Write It From Scratch
Read the prompt aloud and hand over the starter code. Step back and observe — what they write unprompted (bounds checks, Drop impls, memory ordering choices) is far more signal than what they write only after being asked. Reveal solution keys only after they finish or are genuinely stuck.
98 exercises 15–30 min each (W1–W41) · 45–90 min each (W42–W83) · 30–60 min (W84–W98) Pick one or two per interview
// Write Exercise 01 · 15 min
W1 · Generic Stack<T>
generics Option ownership Easy
Read this prompt aloud — do not show the solution
"Implement a generic Stack<T> backed by a Vec<T>. It needs push(&mut self, T), pop(&mut self) -> Option<T>, peek(&self) -> Option<&T>, len(&self) -> usize, and is_empty(&self) -> bool. Make it work for any type, including non-Copy types like String."
Starter code to hand to candidate
struct Stack<T> {
    items: Vec<T>,
}

impl<T> Stack<T> {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self { items: Vec::new() }
    }

    // TODO: push, pop, peek, len, is_empty
}


fn main() {
    let mut s: Stack<String> = Stack::new();
    assert!(s.is_empty());
    s.push("a".to_string());
    s.push("b".to_string());
    assert_eq!(s.peek(), Some(&"b".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(s.pop(), Some("b".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(s.len(), 1);
    assert_eq!(s.pop(), Some("a".to_string()));
    assert!(s.is_empty());
    assert_eq!(s.pop(), None);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
impl<T> Stack<T> {
    fn push(&mut self, item: T) {
        self.items.push(item);
    }

    fn pop(&mut self) -> Option<T> {
        self.items.pop()  // Vec::pop already returns Option — no unwrap, no panic on empty
    }

    fn peek(&self) -> Option<&T> {
        self.items.last()
    }

    fn len(&self) -> usize {
        self.items.len()
    }

    fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
        self.items.is_empty()
    }
}

// Bonus, often volunteered unprompted: implement IntoIterator so `for x in stack` works,
// or Default so Stack::default() works alongside Stack::new().
impl<T> Default for Stack<T> {
    fn default() -> Self { Self::new() }
}

fn main() {
    let mut s: Stack<String> = Stack::new();
    assert!(s.is_empty());
    s.push("a".to_string());
    s.push("b".to_string());
    assert_eq!(s.peek(), Some(&"b".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(s.pop(), Some("b".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(s.len(), 1);
    assert_eq!(s.pop(), Some("a".to_string()));
    assert!(s.is_empty());
    assert_eq!(s.pop(), None);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Uses Vec::pop()'s existing Option<T> return directly rather than manually checking is_empty() then indexing/unwrapping — recognizes the underlying Vec already solves this exact problem.
  • ★★Doesn't add a T: Clone or T: Copy bound anywhere unless genuinely needed — a common over-constraining mistake from candidates more used to languages where generic containers need such bounds by default.
  • ★Volunteers Default or IntoIterator without being asked — shows familiarity with idiomatic collection-type ergonomics beyond the bare minimum.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Why does peek() return Option<&T> rather than Option<T>?" — Returning T by value would require either moving it out of the Vec (leaving a hole — not allowed without also removing it) or cloning it (requires a Clone bound, and is wasteful for large T). Returning a reference lets you inspect the top item without taking ownership or requiring any bound on T at all.
  • P2"What happens if you call push() many times in a row — does Vec reallocate every time?" — No — Vec grows its capacity geometrically (typically doubling) when it needs to reallocate, so push() is amortised O(1), not O(n) per call, even though any individual push() might occasionally trigger a realloc.
  • P3"How would you make this work for a fixed maximum capacity, rejecting pushes beyond it, without changing the public API's return types?" — Change push to return Result<(), T> (Err returning the rejected item back to the caller so it isn't silently dropped) or bool, and check self.items.len() against a stored capacity field before pushing — a good prompt for whether they instinctively return the rejected value rather than just dropping it.
🎯 Senior angle
This is intentionally the easiest exercise in the packet — use it as a fast warm-up/calibration exercise rather than a serious signal generator; the goal is watching how quickly and cleanly someone writes idiomatic Rust before moving to something with real design decisions.

Extends W1. Add drain(&mut self) -> impl Iterator<Item = T> that empties the stack, yielding owned values. Partial drain + Drop of the iterator must not leak/double-pop wrongly.

struct Drain<'a, T> { /* TODO: tie to &mut Stack<T> */ }

fn main() {
    let mut s = Stack::new();
    s.push(1);
    s.push(2);
    s.push(3);
    {
        let mut d = s.drain();
        assert_eq!(d.next(), Some(3));
        assert_eq!(d.next(), Some(2));
        // drop mid-drain — remaining must be cleaned up
    }
    assert!(s.is_empty());
    s.push(9);
    assert_eq!(s.drain().collect::<Vec<_>>(), vec![9]);
}

// Write Exercise 02 · 15 min
W2 · Thread-Safe Counter
atomics Arc threading Easy–Medium
Prompt
"Spawn 10 threads, each incrementing a shared counter 100,000 times. Print the final count — it must always be exactly 1,000,000. Implement it two ways: once using an atomic, once using a mutex — then tell me which you'd actually use in production and why."
Starter code
use std::thread;


fn main() {
    use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
    use std::sync::Arc;
    let counter = Arc::new(AtomicU64::new(0));
    let handles: Vec<_> = (0..10)
        .map(|_| {
            let counter = Arc::clone(&counter);
            thread::spawn(move || {
                for _ in 0..100_000 {
                    counter.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
                }
            })
        })
        .collect();
    for h in handles {
        h.join().unwrap();
    }
    assert_eq!(counter.load(Ordering::Relaxed), 1_000_000);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
// Version 1: atomic — no lock, minimal overhead per increment
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::thread;

fn atomic_version() {
    let counter = Arc::new(AtomicU64::new(0));
    let handles: Vec<_> = (0..10)
        .map(|_| {
            let counter = Arc::clone(&counter);
            thread::spawn(move || {
                for _ in 0..100_000 {
                    counter.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);  // no ordering needed between iterations of a plain sum
                }
            })
        })
        .collect();
    for h in handles { h.join().unwrap(); }
    println!("atomic total: {}", counter.load(Ordering::Relaxed));
}

// Version 2: mutex — same structure, correctness via exclusive access instead of atomicity
use std::sync::Mutex;

fn mutex_version() {
    let counter = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0u64));
    let handles: Vec<_> = (0..10)
        .map(|_| {
            let counter = Arc::clone(&counter);
            thread::spawn(move || {
                for _ in 0..100_000 {
                    *counter.lock().unwrap() += 1;
                }
            })
        })
        .collect();
    for h in handles { h.join().unwrap(); }
    println!("mutex total: {}", *counter.lock().unwrap());
}

fn main() {
    use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
    use std::sync::Arc;
    let counter = Arc::new(AtomicU64::new(0));
    let handles: Vec<_> = (0..10)
        .map(|_| {
            let counter = Arc::clone(&counter);
            thread::spawn(move || {
                for _ in 0..100_000 {
                    counter.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
                }
            })
        })
        .collect();
    for h in handles {
        h.join().unwrap();
    }
    assert_eq!(counter.load(Ordering::Relaxed), 1_000_000);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Uses Arc, not plain Rc — and if they try Rc first, immediately understands and can articulate the resulting Send-related compile error rather than being confused by it.
  • ★★★Chooses Ordering::Relaxed and can justify it — a plain independent-increment counter has no data dependency between iterations requiring stronger ordering; picking SeqCst without being able to explain why anything stronger is needed is a weaker (though not wrong) answer.
  • ★★Collects JoinHandles into a Vec before joining rather than joining immediately inside the spawn loop — joining immediately would serialise the threads, defeating the whole point of spawning them concurrently.
  • ★States the production preference clearly: atomic for a single primitive counter — simpler, faster, no lock overhead — reserving mutex for when multiple related values need to be updated together as one atomic unit.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Would Ordering::Relaxed still be correct if each thread's increment depended on reading some other shared flag first?" — No — Relaxed only guarantees atomicity of the operation itself, not any ordering relative to other memory operations. If correctness depended on observing another thread's prior write, you'd need Acquire/Release (or SeqCst) as covered in the atomics topic.
  • P2"What would happen if you used Rc<AtomicU64> instead of Arc<AtomicU64>?" — Compile error — thread::spawn requires its closure to be Send, and Rc is deliberately not Send. This is exactly the compile-time-enforced guarantee discussed in the smart pointers topic; the compiler catches this before the program ever runs, unlike an equivalent mistake in C++.
  • P3"If you swapped 10 threads for 10,000 short-lived tasks, would you still use std::thread here?" — Probably not — spawning 10,000 OS threads is expensive (each has real memory/scheduling overhead); this shifts toward either a bounded thread pool (rayon, or a hand-rolled pool as in W5) or, if the work were I/O-bound rather than this CPU-bound busy loop, Tokio tasks instead — a good moment to see if they connect this back to the CPU-bound-vs-I/O-bound and thread-pool-sizing material elsewhere in this packet.
🎯 Senior angle
The real signal in this exercise isn't whether the final count is correct (both approaches trivially are) — it's whether the candidate can articulate why Relaxed ordering is sufficient here specifically, rather than defaulting to SeqCst everywhere out of uncertainty.

fn main() {
    use std::sync::Arc;
    use std::thread;
    let state = Arc::new(Mutex::new(State { count: 0, last_thread: 0 }));
    let mut handles = vec![];
    for tid in 0..4usize {
        let s = Arc::clone(&state);
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            for _ in 0..1000 {
                inc(&s, tid);
            }
        }));
    }
    for h in handles {
        h.join().unwrap();
    }
    let g = state.lock().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(g.count, 4000);
    assert!(g.last_thread < 4);
}

// Write Exercise 03 · 25 min
W3 · Mini Rc<T> From Scratch
unsafe smart pointers raw pointers Hard
Prompt
"Implement a simplified, single-threaded MiniRc<T> — a reference-counted smart pointer, without using std::rc::Rc internally. It must support clone() to create a new handle sharing the same allocation and incrementing the count, Deref to access the inner value, and correctly free the allocation when the last handle is dropped. You'll need unsafe — think carefully about what invariant each unsafe block relies on."
Starter code
use std::ops::Deref;
use std::ptr::NonNull;

struct MiniRcInner<T> {
    value: T,
    count: usize,
}

struct MiniRc<T> {
    ptr: NonNull<MiniRcInner<T>>,
}

impl<T> MiniRc<T> {
    fn new(value: T) -> Self {
        let boxed = Box::new(MiniRcInner { value, count: 1 });
        Self { ptr: NonNull::from(Box::leak(boxed)) }
    }

    // TODO: clone(&self) -> Self — increment count, return a new MiniRc sharing the pointer
    // TODO: impl Deref -- access the inner value
    // TODO: impl Drop -- decrement count; free the allocation if it was the last handle
    // TODO: strong_count(&self) -> usize -- for testing
}


fn main() {
    let a = MiniRc::new(vec![1, 2, 3]);
    assert_eq!(a.strong_count(), 1);
    let b = a.clone();
    assert_eq!(a.strong_count(), 2);
    assert_eq!(*b, vec![1, 2, 3]);
    drop(b);
    assert_eq!(a.strong_count(), 1);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
impl<T> MiniRc<T> {
    fn strong_count(&self) -> usize {
        unsafe { self.ptr.as_ref().count }
    }
}

impl<T> Clone for MiniRc<T> {
    fn clone(&self) -> Self {
        unsafe {
            // SAFETY: self.ptr is valid as long as self is alive (invariant of MiniRc);
            // no other thread can be mutating count concurrently — single-threaded only.
            (*self.ptr.as_ptr()).count += 1;
        }
        Self { ptr: self.ptr }
    }
}

impl<T> Deref for MiniRc<T> {
    type Target = T;
    fn deref(&self) -> &T {
        // SAFETY: ptr is non-null and was allocated via Box, guaranteed live while self exists.
        &unsafe { self.ptr.as_ref() }.value
    }
}

impl<T> Drop for MiniRc<T> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        unsafe {
            (*self.ptr.as_ptr()).count -= 1;
            if self.ptr.as_ref().count == 0 {
                // SAFETY: count reached 0 means this is provably the last handle —
                // reconstruct the Box to run T's destructor and free the allocation.
                drop(Box::from_raw(self.ptr.as_ptr()));
            }
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let a = MiniRc::new(vec![1, 2, 3]);
    assert_eq!(a.strong_count(), 1);
    let b = a.clone();
    assert_eq!(a.strong_count(), 2);
    assert_eq!(*b, vec![1, 2, 3]);
    drop(b);
    assert_eq!(a.strong_count(), 1);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Writes a // SAFETY: comment above every unsafe block without being asked — explaining exactly which invariant justifies it. This is the single highest-value signal in this whole exercise, directly connecting to the soundness discussion in the unsafe topic.
  • ★★★Uses Box::leak / Box::from_raw as the allocate/deallocate pair rather than raw alloc/dealloc calls — recognizes Box already provides a correct, audited allocation primitive to build on.
  • ★★Decrements count BEFORE checking if it's zero in Drop, not after — get the order backwards and you'd free the allocation while count still incorrectly reads 1, or check a stale value.
  • ★Volunteers, unprompted, that this type should not be Send or Sync — and that making it so would require switching the plain usize count to an atomic, i.e. reinventing Arc.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Is this MiniRc Send or Sync as written? Should it be?" — No, and it should not be — the count field is a plain, non-atomic usize; two threads cloning/dropping concurrently would race on it exactly like the B3-style data race discussed earlier in this packet. It's neither Send nor Sync automatically, since NonNull<T> isn't — good, that's the correct default here, and adding unsafe impl Send/Sync without also making count atomic would reproduce the B9 bug exercise's exact mistake.
  • P2"What would you need to change to add a Weak-equivalent to this?" — You'd need a second, separate weak count (as real Rc does internally) so a Weak reference doesn't keep the allocation's value alive but can still detect whether it's still valid — and upgrade() would need to check the strong count is still > 0 before creating a new strong MiniRc, atomically with incrementing it (a genuine subtlety even in the real single-threaded Rc implementation).
  • P3"Why NonNull<T> instead of a plain *mut T?" — NonNull encodes a non-null invariant directly in the type, which (a) documents the invariant to future readers, and (b) allows the compiler to apply the null-pointer optimisation to Option<MiniRc<T>> the same way it does for Option<Box<T>> — a plain raw pointer wouldn't get that layout optimisation since it could legitimately be null.
  • P4"How would you test that this doesn't leak or double-free?" — cargo miri test is the direct answer here — it would catch a use-after-free or double-free immediately if the Drop logic had an off-by-one error, exactly the kind of bug this hand-rolled unsafe code is prone to and exactly the tool built to catch it, as discussed in the unsafe and testing topics.
🎯 Senior angle
This exercise exists specifically to test unsafe-code discipline under pressure — the SAFETY comment habit, correct ordering of the decrement-then-check in Drop, and instinctive caution about Send/Sync are all far higher-value signals here than whether the candidate gets every line syntactically correct on the first try.

Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
struct Inner<T> {
    queue: VecDeque<T>,
}

struct BoundedQueue<T> {
    capacity: usize,
    inner: Mutex<Inner<T>>,
    not_full: Condvar,
    not_empty: Condvar,
}

impl<T> BoundedQueue<T> {
    fn new(capacity: usize) -> Self {
        Self {
            capacity,
            inner: Mutex::new(Inner { queue: VecDeque::new() }),
            not_full: Condvar::new(),
            not_empty: Condvar::new(),
        }
    }

    fn push(&self, item: T) {
        let mut guard = self.inner.lock().unwrap();
        while guard.queue.len() == self.capacity {   // `while`, not `if` — handles spurious wakeups
            guard = self.not_full.wait(guard).unwrap();
        }
        guard.queue.push_back(item);
        self.not_empty.notify_one();  // exactly one waiter can make progress from this push
    }

    fn pop(&self) -> T {
        let mut guard = self.inner.lock().unwrap();
        while guard.queue.is_empty() {
            guard = self.not_empty.wait(guard).unwrap();
        }
        let item = guard.queue.pop_front().unwrap();
        self.not_full.notify_one();
        item
    }
}

fn main() {
    use std::sync::Arc;
    use std::thread;
    use std::time::Duration;
    let q = Arc::new(BoundedQueue::new(2));
    let q2 = Arc::clone(&q);
    let producer = thread::spawn(move || {
        q2.push(1);
        q2.push(2);
        q2.push(3);
    });
    thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(30));
    assert_eq!(q.pop(), 1);
    assert_eq!(q.pop(), 2);
    assert_eq!(q.pop(), 3);
    producer.join().unwrap();
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Uses a while loop, not an if, around the condvar wait — knows about spurious wakeups (a Condvar::wait may return without the underlying condition actually being true) and re-checks the condition after waking rather than assuming it holds.
  • ★★★Correctly re-assigns the guard from Condvar::wait()'s return value (guard = self.not_full.wait(guard).unwrap()) — Rust's Condvar API consumes and returns the guard (rather than C++'s in-place unlock/relock on the same object), and forgetting this is a common first-attempt mistake.
  • ★★Uses two separate Condvars (not_full / not_empty) rather than one shared condvar requiring notify_all on every operation.
  • ★Uses notify_one, not notify_all, in the ordinary push/pop path — correctly reasoning that only one waiter can make progress from a single push or pop.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What's a spurious wakeup, and can it actually happen on the specific platform you're running on?" — A Condvar::wait can return even though no notify was called and the condition hasn't changed — this is explicitly permitted by the API contract regardless of the underlying OS's actual behaviour, precisely so the standard library doesn't need to guarantee something no OS's implementation universally provides. Always checking the condition in a loop after waking is the only fully portable-correct pattern, independent of whether the specific OS happens to exhibit spurious wakeups in practice.
  • P2"How would you add a close()/shutdown mechanism that unblocks all waiting threads?" — Add a `closed: bool` field inside Inner, checked in both wait-loop conditions (e.g. `while queue.is_empty() && !closed`), and a close() method that sets it under the lock then calls notify_all() on BOTH condvars — mirroring the C++ BoundedQueue exercise's close() design, and testing whether they generalize the pattern to Rust's Condvar API correctly.
  • P3"Why would you reach for tokio::sync::mpsc or crossbeam_channel instead of this hand-rolled version in most real code?" — This hand-rolled Mutex+Condvar version is correct but is exactly the kind of primitive that's easy to get subtly wrong (as this exercise itself demonstrates) — for sync code, crossbeam_channel::bounded() provides the same semantics, battle-tested and typically faster under contention; for async code, tokio::sync::mpsc with a bounded capacity is the direct equivalent. Hand-rolling this is a good learning exercise, not typically the production choice.
🎯 Senior angle
The while-vs-if distinction around condvar waits is one of the most reliable "have they actually written condition-variable code before, versus just read about it" signals in the entire packet — it's a small detail that's very easy to get right in theory and very easy to forget under live coding pressure.

Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
type Job = Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send + 'static>;

struct Worker {
    handle: Option<thread::JoinHandle<()>>,
}

struct ThreadPool {
    workers: Vec<Worker>,
    sender: Option<mpsc::Sender<Job>>,
}

impl ThreadPool {
    fn new(size: usize) -> Self {
        let (sender, receiver) = mpsc::channel::<Job>();
        let receiver = Arc::new(Mutex::new(receiver));  // mpsc::Receiver isn't Sync — share it via Mutex

        let workers = (0..size)
            .map(|_| {
                let receiver = Arc::clone(&receiver);
                let handle = thread::spawn(move || loop {
                    // lock, receive, THEN drop the lock before running the job —
                    // holding the lock while running the job would serialise all workers.
                    let job = receiver.lock().unwrap().recv();
                    match job {
                        Ok(job) => job(),
                        Err(_) => break,  // sender dropped — channel closed, time to shut down
                    }
                });
                Worker { handle: Some(handle) }
            })
            .collect();

        Self { workers, sender: Some(sender) }
    }

    fn execute<F: FnOnce() + Send + 'static>(&self, job: F) {
        let job: Job = Box::new(job);
        self.sender.as_ref().unwrap().send(job).unwrap();
    }
}

impl Drop for ThreadPool {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        self.sender.take();  // drop the sender — recv() in workers now returns Err, breaking their loops
        for worker in &mut self.workers {
            if let Some(handle) = worker.handle.take() {
                handle.join().unwrap();  // wait for the in-flight job (if any) to actually finish
            }
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
    use std::sync::Arc;
    let pool = ThreadPool::new(4);
    let counter = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    for _ in 0..100 {
        let c = Arc::clone(&counter);
        pool.execute(move || {
            c.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
        });
    }
    drop(pool);
    assert_eq!(counter.load(Ordering::Relaxed), 100);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Drops the mutex lock before running the job, not around it — locking to receive, then explicitly ending the lock's scope before calling job(), is essential; holding it across job execution would fully serialise the "pool," defeating its entire purpose. Watch closely for this — it's an extremely easy mistake to make.
  • ★★★Wraps sender in Option specifically to enable dropping it early in Drop::drop — recognizing that Drop only gives you &mut self, not ownership, so you need Option::take() to actually move the sender out and drop it deliberately rather than waiting for the whole struct's implicit field-by-field drop order.
  • ★★Correctly identifies why Receiver needs Arc<Mutex<...>> — std's mpsc Receiver is designed for single-consumer use and isn't Sync, so sharing one receiver across multiple worker threads requires the Mutex wrapper, unlike the Sender half which is already Clone + Send on its own.
  • ★Uses Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send + 'static> as the Job type alias — recognizing that heterogeneous closures of different concrete (unnameable) types need to go behind a trait object to be stored uniformly in a channel.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What happens on drop if you forget to call handle.join() on each worker?" — The JoinHandles would simply be dropped without joining — the underlying OS threads keep running detached in the background; the process wouldn't necessarily wait for them before continuing, potentially exiting main() while workers are still mid-job, or just leaking thread resources for the remainder of the program's life. Rust does not automatically join threads on JoinHandle drop (unlike some other languages' thread-handle types) — this is a deliberate design choice you need to know about.
  • P2"Why does recv() returning Err(_) correctly signal shutdown, rather than something you need to signal explicitly with a boolean flag?" — mpsc's Receiver::recv() returns Err specifically when all Senders have been dropped and no more messages will ever arrive — this is exactly the shutdown signal already built into the channel's own semantics, so dropping the pool's stored Sender (which is the last remaining clone) is sufficient without needing a separate explicit "shutdown" boolean or message type.
  • P3"How would you extend execute() to return a value from the job, similar to std::thread::spawn's JoinHandle?" — Use a oneshot channel (or std::sync::mpsc with a single expected message) per job: execute() creates a (tx, rx) pair, wraps the job to send its result through tx when done, and returns rx (or a future wrapping it) to the caller — conceptually very close to how a real work-stealing thread pool or futures executor bridges a spawned unit of work back to a caller awaiting its result.
  • P4"Would this design work equally well if 'workers' were Tokio tasks instead of OS threads?" — The overall shape (a shared queue, workers pulling and executing) is similar, but Tokio already provides a multi-worker task scheduler out of the box — you generally wouldn't hand-roll this for async work at all; you'd just tokio::spawn each unit of work directly and let Tokio's own scheduler distribute it across its worker threads, which is exactly why this exercise is framed around raw OS threads rather than async tasks.
🎯 Senior angle
The "drop the lock before running the job" mistake is extremely common even among experienced engineers under live-coding pressure — watching whether the candidate catches it themselves (perhaps after running/reasoning through concurrent execution) versus needing it pointed out is a meaningful signal on its own.

trait Logger {
    fn log(&self, msg: &str);
}

struct ConsoleLogger;
impl Logger for ConsoleLogger {
    fn log(&self, msg: &str) {
        println!("[console] {msg}");
    }
}

struct PrefixLogger {
    inner: Box<dyn Logger>,  // owns any Logger implementation behind a trait object
    prefix: String,
}
impl Logger for PrefixLogger {
    fn log(&self, msg: &str) {
        self.inner.log(&format!("{}{}", self.prefix, msg));
    }
}


fn main() {
    use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
    struct SharedLogger(Arc<Mutex<Vec<String>>>);
    impl Logger for SharedLogger {
        fn log(&self, msg: &str) {
            self.0.lock().unwrap().push(msg.to_string());
        }
    }
    let buf = Arc::new(Mutex::new(Vec::<String>::new()));
    let loggers: Vec<Box<dyn Logger>> = vec![
        Box::new(SharedLogger(buf.clone())),
        Box::new(PrefixLogger {
            inner: Box::new(SharedLogger(buf.clone())),
            prefix: "[ERROR] ".to_string(),
        }),
    ];
    for l in &loggers {
        l.log("system startup");
    }
    assert_eq!(
        *buf.lock().unwrap(),
        vec![
            "system startup".to_string(),
            "[ERROR] system startup".to_string()
        ]
    );
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Correctly identifies that PrefixLogger's field must be Box<dyn Logger>, not a generic parameter — since the collection needs to hold heterogeneous logger types uniformly, and PrefixLogger itself needs to wrap an arbitrary, unknown-at-compile-time Logger implementation (this is the classic case for dyn dispatch over generics, as covered in the traits topic).
  • ★★Types the Vec as Vec<Box<dyn Logger>> without needing it spelled out — a very common early stumbling point is trying `Vec` or `Vec<&dyn Logger>` first and needing to work through why neither compiles (unsized type; lifetime issues with borrowed loggers).
  • ★Considers whether Logger should require Send/Sync if asked about using this from multiple threads, without being told this is coming.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Why can't the Vec just be Vec?" — Logger is a trait, not a concrete sized type — different implementors can have wildly different sizes (ConsoleLogger is zero-sized, PrefixLogger contains a Box and a String), so the compiler has no fixed size to allocate slots for in a Vec. dyn Logger behind a Box (or &) gives every element a uniform, fixed-size (pointer-sized) representation regardless of the concrete implementor's actual size.
  • P2"How would you make PrefixLoggers chainable — a PrefixLogger wrapping a PrefixLogger wrapping a ConsoleLogger?" — This already works with zero changes, since PrefixLogger's inner field is Box<dyn Logger> and PrefixLogger itself implements Logger — you can construct arbitrarily deep wrapping chains. Pointing this out unprompted, and recognizing that this is exactly the decorator pattern, is a good sign of design fluency.
  • P3"If you wanted maximum performance and knew at compile time exactly which logger types you'd use, how would you avoid the dyn dispatch cost here?" — Make the code generic over the Logger type instead (impl Logger for PrefixLogger { inner: L, ... }) — this monomorphises per concrete inner type, avoiding vtable dispatch entirely, at the cost of losing the ability to store different logger types in one homogeneous collection. This is the same generics-vs-dyn trade-off from the generics and traits topics, applied concretely.
  • P4"What would you need to add to make this usable from a Tokio async context across threads?" — Change the trait bound requirements to Logger: Send + Sync (or require the Box), and reconsider whether ConsoleLogger's println! (a synchronous, potentially blocking-on-stdout-lock call) belongs inside async code at all without wrapping it — connecting back to the blocking-the-runtime discussion elsewhere in this packet.
🎯 Senior angle
The "one Logger owning another Logger" requirement is deliberately included to force the Box<dyn Logger> field decision rather than letting the candidate get away with a trivial flat implementation — it's a compact way to test the exact generics-vs-dyn-dispatch reasoning this packet covers at length in the traits and generics topics.

// Write Exercise 07 · 30 min
W7 · Lock-Free Stack (Treiber Stack)
atomics CAS lock-free Hard — staff calibration
Prompt
"Implement a lock-free, thread-safe stack using a compare-and-swap loop on an atomic head pointer (a 'Treiber stack') — push(T) and pop() -> Option<T>, safe to call concurrently from many threads with no mutex anywhere. You do not need to solve memory reclamation (ABA / use-after-free on pop) perfectly — but you must be able to explain exactly where that problem exists in your implementation and what a real fix would require."
Starter code
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicPtr, Ordering};

struct Node<T> {
    value: T,
    next: *mut Node<T>,
}

struct TreiberStack<T> {
    head: AtomicPtr<Node<T>>,
}

impl<T> TreiberStack<T> {
    fn new() -> Self { Self { head: AtomicPtr::new(std::ptr::null_mut()) } }
    fn push(&self, value: T) { todo!() }
    fn pop(&self) -> Option<T> { todo!() }
}

fn main() {
    use std::sync::Arc;
    use std::thread;
    let stack = Arc::new(TreiberStack::new());
    let mut handles = vec![];
    for t in 0..4 {
        let s = Arc::clone(&stack);
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            for i in 0..1000 {
                s.push(t * 1000 + i);
            }
        }));
    }
    for h in handles {
        h.join().unwrap();
    }
    let mut count = 0;
    while stack.pop().is_some() {
        count += 1;
    }
    assert_eq!(count, 4000);
    assert_eq!(stack.pop(), None);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
impl<T> TreiberStack<T> {
    fn push(&self, value: T) {
        let new_node = Box::into_raw(Box::new(Node { value, next: std::ptr::null_mut() }));
        loop {
            let old_head = self.head.load(Ordering::Acquire);
            unsafe { (*new_node).next = old_head; }
            // CAS: only succeeds if head is still old_head — i.e. no one else pushed/popped since we read it
            if self.head
                .compare_exchange(old_head, new_node, Ordering::Release, Ordering::Acquire)
                .is_ok()
            {
                break;  // success — new_node is now the head
            }
            // CAS failed — someone else modified head concurrently; retry with the new head value
        }
    }

    fn pop(&self) -> Option<T> {
        loop {
            let old_head = self.head.load(Ordering::Acquire);
            if old_head.is_null() {
                return None;  // stack is empty
            }
            let next = unsafe { (*old_head).next };
            if self.head
                .compare_exchange(old_head, next, Ordering::Release, Ordering::Acquire)
                .is_ok()
            {
                // SAFETY (with a caveat, see below): we "won" the CAS, so we believe we exclusively
                // own old_head now — reconstruct the Box to take ownership of its value and free it.
                let boxed = unsafe { Box::from_raw(old_head) };
                return Some(boxed.value);
            }
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    use std::sync::Arc;
    use std::thread;
    let stack = Arc::new(TreiberStack::new());
    let mut handles = vec![];
    for t in 0..4 {
        let s = Arc::clone(&stack);
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            for i in 0..1000 {
                s.push(t * 1000 + i);
            }
        }));
    }
    for h in handles {
        h.join().unwrap();
    }
    let mut count = 0;
    while stack.pop().is_some() {
        count += 1;
    }
    assert_eq!(count, 4000);
    assert_eq!(stack.pop(), None);
}
The memory reclamation problem this implementation does NOT solve
This is a genuine use-after-free / ABA hazard: suppose thread A calls pop(), reads old_head and next, but is preempted before its CAS runs. Thread B then pops the same node (freeing it via Box::from_raw), and — critically — the freed memory happens to get reused for a brand-new allocation (e.g. another thread's concurrent push() landing at the same address). Thread A resumes and its CAS on head succeeds (because head now happens to hold the same pointer value old_head again, coincidentally, from the new allocation) — thread A now believes it "won" and calls Box::from_raw(old_head) on memory that a completely different, currently-live node is using, freeing memory still in active use — this is exactly the ABA problem described in the atomics topic, applied concretely to this data structure. A candidate who reaches this far and can articulate this specific scenario unprompted is demonstrating genuinely staff-level lock-free programming awareness — most engineers, including many who ship production Rust, have never had to reason through this personally.
What a real fix requires (discuss verbally — full implementation is out of scope for a live exercise)
A production-grade lock-free stack needs a proper memory-reclamation scheme that defers freeing a node until it's provably safe — epoch-based reclamation (the crossbeam-epoch crate implements exactly this, and is what most real Rust lock-free data structures, including parts of crossbeam's own concurrent collections, actually use) or hazard pointers (threads publish which nodes they're currently dereferencing, and reclamation waits until no thread has published a hazard pointer to a given node). Either way, the takeaway to state explicitly: hand-rolling a fully correct lock-free data structure from raw atomics, with sound memory reclamation, is hard enough that even experienced systems engineers reach for an audited crate (crossbeam) rather than writing one from scratch for production use — this exercise is valuable precisely because it makes candidates feel that difficulty firsthand, not because hand-rolling this is something you'd actually want to ship.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Why Acquire on load and Release on the CAS's success ordering?" — The load needs Acquire so subsequent reads (like dereferencing old_head to get next) see a consistent view of memory published by whichever thread most recently updated head. The CAS's success ordering uses Release so that this thread's writes (constructing new_node, or freeing old_head after a successful pop) become visible to the next thread that acquires the head pointer — this Acquire/Release pairing is exactly the publish/subscribe pattern discussed in the atomics topic.
  • P2"Is this implementation's push() susceptible to the same ABA/reclamation issue as pop()?" — push() itself doesn't free anything, so it doesn't suffer the use-after-free half of the problem directly — but it still participates in the overall hazard, since a node it links via `next` could theoretically be concurrently freed by another thread's pop() if that other pop() incorrectly believes it owns the node exclusively — the reclamation problem is really about pop()'s freeing logic, and push() is a bystander that could still be affected by it.
  • P3"Given how hard this is to get fully right, when would hand-rolling a structure like this actually be justified over crossbeam?" — Very rarely for application code — mainly when building a specialized allocator, a kernel/embedded context without access to crates, or genuinely novel research into concurrent data structures. For virtually all production Rust systems work, crossbeam's audited primitives (or simply a Mutex, measured and found insufficient first) are the right default, and this exercise's difficulty is itself the argument for that default.
🎯 Senior angle
Reserve this exercise for staff-level calibration or candidates who've specifically claimed deep lock-free/ systems programming experience — for most senior interviews, getting the push/pop CAS loops correct and being able to name the ABA/reclamation gap (without necessarily fixing it live) is already an excellent outcome; demanding a fully correct hazard-pointer implementation in a live interview is unrealistic and not representative of real-world expectations.

W8 · LRU Cache
HashMap VecDeque data structures Medium
Prompt
"Implement an LruCache<K, V> with a fixed capacity. get(&mut self, &K) -> Option<&V> should return the value if present and mark it as most-recently-used; put(&mut self, K, V) should insert or update a value, evicting the least-recently-used entry if the cache is at capacity. Both operations should be O(1) amortised — a naive linear scan for recency does not meet the bar here."
Starter code
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::hash::Hash;

struct LruCache<K, V> {
    capacity: usize,
    // TODO: what structure(s) give O(1) lookup AND O(1) "move to most-recently-used"?
}

    fn new(capacity: usize) -> Self { todo!() }

fn main() {
    let mut cache = LruCache::new(2);
    cache.put("a", 1);
    cache.put("b", 2);
    assert_eq!(cache.get(&"a"), Some(&1));
    cache.put("c", 3);

Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes
The classic O(1) design is a HashMap of key → value plus recency metadata, combined with an intrusive doubly-linked list for recency order — but a hand-rolled doubly-linked list in safe Rust is painful (it's the textbook motivating example for needing unsafe or Rc/RefCell, discussed in the lifetimes and smart-pointers topics). A pragmatic, fully-safe alternative that still hits the O(1) bar in practice: use the indexmap or linked-hash-map crate — or, for a from -scratch answer without external crates, a HashMap<K, V> plus a separate HashMap<K, u64> of last-access "timestamps" (a monotonically increasing counter) and periodic O(n) compaction is a reasonable, honestly-caveated compromise for a live-coding setting. The cleanest genuinely-O(1) from-scratch answer most candidates can actually produce live: 
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::hash::Hash;

struct LruCache<K: Eq + Hash + Clone, V> {
    capacity: usize,
    map: HashMap<K, V>,
    order: Vec<K>,  // front = least recently used, back = most recently used
}

impl<K: Eq + Hash + Clone, V> LruCache<K, V> {
    fn new(capacity: usize) -> Self {
        Self { capacity, map: HashMap::new(), order: Vec::new() }
    }

    fn touch(&mut self, key: &K) {
        if let Some(pos) = self.order.iter().position(|k| k == key) {
            let k = self.order.remove(pos);
            self.order.push(k);
        }
    }

    fn get(&mut self, key: &K) -> Option<&V> {
        if self.map.contains_key(key) {
            self.touch(key);
            self.map.get(key)
        } else {
            None
        }
    }

    fn put(&mut self, key: K, value: V) {
        if self.map.contains_key(&key) {
            self.map.insert(key.clone(), value);
            self.touch(&key);
            return;
        }
        if self.map.len() >= self.capacity {
            let lru_key = self.order.remove(0);  // evict the front — least recently used
            self.map.remove(&lru_key);
        }
        self.map.insert(key.clone(), value);
        self.order.push(key);
    }
}
// Honest caveat to raise unprompted: order.remove(pos) / order.remove(0) are O(n),
// not O(1) — this version is O(n) touch/evict, not the theoretically optimal O(1).
// True O(1) requires an intrusive linked list (unsafe or Rc>) or a crate.

fn main() {
    let mut cache = LruCache::new(2);
    cache.put("a", 1);
    cache.put("b", 2);
    assert_eq!(cache.get(&"a"), Some(&1));
    cache.put("c", 3);
    assert_eq!(cache.get(&"b"), None);
    assert_eq!(cache.get(&"a"), Some(&1));
    assert_eq!(cache.get(&"c"), Some(&3));
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Proactively admits the Vec-based order tracking is O(n), not O(1) — rather than presenting it as if it fully meets the stated bar. Recognizing and stating your own solution's shortfall is more valuable here than silently hoping it goes unnoticed.
  • ★★★Names the intrusive-doubly-linked-list design (even without fully implementing it) as the "real" O(1) answer, and can explain why it's awkward in safe Rust — nodes needing to be reachable from both a HashMap and their neighbours in the list is exactly the shared-mutable-ownership problem discussed in the lifetimes/smart-pointers topics.
  • ★★Considers linked-hash-map or the standard library's absence of a built-in LRU type and mentions that this is a case where reaching for a crate rather than hand-rolling is the practical real-world answer.
  • ★Correctly handles the update-existing-key case in put() — updating an existing key's value should also refresh its recency, and a common bug is forgetting to touch() in that branch.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Sketch, without fully implementing, what the intrusive-linked-list version's node type would look like, and why it needs unsafe or Rc/RefCell." — Each node needs pointers to both its list neighbours AND the map needs to be able to reach a node directly by key (typically storing raw pointers or indices into an arena as map values) — multiple simultaneous mutable-ish access paths to the same node (from the map, and from list traversal) is exactly the shared-ownership problem that either Rc> (with runtime cost and cycle-risk from the earlier bug exercise) or careful unsafe raw-pointer code (with its own soundness burden) is needed to resolve safely.
  • P2"How would you make this cache safe to share across threads?" — Wrap the whole LruCache in a Mutex (Arc>>) — since both get() and put() need &mut self anyway (recency tracking mutates state even on a 'read'), there's no read/write asymmetry to exploit with an RwLock the way there might be for a pure lookup structure; a plain Mutex is the natural fit here specifically because LRU's own bookkeeping makes even 'reads' into writes.
  • P3"For a real production cache, would you reach for this hand-rolled structure or something like the moka crate?" — For production use, a crate like moka (mentioned in the rate-limiter system design exercise too) provides a battle-tested, properly-O(1), often also TTL-aware and concurrent-safe cache out of the box — hand-rolling an LRU cache is a great interview exercise specifically because it's a well-understood, self-contained data structure problem, but it's not typically what you'd ship without a strong specific reason.
🎯 Senior angle
This exercise is deliberately designed so that the "obvious" implementation candidates reach for under time pressure doesn't actually meet the stated O(1) bar — the real signal is whether they notice and say so themselves, and can articulate what the fully-correct version would require, rather than presenting an O(n) solution as if it satisfies the original ask.

W9 · Custom Iterator — Sliding Window
Iterator trait laziness adapters Easy–Medium
Prompt
"Implement windows(slice: &[T], size: usize) -> Windows<T> yourself — without calling the standard library's own slice::windows() — returning a lazy iterator that yields overlapping windows of length size as &[T] slices. It must work with all the standard iterator adapters (.map(), .take(), for loops, etc.) with zero extra work on your part."
Starter code
struct Windows<'a, T> {
    slice: &'a [T],
    size: usize,
    pos: usize,
}

fn windows<T>(slice: &[T], size: usize) -> Windows<T> {
    Windows { slice, size, pos: 0 }
}

// TODO: impl Iterator for Windows


fn main() {
    let data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
    let got: Vec<&[i32]> = windows(&data, 3).collect();
    assert_eq!(got, vec![&[1, 2, 3][..], &[2, 3, 4][..], &[3, 4, 5][..]]);
    let sums: Vec<i32> = windows(&data, 2).map(|w| w.iter().sum()).collect();
    assert_eq!(sums, vec![3, 5, 7, 9]);
    assert_eq!(windows(&data, 6).count(), 0);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
impl<'a, T> Iterator for Windows<'a, T> {
    type Item = &'a [T];

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        if self.pos + self.size > self.slice.len() {
            return None;
        }
        let window = &self.slice[self.pos..self.pos + self.size];
        self.pos += 1;
        Some(window)
    }

    fn size_hint(&self) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {  // optional but shows real fluency
        let remaining = self.slice.len().saturating_sub(self.pos + self.size - 1);
        (remaining, Some(remaining))
    }
}

fn main() {
    let data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
    let got: Vec<&[i32]> = windows(&data, 3).collect();
    assert_eq!(got, vec![&[1, 2, 3][..], &[2, 3, 4][..], &[3, 4, 5][..]]);
    let sums: Vec<i32> = windows(&data, 2).map(|w| w.iter().sum()).collect();
    assert_eq!(sums, vec![3, 5, 7, 9]);
    assert_eq!(windows(&data, 6).count(), 0);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Only implements next() and gets .map(), .take(), for loops etc. "for free" — recognizing that Iterator's default-method design means every other adapter is built on top of next() alone.
  • ★★Correctly guards the boundary check (pos + size > slice.len()) rather than something off-by-one, and doesn't panic on empty input or size > slice.len().
  • ★Implements size_hint() unprompted — a sign of having actually read the Iterator trait's full surface rather than just next().
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Why does the Item type need to borrow from the slice with lifetime 'a rather than just being &[T] with an inferred lifetime?" — Without tying Item's lifetime explicitly to the struct's own 'a, the compiler can't verify the returned slice reference stays valid relative to the original input slice's lifetime — the explicit 'a on both the struct and the impl block is what lets the borrow checker connect "how long the windows live" to "how long the original slice lives."
  • P2"Would this iterator work with an infinite/unbounded source, like a generator function instead of a fixed slice?" — Not as written — it fundamentally depends on Windows knowing slice.len() up front for its bounds check; a windows-over-a-stream version would need to buffer size elements internally (e.g. a VecDeque) and pull from an inner iterator instead of indexing a fixed slice.
  • P3"Is this iterator's next() O(1)? What about collecting all windows into a Vec> instead of &[T]?" — next() itself is O(1) — slicing is a cheap pointer+length operation. But collecting into owned Vec> would require cloning each window's elements (needing a Clone bound on T), turning the whole traversal into O(n·size) — a good moment to see if they distinguish "iterating is cheap" from "materializing owned copies is not."
🎯 Senior angle
The real test here is whether the candidate reaches for implementing only next() instead of trying to hand-write map/take/collection logic themselves — that instinct is the clearest signal of genuinely understanding how Rust's iterator trait composes, rather than just knowing the syntax to call iterator methods.

Prompt

Design a single custom ConfigError enum that can represent both failure modes, and make the ? operator work directly against both underlying error types with no .map_err() calls anywhere in load_config."
Starter code

use std::io;
use std::num::ParseIntError;

// TODO: design ConfigError so `?` works for both io::Error and ParseIntError below

        .ok_or(/* what goes here for a "missing key" case with no underlying error? */)?;

fn main() {
    use std::io::Write;
    let dir = std::env::temp_dir().join("w10_config_test");
    let _ = std::fs::create_dir_all(&dir);
    let path = dir.join("app.conf");

        let mut f = std::fs::File::create(&path).unwrap();
        writeln!(f, "port=8080").unwrap();

    assert_eq!(cfg.port, 8080);

    let bad = dir.join("bad.conf");
    {
        let mut f = std::fs::File::create(&bad).unwrap();
        writeln!(f, "port=xyz").unwrap();
    }

    let missing = dir.join("missing.conf");
    {

Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
enum ConfigError {
    Io(io::Error),
    Parse(ParseIntError),
    MissingKey(String),
}

// From impls are what let `?` auto-convert — this is the whole trick
impl From<io::Error> for ConfigError {
    fn from(e: io::Error) -> Self { ConfigError::Io(e) }
}
impl From<ParseIntError> for ConfigError {
    fn from(e: ParseIntError) -> Self { ConfigError::Parse(e) }
}

// Good practice, often volunteered unprompted: implement Display + Error too
impl std::fmt::Display for ConfigError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter) -> std::fmt::Result {
        match self {
            ConfigError::Io(e) => write!(f, "I/O error: {e}"),
            ConfigError::Parse(e) => write!(f, "invalid port number: {e}"),
            ConfigError::MissingKey(k) => write!(f, "missing config key: {k}"),
        }
    }
}
impl std::error::Error for ConfigError {}

fn load_config(path: &str) -> Result<Config, ConfigError> {
    let contents = fs::read_to_string(path)?;
    let line = contents.lines().find(|l| l.starts_with("port="))
        .ok_or_else(|| ConfigError::MissingKey("port".to_string()))?;
    let port: u16 = line[5..].parse()?;
    Ok(Config { port })
}

fn main() {
    use std::io::Write;
    let dir = std::env::temp_dir().join("w10_config_test");
    let _ = std::fs::create_dir_all(&dir);
    let path = dir.join("app.conf");
    {
        let mut f = std::fs::File::create(&path).unwrap();
        writeln!(f, "port=8080").unwrap();
    }
    let cfg = load_config(path.to_str().unwrap()).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(cfg.port, 8080);

    let bad = dir.join("bad.conf");
    {
        let mut f = std::fs::File::create(&bad).unwrap();
        writeln!(f, "port=xyz").unwrap();
    }
    assert!(load_config(bad.to_str().unwrap()).is_err());

    let missing = dir.join("missing.conf");
    {
        let mut f = std::fs::File::create(&missing).unwrap();
        writeln!(f, "host=localhost").unwrap();
    }
    assert!(load_config(missing.to_str().unwrap()).is_err());
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Writes impl From<io::Error> and impl From<ParseIntError> rather than reaching for .map_err(|e| ...) at every call site — recognizing that ? automatically calls Into::into() (via the target error type's From impl) on the error before propagating, which is precisely why the prompt bans .map_err().
  • ★★Uses ok_or_else with a closure, not ok_or with an eagerly-constructed value, for the missing-key case — ok_or's argument is evaluated unconditionally even on the Some path, which is wasteful (and would be a real cost if constructing the error were expensive) — a subtle but real API-design signal.
  • ★Volunteers impl std::error::Error (and usually Display alongside it) without being asked, recognizing that a "real" library-quality error type should implement the standard Error trait so it composes with Box<dyn Error>, anyhow, and error-reporting tools.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What exactly does the ? operator expand to, mechanically?" — Roughly: `match expr { Ok(v) => v, Err(e) => return Err(From::from(e)) }` — the key detail most candidates miss is the implicit From::from(e) call on the error path, which is exactly the mechanism that makes the From impls in this exercise necessary and sufficient.
  • P2"If this were a library crate rather than application code, would you still hand-write these From impls, or reach for a crate?" — For a library, thiserror is the standard answer — its #[derive(Error)] and #[from] attribute generate exactly this From-impl boilerplate from a declarative annotation, while still producing a fully typed, matchable public enum (unlike anyhow, which is more suited to application code that doesn't need callers to match on specific error variants).
  • P3"What would go wrong if you had two different underlying error types that both wanted to convert into the same variant?" — Nothing wrong in principle — you'd just write multiple From impls, each targeting a different ConfigError variant (or the same variant, if that's semantically right) — Rust allows arbitrarily many From for Y impls for the same Y as long as each X is a distinct source type; the coherence/orphan rule only restricts implementing traits for types you don't own, not having multiple impls for types you do own.
🎯 Senior angle
This exercise's real constraint — "no .map_err() anywhere" — forces the candidate to actually understand and use ?'s implicit From::from() conversion rather than working around it, which is exactly the mechanism most engineers use correctly by copying examples without ever being asked to explain.

Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
struct RequestBuilder {
    url: String,
    headers: Vec<(String, String)>,
    timeout_ms: u64,  // sensible default rather than Option — no failure mode for this field
}

enum BuildError {
    EmptyUrl,
}

impl RequestBuilder {
    fn new(url: &str) -> Self {
        Self { url: url.to_string(), headers: Vec::new(), timeout_ms: 30_000 }
    }

    fn header(mut self, key: &str, value: &str) -> Self {  // consumes and returns self — enables chaining
        self.headers.push((key.to_string(), value.to_string()));
        self
    }

    fn timeout_ms(mut self, ms: u64) -> Self {
        self.timeout_ms = ms;
        self
    }

    fn build(self) -> Result<Request, BuildError> {
        if self.url.is_empty() {
            return Err(BuildError::EmptyUrl);
        }
        Ok(Request { url: self.url, headers: self.headers, timeout_ms: self.timeout_ms })
    }
}

fn main() {
    let req = RequestBuilder::new("https://example.com")
        .header("Accept", "application/json")
        .timeout_ms(1500)
        .build()
        .unwrap();
    assert_eq!(req.url, "https://example.com");
    assert!(req.headers.iter().any(|(k, v)| k == "Accept" && v == "application/json"));
    assert_eq!(req.timeout_ms, 1500);
    assert!(RequestBuilder::new("").build().is_err());
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Takes and returns self by value (consuming) in every chainable method, not &mut self returning &mut Self — the consuming-self style is idiomatic in Rust specifically because it lets build() also consume self at the end to move fields out without cloning, and prevents a half-built builder from being reused unexpectedly.
  • ★★Uses a plain u64 with a default, not Option<u64>, for timeout_ms — correctly distinguishing "has a sensible default, never fails" fields from "must be validated at build() time" fields like the URL.
  • ★Considers whether repeated .header() calls with the same key should overwrite or accumulate, and states the choice explicitly (real HTTP headers can legitimately repeat, e.g. multiple Set-Cookie — accumulating via Vec rather than a HashMap models this correctly).
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What would break if header() took &mut self and returned &mut Self instead of consuming self?" — Chaining would still compile in the simple case, but you'd lose the ability to move the builder around by value across chain steps and, more importantly, build() couldn't move fields out of self at the end (a &mut self receiver only gives you a mutable reference, not ownership) — you'd be forced to clone the headers Vec and url String inside build(), an unnecessary allocation.
  • P2"How would you enforce, at compile time, that .header() must be called at least once before .build() is callable — without a runtime check?" — This is the "typestate builder" pattern: introduce marker generic parameters (e.g. RequestBuilder vs RequestBuilder) so that build() is only defined in an impl block generic over HasUrl, making it a compile error to call build() on a builder that hasn't set the URL yet — a genuinely advanced pattern worth naming even if not implementing live.
  • P3"Would you reach for the derive_builder crate in a real project instead of hand-writing this?" — For a struct with many optional fields, derive_builder (or similar) eliminates exactly this boilerplate via a derive macro — hand-writing it is a fine interview exercise and occasionally justified for a small, stable, hand-tuned public API, but it's not what most engineers would type out repeatedly in application code.
🎯 Senior angle
Watch specifically for the consuming-self vs. &mut self choice — it's a small detail that reveals whether the candidate has internalized Rust's ownership-based API design idioms or is translating a builder pattern learned in a garbage-collected language without adapting it.

// Write Exercise 12 · 30 min
W12 · Hand-Rolled Future — a Minimal Delay
Future trait Waker Pin Hard
Prompt
"Implement std::future::Future by hand for a Delay type — no async fn, no tokio::time::sleep — such that Delay::new(Duration::from_millis(200)).await works inside any async runtime (Tokio is fine to test with) and resolves after roughly the given duration. You'll need to spawn a helper OS thread that sleeps and then wakes the task — think carefully about what happens on the first poll versus subsequent polls."
Starter code

use std::time::Duration;

Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
struct SharedState {
    completed: bool,
    waker: Option<Waker>,
}

struct Delay {
    state: Arc<Mutex<SharedState>>,
}

impl Delay {
    fn new(duration: Duration) -> Self {
        let state = Arc::new(Mutex::new(SharedState { completed: false, waker: None }));
        let thread_state = Arc::clone(&state);
        std::thread::spawn(move || {
            std::thread::sleep(duration);
            let mut s = thread_state.lock().unwrap();
            s.completed = true;
            if let Some(waker) = s.waker.take() {
                waker.wake();  // tells the executor "re-poll this task" — nothing happens without this
            }
        });
        Delay { state }
    }
}

impl Future for Delay {
    type Output = ();

    fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<()> {
        let mut s = self.state.lock().unwrap();
        if s.completed {
            Poll::Ready(())
        } else {
            // Store (or refresh) the waker EVERY pending poll — the executor may hand us
            // a different Waker on each call (e.g. if the task moves between threads).
            s.waker = Some(cx.waker().clone());
            Poll::Pending
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let rt = tokio::runtime::Runtime::new().unwrap();
    rt.block_on(async {
        let start = std::time::Instant::now();
        Delay::new(std::time::Duration::from_millis(50)).await;
        assert!(start.elapsed() >= std::time::Duration::from_millis(40));
    });
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Calls waker.wake() from the spawned thread after setting completed = true, not before — and recognizes that forgetting to call wake() at all is the single most common mistake: the future would simply never be polled again, hanging forever even though the condition is technically satisfied.
  • ★★★Re-clones and stores the waker on every Pending poll, not just the first — recognizing that an executor is permitted to give a task a different Waker across polls (for instance if work-stealing moves the task to a different worker), so caching only the first one is a latent bug.
  • ★★Doesn't try to store a &mut self reference or otherwise fight Pin — this particular future has no internal self-references needing pinning, so self: Pin<&mut Self> can just be used via auto-deref without any unsafe — recognizing when Pin is a non-issue is as valuable as knowing when it matters.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What would happen if poll() were called and returned Pending, but the future's task was then dropped before the sleeping thread finished — does anything leak or panic?" — The Arc> keeps the shared state alive as long as either side (the Delay/task or the spawned thread) holds a reference, so no use-after-free — the spawned thread will still complete, lock, set completed, and try to wake a Waker that may now point to a dropped task; calling wake() on a stale waker for an already-dropped task is safe (a no-op essentially) precisely because Waker's contract is designed to tolerate this.
  • P2"Why does this need a background OS thread at all — why can't poll() just check std::time::Instant::now() directly?" — You could poll-and-compare against a stored deadline instead of using a thread+Waker — but then nothing would ever call wake(), so the executor would have no signal to re-poll the future; it would either need to busy-poll (wasteful) or simply never get re-scheduled at all if the executor only re-polls in response to a wake() call, which is how most real executors, including Tokio's, actually work.
  • P3"In real code, would you ever hand-roll this instead of using tokio::time::sleep?" — Essentially never for a plain delay — this exercise exists purely to build genuine intuition for how async/await desugars to poll-based state machines under the hood; production code should always prefer the runtime's own, already-integrated-with-its-timer-wheel sleep primitive.
🎯 Senior angle
Very few engineers who use async/await daily have ever manually implemented Future::poll — this exercise is one of the highest-signal ways to distinguish "knows how to write async Rust" from "understands what async Rust actually compiles down to," which matters enormously when debugging a stuck or leaking task in production.

W13 · Retry With Exponential Backoff
async generics Tokio resilience Medium

It should return the first success or the last error if all attempts are exhausted."
Starter code

use std::time::Duration;

fn main() {
    let rt = tokio::runtime::Runtime::new().unwrap();
    rt.block_on(async {
        use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU32, Ordering};
        let attempts = AtomicU32::new(0);
        let result = retry_with_backoff(
            || async {
                let n = attempts.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst) + 1;
                if n < 3 {

                } else {

Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
async fn retry_with_backoff<F, Fut, T, E>(
    mut f: F,
    max_attempts: u32,
    base_delay: Duration,
) -> Result<T, E>
where
    F: FnMut() -> Fut,          // called fresh each attempt — produces a NEW future each time
    Fut: Future<Output = Result<T, E>>,
{
    let mut attempt = 0;
    let mut delay = base_delay;

    loop {
        attempt += 1;
        match f().await {
            Ok(value) => return Ok(value),
            Err(e) if attempt >= max_attempts => return Err(e),
            Err(_) => {
                tokio::time::sleep(delay).await;
                delay *= 2;  // exponential backoff — consider capping this with delay.min(max_delay) in production
            }
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let rt = tokio::runtime::Runtime::new().unwrap();
    rt.block_on(async {
        use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU32, Ordering};
        let attempts = AtomicU32::new(0);
        let result = retry_with_backoff(
            || async {
                let n = attempts.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst) + 1;
                if n < 3 {
                    Err("fail")
                } else {
                    Ok(42)
                }
            },
            5,
            std::time::Duration::from_millis(1),
        )
        .await;
        assert_eq!(result, Ok(42));
        assert_eq!(attempts.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 3);
    });
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Uses FnMut() -> Fut where Fut: Future<Output = Result<T, E>>, not a single async fn signature — recognizing that a closure returning a future is the correct shape to let each call produce a fresh, independently-pollable future (you can't .await the same future object twice).
  • ★★Awaits the sleep between attempts, not a blocking std::thread::sleep — using a blocking sleep inside an async fn would stall the entire runtime worker thread, directly connecting to the blocking-the-runtime pitfall covered elsewhere in this packet.
  • ★Volunteers a cap on the maximum delay (e.g. delay = delay.min(max_delay)) unprompted, recognizing that naive doubling grows unbounded and could eventually wait for absurdly long, impractical durations.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Why does F need to be FnMut and not Fn — why can't the closure be called only once and its future reused?" — A single Future value represents one specific unit of work in progress; polling it to completion (or having it fail) consumes it conceptually — Future doesn't implement Clone, and re-polling an already-completed future is explicitly documented as allowed to panic. FnMut lets you call f() again to get a brand new Fut for each retry attempt, which is the only sound way to "try the operation again."
  • P2"What's missing here for real production use — specifically around retrying non-idempotent operations?" — Blind retrying is only safe for idempotent operations (a GET, or a PUT with the same payload) — retrying a non-idempotent operation like "charge this credit card" without deduplication (e.g. an idempotency key) can cause duplicate side effects; a senior answer should flag this as a correctness concern that backoff logic alone doesn't address.
  • P3"How would you add jitter to this, and why does jitter matter?" — Add a small random component to each delay (e.g. delay + Duration::from_millis(rng.gen_range(0..50))) — without jitter, many clients retrying a shared, temporarily-overloaded service in lockstep after the same fixed backoff interval can create synchronized retry storms that repeatedly re-overload the service; jitter spreads retries out in time to avoid this thundering-herd effect.
🎯 Senior angle
The FnMut() -> Fut generic bound is a small piece of syntax that trips up even experienced Rust engineers on the first attempt — watching whether the candidate arrives at it through reasoning about what a "repeatable async operation" needs to look like, versus getting stuck fighting the compiler, is genuinely useful signal.

// Write Exercise 14 · 25 min
W14 · Token Bucket Rate Limiter
Instant/Duration Mutex systems Medium
Prompt
"Implement a thread-safe TokenBucket rate limiter: capacity max tokens, refilling at refill_rate tokens per second continuously (not in discrete ticks). try_acquire(&self, n: u32) -> bool should atomically check-and-deduct n tokens, returning true if there were enough, false otherwise (no blocking). Refilling should happen lazily, computed from elapsed time, not via a background thread or timer."
Starter code
use std::sync::Mutex;
use std::time::Instant;

struct TokenBucket {
    capacity: f64,
    refill_rate: f64,  // tokens per second
    state: Mutex<State>,
}

struct State { tokens: f64, last_refill: Instant }

impl TokenBucket {
    fn new(capacity: f64, refill_rate: f64) -> Self { todo!() }
    fn try_acquire(&self, n: f64) -> bool { todo!() }
}

fn main() {
    let bucket = TokenBucket::new(2.0, 1000.0);
    assert!(bucket.try_acquire(1.0));
    assert!(bucket.try_acquire(1.0));
    assert!(!bucket.try_acquire(1.0)); // empty
    std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(5));
    assert!(bucket.try_acquire(1.0)); // refilled
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
impl TokenBucket {
    fn new(capacity: f64, refill_rate: f64) -> Self {
        Self {
            capacity,
            refill_rate,
            state: Mutex::new(State { tokens: capacity, last_refill: Instant::now() }),
        }
    }

    fn try_acquire(&self, n: f64) -> bool {
        let mut state = self.state.lock().unwrap();

        // Lazy refill: compute exactly how many tokens would have accrued since last_refill,
        // rather than running a background timer — no wasted wakeups when the bucket is idle.
        let now = Instant::now();
        let elapsed = now.duration_since(state.last_refill).as_secs_f64();
        let refilled = elapsed * self.refill_rate;
        state.tokens = (state.tokens + refilled).min(self.capacity);
        state.last_refill = now;

        if state.tokens >= n {
            state.tokens -= n;
            true
        } else {
            false
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let bucket = TokenBucket::new(2.0, 1000.0);
    assert!(bucket.try_acquire(1.0));
    assert!(bucket.try_acquire(1.0));
    assert!(!bucket.try_acquire(1.0)); // empty
    std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(5));
    assert!(bucket.try_acquire(1.0)); // refilled
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Refills lazily based on elapsed Instant delta on every call, rather than spawning a background thread/timer to "tick" the bucket periodically — this is a meaningfully better design (no wasted wakeups, works correctly even under bursty or sparse traffic) and is exactly what the prompt is testing for.
  • ★★★Clamps refilled tokens to capacity with .min() — without this, a bucket left idle for a long time would accumulate unbounded "banked" tokens, letting a client burst far beyond its intended rate the next time it's used.
  • ★★Performs the check-and-deduct as one atomic critical section under the single lock, not as two separate locked operations — a check-then-later-deduct split would reintroduce a race between concurrent callers.
  • ★Uses Instant, not SystemTime, for measuring elapsed durations — recognizing that Instant is monotonic and unaffected by system clock adjustments (NTP sync, manual changes), which matters for any duration/elapsed-time calculation.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"How would you extend this to work across multiple server instances behind a load balancer, not just within one process?" — This in-memory version only rate-limits within a single process — a distributed version needs shared external state, typically Redis with an atomic Lua script (or Redis's own token-bucket-style commands) implementing the same check-and-deduct logic atomically server-side, exactly as discussed in this packet's rate-limiter system-design scenario.
  • P2"What's the actual behavioral difference between this token-bucket approach and a fixed-window counter (e.g. 'max 100 requests per calendar minute')?" — Fixed windows allow a burst of up to 2x the intended rate right at a window boundary (100 requests in the last millisecond of one window plus 100 more in the first millisecond of the next) — token bucket's continuous refill avoids this boundary-burst problem entirely by tracking a smoothly-accruing budget rather than resetting a counter at fixed instants.
  • P3"Is a Mutex the right choice here, or would you reach for atomics instead?" — Since a correct refill+check+deduct requires reading and writing both tokens and last_refill together as one consistent unit, a Mutex around a small State struct is the natural fit — you could attempt a fully lock-free CAS-loop version using packed atomics, but the added complexity is rarely justified for a rate limiter's typically modest contention levels; a good answer names this trade-off explicitly rather than reflexively reaching for atomics everywhere.
🎯 Senior angle
The lazy-refill-via-elapsed-time technique is the crux of this exercise — candidates who reach for a background thread that ticks the bucket on an interval are solving the problem in a less efficient, more complex, and more failure-prone way than the codebase actually needs, and noticing that yourself unprompted is a mark of practical systems judgment.
