W15 · Recursive-Descent JSON Parser
enums recursion parsing Hard
Prompt
"Without serde_json or any parsing crate, write a parser for a subset of JSON — objects, arrays, strings, numbers, true/false/null — into an enum Json. fn parse(input: &str) -> Result<Json, String> is the entry point. You don't need to handle escaped characters inside strings or full float exponent syntax — focus on getting the recursive structure and control flow right."
Starter code
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::iter::Peekable;
use std::str::Chars;

enum Json {
    Null,
    Bool(bool),
    Number(f64),
    Str(String),
    Array(Vec<Json>),
    Object(HashMap<String, Json>),
}

fn parse(input: &str) -> Result<Json, String> {
    let mut chars = input.chars().peekable();
    parse_value(&mut chars)
}

// TODO: parse_value, plus helpers for object/array/string/number, skipping whitespace
fn parse_value(chars: &mut Peekable<Chars>) -> Result<Json, String> {
    todo!()
}

fn main() {
    match parse(r#"{"a": [1, true, null]}"#) {
        Ok(Json::Object(map)) => {
            match map.get("a") {
                Some(Json::Array(items)) => {
                    assert_eq!(items.len(), 3);
                    assert!(matches!(items[0], Json::Number(_)));
                    assert!(matches!(items[1], Json::Bool(true)));
                    assert!(matches!(items[2], Json::Null));
                }
                other => panic!("expected array, got {other:?}"),
            }
        }
        other => panic!("parse failed: {other:?}"),
    }
    assert!(parse("{").is_err());
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
fn skip_whitespace(chars: &mut Peekable<Chars>) {
    while let Some(&c) = chars.peek() {
        if c.is_whitespace() { chars.next(); } else { break; }
    }
}

fn parse_value(chars: &mut Peekable<Chars>) -> Result<Json, String> {
    skip_whitespace(chars);
    match chars.peek() {
        Some('{') => parse_object(chars),
        Some('[') => parse_array(chars),
        Some('"') => parse_string(chars).map(Json::Str),
        Some('t') | Some('f') => parse_bool(chars),
        Some('n') => parse_null(chars),
        Some(c) if c.is_ascii_digit() || *c == '-' => parse_number(chars),
        Some(c) => Err(format!("unexpected character: {c}")),
        None => Err("unexpected end of input".to_string()),
    }
}

fn parse_object(chars: &mut Peekable<Chars>) -> Result<Json, String> {
    chars.next();  // consume '{'
    let mut map = HashMap::new();
    skip_whitespace(chars);
    if chars.peek() == Some(&'}') { chars.next(); return Ok(Json::Object(map)); }

    loop {
        skip_whitespace(chars);
        let key = parse_string(chars)?;
        skip_whitespace(chars);
        if chars.next() != Some(':') { return Err("expected ':'".to_string()); }
        let value = parse_value(chars)?;  // recursion — values can be objects/arrays too
        map.insert(key, value);
        skip_whitespace(chars);
        match chars.next() {
            Some(',') => continue,
            Some('}') => return Ok(Json::Object(map)),
            _ => return Err("expected ',' or '}'".to_string()),
        }
    }
}

fn parse_array(chars: &mut Peekable<Chars>) -> Result<Json, String> {
    chars.next();  // consume '['
    let mut items = Vec::new();
    skip_whitespace(chars);
    if chars.peek() == Some(&']') { chars.next(); return Ok(Json::Array(items)); }

    loop {
        items.push(parse_value(chars)?);
        skip_whitespace(chars);
        match chars.next() {
            Some(',') => continue,
            Some(']') => return Ok(Json::Array(items)),
            _ => return Err("expected ',' or ']'".to_string()),
        }
    }
}

fn parse_string(chars: &mut Peekable<Chars>) -> Result<String, String> {
    skip_whitespace(chars);
    if chars.next() != Some('"') { return Err("expected '\"'".to_string()); }
    let mut s = String::new();
    while let Some(c) = chars.next() {
        if c == '"' { return Ok(s); }
        s.push(c);
    }
    Err("unterminated string".to_string())
}

fn parse_number(chars: &mut Peekable<Chars>) -> Result<Json, String> {
    let mut s = String::new();
    while let Some(&c) = chars.peek() {
        if c.is_ascii_digit() || c == '.' || c == '-' { s.push(c); chars.next(); } else { break; }
    }
    s.parse::<f64>().map(Json::Number).map_err(|e| e.to_string())
}

fn parse_bool(chars: &mut Peekable<Chars>) -> Result<Json, String> {
    if chars.clone().take(4).collect::<String>() == "true" {
        for _ in 0..4 { chars.next(); }
        return Ok(Json::Bool(true));
    }
    if chars.clone().take(5).collect::<String>() == "false" {
        for _ in 0..5 { chars.next(); }
        return Ok(Json::Bool(false));
    }
    Err("expected true/false".to_string())
}

fn parse_null(chars: &mut Peekable<Chars>) -> Result<Json, String> {
    if chars.clone().take(4).collect::<String>() == "null" {
        for _ in 0..4 { chars.next(); }
        return Ok(Json::Null);
    }
    Err("expected null".to_string())
}

fn main() {
    match parse(r#"{"a": [1, true, null]}"#) {
        Ok(Json::Object(map)) => {
            match map.get("a") {
                Some(Json::Array(items)) => {
                    assert_eq!(items.len(), 3);
                    assert!(matches!(items[0], Json::Number(_)));
                    assert!(matches!(items[1], Json::Bool(true)));
                    assert!(matches!(items[2], Json::Null));
                }
                other => panic!("expected array, got {other:?}"),
            }
        }
        other => panic!("parse failed: {other:?}"),
    }
    assert!(parse("{").is_err());
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Uses Peekable<Chars> and structures the whole parser around peek()-then-next() — recognizing that you often need to look at the next character to decide what to parse before committing to consuming it, which is the core recursive-descent technique.
  • ★★Handles the empty-object/empty-array case ({}, []) as a special early check before entering the comma-separated loop — a very common off-by-one/infinite-loop source if skipped.
  • ★Recognizes the recursive call to parse_value inside parse_object/parse_array is what naturally handles arbitrarily nested JSON — no special-casing needed for nested structures.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What happens with deeply nested input, like 10,000 levels of nested arrays — is there a risk here?" — Yes — this parser is directly recursive, so extremely deep nesting can exhaust the call stack and cause a stack overflow (a crash, not a graceful error) — real-world parsers (including serde_json) impose a maximum recursion depth specifically to convert this into a clean, catchable error instead of a process crash.
  • P2"Why iterate over chars() rather than bytes(), given JSON files are often read as raw bytes from a file or network socket?" — chars() correctly handles multi-byte UTF-8 sequences as single logical characters, which matters for JSON string content containing non-ASCII text — iterating raw bytes would require manually handling UTF-8 decoding to avoid splitting a multi-byte character in the middle, which str::chars() already does correctly and for free.
  • P3"In real production code, would you ship this, or reach for serde_json?" — serde_json, without question, for virtually any real use case — it's extensively fuzzed, handles the full JSON spec correctly (escape sequences, exponents, surrogate pairs, etc.), and is highly optimized. This exercise is valuable specifically as a controlled way to test recursive-descent parsing fundamentals and enum-based AST design, not as a preview of production code.
🎯 Senior angle
This is one of the meatier exercises in the packet — it simultaneously tests enum-based AST modeling, recursive control flow, string/iterator manipulation, and careful error propagation, making it a strong single exercise to fill a full 30-minute block when you want maximum coverage from one prompt.

                    assert_eq!(items.len(), 3);
                    assert!(matches!(items[0], Json::Number(_)));
                    assert!(matches!(items[1], Json::Bool(true)));
                    assert!(matches!(items[2], Json::Null));
                }
                other => panic!("expected array, got {other:?}"),
            }
        }
        other => panic!("parse failed: {other:?}"),
    }
    assert!(parse("{").is_err());
}

W16 · Graph BFS — Shortest Path
HashMap VecDeque algorithms Medium
Prompt
"Implement a generic Graph<T> using an adjacency-list representation, with add_edge(&mut self, from: T, to: T) (undirected) and shortest_path(&self, start: &T, end: &T) -> Option<Vec<T>> that returns the shortest path (by edge count) between two nodes using breadth-first search, or None if unreachable."
Starter code
use std::collections::{HashMap, HashSet, VecDeque};
use std::hash::Hash;

struct Graph<T: Eq + Hash + Clone> {
    adjacency: HashMap<T, Vec<T>>,
}

impl<T: Eq + Hash + Clone> Graph<T> {
    fn new() -> Self { Self { adjacency: HashMap::new() } }
    fn add_edge(&mut self, from: T, to: T) { todo!() }
    fn shortest_path(&self, start: &T, end: &T) -> Option<Vec<T>> { todo!() }
}

fn main() {
    let mut g = Graph::new();
    g.add_edge("a", "b");
    g.add_edge("b", "c");
    g.add_edge("a", "c");
    assert_eq!(g.shortest_path(&"a", &"c"), Some(vec!["a".into(), "c".into()]));
    assert_eq!(g.shortest_path(&"c", &"a"), None);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
impl<T: Eq + Hash + Clone> Graph<T> {
    fn add_edge(&mut self, from: T, to: T) {
        self.adjacency.entry(from.clone()).or_default().push(to.clone());
        self.adjacency.entry(to).or_default().push(from);  // undirected — add both directions
    }

    fn shortest_path(&self, start: &T, end: &T) -> Option<Vec<T>> {
        if start == end { return Some(vec![start.clone()]); }

        let mut visited: HashSet<T> = HashSet::new();
        let mut came_from: HashMap<T, T> = HashMap::new();  // tracks predecessor for path reconstruction
        let mut queue: VecDeque<T> = VecDeque::new();

        queue.push_back(start.clone());
        visited.insert(start.clone());

        while let Some(current) = queue.pop_front() {
            if let Some(neighbors) = self.adjacency.get(&current) {
                for neighbor in neighbors {
                    if !visited.contains(neighbor) {
                        visited.insert(neighbor.clone());
                        came_from.insert(neighbor.clone(), current.clone());
                        if neighbor == end {
                            return Some(reconstruct_path(&came_from, start, end));  // found — stop early, BFS guarantees shortest
                        }
                        queue.push_back(neighbor.clone());
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        None  // queue exhausted without reaching `end` — unreachable
    }
}

fn reconstruct_path<T: Eq + Hash + Clone>(came_from: &HashMap<T, T>, start: &T, end: &T) -> Vec<T> {
    let mut path = vec![end.clone()];
    let mut current = end;
    while current != start {
        current = &came_from[current];
        path.push(current.clone());
    }
    path.reverse();  // we walked backward from end to start via came_from — flip it
    path
}

fn main() {
    let mut g = Graph::new();
    g.add_edge("a", "b");
    g.add_edge("b", "c");
    g.add_edge("a", "c");
    assert_eq!(g.shortest_path(&"a", &"c"), Some(vec!["a".into(), "c".into()]));
    assert_eq!(g.shortest_path(&"c", &"a"), None);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Marks nodes visited at the moment they're enqueued, not when dequeued — marking on dequeue instead is a classic BFS bug that allows the same node to be pushed onto the queue multiple times from different neighbors before it's ever processed.
  • ★★★Uses a came_from map to reconstruct the path, rather than storing the whole path-so-far in the queue at every node — storing full paths works but is far more memory-intensive (O(V²) in the worst case) than tracking one predecessor per node (O(V)).
  • ★★Uses VecDeque, not Vec, for the BFS frontier — recognizing that BFS needs FIFO order (push_back/pop_front), and popping from the front of a Vec would be an O(n) operation every time versus VecDeque's O(1).
  • ★Adds the edge in both directions in add_edge for the stated undirected-graph requirement, and uses entry().or_default() rather than manually checking-then-inserting.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Why does BFS guarantee the shortest path here, but wouldn't if edges had different weights?" — BFS explores nodes in strictly increasing order of edge-count distance from the start (all distance-1 nodes before any distance-2 node, etc.), which only corresponds to "shortest path" when every edge has equal weight (or no weight, as here). With weighted edges, a longer-edge-count path could have smaller total weight, requiring Dijkstra's algorithm (a priority-queue-driven approach) instead.
  • P2"What's the time and space complexity here, in terms of V (nodes) and E (edges)?" — O(V + E) time — each node is enqueued/dequeued once, and each edge is examined at most twice (once from each endpoint in an undirected graph) — and O(V) additional space for visited, came_from, and the queue, on top of the O(V + E) graph representation itself.
  • P3"If T were an expensive-to-clone type like a large struct or String, would you change anything about this design?" — Cloning T repeatedly (in add_edge, visited.insert, came_from, and path reconstruction) could get expensive — a real-world refinement would intern node identities into a cheap Copy index type (e.g. a usize NodeId) up front and keep the actual T values in a separate side table, so the graph algorithm itself only ever copies small indices.
🎯 Senior angle
Watch closely for the visited-on-enqueue-vs-dequeue distinction — it's the single most common subtle bug in hand-written BFS, and candidates who get it right without prompting are demonstrating they've actually internalized the algorithm's invariants rather than pattern-matching a remembered template.

// Write Exercise 17 · 30 min
W17 · Bump Allocator (Arena) — Unsafe
unsafe raw pointers alignment Hard — staff calibration
Prompt
"Implement a simple bump allocator arena: a fixed-size backing buffer that hands out individual T allocations via alloc<T>(&self, value: T) -> &mut T by simply advancing an offset — no per-allocation bookkeeping, no individual frees. Note the &self (not &mut self) — this needs to support allocating multiple times without exclusive borrows piling up. You must respect T's alignment requirement, not just its size, and must not overrun the buffer."
Starter code
use std::cell::Cell;

struct Arena {
    buf: Vec<u8>,
    offset: Cell<usize>,
}

impl Arena {
    fn new(capacity: usize) -> Self {
        Self { buf: vec![0u8; capacity], offset: Cell::new(0) }
    }

// TODO: fn alloc(&self, value: T) -> &mut T
// - compute a properly aligned offset for T within `buf`
// - bump `offset` past this allocation
// - write `value` into that location and return a mutable reference to it
// - what happens if there isn't enough room?
}

fn main() {
    let arena = Arena::new(1024);
    let a = arena.alloc(1u32);
    let b = arena.alloc(2u32);
    assert_eq!(*a, 1);
    assert_eq!(*b, 2);
    *a = 9;
    assert_eq!(*a, 9);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
impl Arena {
    fn alloc<T>(&self, value: T) -> &mut T {
        let align = std::mem::align_of::<T>();
        let size = std::mem::size_of::<T>();

        let current = self.offset.get();
        let aligned = (current + align - 1) / align * align;  // round up to the next multiple of `align`

        if aligned + size > self.buf.len() {
            panic!("arena out of memory");  // simplest correct behavior — see follow-up P2 for alternatives
        }

        unsafe {
            // SAFETY: `aligned + size 
            // `aligned` satisfies T's alignment by construction. `buf` outlives the returned
            // reference because Arena itself must outlive it (tied via the &self borrow's lifetime).
            let ptr = self.buf.as_ptr().add(aligned) as *mut T;
            ptr.write(value);
            self.offset.set(aligned + size);
            &mut *ptr
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let arena = Arena::new(1024);
    let a = arena.alloc(1u32);
    let b = arena.alloc(2u32);
    assert_eq!(*a, 1);
    assert_eq!(*b, 2);
    *a = 9;
    assert_eq!(*a, 9);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Rounds the offset up to satisfy T's alignment, not just checking there's enough remaining size — an allocator that ignores alignment can hand out a pointer that's technically in-bounds but misaligned for T, which is undefined behavior the moment you dereference or write through it, even if nothing crashes immediately.
  • ★★★Uses Cell<usize> for the offset, recognizing that &self (required so multiple allocations can happen without an exclusive borrow) rules out a plain usize field mutated directly — Cell gives interior mutability for a Copy type with zero runtime overhead, appropriate here specifically because Arena isn't meant to be shared across threads (no need for a Mutex/atomic).
  • ★★Uses ptr::write, not a plain pointer dereference assignment, to place the value into uninitialized memory — writing via *ptr = value on uninitialized memory would first try to drop whatever "old value" is notionally there (garbage), which is unsound; write is specifically designed to skip that.
  • ★Writes a // SAFETY: comment covering both the bounds check and the alignment argument explicitly, without being asked.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What's unsound about the returned lifetime here — could you get two overlapping &mut T references out of this arena by accident?" — As written, every alloc() call returns an independent &mut T pointing to a disjoint region of the buffer (since offset only ever increases), so no two calls alias the same memory — but nothing in the type system prevents a caller from calling arena.alloc() again while holding an earlier &mut T reference indefinitely; that's fine memory-safety-wise (they point to different bytes) but is worth naming as a place where the compiler is trusting the implementation's internal bookkeeping rather than verifying it structurally.
  • P2"panic! on out-of-memory is one option — what are the alternatives, and their trade-offs?" — Return Option<&mut T> (or Result) so callers can handle exhaustion gracefully, at the cost of every call site needing to handle the failure case; or grow the backing buffer dynamically (much closer to how bumpalo's real chunked-arena design works, allocating additional chunks on demand) — panicking is the simplest correct choice for a fixed-capacity toy arena but is rarely the right default for a general-purpose allocator.
  • P3"Does this arena ever call any T's Drop impl? Is that a problem?" — No — values written via ptr::write are never automatically dropped when the Arena itself is dropped (the Arena only holds raw Vec bytes, which know nothing about the T values logically stored inside them); for Copy types or types that don't own external resources (heap allocations, file handles) this is harmless, but for a real arena allocator meant to store arbitrary droppable types, you'd need to separately track and manually drop each allocated value — this is exactly why bumpalo's real API requires T: 'static and documents this limitation carefully, and is a strong signal if raised unprompted.
🎯 Senior angle
Reserve this for candidates who've specifically claimed low-level/allocator/performance experience — the alignment-rounding detail and the interior-mutability-via-Cell choice are both easy to get wrong under pressure, and getting them right unprompted is a strong indicator of genuine systems-level Rust fluency rather than surface familiarity with unsafe syntax.

Expose a cheaply cloneable CounterHandle with async methods increment(&self) and get(&self) -> u64 that many callers, across many tasks, can use concurrently."

}

Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
impl CounterHandle {
    fn new() -> Self {
        let (tx, mut rx) = mpsc::channel::<Command>(32);

        tokio::spawn(async move {
            let mut count: u64 = 0;  // owned exclusively by this task — never shared, never locked
            while let Some(cmd) = rx.recv().await {
                match cmd {
                    Command::Increment => count += 1,
                    Command::Get(reply) => {
                        let _ = reply.send(count);  // ignore error — caller may have dropped their receiver
                    }
                }
            }
        });

        Self { tx }
    }

    async fn increment(&self) {
        let _ = self.tx.send(Command::Increment).await;
    }

    async fn get(&self) -> u64 {
        let (reply_tx, reply_rx) = oneshot::channel();
        let _ = self.tx.send(Command::Get(reply_tx)).await;
        reply_rx.await.unwrap_or(0)  // actor task gone — a real impl would surface this as an error, not silently 0
    }
}

fn main() {
    let rt = tokio::runtime::Runtime::new().unwrap();
    rt.block_on(async {
        let handle = CounterHandle::new();
        handle.increment().await;
        handle.increment().await;
        assert_eq!(handle.get().await, 2);
    });
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Uses a plain, un-synchronized u64 local variable inside the spawned task for the counter state — recognizing that because only the actor task itself ever touches count, there is no shared mutable state at all, and therefore no Mutex is needed anywhere. This is the entire point of the actor pattern.
  • ★★★Uses a oneshot channel for the Get reply path, not the main mpsc channel — recognizing that a request needing exactly one specific response back to exactly one specific caller is a different shape than the many-producers-one-consumer command channel, and reaching for the right primitive rather than overloading the one channel.
  • ★★Derives Clone on CounterHandle and recognizes that cloning it is cheap (just cloning an mpsc::Sender, which is designed to be cheaply cloneable) — this is what lets "many callers across many tasks" share one handle without any Arc wrapper needed.
  • ★Doesn't panic or propagate an error loudly on a failed send to a possibly-dropped receiver — acknowledges this could happen (e.g. caller cancelled) and handles it gracefully, even if just by ignoring the result for this exercise's scope.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What's the actual advantage of this over just wrapping the counter in Arc> directly, for this specific example?" — For a trivial counter, genuinely not much — Arc would be simpler and faster here. The actor pattern's real value shows up when the shared state is more complex than a single primitive: multiple related fields that must be updated together, state machines with invariants that are easy to violate under concurrent direct mutation, or when you want all mutation funneled through one auditable, sequential code path rather than scattered across lock-acquisition call sites everywhere.
  • P2"What happens to in-flight increment() calls if the actor task panics?" — The spawned task dying (whether by panic or the channel's rx.recv() loop ending because all senders were dropped) means the receiving end of the mpsc channel is gone — subsequent send() calls from any CounterHandle will return an error (which this implementation currently discards) rather than hanging forever, so callers won't deadlock, but they will silently get no counter behavior at all unless the discarded error is surfaced.
  • P3"How would you add a graceful shutdown that waits for all pending commands to be processed before the actor task exits?" — Add a Shutdown command variant, or rely on the natural behavior that when the last CounterHandle (and thus the last Sender clone) is dropped, rx.recv().await naturally returns None and the while-let loop exits on its own — this natural drain-and-exit-on-channel-close behavior is one of the actor pattern's underrated advantages over manually coordinating thread shutdown flags.
🎯 Senior angle
The actor pattern is one of the more distinctly "Rust-flavored" concurrency idioms candidates from other ecosystems often haven't encountered — a candidate who's used it before will typically volunteer the "ownership funnels through one task" framing unprompted, which is a strong positive signal for async Rust design taste specifically.

W19 · Custom Semaphore From Scratch
Condvar RAII guard concurrency primitive Medium
Prompt
"Implement a counting Semaphore from scratch using Mutex + Condvar (no tokio::sync::Semaphore, no external crates). acquire(&self) should block while there are zero available permits, then take one; releasing a permit should happen automatically via RAII when a returned guard type is dropped — callers should never be able to forget to release a permit they acquired."
Starter code
use std::sync::{Condvar, Mutex};

    count: Mutex<usize>,
    condvar: Condvar,
}

// TODO: what type does acquire() return, and how does it release the permit on drop?

    fn new(permits: usize) -> Self { todo!() }
    fn acquire(&self) -> /* ??? */ { todo!() }

fn main() {
    use std::sync::Arc;
    use std::thread;
    use std::time::{Duration, Instant};
    let sem = Arc::new(Semaphore::new(1));
    let s2 = Arc::clone(&sem);
    let t0 = Instant::now();
    let h = thread::spawn(move || {
        let _g = s2.acquire();
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(50));
    });

Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
struct Semaphore {
    count: Mutex<usize>,
    condvar: Condvar,
}

// The guard borrows the Semaphore for its whole lifetime, guaranteeing it can't
// outlive the semaphore it releases a permit back to.
struct SemaphoreGuard<'a> {
    semaphore: &'a Semaphore,
}

impl<'a> Drop for SemaphoreGuard<'a> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        let mut count = self.semaphore.count.lock().unwrap();
        *count += 1;
        self.semaphore.condvar.notify_one();  // wake exactly one waiter — one permit just freed up
    }
}

impl Semaphore {
    fn new(permits: usize) -> Self {
        Self { count: Mutex::new(permits), condvar: Condvar::new() }
    }

    fn acquire(&self) -> SemaphoreGuard<'_> {
        let mut count = self.count.lock().unwrap();
        while *count == 0 {                                 // while, not if — spurious wakeups
            count = self.condvar.wait(count).unwrap();
        }
        *count -= 1;
        SemaphoreGuard { semaphore: self }
    }
}

fn main() {
    use std::sync::Arc;
    use std::thread;
    use std::time::{Duration, Instant};
    let sem = Arc::new(Semaphore::new(1));
    let s2 = Arc::clone(&sem);
    let t0 = Instant::now();
    let h = thread::spawn(move || {
        let _g = s2.acquire();
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(50));
    });
    thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(10));
    let _g = sem.acquire();
    assert!(t0.elapsed() >= Duration::from_millis(40));
    h.join().unwrap();
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Introduces a guard type with a Drop impl as the return value of acquire(), rather than a bare release() method callers must remember to call — this is the exact same RAII principle behind MutexGuard, applied to a hand-rolled primitive, and directly prevents an entire class of "forgot to release the permit" bugs.
  • ★★★Gives the guard a lifetime tied to the semaphore (&'a Semaphore) — ensuring the guard cannot outlive the semaphore it needs to release a permit back to, letting the borrow checker enforce a correctness property that would otherwise need a runtime check or documentation-only convention.
  • ★★Calls notify_one(), not notify_all(), in the guard's Drop impl — recognizing that releasing exactly one permit can wake at most one additional waiter usefully.
  • ★Uses while around the condvar wait, consistent with the spurious-wakeup awareness tested elsewhere in this packet (W4).
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What would go wrong if SemaphoreGuard didn't borrow the Semaphore and instead held an owned Arc?" — Nothing would go "wrong" per se — it's actually a common and reasonable alternative design, useful specifically when the guard needs to be moved across an await point or into another task/thread that doesn't otherwise have access to the semaphore. The borrowed-reference version is simpler and zero-cost but ties the guard's lifetime (and usability) tightly to the semaphore's own scope; Arc trades a small refcount overhead for much more flexibility in where the guard can travel.
  • P2"How would you adapt this into an async semaphore usable inside Tokio tasks, rather than this blocking, thread-based version?" — Condvar::wait blocks the calling OS thread, which would stall a Tokio worker thread exactly like the blocking-the-runtime pitfall discussed elsewhere in this packet — an async version needs a fundamentally different waiting mechanism (a queue of Wakers, notified on release, similar to the hand-rolled Future exercise) — which is exactly what tokio::sync::Semaphore implements internally.
  • P3"When would you reach for this pattern versus just using a Mutex directly?" — A semaphore generalizes a mutex — a Mutex is really just a semaphore with exactly 1 permit. Reach for a full semaphore specifically when you need to allow N concurrent holders rather than strictly 1 — for example, limiting concurrent outbound connections to some external service to at most N at a time, which is exactly the shape of the connection-pool system-design scenario elsewhere in this packet.
🎯 Senior angle
The guard-with-Drop design is the single highest-value thing to look for here — candidates who reach for it unprompted are demonstrating they understand RAII as a general design principle for resource management, not just something the standard library happens to do for you with MutexGuard.

// Write Exercise 20 · 20 min
W20 · Union-Find / Disjoint Set
data structures amortized complexity algorithms Medium
Prompt
"Implement a DisjointSet (union-find) over indices 0..n, with find(&mut self, x: usize) -> usize (returns the representative/root of x's set) and union(&mut self, a: usize, b: usize) (merges the two sets). Implement both path compression and union by rank — a version without either is not sufficient here."
Starter code
struct DisjointSet {
    parent: Vec<usize>,
    rank: Vec<usize>,
}

impl DisjointSet {
    fn new(n: usize) -> Self {
        Self { parent: (0..n).collect(), rank: vec![0; n] }  // everyone starts as their own root
    }
    fn find(&mut self, x: usize) -> usize { todo!() }
    fn union(&mut self, a: usize, b: usize) { todo!() }
}

fn main() {
    let mut ds = DisjointSet::new(5);
    ds.union(0, 1);
    ds.union(1, 2);
    assert_eq!(ds.find(0), ds.find(2));
    assert_ne!(ds.find(0), ds.find(3));
    ds.union(3, 4);
    ds.union(2, 3);
    assert_eq!(ds.find(0), ds.find(4));
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
impl DisjointSet {
    fn find(&mut self, x: usize) -> usize {
        if self.parent[x] != x {
            self.parent[x] = self.find(self.parent[x]);  // path compression: point directly at the root
        }
        self.parent[x]
    }

    fn union(&mut self, a: usize, b: usize) {
        let root_a = self.find(a);
        let root_b = self.find(b);
        if root_a == root_b { return; }  // already in the same set

        // union by rank: attach the shorter tree under the taller one's root, keeping trees flat
        if self.rank[root_a] < self.rank[root_b] {
            self.parent[root_a] = root_b;
        } else if self.rank[root_a] > self.rank[root_b] {
            self.parent[root_b] = root_a;
        } else {
            self.parent[root_b] = root_a;
            self.rank[root_a] += 1;
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut ds = DisjointSet::new(5);
    ds.union(0, 1);
    ds.union(1, 2);
    assert_eq!(ds.find(0), ds.find(2));
    assert_ne!(ds.find(0), ds.find(3));
    ds.union(3, 4);
    ds.union(2, 3);
    assert_eq!(ds.find(0), ds.find(4));
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Implements path compression by writing self.parent[x] = self.find(self.parent[x]), not just returning the root without updating the structure — compression is what gives near-flat trees over repeated calls; without it the structure degrades to a plain linked-list-like chain in the worst case.
  • ★★★Attaches the shorter-rank tree under the taller one in union, only incrementing rank when the two ranks are equal — getting this backwards (attaching the taller tree under the shorter one) still produces a correct union-find but degrades the amortized time complexity guarantee.
  • ★★Checks root_a == root_b and returns early in union before touching rank — merging a set with itself should be a no-op, not accidentally increment rank or reassign a root to itself.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What's the actual amortized time complexity of find() with both optimizations, and why does it matter that it's 'amortized' rather than worst-case-per-call?" — With both path compression and union by rank, a sequence of m operations on n elements runs in O(m · α(n)) total, where α is the inverse Ackermann function — for any practically conceivable n, α(n) is at most 4 or 5, making this "effectively constant" per operation on average, even though any single find() call could in principle still walk a longer chain before compression fully flattens things out.
  • P2"This find() is recursive — is that a concern, and how would you rewrite it iteratively?" — For pathological input (a very deep chain before compression kicks in) recursion depth could theoretically be a stack-overflow concern, though path compression makes this self-limiting in practice after the first few calls flatten things. An iterative version: walk up parent[x] in a loop collecting visited nodes, find the root, then do a second pass setting every visited node's parent directly to the root.
  • P3"What's a real system where you'd reach for union-find specifically?" — Classic uses: detecting cycles or connected components while building a graph incrementally (e.g. Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm), network connectivity tracking, image processing (connected-component labeling), or grouping/deduplication problems where "these two things are the same" relationships arrive as a stream of pairwise union operations rather than all at once.
🎯 Senior angle
This is a classic CS-fundamentals exercise rather than a Rust-specific one — its value in a Rust interview is testing whether the candidate can translate a textbook algorithm into clean, borrow-checker-friendly code (notice the solution never needs more than one active mutable borrow of self at a time) without reaching for Rc<RefCell<_>> or unsafe out of reflexive caution.

W21 · Closures as Parameters — Generic vs dyn
closures FnMut generics vs dyn Easy
Prompt
"Write apply_n_times_generic, generic over a closure type bounded by FnMut(i32) -> i32, and apply_n_times_dyn, taking the closure as &mut dyn FnMut(i32) -> i32 instead — both apply the closure to a starting value n times and return the final result. Then write run_pipeline, which takes a Vec<Box<dyn FnMut(i32) -> i32>> of different closures and threads a value through all of them in order."
Starter code to hand to candidate
fn apply_n_times_generic<F>(start: i32, n: u32, f: F) -> i32
where
    F: FnMut(i32) -> i32,
{
    todo!()
}

fn apply_n_times_dyn(start: i32, n: u32, f: &mut dyn FnMut(i32) -> i32) -> i32 {
    todo!()
}

fn run_pipeline(start: i32, pipeline: &mut Vec<Box<dyn FnMut(i32) -> i32>>) -> i32 {
    todo!()
}


fn main() {
    assert_eq!(apply_n_times_generic(1, 5, |x| x * 2), 32);
    let mut total_calls = 0;
    let mut counting = |x: i32| {
        total_calls += 1;
        x + 1
    };
    assert_eq!(apply_n_times_dyn(0, 3, &mut counting), 3);
    assert_eq!(total_calls, 3);
    let mut pipeline: Vec<Box<dyn FnMut(i32) -> i32>> = vec![
        Box::new(|x| x + 1),
        Box::new(|x| x * 2),
    ];
    assert_eq!(run_pipeline(5, &mut pipeline), 12);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
fn apply_n_times_generic<F>(start: i32, n: u32, mut f: F) -> i32
where
    F: FnMut(i32) -> i32,
{
    let mut value = start;
    for _ in 0..n { value = f(value); }  // takes F by value but must re-declare `mut f` to call it repeatedly
    value
}

fn apply_n_times_dyn(start: i32, n: u32, f: &mut dyn FnMut(i32) -> i32) -> i32 {
    let mut value = start;
    for _ in 0..n { value = f(value); }
    value
}

fn run_pipeline(start: i32, pipeline: &mut Vec<Box<dyn FnMut(i32) -> i32>>) -> i32 {
    pipeline.iter_mut().fold(start, |acc, f| f(acc))  // fold threads the value through every boxed closure in order
}

fn main() {
    assert_eq!(apply_n_times_generic(1, 5, |x| x * 2), 32);
    let mut total_calls = 0;
    let mut counting = |x: i32| {
        total_calls += 1;
        x + 1
    };
    assert_eq!(apply_n_times_dyn(0, 3, &mut counting), 3);
    assert_eq!(total_calls, 3);
    let mut pipeline: Vec<Box<dyn FnMut(i32) -> i32>> = vec![
        Box::new(|x| x + 1),
        Box::new(|x| x * 2),
    ];
    assert_eq!(run_pipeline(5, &mut pipeline), 12);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Writes mut f: F in the generic version's parameter list (or shadows it with let mut f = f; in the body) — the bound is FnMut, and calling a FnMut more than once requires an exclusive binding, a detail easy to skip when copy-pasting a signature from a Fn example.
  • ★★★Reaches for Box<dyn FnMut> specifically to make Vec storage possible in run_pipeline, and can explain unprompted that a Vec<F> with a generic F: FnMut could never hold two different closure literals — each closure expression has its own distinct, anonymous type.
  • ★★Uses &mut dyn FnMut (a borrow) rather than Box<dyn FnMut> for the plain apply_n_times_dyn parameter — no ownership transfer or allocation is needed just to call a closure the caller already owns.
  • ★Uses .fold() for run_pipeline rather than a hand-written mutable-accumulator loop — both are equally correct, but reaching for the combinator here is a small idiomatic-fluency signal.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Could apply_n_times_generic and apply_n_times_dyn share one implementation instead of duplicating the loop body?" — Not directly with today's stable trait system (no blanket way to have one function body work identically for both a generic F and a dyn FnMut without one calling into the other), but you could have the dyn version call the generic one by exploiting that &mut dyn FnMut(i32) -> i32 itself implements FnMut(i32) -> i32 — so apply_n_times_dyn's body could just be apply_n_times_generic(start, n, f) once f is a reference implementing the trait, eliminating the duplication entirely.
  • P2"What would you need to change to run one of these closures on a separate thread?" — The closure type would need a Send bound (F: FnMut(i32) -> i32 + Send for the generic version, or Box i32 + Send> for the boxed one) and typically also 'static, since thread::spawn requires both — a closure capturing a non-Send type (like an Rc) would fail to compile at the spawn call site, not inside this function.
  • P3"Why does main's `counting` closure need `let mut total_calls` outside it, rather than incrementing some field on the closure itself?" — total_calls is captured by unique reference (&mut i32) inside the FnMut closure, so mutating it inside the closure body is mutating the captured variable in the enclosing scope directly — there's no separate "field on the closure" concept exposed to the programmer; the closure's hidden struct holds the capture, and this is exactly the mechanism that makes the closure only satisfy FnMut (mutates a capture) rather than Fn.
🎯 Senior angle
The single highest-value moment in this exercise is watching whether a candidate reaches for Box<dyn FnMut> specifically and only when heterogeneous storage in a Vec actually requires it, rather than defaulting to dyn everywhere out of unfamiliarity with the generic form — or the opposite failure mode, insisting on generics for run_pipeline and getting stuck when the compiler rejects mixing closure types in one Vec<F>.

// Write Exercise 22 · 20 min
W22 · File I/O — Word Frequency Counter
std::fs BufReader/BufWriter io::Result Easy
Prompt
"Write word_frequencies(input_path: &str, output_path: &str) -> io::Result<()> that reads a text file line by line (don't load the whole file with read_to_string), counts word frequency case-insensitively, and writes word count pairs to the output file sorted by descending frequency, using buffered I/O for both the read and the write side."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{self, BufRead, BufReader, BufWriter, Write};

fn word_frequencies(input_path: &str, output_path: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
    todo!()
}

fn main() {
    use std::io::Write;
    let dir = std::env::temp_dir().join("w22_wordfreq");
    let _ = std::fs::create_dir_all(&dir);
    let inp = dir.join("in.txt");
    let out = dir.join("out.txt");
    {
        let mut f = std::fs::File::create(&inp).unwrap();
        writeln!(f, "Hello hello world").unwrap();
    }
    word_frequencies(inp.to_str().unwrap(), out.to_str().unwrap()).unwrap();
    let text = std::fs::read_to_string(&out).unwrap();
    assert!(text.to_lowercase().contains("hello"));
    assert!(text.contains('2') || text.contains("hello 2"));
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
fn word_frequencies(input_path: &str, output_path: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
    let file = File::open(input_path)?;
    let reader = BufReader::new(file);
    let mut counts: HashMap<String, u32> = HashMap::new();

    for line in reader.lines() {
        let line = line?;  // lines() yields io::Result — propagate per-line errors, don't unwrap
        for word in line.split_whitespace() {
            *counts.entry(word.to_lowercase()).or_insert(0) += 1;
        }
    }

    let mut pairs: Vec<(String, u32)> = counts.into_iter().collect();
    pairs.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.cmp(&a.1).then_with(|| a.0.cmp(&b.0)));  // tie-break alphabetically for determinism

    let out_file = File::create(output_path)?;
    let mut writer = BufWriter::new(out_file);
    for (word, count) in pairs {
        writeln!(writer, "{word} {count}")?;
    }
    writer.flush()?;  // explicit flush so any write failure is observable via ?, not swallowed on Drop
    Ok(())
}

fn main() {
    use std::io::Write;
    let dir = std::env::temp_dir().join("w22_wordfreq");
    let _ = std::fs::create_dir_all(&dir);
    let inp = dir.join("in.txt");
    let out = dir.join("out.txt");
    {
        let mut f = std::fs::File::create(&inp).unwrap();
        writeln!(f, "Hello hello world").unwrap();
    }
    word_frequencies(inp.to_str().unwrap(), out.to_str().unwrap()).unwrap();
    let text = std::fs::read_to_string(&out).unwrap();
    assert!(text.to_lowercase().contains("hello"));
    assert!(text.contains('2') || text.contains("hello 2"));
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Wraps both the input File and output File in BufReader/BufWriter rather than calling .read()/.write() directly — the difference between a syscall per line and one syscall per buffer-full.
  • ★★★Propagates errors from reader.lines() with line? inside the loop, rather than .unwrap() or silently skipping — each yielded item is io::Result<String>, not a bare String.
  • ★★Calls .flush() explicitly before returning Ok(()) — BufWriter does flush on Drop, but a drop-time flush failure has nowhere to propagate to and is silently discarded.
  • ★Uses the entry API (*counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1) for counting rather than a manual contains_key/insert/get_mut sequence.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"This scales fine for a huge file in terms of memory — why?" — Because the function streams line-by-line rather than loading the whole file, and the counts HashMap only grows with the number of unique words, not the file's total size — a multi-gigabyte file with a bounded vocabulary still uses a small, bounded amount of memory for the counting step itself.
  • P2"What happens if the file contains invalid UTF-8?" — reader.lines() will return an Err for that line (io::Error with an InvalidData-style kind), since String must be valid UTF-8 — the `line?` propagates it and the whole function returns early. A tolerant version could instead read raw bytes and use String::from_utf8_lossy to substitute replacement characters rather than failing outright.
  • P3"Why sort_by with a tie-breaker instead of just sort_by_key(|p| p.1)?" — HashMap iteration order is unspecified and can vary between runs; without a secondary tie-break on the word itself, two words with equal counts could appear in a different relative order each time you run the program, making output non-deterministic and harder to diff/test against an expected file.
🎯 Senior angle
Ask what changes if this needs to run as part of a request handler in an async web service — the correct answer is wrapping the blocking file I/O in tokio::task::spawn_blocking (or using tokio::fs's async equivalents), tying this exercise directly back to the "blocking the async runtime" pitfall covered in the Async/Tokio topic.

W23 · Memory-Mapped File Scanner
memmap2 unsafe performance Medium
Prompt
"Using the memmap2 crate, write mmap_line_count(path: &str) -> io::Result<usize> (count newline bytes) and mmap_contains(path: &str, pattern: &[u8]) -> io::Result<bool> (check if a byte pattern exists anywhere in the file) — neither should ever copy the file's contents into a Vec<u8> you allocate yourself."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use memmap2::Mmap;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io;

fn mmap_line_count(path: &str) -> io::Result<usize> {
    todo!()
}

fn mmap_contains(path: &str, pattern: &[u8]) -> io::Result<bool> {
    todo!()
}

fn main() {
    use std::io::Write;
    let path = std::env::temp_dir().join("w23_mmap.txt");
    {
        let mut f = std::fs::File::create(&path).unwrap();
        write!(f, "one\ntwo\nthree").unwrap();
    }
    let p = path.to_str().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(mmap_line_count(p).unwrap(), 2);
    assert!(mmap_contains(p, b"two").unwrap());
    assert!(!mmap_contains(p, b"four").unwrap());
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
fn mmap_line_count(path: &str) -> io::Result<usize> {
    let file = File::open(path)?;
    // SAFETY: we assume nothing else truncates/mutates this file while it's mapped —
    // a real service would need a stronger guarantee (e.g. exclusive open, or a read-only snapshot).
    let mmap = unsafe { Mmap::map(&file)? };
    Ok(mmap.iter().filter(|&&b| b == b'\n').count())  // Mmap derefs to &[u8] — plain iterator/slice methods just work
}

fn mmap_contains(path: &str, pattern: &[u8]) -> io::Result<bool> {
    let file = File::open(path)?;
    let mmap = unsafe { Mmap::map(&file)? };
    if pattern.is_empty() || pattern.len() > mmap.len() {  // guard first — .windows(0) panics, and len() > mmap.len() would too
        return Ok(pattern.is_empty());
    }
    Ok(mmap.windows(pattern.len()).any(|w| w == pattern))
}

fn main() {
    use std::io::Write;
    let path = std::env::temp_dir().join("w23_mmap.txt");
    {
        let mut f = std::fs::File::create(&path).unwrap();
        write!(f, "one\ntwo\nthree").unwrap();
    }
    let p = path.to_str().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(mmap_line_count(p).unwrap(), 2);
    assert!(mmap_contains(p, b"two").unwrap());
    assert!(!mmap_contains(p, b"four").unwrap());
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Writes an actual // SAFETY: comment above the unsafe block naming the real assumption being relied on (file not mutated/truncated during the mapping) — not just an empty or generic comment, but the specific invariant this particular call site depends on.
  • ★★★Guards against pattern.len() > mmap.len() and an empty pattern before calling .windows(), which panics if the window size is 0 or exceeds the slice length — an easy oversight when translating "just call windows()" straight from the topic explanation into code.
  • ★★Treats mmap as a plain &[u8] after the single unsafe mapping call — no further unsafe code needed for the actual scanning logic, correctly scoping the unsafe surface area to just the mapping itself.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Concretely, what's the worst thing that can happen if another process truncates this file while it's mapped?" — Accessing a page that's now past the file's new end can raise a SIGBUS signal, which Rust's normal panic/unwind machinery does not handle — this can crash the process outright rather than producing a recoverable error, which is exactly why the mapping call itself is unsafe even though the resulting type looks like an ordinary safe slice.
  • P2"For mmap_line_count specifically, would BufReader::lines().count() be just as fast?" — For a single sequential full-file scan like this one, quite possibly yes — the OS's own read-ahead and page cache do most of the same work either way; mmap's real advantage shows up for random access or avoiding a second in-process copy, not necessarily for a one-shot linear scan like counting newlines.
  • P3"How would you share this mapping read-only across multiple threads?" — Wrap it in an Arc — memmap2's Mmap is Send + Sync for read-only mappings, since the underlying pages are just shared memory with no interior mutability exposed through the safe API, so multiple threads can each hold a cloned Arc and read concurrently with zero additional synchronization needed.
🎯 Senior angle
The // SAFETY: comment is the single most important artifact from this exercise — a candidate who writes unsafe { Mmap::map(&file)? } with no comment at all, versus one who names the specific external-mutation invariant being relied on, are giving you very different signals about how they'd behave in a codebase full of other people's unsafe blocks.

// Write Exercise 24 · 25 min
W24 · async fn in Traits — Native vs Object-Safe
async traits object safety Pin<Box<dyn Future>> Hard
Prompt
"Define trait DataSource { async fn fetch(&self, id: u64) -> Result<String, FetchError>; } using native async-fn-in-traits syntax and implement it for InMemory and SlowRemote (which awaits tokio::time::sleep). Then define DataSourceDyn — an object-safe equivalent that can be stored as Box<dyn DataSourceDyn> — and a blanket impl bridging any DataSource into DataSourceDyn automatically."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::time::Duration;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct FetchError(String);

trait DataSource {
    async fn fetch(&self, id: u64) -> Result<String, FetchError>;
}

struct InMemory { data: HashMap<u64, String> }
struct SlowRemote;

// TODO: impl DataSource for InMemory and SlowRemote

// TODO: define an object-safe DataSourceDyn, storable as Box,
// plus a blanket `impl DataSourceDyn for T` bridging the two.

fn main() {
    let rt = tokio::runtime::Runtime::new().unwrap();
    rt.block_on(async {
        use std::collections::HashMap;
        let mem = InMemory {
            data: HashMap::from([(1, "ok".into())]),
        };
        assert_eq!(mem.fetch(1).await.unwrap(), "ok");
        let sources: Vec<Box<dyn DataSourceDyn>> = vec![Box::new(mem)];
        let v = sources[0].fetch(1).await.unwrap();
        assert_eq!(v, "ok");
    });
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
impl DataSource for InMemory {
    async fn fetch(&self, id: u64) -> Result<String, FetchError> {
        self.data.get(&id).cloned().ok_or_else(|| FetchError(format!("no entry for {id}")))
    }
}

impl DataSource for SlowRemote {
    async fn fetch(&self, id: u64) -> Result<String, FetchError> {
        tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(50)).await;  // simulated network latency
        Ok(format!("remote-value-{id}"))
    }
}

use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::Pin;

// Object-safe: every impl's future is boxed and erased to one fixed, vtable-compatible return type.
trait DataSourceDyn {
    fn fetch<'a>(&'a self, id: u64) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = Result<String, FetchError>> + Send + 'a>>;
}

// Bridge: any DataSource automatically gets a DataSourceDyn impl for free — no manual duplication per type.
impl<T: DataSource + Sync> DataSourceDyn for T {
    fn fetch<'a>(&'a self, id: u64) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = Result<String, FetchError>> + Send + 'a>> {
        Box::pin(DataSource::fetch(self, id))  // Box::pin erases the concrete, per-impl future type into one uniform pointer
    }
}

async fn fetch_all(sources: &[Box<dyn DataSourceDyn>], id: u64) {
    for s in sources {
        let _ = s.fetch(id).await;
    }
}

fn main() {
    let rt = tokio::runtime::Runtime::new().unwrap();
    rt.block_on(async {
        use std::collections::HashMap;
        let mem = InMemory {
            data: HashMap::from([(1, "ok".into())]),
        };
        assert_eq!(mem.fetch(1).await.unwrap(), "ok");
        let sources: Vec<Box<dyn DataSourceDyn>> = vec![Box::new(mem)];
        let v = sources[0].fetch(1).await.unwrap();
        assert_eq!(v, "ok");
    });
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Correctly predicts that Box<dyn DataSource> fails to compile for the native-syntax trait, and can articulate why (each impl's async fn desugars to a differently-shaped, differently-sized anonymous future type — no single vtable slot can represent all of them).
  • ★★★Writes the exact Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ...> + Send + 'a>> return type by hand — this is genuinely one of the least memorable exact signatures in the language, and correctly reproducing it (or getting close and self-correcting) is a strong signal of having actually worked with this pattern before, not just read about it.
  • ★★Writes a blanket impl<T: DataSource> DataSourceDyn for T rather than manually re-implementing DataSourceDyn separately for InMemory and SlowRemote — recognizing that the bridge logic (Box::pin(...)) is identical for every type and should be written exactly once.
  • ★Adds the + Send bound on the boxed future without being told — necessary for the future to be spawnable/movable across threads on a multi-threaded Tokio runtime.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What is this exercise doing manually that the async-trait crate would do for you with one attribute macro?" — Exactly this: #[async_trait] rewrites an async fn trait method into the same Pin + Send + '_>> shape automatically. Doing it by hand once is valuable for understanding the mechanism; in real production code, reaching for async-trait when you specifically need object safety is perfectly idiomatic and far less error-prone than hand-writing this repeatedly.
  • P2"Does boxing here cost anything at runtime, and does it matter for SlowRemote specifically?" — Yes: one heap allocation per fetch() call for the boxed future, plus dynamic dispatch through the vtable to poll it. For SlowRemote, awaiting a real ~50ms simulated network delay completely dwarfs that overhead — the cost only becomes worth worrying about for extremely hot, low-latency call paths, not for typical I/O-bound async work.
  • P3"Why + Sync on the blanket impl's bound (T: DataSource + Sync), given the trait method itself only takes &self?" — Because the resulting boxed future carries a borrow of self across .await points inside async code that Tokio may move between worker threads while polling — for that future to itself be Send (required by the trait), the data it borrows (self) generally needs to be Sync, so multiple threads could in principle observe it through that shared reference over the future's lifetime.
🎯 Senior angle
This exercise is deliberately the hardest one to write from memory in the entire packet — few engineers keep the exact Pin<Box<dyn Future>> incantation memorized, and that's fine. What actually matters for a senior signal is recognizing when this ceremony is necessary (storing trait objects) versus when plain native async fn in a trait is all you need (everywhere else) — reaching for async-trait or this manual boxing pattern reflexively on every async trait, "just in case," is itself a mild anti-signal.

W25 · Static vs Dynamic Dispatch — Shapes
monomorphisation dyn Trait vtables Easy
Prompt
"Define trait Shape { fn area(&self) -> f64; }, implement it for Circle and Rectangle. Write total_area_generic<T: Shape>(shapes: &[T]) -> f64 and total_area_dyn(shapes: &[Box<dyn Shape>]) -> f64. Then explain: why can't you put a Circle and a Rectangle in the same slice passed to total_area_generic, and what does that function actually compile down to for two different call sites?"
Starter code to hand to candidate
trait Shape { fn area(&self) -> f64; }

struct Circle { radius: f64 }
struct Rectangle { width: f64, height: f64 }

// TODO: impl Shape for Circle and Rectangle

fn total_area_generic<T: Shape>(shapes: &[T]) -> f64 { todo!() }
fn total_area_dyn(shapes: &[Box<dyn Shape>]) -> f64 { todo!() }

fn main() {
    let circles = vec![Circle { radius: 1.0 }, Circle { radius: 2.0 }];
    let generic_total = total_area_generic(&circles);
    assert!((generic_total - (std::f64::consts::PI * 5.0)).abs() < 1e-6);
    let mixed: Vec<Box<dyn Shape>> = vec![
        Box::new(Circle { radius: 1.0 }),
        Box::new(Rectangle {
            width: 2.0,
            height: 3.0,
        }),
    ];
    let dyn_total = total_area_dyn(&mixed);
    assert!((dyn_total - (std::f64::consts::PI + 6.0)).abs() < 1e-6);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
impl Shape for Circle {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 { std::f64::consts::PI * self.radius * self.radius }
}
impl Shape for Rectangle {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.width * self.height }
}

fn total_area_generic<T: Shape>(shapes: &[T]) -> f64 {
    shapes.iter().map(|s| s.area()).sum()  // monomorphised — a fresh copy of this whole function per concrete T
}

fn total_area_dyn(shapes: &[Box<dyn Shape>]) -> f64 {
    shapes.iter().map(|s| s.area()).sum()  // one compiled body — s.area() is a vtable call for every element
}


fn main() {
    let circles = vec![Circle { radius: 1.0 }, Circle { radius: 2.0 }];
    let generic_total = total_area_generic(&circles);
    assert!((generic_total - (std::f64::consts::PI * 5.0)).abs() < 1e-6);
    let mixed: Vec<Box<dyn Shape>> = vec![
        Box::new(Circle { radius: 1.0 }),
        Box::new(Rectangle {
            width: 2.0,
            height: 3.0,
        }),
    ];
    let dyn_total = total_area_dyn(&mixed);
    assert!((dyn_total - (std::f64::consts::PI + 6.0)).abs() < 1e-6);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Explains unprompted that total_area_generic::<Circle> and a hypothetical total_area_generic::<Rectangle> are two entirely separate, independently-compiled functions — monomorphisation, not one function handling both — which is precisely why a single call can only ever take one concrete T, never a mix.
  • ★★Identifies &[impl Shape] as sugar for the same generic constraint when asked if it's an alternative — correctly noting it does not solve the heterogeneity problem either, for the same underlying reason.
  • ★Notes both function bodies are textually identical — the difference between static and dynamic dispatch here lives entirely in the parameter type, not the logic, which is exactly the point of the exercise.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"How would you actually verify whether the vtable indirection in total_area_dyn matters for performance here?" — Write a criterion benchmark comparing total_area_generic on a slice of one shape type against total_area_dyn on an equivalent Vec>, at realistic collection sizes — intuition about dispatch overhead is frequently wrong in either direction, and this is cheap to actually measure rather than assume.
  • P2"Is there a way to get heterogeneous storage without one heap allocation per shape?" — Yes: an enum wrapping each concrete variant, `enum AnyShape { Circle(Circle), Rectangle(Rectangle) }`, with area() implemented via a match — stores every variant inline (stack or contiguous in a Vec, no per-element Box), trading the ability to add new shape types without modifying the enum for eliminating both the allocation and the vtable call.
  • P3"When does the generic version's binary-size cost from monomorphisation actually start to bite in a real codebase?" — When a heavily-generic function like this one is called with many distinct concrete types across a large codebase — each instantiation is a full separate copy in the final binary, which is why generics-heavy libraries sometimes intentionally keep a small non-generic core function and make the generic wrapper a thin, easily-inlined shim around it, limiting how much code gets duplicated per instantiation.
🎯 Senior angle
This is the cleanest possible minimal example of the generic-vs-dyn decision entirely stripped of closures — use it to confirm a candidate's mental model generalizes beyond "closures specifically" to the dispatch decision in general, since some candidates who handle the closure-flavored version fluently (W21) still stumble when the exact same trade-off shows up on an ordinary trait.

// Write Exercise 26 · 20 min
W26 · Threads + Arc — Parallel Chunked Sum
thread::spawn Arc Send + 'static Medium
Prompt
"Write parallel_sum(data: Arc<Vec<i64>>, num_threads: usize) -> i64 that splits data into num_threads roughly-equal contiguous chunks, sums each chunk on its own spawned OS thread, and combines the partial sums — sharing the underlying vector across threads via Arc without cloning the Vec's contents."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::thread;

fn parallel_sum(data: Arc<Vec<i64>>, num_threads: usize) -> i64 {
    todo!()
}

fn main() {
    let data = std::sync::Arc::new((0..10_000i64).collect::<Vec<_>>());
    let expected: i64 = data.iter().sum();
    assert_eq!(parallel_sum(std::sync::Arc::clone(&data), 1), expected);
    assert_eq!(parallel_sum(std::sync::Arc::clone(&data), 4), expected);
    assert_eq!(parallel_sum(std::sync::Arc::clone(&data), 8), expected);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
fn parallel_sum(data: Arc<Vec<i64>>, num_threads: usize) -> i64 {
    let len = data.len();
    let chunk_size = (len + num_threads - 1) / num_threads;  // ceiling division — last chunk may be smaller
    let mut handles = Vec::with_capacity(num_threads);

    for i in 0..num_threads {
        let data = Arc::clone(&data);  // clones the Arc handle (refcount bump) — NOT the underlying Vec's contents
        let start = i * chunk_size;
        let end = (start + chunk_size).min(len);
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {  // move: the closure owns its cloned Arc, satisfying 'static
            if start >= end { return 0; }
            data[start..end].iter().sum::<i64>()
        }));
    }

    handles.into_iter().map(|h| h.join().unwrap()).sum()  // join every handle AFTER all threads are spawned, not one at a time
}

fn main() {
    let data = std::sync::Arc::new((0..10_000i64).collect::<Vec<_>>());
    let expected: i64 = data.iter().sum();
    assert_eq!(parallel_sum(std::sync::Arc::clone(&data), 1), expected);
    assert_eq!(parallel_sum(std::sync::Arc::clone(&data), 4), expected);
    assert_eq!(parallel_sum(std::sync::Arc::clone(&data), 8), expected);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Calls Arc::clone(&data) once per thread before the move closure — cloning the Arc handle (a cheap atomic refcount increment) rather than the Vec's contents, and understanding that move is what transfers ownership of that specific clone into the spawned thread.
  • ★★★Spawns every thread first, collects all the JoinHandles into a Vec, and only then joins them in a second pass — joining immediately after each spawn would serialize all the work and defeat the entire purpose of parallelising it.
  • ★★Uses ceiling division for chunk_size and clamps the last chunk's end with .min(len) — correctly handling a length that doesn't divide evenly by num_threads without an out-of-bounds slice panic.
  • ★Guards the empty-range case (start >= end) for when num_threads exceeds len, returning 0 for that thread instead of panicking on an empty/invalid slice range.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What if you passed Rc> instead of Arc?" — It wouldn't compile: thread::spawn requires its closure (and everything captured by it) to be Send + 'static. Rc's reference count is a plain non-atomic integer, so Rc is explicitly not Send — the compiler rejects moving one into a spawned thread at the exact call site, which is a compile-time guarantee against exactly the kind of data race an unsynchronized shared refcount would cause.
  • P2"What does .join() actually return, and what happens if a spawned thread panics?" — JoinHandle::join() returns Result> — Err specifically if the thread panicked, carrying the panic payload. Calling .unwrap() on that Result re-panics on the joining thread if any worker panicked — production code processing untrusted or fallible per-chunk logic might instead match on the Result to handle a failed chunk gracefully rather than propagating the panic.
  • P3"When would rayon's par_iter() be a better fit than this hand-rolled version?" — Almost always, for exactly this data-parallel shape — rayon handles chunking, load-balancing via work-stealing, and thread-pool reuse (avoiding the overhead of spawning brand-new OS threads on every call) automatically. Hand-rolling with thread::spawn is worth doing once to understand the Send/'static/Arc mechanics directly, but rayon is the practical default for this exact pattern in production Rust.
🎯 Senior angle
Watch specifically for whether the candidate clones the Arc inside the loop, once per thread, versus trying to move the single original Arc into the first closure and then being stuck for the second iteration — a very common live-coding stumble that reveals whether "clone an Arc per thread" is genuine muscle memory or something they've only ever seen written by someone else.

// Write Exercise 27 · 20 min
W27 · Generic Over Read/Write — Not File-Specific
Read / Write bounds short reads write_all Medium
Prompt
"Write copy_uppercase_ascii<R: Read, W: Write>(reader: &mut R, writer: &mut W) -> io::Result<u64> that reads bytes from any Read source, uppercases ASCII letters, writes the result to any Write sink, and returns the total byte count — then call it once against real Files and once against a &[u8] / Vec<u8> pair, with no changes to the function itself."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::io::{self, Read, Write};

fn copy_uppercase_ascii<R: Read, W: Write>(reader: &mut R, writer: &mut W) -> io::Result<u64> {
    todo!()
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    // Works unchanged against real files...
    let mut input = File::open("in.txt")?;
    let mut output = File::create("out.txt")?;
    copy_uppercase_ascii(&mut input, &mut output)?;

    // ...and against plain in-memory buffers, with zero code changes — the whole point of the bound.
    let mut mem_in: &[u8] = b"hello world";
    let mut mem_out: Vec<u8> = Vec::new();
    copy_uppercase_ascii(&mut mem_in, &mut mem_out)?;
    assert_eq!(mem_out, b"HELLO WORLD");
    Ok(())
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
fn copy_uppercase_ascii<R: Read, W: Write>(reader: &mut R, writer: &mut W) -> io::Result<u64> {
    let mut buf = [0u8; 8192];
    let mut total = 0u64;
    loop {
        let n = reader.read(&mut buf)?;  // Ok(0) is the ONE true EOF signal — Ok(n) with n < buf.len() is not an error
        if n == 0 {
            break;
        }
        for byte in &mut buf[..n] {
            byte.make_ascii_uppercase();
        }
        writer.write_all(&buf[..n])?;  // write_all loops internally until every byte is accepted — write() alone may do a short write
        total += n as u64;
    }
    Ok(total)
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    // Works unchanged against real files...
    let mut input = File::open("in.txt")?;
    let mut output = File::create("out.txt")?;
    copy_uppercase_ascii(&mut input, &mut output)?;

    // ...and against plain in-memory buffers, with zero code changes — the whole point of the bound.
    let mut mem_in: &[u8] = b"hello world";
    let mut mem_out: Vec<u8> = Vec::new();
    copy_uppercase_ascii(&mut mem_in, &mut mem_out)?;
    assert_eq!(mem_out, b"HELLO WORLD");
    Ok(())
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Reads into a fixed-size stack buffer in a loop and treats Ok(0) as the sole EOF condition — not Ok(n) where n < buf.len(), which is a perfectly legal "short read" and not an error or an end-of-stream signal by itself.
  • ★★★Writes with write_all, not a bare write call — understanding that write() is permitted to accept fewer bytes than handed to it in a single call, and only write_all guarantees the entire slice was actually written (or an error was returned) before moving on.
  • ★★Exercises the function against &[u8] and Vec<u8> directly, with no wrapping in a File-like adapter — recognizing both already implement Read/Write natively, not just realizing it after being told.
  • ★Takes reader/writer as generic type parameters bounded by the trait (R: Read, not a concrete File or Box<dyn Read>) — the signature itself is the point of the exercise, not just the loop body.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Why not just use io::copy?" — io::copy(reader, writer) already does almost exactly this loop (chunked reads, Ok(0)-is-EOF, internally uses write_all-equivalent logic) — but it copies bytes unchanged and gives you no hook to transform them in flight. io::copy is the right call whenever you're not touching the bytes; this hand-rolled loop is what you fall back to the moment you need to touch every byte, exactly as here.
  • P2"What if the reader is a network socket that only ever delivers a few bytes at a time?" — Already handled correctly: read() is explicitly permitted to return fewer bytes than requested for reasons with nothing to do with EOF (only some bytes have arrived over the wire so far, for instance) — the loop keeps calling read() until it sees Ok(0), the only reliable EOF signal, so this function needs zero changes to work correctly against a slow, partial-delivery source.
  • P3"Could you have bounded this by BufRead and used .lines() instead?" — Only if you already know the data is UTF-8 text delimited by newlines — .lines()/BufRead is a text-oriented abstraction layered on top of Read. This exercise is deliberately byte-oriented (it has to work on arbitrary binary data), so bounding by the more general Read/Write traits rather than the narrower BufRead is the correct, more widely-applicable choice here.
🎯 Senior angle
Because the function is generic over the trait rather than tied to File, file- or socket-processing logic like this can be unit-tested with zero real I/O — no tempfile, no actual socket, just a &[u8] in and a Vec<u8> out. A candidate who writes the function this way from the start, unprompted, is telling you something concrete about how they'd approach testing I/O-adjacent code in a real codebase.

W28 · Raw TCP Echo Server — Event Loop Over .lines()
TcpListener / TcpStream try_clone thread-per-connection Medium
Prompt
"Using only std::net (no async runtime, no framework), write a line-oriented TCP echo server: run_echo_server(addr: &str) -> io::Result<()> accepts connections in a loop and handles each one on its own thread; handle_client(stream: TcpStream) -> io::Result<()> reads lines from the client with .lines() and echoes each one straight back until the client disconnects."
Starter code to hand to candidate

use std::net::{TcpListener, TcpStream};
use std::thread;

fn run_echo_server(addr: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
    todo!()
}

fn handle_client(stream: TcpStream) -> io::Result<()> {
    todo!()

#[cfg(test)]

    use super::*;
    use std::io::{BufRead, BufReader, Write};
    use std::net::TcpStream;
    use std::thread;
    use std::time::Duration;

    fn echoes_a_line() {
        let listener = std::net::TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0").unwrap();
        let addr = listener.local_addr().unwrap();
        thread::spawn(move || {
            let (stream, _) = listener.accept().unwrap();
            let _ = handle_client(stream);
        });
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(20));
        let mut client = TcpStream::connect(addr).unwrap();
        writeln!(client, "hello").unwrap();
        let mut reader = BufReader::new(client.try_clone().unwrap());
        let mut line = String::new();

Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
fn run_echo_server(addr: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
    let listener = TcpListener::bind(addr)?;
    for incoming in listener.incoming() {  // blocks here until a new connection arrives — this IS the accept loop
        let stream = incoming?;
        thread::spawn(move || {  // one OS thread per connection — a slow/idle client never blocks anyone else
            if let Err(e) = handle_client(stream) {
                eprintln!("client error: {e}");  // log and move on — one bad client must not take down the server
            }
        });
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn handle_client(mut stream: TcpStream) -> io::Result<()> {
    let reader_half = stream.try_clone()?;  // BufReader::new() needs to OWN a reader, but `stream` is still needed below to write
    let reader = BufReader::new(reader_half);

    for line in reader.lines() {  // the event loop: blocks per iteration until a full line arrives, or the peer disconnects
        let line = line?;  // the iterator ending (None) — not an Err here — is what "client disconnected" looks like
        writeln!(stream, "{line}")?;  // echo straight back over the ORIGINAL handle, not the cloned reader half
    }
    Ok(())
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    use std::io::{BufRead, BufReader, Write};
    use std::net::TcpStream;
    use std::thread;
    use std::time::Duration;

    #[test]
    fn echoes_a_line() {
        let listener = std::net::TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0").unwrap();
        let addr = listener.local_addr().unwrap();
        thread::spawn(move || {
            let (stream, _) = listener.accept().unwrap();
            let _ = handle_client(stream);
        });
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(20));
        let mut client = TcpStream::connect(addr).unwrap();
        writeln!(client, "hello").unwrap();
        let mut reader = BufReader::new(client.try_clone().unwrap());
        let mut line = String::new();
        reader.read_line(&mut line).unwrap();
        assert_eq!(line.trim(), "hello");
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("run `cargo test` for W28 echo checks");
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Reaches for stream.try_clone() unprompted the moment they need to both read and write the same connection — recognizing that BufReader::new(stream) would take ownership of stream entirely, leaving nothing behind to write the echoed line back with, and that try_clone() (both clones referring to the same underlying OS socket) is the fix, not fighting the borrow checker.
  • ★★★Spawns a new OS thread per accepted connection inside the accept loop, so one slow or idle client can't stall every other client — the thread-per-connection model, correctly identified as the reason this design scales to hundreds but not tens of thousands of concurrent clients if asked.
  • ★★Treats the for line in reader.lines() loop ending naturally as "client disconnected" — no explicit break-on-empty-string logic anywhere, because a .lines() iterator yielding None is precisely what happens once the underlying read_line sees Ok(0).
  • ★Logs and continues (if let Err(e) = handle_client(...)) rather than .unwrap()ing inside the spawned closure — an unwrap on one client's I/O error would only panic that one thread, but a candidate reaching for structured error handling here is the more senior habit regardless.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Why try_clone() instead of some kind of split()?" — Plain blocking std::net::TcpStream has no built-in split() (that's a tokio::io concept for async sockets) — try_clone() duplicates the underlying file descriptor/socket handle itself, so both clones refer to the exact same OS-level connection; reads on one and writes on the other both operate on that one real socket. It's the standard way to get an independent read-half and write-half of one blocking connection.
  • P2"What breaks first under load with thousands of simultaneous idle clients?" — Thread count: each spawned OS thread carries its own stack (megabytes by default) and the OS scheduler has real context-switch overhead once thread counts climb into the thousands — this model degrades well before an equivalent async design (one lightweight Tokio task per connection, all multiplexed onto a small thread pool) would, which is exactly the problem async I/O exists to solve.
  • P3"What if a client sends one enormous line with no newline, ever?" — reader.lines() keeps buffering into that single line indefinitely — BufReader's internal buffer just keeps refilling and read_line keeps appending until it finds a \n or hits real EOF, with no built-in cap. That makes this naive server vulnerable to a memory-exhaustion DoS from a single misbehaving connection; a hardened version would wrap the reader in a `.take(MAX_LINE_BYTES)` (or otherwise bound a single line's length) before erroring out.
🎯 Senior angle
The try_clone()-for-read/write-split step is one of the clearest "know the theory vs. have actually typed this" tells in the whole packet — ask a candidate to write this echo server cold and watch whether they reach for try_clone() unprompted the instant they need both halves, or get visibly stuck fighting stream's ownership instead.
