W29 · Implement the Read Trait Yourself
impl Read read() contract short reads vs EOF Medium
Prompt
"Implement Read for struct RepeatN { byte: u8, remaining: usize }, a source that yields byte exactly remaining times and then signals end-of-stream — so it can be dropped into anything generic over Read, including BufReader and read_to_string, with no special-casing."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::io::{self, Read};

struct RepeatN { byte: u8, remaining: usize }

impl Read for RepeatN {
    fn read(&mut self, buf: &mut [u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
        todo!()
    }
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let source = RepeatN { byte: b'x', remaining: 5 };
    let mut out = String::new();
    io::BufReader::new(source).read_to_string(&mut out)?;  // BufReader/read_to_string work on RepeatN exactly as on a File — it's just Read
    assert_eq!(out, "xxxxx");
    Ok(())
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
impl Read for RepeatN {
    fn read(&mut self, buf: &mut [u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
        let n = buf.len().min(self.remaining);  // never write more than either side can actually hold
        for slot in &mut buf[..n] {
            *slot = self.byte;
        }
        self.remaining -= n;
        Ok(n)  // n == 0 (remaining exhausted) IS the EOF signal — nothing else needs to happen
    }
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let source = RepeatN { byte: b'x', remaining: 5 };
    let mut out = String::new();
    io::BufReader::new(source).read_to_string(&mut out)?;  // BufReader/read_to_string work on RepeatN exactly as on a File — it's just Read
    assert_eq!(out, "xxxxx");
    Ok(())
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Clamps n to buf.len().min(self.remaining) — never writes past the caller's buffer, and never claims more bytes were produced than actually exist left to give.
  • ★★★Returns Ok(0) only once remaining hits zero, and can state unprompted that this is the one and only meaning of Ok(0) from read() — "no more data, ever" — not "temporarily nothing available right now" (that second case, for something like a non-blocking socket, is signalled with a distinct WouldBlock error kind instead).
  • ★★Writes a plain slice loop/index over &mut buf[..n] rather than reaching for unsafe or an unnecessary manual byte-by-byte iterator dance — the safe, idiomatic shape for filling a buffer.
  • ★Notices unprompted that implementing this one required method unlocks a whole family of default-provided behavior — read_to_string, read_to_end, bytes(), and wrapping in BufReader all become available for free, the same "implement one method, get many" theme as the custom Iterator exercise elsewhere in this packet.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Could read_to_string ever fail on this specific type, and why would that be, generally?" — Only if the bytes produced aren't valid UTF-8: read_to_string reads into a byte buffer internally, then validates the whole thing as UTF-8 in one pass, erroring if that validation fails. For RepeatN specifically it can't happen (byte is one fixed value chosen by the caller), but it's a real and common failure mode for less trivial Read implementors.
  • P2"When would you implement Read yourself instead of just handing callers a Cursor>?" — A Cursor> (or &[u8]) is right whenever the data already fully exists in memory up front. Implementing Read directly is for when the data is generated or fetched lazily/on demand — exactly like RepeatN here, or a network response streamed in, or a compressed stream decoded chunk by chunk as the caller asks for more.
  • P3"How would you make RepeatN return bytes in small chunks even when buf is huge, to simulate a flaky real source in a test?" — Cap n with an extra artificial limit, e.g. `let n = buf.len().min(self.remaining).min(64);`, so read() never hands back more than 64 bytes per call no matter how large buf is — a genuinely useful technique for writing a test double that exercises whether a caller correctly handles "read() may do a short read," since a caller that (incorrectly) assumes one call always fills the whole buffer will visibly fail against a double like this.
🎯 Senior angle
Most engineers spend years exclusively consuming Read/Write and never once implement either — being on the implementor side, even for a toy type this small, is what makes the read() contract (short reads are legal and normal, Ok(0) is the one true EOF signal) fully click as a lived rule rather than a memorized one.

// Write Exercise 30 · 20 min
W30 · Stdin/Stdout Event Loop — Testable REPL
BufRead::lines() generic over Read/Write flush semantics Easy
Prompt
"Write run_repl<R: BufRead, W: Write>(input: R, output: W) -> io::Result<()> that prints a > prompt, reads one command per line, supports echo <text> and quit/exit, and exits cleanly on real EOF. Wire it to real stdin/stdout in main, then write a unit test that drives it with an in-memory buffer — no terminal involved."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};

fn run_repl<R: BufRead, W: Write>(input: R, mut output: W) -> io::Result<()> {
    todo!()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn echoes_and_quits_without_a_real_terminal() {
        let input: &[u8] = b"echo hello\nquit\n";  // &[u8] implements BufRead — no real stdin needed at all
        let mut output = Vec::new();
        run_repl(input, &mut output).unwrap();
        let text = String::from_utf8(output).unwrap();
        assert!(text.contains("hello"));
    }
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
fn run_repl<R: BufRead, W: Write>(input: R, mut output: W) -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut lines = input.lines();  // BufRead::lines() -> impl Iterator> — the event loop drives this
    loop {
        write!(output, "> ")?;
        output.flush()?;  // stdout is fully-buffered (not line-buffered) once it's piped/redirected — unflushed, this prompt may never appear

        let line = match lines.next() {
            Some(line) => line?,
            None => break,  // iterator exhausted == true EOF (Ctrl+D, or piped input ran out) — the loop's only clean exit
        };

        let cmd = line.trim();
        match cmd {
            "quit" | "exit" => break,
            "" => continue,
            _ if cmd.starts_with("echo ") => writeln!(output, "{}", &cmd[5..])?,
            other => writeln!(output, "unknown command: {other}")?,
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let stdin = io::stdin();
    run_repl(stdin.lock(), io::stdout())
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn echoes_and_quits_without_a_real_terminal() {
        let input: &[u8] = b"echo hello\nquit\n";  // &[u8] implements BufRead — no real stdin needed at all
        let mut output = Vec::new();
        run_repl(input, &mut output).unwrap();
        let text = String::from_utf8(output).unwrap();
        assert!(text.contains("hello"));
    }
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Explicitly .flush()es right after writing the prompt, before blocking on the next read — knowing stdout's buffering mode changes depending on context (line-buffered when attached to a real terminal, fully block-buffered once piped/redirected), so an unflushed prompt can simply sit in the buffer and never actually appear in non-interactive runs.
  • ★★★Treats lines.next() returning None as the one true "input is done" exit — the same shape as the TCP server's .lines() loop ending naturally elsewhere in this packet — and does not confuse it with an empty-string line (""), which is legitimate blank input, not EOF.
  • ★★Writes the function generic over R: BufRead, W: Write instead of hardcoding io::Stdin/io::Stdout directly inside the core loop — specifically so it can be driven by a &[u8]/Vec<u8> pair in a test with no real terminal involved.
  • ★Locks stdin exactly once in main (let stdin = io::stdin(); stdin.lock()) and passes the locked guard into the loop, rather than calling io::stdin() repeatedly inside the loop body for no reason.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Why does main() bind `let stdin = io::stdin();` on its own line instead of writing `io::stdin().lock()` inline?" — .lock() borrows from the Stdin handle it's called on. `io::stdin().lock()` written as one expression would try to borrow from a temporary value that gets dropped at the end of that statement — the compiler rejects this ("temporary value dropped while borrowed"). Binding stdin to a named variable first gives the lock something with a long enough lifetime to actually reference.
  • P2"How exactly does the test avoid touching a real terminal?" — By passing a `&[u8]` as the `R: BufRead` argument (a byte slice implements BufRead directly, no wrapping needed) and a `Vec` as the `W: Write` argument, then asserting on the bytes the function wrote into that Vec — this dependency-injection-via-trait-bound pattern is exactly why testable CLI tools are written generic over BufRead/Write rather than calling io::stdin()/io::stdout() directly inside their core logic.
  • P3"What if a command handler itself needs to fail with something other than an I/O error, like a parse error?" — The current signature can only propagate io::Error via ?. A more realistic REPL would define its own error enum with `From` (or lean on anyhow) so a malformed-command failure and an actual write failure can both flow through the same ?-based path without conflating "the terminal write failed" with "the user typed something invalid."
🎯 Senior angle
This exact shape — generic over BufRead/Write, fully testable without a real terminal — is the difference between a CLI tool you can only "test" by running it by hand and one you can unit-test in CI in milliseconds. Ask whether a candidate reaches for io::stdin()/ io::stdout() directly inside their core logic function (a real anti-pattern for testability) versus threading generic reader/writer parameters through — the same dependency-injection instinct as axum's extractor pattern elsewhere in this packet, just applied to a plain CLI loop instead of an HTTP handler.

W31 · Trie-Based Autocomplete System
Trie / prefix tree HashMap-backed nodes bounded DFS Medium
Prompt
"Implement a Trie (prefix tree) with insert(&mut self, word: &str) and autocomplete(&self, prefix: &str, limit: usize) -> Vec<String>, returning up to limit stored words that start with prefix — the classic engine behind a search box or command-palette autocomplete feature."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Default)]
struct TrieNode {
    children: HashMap<char, TrieNode>,
    is_end: bool,
}

#[derive(Default)]
struct Trie { root: TrieNode }

impl Trie {
    fn insert(&mut self, word: &str) {
        todo!()
    }

    fn autocomplete(&self, prefix: &str, limit: usize) -> Vec<String> {
        todo!()
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut trie = Trie::default();
    for word in ["cat", "car", "card", "care", "dog"] {
        trie.insert(word);
    }
    assert_eq!(trie.autocomplete("ca", 10), vec!["car", "card", "care", "cat"]);
    assert_eq!(trie.autocomplete("xy", 10), Vec::<String>::new());
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
impl Trie {
    fn insert(&mut self, word: &str) {
        let mut node = &mut self.root;
        for c in word.chars() {
            node = node.children.entry(c).or_default();  // or_default() works because TrieNode derives Default
        }
        node.is_end = true;
    }

    fn autocomplete(&self, prefix: &str, limit: usize) -> Vec<String> {
        let mut node = &self.root;  // walk down to the node for `prefix` — O(prefix.len()), independent of how many words are stored
        for c in prefix.chars() {
            match node.children.get(&c) {
                Some(next) => node = next,
                None => return Vec::new(),  // prefix isn't in the trie at all — nothing to suggest
            }
        }

        let mut results = Vec::new();
        let mut buf = prefix.to_string();
        Self::collect(node, &mut buf, &mut results, limit);
        results
    }

    fn collect(node: &TrieNode, buf: &mut String, out: &mut Vec<String>, limit: usize) {
        if out.len() >= limit {
            return;  // abandon this whole subtree once we already have enough — bounded, not exhaustive
        }
        if node.is_end {
            out.push(buf.clone());
        }

        let mut chars: Vec<&char> = node.children.keys().collect();
        chars.sort();  // HashMap iteration order is unspecified — sort for deterministic, repeatable output

        for &c in &chars {
            if out.len() >= limit {
                return;
            }
            buf.push(*c);
            Self::collect(&node.children[c], buf, out, limit);
            buf.pop();  // backtrack: undo the char we just tried before exploring the next sibling
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut trie = Trie::default();
    for word in ["cat", "car", "card", "care", "dog"] {
        trie.insert(word);
    }
    assert_eq!(trie.autocomplete("ca", 10), vec!["car", "card", "care", "cat"]);
    assert_eq!(trie.autocomplete("xy", 10), Vec::<String>::new());
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Uses HashMap<char, TrieNode> for children directly, with no Box — recognizing that HashMap's own storage is already heap-indirect, so there's no infinite-size-at-compile-time problem the way a directly self-referential enum (enum List { Cons(T, List) }) would have.
  • ★★★Builds output with one shared, mutable String buffer (buf.push/buf.pop) during the DFS, rather than concatenating/cloning a new String at every level of recursion — the classic "backtracking with a shared buffer" technique.
  • ★★Sorts the children's keys before recursing, unprompted — recognizing HashMap iteration order is unspecified, so without sorting, autocomplete could return words in a different order across different runs of the very same program.
  • ★Checks out.len() >= limit at the top of collect, not only right before pushing — abandoning the whole remaining subtree once enough results exist, rather than walking everything and truncating the final list.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What's the time complexity of insert and the prefix-walk step of autocomplete, and why doesn't it depend on how many words are stored?" — Both are O(length of the word/prefix) — each character does exactly one HashMap lookup/insert descending one level, completely independent of the total number of words in the trie. Compare that to a naive Vec<String> scanned with word.starts_with(prefix), which is O(number of stored words × prefix length) — turning "search" from something that scales with dataset size into something that only scales with query length is the entire value proposition of a trie.
  • P2"How would you rank results by popularity instead of alphabetically?" — Store a score (e.g. a search-count u32) on each is_end node instead of a plain bool, then instead of the current alphabetical DFS, collect a candidate set and select the top-scoring k from it — this is exactly where a BinaryHeap-based top-k selection becomes the natural next step once "alphabetical" isn't a good enough ranking anymore.
  • P3"Is this in-memory structure actually a good fit for a production autocomplete feature?" — For a bounded, largely static dictionary that comfortably fits in memory on one process (CLI command names, a product catalog, a fixed list of city names), yes — this is genuinely close to what many editors and shells do today. For a large, constantly-updated, or multi-instance search product you'd typically reach for a dedicated search index instead — but understanding this exact mechanism is precisely what a live "build me a trie" round is testing.
🎯 Senior angle
Ask what changes if insert needs to be callable safely from multiple threads while autocomplete reads are happening concurrently — the honest, pragmatic answer is wrapping the whole Trie in a RwLock (cheap, obviously correct, and the right default), not a bespoke lock-free trie. Watch for whether a candidate reaches for the simple correct answer first, versus reflexively over-engineering a concurrency-control scheme nobody asked for.

W32 · BinaryHeap — Top-K Frequent Elements
BinaryHeap std::cmp::Reverse top-K pattern Medium
Prompt
"Write top_k_frequent(nums: &[i32], k: usize) -> Vec<i32>, returning the k most frequent values in nums. Use a BinaryHeap bounded to size k throughout — don't sort every distinct value just to keep the top few."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::collections::HashMap;

fn top_k_frequent(nums: &[i32], k: usize) -> Vec<i32> {
    todo!()
}

fn main() {
    let nums = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3];
    let mut result = top_k_frequent(&nums, 2);
    result.sort();
    assert_eq!(result, vec![1, 2]);  // 1 appears 3x, 2 appears 2x, 3 appears 1x — top 2 are 1 and 2
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::cmp::Reverse;
use std::collections::BinaryHeap;

fn top_k_frequent(nums: &[i32], k: usize) -> Vec<i32> {
    let mut counts: HashMap<i32, usize> = HashMap::new();
    for &n in nums {
        *counts.entry(n).or_insert(0) += 1;
    }

    let mut heap: BinaryHeap<Reverse<(usize, i32)>> = BinaryHeap::new();  // Reverse flips BinaryHeap's default max-heap into a min-heap
    for (val, count) in counts {
        heap.push(Reverse((count, val)));
        if heap.len() > k {
            heap.pop();  // evicts the CURRENT smallest-frequency entry, keeping the heap bounded at size k the whole time
        }
    }

    heap.into_iter().map(|Reverse((_, val))| val).collect()  // destructure straight back out of Reverse((count, val))
}

fn main() {
    let nums = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3];
    let mut result = top_k_frequent(&nums, 2);
    result.sort();
    assert_eq!(result, vec![1, 2]);  // 1 appears 3x, 2 appears 2x, 3 appears 1x — top 2 are 1 and 2
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Knows unprompted that std::collections::BinaryHeap is a max-heap — .pop() returns the greatest element first — and reaches for std::cmp::Reverse to flip the ordering into a min-heap, exactly the trick this problem needs.
  • ★★★Bounds the heap to size k throughout the loop (popping the instant heap.len() > k), rather than pushing every distinct value and trimming at the end — recognizing this is precisely what makes the approach O(n log k) instead of O(n log n).
  • ★★Pushes a (count, val) tuple, not a bare count — needs val alongside the count to know which original number each heap entry belongs to when extracting the final result, and gets a free, deterministic tie-break on val via tuple Ord's lexicographic comparison.
  • ★Uses the entry API (*counts.entry(n).or_insert(0) += 1) to build the frequency map, consistent with the same counting idiom used elsewhere in this packet (word-frequency file exercise, etc.).
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Why (usize, i32) instead of pushing just the count?" — Need val alongside the count to know which original number each heap entry refers to once results are extracted — pushing bare counts would tell you the top-k frequencies exist but not which numbers had them. Tuple Ord compares the first field first (count), only falling back to the second (val) on an exact tie, which also happens to make the result fully deterministic rather than depending on HashMap iteration order.
  • P2"When would a plain sort_by_key beat this heap approach?" — When k is close to n — the heap approach's advantage (O(n log k) vs. a full sort's O(n log n)) shrinks toward nothing as k approaches n, and the extra bookkeeping (wrapping/unwrapping Reverse, conditional pops) can lose to a straightforward sort_by_key + truncate for a k that isn't meaningfully smaller than the input. Worth actually benchmarking with criterion rather than assuming — especially since real-world k is often a small fixed constant like "top 10," which is exactly the regime where the heap wins clearly.
  • P3"Could you implement BinaryHeap's push/pop yourself on a plain Vec? What are the two operations that maintain the heap invariant?" — sift_up (after appending a new element at the end, repeatedly swap it with its parent while it's out of order, bubbling toward the root) and sift_down (after removing the root by swapping it with the last element and popping, repeatedly swap that relocated element with its larger/smaller child, bubbling toward a leaf) — both run in O(log n). Being able to sketch these two operations is the standard senior follow-up to "have you used BinaryHeap," probing whether the abstraction is genuinely understood or just called.
🎯 Senior angle
"Max-heap by default, wrap in Reverse for a min-heap" is one of those small standard-library facts that's trivial once known but genuinely stumps people mid-interview if they haven't reached for it recently — watch for whether a candidate reaches for Reverse the instant they realize they need a min-heap, versus getting visibly confused about why .pop() keeps handing back the largest element.

// Write Exercise 33 · 20 min
W33 · Quicksort From Scratch — In Place
in-place partitioning split_at_mut recursion Medium
Prompt
"Implement quicksort in place on &mut [i32] — no allocating a second Vec — using Lomuto partitioning. Then explain the worst-case complexity of this exact implementation and one concrete way to avoid triggering it in practice."
Starter code to hand to candidate
fn quicksort(slice: &mut [i32]) {
    todo!()
}

fn main() {
    let mut data = vec![5, 3, 8, 1, 9, 2];
    quicksort(&mut data);
    assert_eq!(data, vec![1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9]);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
fn quicksort(slice: &mut [i32]) {
    if slice.len() <= 1 {
        return;  // 0 or 1 elements: nothing to compare, recursion must terminate here
    }
    let pivot_index = partition(slice);
    let (left, right) = slice.split_at_mut(pivot_index);  // two genuinely disjoint &mut sub-slices — the idiomatic way to recurse on both halves
    quicksort(left);
    quicksort(&mut right[1..]);  // right[0] is the pivot itself, already in its final sorted position — skip it
}

fn partition(slice: &mut [i32]) -> usize {
    let pivot = slice[slice.len() - 1];
    let mut store_index = 0;
    for i in 0..slice.len() - 1 {
        if slice[i] < pivot {
            slice.swap(i, store_index);
            store_index += 1;
        }
    }
    slice.swap(store_index, slice.len() - 1);
    store_index
}

fn main() {
    let mut data = vec![5, 3, 8, 1, 9, 2];
    quicksort(&mut data);
    assert_eq!(data, vec![1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9]);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Uses slice.split_at_mut(pivot_index) to get two disjoint &mut sub-slices for the two recursive calls, rather than fighting the borrow checker trying to produce two simultaneous mutable borrows of the same slice by hand.
  • ★★★Sorts genuinely in place — swaps elements within the given slice via .swap(), never allocates a second Vec to build a sorted copy into.
  • ★★Handles the base case (len() <= 1) before attempting to partition — a slice of 0 or 1 elements has no valid comparison to make, and this is where the recursion has to bottom out.
  • ★Recurses on &mut right[1..], correctly skipping the pivot's own now-final position rather than re-including it in either recursive call.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What's the average-case and worst-case complexity here, and when does the worst case actually happen?" — Average case is O(n log n); worst case is O(n²), triggered by consistently bad pivot choices. This exact implementation always picks the last element as pivot, so an already-sorted or reverse-sorted input hits the worst case every single time — each partition step shrinks the problem by only one element instead of roughly halving it.
  • P2"What's one concrete way to avoid that worst case in practice?" — Randomize the pivot choice (swap a randomly-selected element into the pivot position before partitioning) or use a median-of-three heuristic (pick the median of the first, middle, and last elements) — either defeats an input specifically crafted (or unluckily shaped) to target a fixed pivot-selection rule, at a small constant-time cost per partition step.
  • P3"In real Rust code, would you ever actually hand-write this instead of calling .sort() or .sort_unstable()?" — Essentially never for general-purpose sorting. Std's sort_unstable (a pattern-defeating quicksort hybrid) and sort (a stable, adaptive merge sort) are both extensively tuned and handle edge cases — nearly-sorted data, many duplicate keys, adversarial inputs — far better than a textbook quicksort. This exercise exists purely to build genuine intuition for in-place partitioning and recursive slicing; production code should reach for the standard library's sort every time.
🎯 Senior angle
Ask which of .sort() vs. .sort_unstable() a candidate would reach for by default, and why — .sort() is stable (equal elements keep their relative order, useful when sorting by one key after already having grouped/sorted by another) at a modest extra-allocation cost; .sort_unstable() gives up that guarantee but is typically faster and allocates nothing extra. Most real code should default to .sort_unstable() unless stability specifically matters — recognizing that trade-off unprompted is a stronger signal than fluently reciting the quicksort algorithm itself.

// Write Exercise 34 · 25 min
W34 · N-Worker Task Pool That Returns Results
type erasure Box<dyn FnOnce> per-job result channel Hard
Prompt
"Extend the classic N-worker thread pool (fixed-size, workers pulling jobs from a shared queue) so submitting a job gives the caller its result back, instead of firing and forgetting: fn execute<T: Send + 'static, F: FnOnce() -> T + Send + 'static>(&self, job: F) -> mpsc::Receiver<T>. The caller calls .recv() on the returned receiver whenever it's ready to wait for that specific job's result."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::sync::mpsc;
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;

type Job = Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send + 'static>;

struct Worker { handle: Option<thread::JoinHandle<()>> }

struct ThreadPool {
    workers: Vec<Worker>,
    sender: Option<mpsc::Sender<Job>>,
}

impl ThreadPool {
    fn new(size: usize) -> Self { todo!() }

    // The interesting part: execute() is generic per-call, even though ThreadPool itself is not.
    fn execute<T, F>(&self, job: F) -> mpsc::Receiver<T>
    where
        T: Send + 'static,
        F: FnOnce() -> T + Send + 'static,
    {
        todo!()
    }
}

fn main() {
    let pool = ThreadPool::new(4);
    let rx = pool.execute(|| {
        2 + 2
    });
    assert_eq!(rx.recv().unwrap(), 4);

    let rx2 = pool.execute(|| format!("done"));
    assert_eq!(rx2.recv().unwrap(), "done");  // a completely different T on the very next call — same pool instance
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
impl ThreadPool {
    fn new(size: usize) -> Self {
        let (sender, receiver) = mpsc::channel::<Job>();
        let receiver = Arc::new(Mutex::new(receiver));  // mpsc::Receiver isn't Sync — share it across workers via Mutex

        let workers = (0..size)
            .map(|_| {
                let receiver = Arc::clone(&receiver);
                let handle = thread::spawn(move || loop {
                    let job = { receiver.lock().unwrap().recv() };  // lock released before running job — don't serialise workers
                    match job {
                        Ok(job) => job(),
                        Err(_) => break,  // all Senders dropped — pool is shutting down
                    }
                });
                Worker { handle: Some(handle) }
            })
            .collect();

        Self { workers, sender: Some(sender) }
    }

    fn execute<T, F>(&self, job: F) -> mpsc::Receiver<T>
    where
        T: Send + 'static,
        F: FnOnce() -> T + Send + 'static,
    {
        let (result_tx, result_rx) = mpsc::channel();  // a FRESH channel per call — one job, one dedicated result path
        let wrapped: Job = Box::new(move || {  // erase T/F down to the one shape the shared queue understands: FnOnce()
            let result = job();
            let _ = result_tx.send(result);  // caller may have dropped result_rx already — a failed send here is not an error
        });
        self.sender.as_ref().unwrap().send(wrapped).unwrap();
        result_rx
    }
}

fn main() {
    let pool = ThreadPool::new(4);
    let rx = pool.execute(|| {
        2 + 2
    });
    assert_eq!(rx.recv().unwrap(), 4);

    let rx2 = pool.execute(|| format!("done"));
    assert_eq!(rx2.recv().unwrap(), "done");  // a completely different T on the very next call — same pool instance
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Recognizes execute must be generic, but the pool's internal shared job queue cannot be — type-erases each submitted job into one uniform Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send + 'static> that closes over both running the job and sending its specifically-typed result down a fresh channel, so genericness lives entirely at the execute boundary, never inside the shared queue itself.
  • ★★★Creates a brand-new mpsc::channel() per call to execute — one dedicated result channel per submitted job — rather than one shared result channel for the whole pool, which would make it impossible for a caller to tell which result belongs to which submitted job.
  • ★★Lets result_tx.send(result)'s Err case pass silently inside the wrapped closure — a caller that drops the returned Receiver before the job finishes makes that send fail harmlessly, and that must never panic or crash the worker thread running it.
  • ★Puts the T/F generic bounds on execute itself, not on ThreadPool — correctly recognizing that the pool struct holds no T or F anywhere in its own fields; only the method submitting a job needs to be generic.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Why not make ThreadPool itself generic over the result type directly?" — Because a single pool instance needs to run many different jobs with many different result types over its lifetime — that's the whole point of a general-purpose pool. A struct generic over T could only ever be specialized to jobs returning that one T. Type-erasing to Box at the boundary, and keeping the specific T confined to a private, per-call result channel, is exactly what lets one pool instance serve arbitrarily many different job/result-type combinations.
  • P2"What happens if the caller never calls .recv() on the returned Receiver?" — Nothing breaks: the job still runs on some worker thread regardless — it was already queued and picked up independently of whether anyone is listening for the result — and result_tx.send(result) simply returns an Err that's silently discarded since the matching Receiver was dropped. This is the same "fire-and-forget is still safe" property mpsc channels provide elsewhere in this packet.
  • P3"Is there a real crate or std API that already gives you exactly this pattern?" — Yes — rayon's thread pool and scoped-spawn APIs hand back join-handle-like results for exactly this shape of "run this closure somewhere, get its output back," and for async code, tokio::task::spawn_blocking returns a JoinHandle you simply .await — the async-native equivalent of this same pattern, without hand-rolling a channel-per-call.
🎯 Senior angle
This is a good gauge of whether a candidate genuinely understands why the type erasure via Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send> is necessary here, versus merely pattern-matching "I've seen a thread pool store a boxed closure before" without being able to explain that the erasure is specifically what lets one pool instance serve heterogeneous job/result-type combinations over its lifetime — ask them to justify the design in their own words, not just reproduce it from memory.

// Write Exercise 35 · 25 min
W35 · Pub/Sub Message Broadcast Queue
fan-out Vec<Sender<T>> prune-on-disconnect Medium
Prompt
"Implement a simple in-memory pub/sub message queue: MessageQueue<T: Clone> with subscribe(&self) -> mpsc::Receiver<T> (registers a new subscriber) and publish(&self, msg: T) (delivers a clone of msg to every currently-registered subscriber). A subscriber that drops its Receiver must not cause publish to error or panic — it should just be quietly dropped from the subscriber list."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::sync::mpsc::{self, Sender, Receiver};
use std::sync::Mutex;

struct MessageQueue<T: Clone> {
    subscribers: Mutex<Vec<Sender<T>>>,
}

impl<T: Clone> MessageQueue<T> {
    fn new() -> Self { todo!() }
    fn subscribe(&self) -> Receiver<T> { todo!() }
    fn publish(&self, msg: T) { todo!() }
}

fn main() {
    let queue = MessageQueue::<String>::new();
    let sub1 = queue.subscribe();
    let sub2 = queue.subscribe();

    queue.publish("hello".to_string());
    assert_eq!(sub1.recv().unwrap(), "hello");
    assert_eq!(sub2.recv().unwrap(), "hello");  // every subscriber independently got its own clone

    drop(sub2);  // simulate a subscriber going away
    queue.publish("still works".to_string());  // must not panic — sub2's dead Sender is pruned silently on this call
    assert_eq!(sub1.recv().unwrap(), "still works");
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
impl<T: Clone> MessageQueue<T> {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self { subscribers: Mutex::new(Vec::new()) }
    }

    fn subscribe(&self) -> Receiver<T> {
        let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();
        self.subscribers.lock().unwrap().push(tx);  // &self, not &mut self — mutation goes through the Mutex's interior mutability
        rx
    }

    fn publish(&self, msg: T) {
        let mut subs = self.subscribers.lock().unwrap();
        subs.retain(|tx| tx.send(msg.clone()).is_ok());  // send() fails exactly when the matching Receiver was dropped — prune it, don't panic
    }
}

fn main() {
    let queue = MessageQueue::<String>::new();
    let sub1 = queue.subscribe();
    let sub2 = queue.subscribe();

    queue.publish("hello".to_string());
    assert_eq!(sub1.recv().unwrap(), "hello");
    assert_eq!(sub2.recv().unwrap(), "hello");  // every subscriber independently got its own clone

    drop(sub2);  // simulate a subscriber going away
    queue.publish("still works".to_string());  // must not panic — sub2's dead Sender is pruned silently on this call
    assert_eq!(sub1.recv().unwrap(), "still works");
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Uses Vec::retain inside publish to prune subscribers whose send() returned Err — treating a dropped Receiver as a completely normal, expected event in a pub/sub system (a subscriber that's no longer interested), never as a bug to panic or .unwrap() on.
  • ★★★Clones msg once per subscriber (tx.send(msg.clone())) and bounds the type by T: Clone — recognizing a single message value can't be moved to more than one destination, and fan-out delivery inherently needs N independent copies (or an Arc<T>, if raised as an optimisation).
  • ★★Keeps the subscribers lock held only for the duration of the retain/send loop in publish — not, say, running arbitrary subscriber-supplied callback logic while holding it — keeping the critical section's scope tight and easy to reason about.
  • ★Writes subscribe(&self), not &mut self — the mutation (pushing a new subscriber) happens through the Mutex's interior mutability, so multiple callers can register concurrently from multiple threads without needing exclusive access to the whole queue.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What if T is expensive to clone — say, a large Vec payload?" — Wrap the message type in an Arc at the API boundary: subscribers receive Arc, and publish clones the Arc, which is just a cheap atomic refcount bump rather than a deep copy — the standard fix for exactly this cost, and worth raising unprompted the moment cloning cost comes up.
  • P2"Multiple threads calling publish() concurrently — is this actually safe, and could messages arrive out of order at a single subscriber?" — Safe: the Mutex serializes the entire publish() body, so no two publish() calls can interleave their retain/send operations against the same Vec. Because that whole critical section is serialized, deliveries to any single subscriber's channel happen in the same relative order publish() calls occurred in, even from different publisher threads — the ordering guarantee comes directly from the mutex, not from anything inherent to mpsc::Sender.
  • P3"How is this different from tokio::sync::broadcast, and when would you reach for this hand-rolled version over it?" — tokio::sync::broadcast is the direct async-native equivalent — a fixed-capacity ring buffer per subscriber, where a lagging subscriber gets an explicit RecvError::Lagged instead of unboundedly blocking others — and is almost always the better choice for real async code. This hand-rolled Vec version is worth building once to internalize the core mechanics (fan-out plus prune-on-disconnect), but production sync code would typically also prefer a maintained crate's pub/sub primitive over re-deriving this from scratch each time.
🎯 Senior angle
Ask what happens to publish()'s throughput as the subscriber count grows into the thousands — every single call becomes an O(subscribers) linear scan while holding one global lock, a real and common scaling wall for naive pub/sub implementations. A production system actually facing that scale usually shards subscribers by topic/partition or moves to a dedicated message broker (Kafka, NATS, Redis pub/sub) rather than trying to out-engineer a single in-process, mutex-protected Vec — watch for whether a candidate volunteers that ceiling unprompted.

W36 · Zero-Copy Tokenizer — Struct Lifetimes + Generic Iterator Bound
explicit struct lifetime Iterator<Item = &'a str> generic over trait, not type Hard
Prompt
"Implement Tokenizer<'a> which borrows a &'a str and, via Iterator<Item = &'a str>, yields each whitespace-separated word as a zero-copy substring — no String allocation anywhere. Then write a generic function fn longest_token<'a, I: Iterator<Item = &'a str>>(tokens: I) -> Option<&'a str> that returns the longest yielded token — generic over any such iterator, not just your specific Tokenizer."
Starter code to hand to candidate
struct Tokenizer<'a> {
    remaining: &'a str,
}

impl<'a> Tokenizer<'a> {
    fn new(source: &'a str) -> Self { todo!() }
}

impl<'a> Iterator for Tokenizer<'a> {
    type Item = &'a str;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<&'a str> {
        todo!()
    }
}

fn longest_token<'a, I: Iterator<Item = &'a str>>(tokens: I) -> Option<&'a str> {
    todo!()
}

fn main() {
    let text = "the quick brown fox jumps extraordinarily".to_string();
    let tokens: Vec<&str> = Tokenizer::new(&text).collect();
    assert_eq!(tokens, vec!["the", "quick", "brown", "fox", "jumps", "extraordinarily"]);
    assert_eq!(longest_token(Tokenizer::new(&text)), Some("extraordinarily"));
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
impl<'a> Tokenizer<'a> {
    fn new(source: &'a str) -> Self {
        Tokenizer { remaining: source.trim_start() }
    }
}

impl<'a> Iterator for Tokenizer<'a> {
    type Item = &'a str;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<&'a str> {
        if self.remaining.is_empty() {
            return None;
        }
        let end = self.remaining.find(char::is_whitespace).unwrap_or(self.remaining.len());
        let (word, rest) = self.remaining.split_at(end);  // both `word` and `rest` are &'a str slices INTO the original source
        self.remaining = rest.trim_start();
        Some(word)
    }
}

fn longest_token<'a, I: Iterator<Item = &'a str>>(tokens: I) -> Option<&'a str> {
    tokens.max_by_key(|s| s.len())  // works on ANY Iterator — not tied to Tokenizer specifically
}

fn main() {
    let text = "the quick brown fox jumps extraordinarily".to_string();
    let tokens: Vec<&str> = Tokenizer::new(&text).collect();
    assert_eq!(tokens, vec!["the", "quick", "brown", "fox", "jumps", "extraordinarily"]);
    assert_eq!(longest_token(Tokenizer::new(&text)), Some("extraordinarily"));
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Declares the struct with an explicit lifetime parameter, struct Tokenizer<'a> { remaining: &'a str } — recognizing that lifetime elision, which works great in function signatures, does not apply to struct field definitions; any struct holding a reference must name its lifetime explicitly, with no exceptions.
  • ★★★Writes type Item = &'a str; tied to the struct's own 'a, not some fresh lifetime implicitly scoped to one call of next(&mut self) — so tokens yielded by the iterator remain valid for as long as the original source string, not merely for the duration of the call that produced them.
  • ★★Writes longest_token generic over I: Iterator<Item = &'a str> rather than hardcoding Tokenizer<'a> as the parameter type — the same "generic over the trait, not the concrete type" instinct tested elsewhere in this packet, here combined with an explicit lifetime on the bound itself.
  • ★Uses split_at/find on the borrowed &str to slice zero-copy substrings, never calling .to_string()/.to_owned() anywhere in the tokenizing path.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What would go wrong if Tokenizer had no lifetime parameter at all — struct Tokenizer { remaining: &str }?" — That's not valid on its own: a struct definition needs an explicitly named lifetime for any reference field, because unlike a function signature, there's no calling context for the compiler to elide a lifetime from. It's a straight compile error asking for a lifetime parameter, before you even get to questions about borrowing or moves.
  • P2"Could a Tokenizer<'a> ever outlive the &'a str it was built from?" — No — the borrow checker ties every Tokenizer<'a> value's usable lifetime to be no longer than 'a, so the original string data it borrows from must still be alive, and (per Rust's aliasing rules) not mutated through any other handle, for as long as any Tokenizer or any &'a str token it yielded is still reachable.
  • P3"How would you extend this to split on custom delimiters (e.g. commas) without giving up the zero-copy property?" — Swap the hand-rolled `find(char::is_whitespace)` for a caller-supplied `impl FnMut(char) -> bool` predicate (or delegate to `str::split` with a closure/pattern) — still calling `split_at`/slicing on the same original `&'a str`. Zero-copy is a property of "we only ever slice the original buffer," which is entirely orthogonal to what predicate decides where the slice boundaries fall.
🎯 Senior angle
Ask a candidate to explain, unprompted, why Tokenizer<'a> needs a lifetime parameter at all when a similarly-shaped struct Counter { count: usize } doesn't. The answer — "any type holding a reference must carry a lifetime parameter recording how long that reference is guaranteed to stay valid; a type holding only owned data carries no such constraint" — is a foundational mental model, and how fluently it comes out is one of the cleanest simple/complex litmus tests in this whole packet.

// Write Exercise 37 · 20 min
W37 · Two Independent Input Lifetimes — Why Naive 'a-Everywhere Fails
independent lifetime params PartialEq bound return-lifetime reasoning Hard
Prompt
"Write fn first_match<'a, 'b, T: PartialEq>(haystack: &'a [T], needle: &'b T) -> Option<&'a T>, returning a reference to the first element of haystack equal to needle. Then explain: why does the return type borrow from 'a and not 'b, and what would break if you instead forced both parameters to share one 'a?"
Starter code to hand to candidate
fn first_match<'a, 'b, T: PartialEq>(haystack: &'a [T], needle: &'b T) -> Option<&'a T> {
    todo!()
}

fn main() {
    let haystack = vec![1, 2, 3, 4];
    let result;
    {
        let needle = 3;                              // needle's lifetime 'b is much shorter than haystack's 'a
        result = first_match(&haystack, &needle);
    }                                              // needle, and 'b, end here — but result never borrowed from needle
    assert_eq!(result, Some(&3));                // still valid — result only ever borrowed from haystack ('a)
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
fn first_match<'a, 'b, T: PartialEq>(haystack: &'a [T], needle: &'b T) -> Option<&'a T> {
    haystack.iter().find(|item| *item == needle)  // returned reference borrows ONLY from haystack ('a) — needle ('b) is just compared against, never returned
}

fn main() {
    let haystack = vec![1, 2, 3, 4];
    let result;
    {
        let needle = 3;                              // needle's lifetime 'b is much shorter than haystack's 'a
        result = first_match(&haystack, &needle);
    }                                              // needle, and 'b, end here — but result never borrowed from needle
    assert_eq!(result, Some(&3));                // still valid — result only ever borrowed from haystack ('a)
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Gives haystack and needle genuinely independent lifetime parameters ('a, 'b) rather than forcing both under one shared 'a — and can explain that forcing a shared lifetime would incorrectly tie the return value's validity to whichever input happens to have the shorter lifetime at a given call site, even though the returned reference never actually borrows from needle at all.
  • ★★★Writes the return type as Option<&'a T>, tied only to haystack — not &'b T, and not some intersection of the two — recognizing the returned reference's lifetime must match wherever the underlying data it points to actually lives, which is unambiguously inside haystack.
  • ★★Constructs (or explains) a scenario where needle goes out of scope before result is used, and correctly states this compiles fine specifically because result never borrowed from needle in the first place.
  • ★Bounds T by PartialEq, not Eq or PartialOrd — the minimal correct bound for the == comparison find's closure needs, and nothing more.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What if you'd written first_match<'a, T: PartialEq>(haystack: &'a [T], needle: &'a T) -> Option<&'a T> instead — does it still compile, and what actually changes?" — It still compiles for this specific function body, but it's a strictly worse signature: it forces every caller to ensure needle lives at least as long as haystack, even though the function body never needs that. That over-constraint would reject perfectly safe call patterns — like the one in main above, where needle's scope ends early — purely because the signature ties together two lifetimes that don't actually need to be related.
  • P2"Is there a version of this problem where the return type genuinely would need to share one lifetime across both inputs?" — Yes — if the function could return a reference pointing into either input depending on some runtime condition (compare something in haystack against something wrapping needle and return whichever "wins"), both inputs would need one shared lifetime, since the return type can't know ahead of time which side it's borrowing from. The independent-lifetimes version here is correct precisely because the return value provably only ever comes from one specific side.
  • P3"How does this connect to the classic longest(x, y) example almost everyone first learns lifetimes from?" — That classic example (fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str) is the mirror-image case: it deliberately DOES need one shared 'a, because the return value could be either x or y depending on which is longer at runtime — the function can't know in advance which parameter it's borrowing from, so both must share a lifetime the return type can safely use. Correctly identifying which of the two shapes — "independent lifetimes are fine" vs. "must share one" — applies to a given function is the actual skill being tested here, not memorizing either example in isolation.
🎯 Senior angle
Most engineers memorize "the longest() example" without internalizing why it needs one shared lifetime, then reflexively give every multi-reference function a single shared 'a "just in case." Over-constraining lifetimes this way is a genuine, if usually harmless, code smell — ask candidates to justify each lifetime parameter's presence individually rather than defaulting to one shared 'a out of habit.

// Write Exercise 38 · 30 min
W38 · The Self-Referential Struct Trap — Fix It Without Unsafe
self-referential structs PhantomData<T> trait bound + assoc. fn Hard
Prompt
"A teammate writes this and it doesn't compile: struct Parser { source: String, current_token: &str } — intended so current_token is a slice into source. Explain exactly why this can never work in safe Rust, no matter how it's annotated. Then implement a corrected, generic Parser<'a, T: Tokenize> that holds a borrowed &'a str (not an owned String) plus current: Option<&'a str>, where Tokenize provides fn next_token(input: &str) -> Option<(&str, &str)> (token, remainder)."
Starter code to hand to candidate
trait Tokenize {
    fn next_token(input: &str) -> Option<(&str, &str)>;  // (token, remainder)
}

// TODO: define Parser — fields, new(), and advance()
// TODO: impl Tokenize for a `Whitespace` marker type

fn main() {
    let source = "parse me please".to_string();  // the OWNER of the data lives OUTSIDE Parser entirely
    let mut parser: Parser<Whitespace> = Parser::new(&source);
    assert_eq!(parser.advance(), Some("parse"));
    assert_eq!(parser.advance(), Some("me"));
    assert_eq!(parser.advance(), Some("please"));
    assert_eq!(parser.advance(), None);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
struct Whitespace;

impl Tokenize for Whitespace {
    fn next_token(input: &str) -> Option<(&str, &str)> {
        let input = input.trim_start();
        if input.is_empty() { return None; }
        let end = input.find(char::is_whitespace).unwrap_or(input.len());
        Some(input.split_at(end))
    }
}

struct Parser<'a, T: Tokenize> {
    remaining: &'a str,
    current: Option<&'a str>,
    _tokenizer: std::marker::PhantomData<T>,  // T never appears in a field otherwise — PhantomData satisfies "parameter T is never used"
}

impl<'a, T: Tokenize> Parser<'a, T> {
    fn new(source: &'a str) -> Self {
        Parser { remaining: source, current: None, _tokenizer: std::marker::PhantomData }
    }

    fn advance(&mut self) -> Option<&'a str> {
        let (token, rest) = T::next_token(self.remaining)?;
        self.remaining = rest;
        self.current = Some(token);
        self.current
    }
}

fn main() {
    let source = "parse me please".to_string();  // the OWNER of the data lives OUTSIDE Parser entirely
    let mut parser: Parser<Whitespace> = Parser::new(&source);
    assert_eq!(parser.advance(), Some("parse"));
    assert_eq!(parser.advance(), Some("me"));
    assert_eq!(parser.advance(), Some("please"));
    assert_eq!(parser.advance(), None);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Explains that the real blocker is structural, not "moves invalidate pointers" — a struct simply has no syntax for "this field borrows from that sibling field defined right next to it." Lifetimes describe borrows of data external to the struct, whose scope the struct doesn't own — there is no vocabulary for a self-relationship between two of a struct's own fields, regardless of whether it would happen to be memory-safe in a given case.
  • ★★★Fixes it by separating ownership from borrowing — Parser<'a, T> holds only &'a str slices, never the owned String itself, pushing responsibility for keeping the source alive onto the caller — rather than reaching for unsafe, raw pointers, or immediately suggesting a crate like ouroboros/self_cell as the first move.
  • ★★Adds PhantomData<T> (or otherwise resolves) once T doesn't appear in any of Parser's actual fields — recognizing the "parameter T is never used" compile error and its standard fix, rather than getting stuck on why the type won't compile.
  • ★Doesn't add unnecessary lifetime annotations inside Tokenize::next_token — one input reference, so both output references in the returned tuple correctly elide to that same lifetime with zero explicit annotation needed.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"If moving a String doesn't actually invalidate a pointer into its heap buffer, why is self-referencing still fundamentally blocked?" — Because the compiler's rule isn't "we specifically detected this exact case is unsafe" — it's structural. There is no lifetime syntax letting one field name "the lifetime of that other field, defined right next to me." Even in cases that would happen to be memory-safe (like this one, since String's heap allocation address is stable across a struct-level move), the type system has no way to express or verify that safety, so it's rejected categorically rather than case-by-case.
  • P2"When would you actually reach for a crate like ouroboros or self_cell instead of the separate-owner fix shown here?" — When restructuring to "just don't own the data in the same struct" is genuinely impractical for the API you need — e.g. a library that must hand callers one self-contained value that internally owns a buffer and borrows from it, so callers don't have to separately manage a source string's lifetime themselves. Those crates use carefully audited unsafe internally to provide a safe-looking external API for exactly this self-referential shape — reaching for them is reasonable once you've confirmed the ownership-separation approach genuinely doesn't fit your API constraints.
  • P3"What's the tradeoff between storing &'a str tokens directly, versus storing (start, end) byte-index pairs into the original string instead?" — Index pairs are plain usize data with no lifetime at all, so a struct storing them can freely be moved, stored in a Vec, or serialized without any borrow-checker entanglement — at the cost of needing to re-slice the original string every time you want the actual text, and needing to separately (manually, not compiler-enforced) guarantee the original string hasn't been mutated or dropped by then. The &'a str version gets that guarantee for free from the borrow checker, at the cost of the struct itself being borrow-checker-entangled with its source's lifetime.
🎯 Senior angle
This exact trap — owned data plus a reference into itself, in one struct — is one of the most common "hits a wall and doesn't know why" moments for engineers coming from garbage-collected languages. Watch whether a candidate's first instinct is to reach for unsafe/raw pointers to force it to work, versus recognizing that restructuring around the constraint (separate ownership from borrowing, or use indices instead of references) is almost always the right move — and is what real Rust codebases do the vast majority of the time.

W39 · Cow<'_, str> — Allocate Only When You Must
Cow::Borrowed vs. Owned two-pass scan-then-write conditional allocation Medium
Prompt
"Write fn normalize_whitespace(input: &str) -> Cow<'_, str> that collapses any run of consecutive whitespace into a single space. If the input already has no such runs, return it borrowed with zero allocation — only allocate a new String when a rewrite is actually necessary."

use std::borrow::Cow;

fn normalize_whitespace(input: &str) -> Cow<'_, str> {
    // Pass 1: read-only scan to DECIDE whether a rewrite is needed — no allocation yet.
    let mut needs_rewrite = false;
    let mut prev_was_space = false;
    for ch in input.chars() {
        if ch.is_whitespace() {
            if prev_was_space || ch != ' ' {
                needs_rewrite = true;
                break;
            }
            prev_was_space = true;
        } else {
            prev_was_space = false;
        }
    }

    if !needs_rewrite {
        return Cow::Borrowed(input);  // zero allocation — common case for already-clean input
    }

    // Pass 2: only reached when a rewrite is actually required.
    let mut out = String::with_capacity(input.len());  // output can't exceed input's byte length
    let mut prev_was_space = false;
    for ch in input.chars() {
        if ch.is_whitespace() {
            if !prev_was_space {
                out.push(' ');
            }
            prev_was_space = true;
        } else {
            out.push(ch);
            prev_was_space = false;
        }
    }
    Cow::Owned(out)
}

fn main() {
    assert!(matches!(normalize_whitespace("already clean"), Cow::Borrowed(_)));  // no allocation happened
    assert_eq!(normalize_whitespace("has  double   spaces"), "has double spaces");
    assert!(matches!(normalize_whitespace("has  double   spaces"), Cow::Owned(_)));
    assert_eq!(normalize_whitespace("tab\there"), "tab here");
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Returns Cow::Borrowed(input) directly when no rewrite is needed, with zero allocation — rather than always building a new String and letting Cow::Owned wrap it unconditionally, which compiles and produces correct output but defeats the entire point of using Cow in the first place.
  • ★★★Scans first with a cheap, read-only pass to decide whether a rewrite is needed, before committing to allocate — doesn't speculatively build the new string and then compare it to the input to decide which variant to return.
  • ★★Writes the signature as Cow<'_, str>, letting the elided lifetime tie itself to input's borrow — not hardcoding an explicit named lifetime, and not falling back to always returning an owned String (which would compile but allocate unconditionally, silently losing the entire optimization).
  • ★Uses String::with_capacity(input.len()) when it does allocate, since the rewritten output's byte length can never exceed the input's.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What's the actual point of Cow here versus just always returning an owned String?" — Cow lets a caller who mostly passes already-clean strings avoid an allocation entirely in the common case, while still handling the rare "needs rewrite" case correctly through the exact same function signature. The two-pass shape — a cheap read-only scan to decide, then optionally a write pass — is the standard structure for this pattern; the goal is deferring the allocation decision until it's known to be necessary, not saving on typing.
  • P2"If a caller does `let s: String = normalize_whitespace(input).into_owned();` on a value that was Cow::Borrowed, does that allocate?" — Yes — `into_owned()` always produces an owned String by cloning in the Borrowed case, so a caller that unconditionally converts to owned afterward has thrown away Cow's benefit entirely. Cow only pays off when downstream code can keep working with a borrowed &str in the common case, not when every call site immediately converts to owned regardless.
  • P3"Where does the standard library itself lean on this exact pattern?" — `String::from_utf8_lossy` is the canonical example: it returns `Cow<'_, str>`, borrowing the input directly when it's already valid UTF-8 (the overwhelmingly common case) and only allocating a new String — substituting the replacement character for invalid bytes — when the input actually contains invalid UTF-8.
🎯 Senior angle
The "scan first, allocate only if needed" two-pass shape shown here is the single most common Cow usage pattern in real Rust code. Recognizing that the type exists specifically to make this optimization ergonomic — instead of requiring two entirely different function signatures for the borrowed and owned cases — is more valuable than being able to recite Cow's variant names from memory.

// Write Exercise 40 · 25 min
W40 · Zero-Copy Binary Header Parser
&'a [u8] slicing from_be_bytes bounds-check before split_at Hard
Prompt
"Implement fn parse_frame(buf: &[u8]) -> Option<Frame<'_>> for a simple wire protocol: 4-byte magic b"FRM1", then a big-endian u16 payload length, then that many payload bytes. Return a Frame<'a> holding the parsed length and a payload: &'a [u8] slice borrowed directly from buf — no copying the payload into an owned Vec<u8>. Handle truncated/malformed buffers by returning None, never panicking."
Starter code to hand to candidate
struct Frame<'a> {
    length: u16,
    payload: &'a [u8],
}

const MAGIC: &[u8] = b"FRM1";

fn parse_frame(buf: &[u8]) -> Option<Frame<'_>> {
    todo!()
}

fn main() {
    let mut buf = Vec::new();
    buf.extend_from_slice(b"FRM1");
    buf.extend_from_slice(&5u16.to_be_bytes());
    buf.extend_from_slice(b"hello");
    buf.extend_from_slice(b"trailing garbage ignored");

    let frame = parse_frame(&buf).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(frame.length, 5);
    assert_eq!(frame.payload, b"hello");

    // Confirm zero-copy: payload's backing pointer literally falls inside buf's allocation.
    let payload_ptr = frame.payload.as_ptr();
    let buf_start = buf.as_ptr();
    let buf_end = unsafe { buf_start.add(buf.len()) };
    assert!(payload_ptr >= buf_start && payload_ptr < buf_end);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
fn parse_frame(buf: &[u8]) -> Option<Frame<'_>> {
    if buf.len() < MAGIC.len() + 2 { return None; }  // bounds-check BEFORE any split_at/indexing
    let (magic, rest) = buf.split_at(MAGIC.len());
    if magic != MAGIC { return None; }

    let (len_bytes, rest) = rest.split_at(2);
    let length = u16::from_be_bytes([len_bytes[0], len_bytes[1]]);  // big-endian — a wire-format convention, not this machine's native endianness

    if rest.len() < length as usize { return None; }  // don't trust the claimed length — verify enough bytes actually remain
    let (payload, _remaining) = rest.split_at(length as usize);

    Some(Frame { length, payload })  // payload borrows directly from buf — zero copy
}

fn main() {
    let mut buf = Vec::new();
    buf.extend_from_slice(b"FRM1");
    buf.extend_from_slice(&5u16.to_be_bytes());
    buf.extend_from_slice(b"hello");
    buf.extend_from_slice(b"trailing garbage ignored");

    let frame = parse_frame(&buf).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(frame.length, 5);
    assert_eq!(frame.payload, b"hello");

    // Confirm zero-copy: payload's backing pointer literally falls inside buf's allocation.
    let payload_ptr = frame.payload.as_ptr();
    let buf_start = buf.as_ptr();
    let buf_end = unsafe { buf_start.add(buf.len()) };
    assert!(payload_ptr >= buf_start && payload_ptr < buf_end);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Returns payload: &'a [u8] borrowed directly from the input buffer, not payload: Vec<u8> — the entire point of the exercise; a candidate defaulting to .to_vec() "to be safe" compiles and passes basic tests but defeats the zero-copy goal entirely.
  • ★★★Validates buffer length BEFORE calling split_at/indexing, at every step, rather than letting a short or malformed buffer panic — split_at panics if the index is out of bounds, and naive indexing like buf[4] panics too. This is untrusted wire input; panicking on malformed network data is a real availability bug, not a style nitpick.
  • ★★Uses u16::from_be_bytes and can state why big-endian — a deliberate wire-format convention, not this machine's native byte order. Using from_le_bytes instead would silently produce a wrong length on this exact input even though every byte was read correctly.
  • ★Doesn't try to validate or consume trailing bytes after the payload — correctly scopes this function to "parse exactly one frame," leaving handling of subsequent frames/trailing data to the caller.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What happens if length is a lie — the header claims 5 bytes of payload but only 2 remain in buf?" — The `if rest.len() < length as usize { return None; }` check catches this before `split_at` is ever called, so a corrupted or malicious length field returns None cleanly. Skipping that check and calling `rest.split_at(length as usize)` directly would panic the instant length exceeds rest.len() — a crash triggered by untrusted network input, exactly the class of bug the defensive check exists to prevent.
  • P2"Frame<'a> borrows from buf — what does that mean for how long the caller must keep buf alive?" — buf (and the data it owns) must remain alive, and not be mutated in a way that invalidates the slice, for as long as any Frame derived from it is still in use. In practice: read a frame's bytes into a buffer, parse it, fully consume whatever's needed from the Frame, and only then reuse or drop that buffer for the next read — you can't hold overlapping in-flight Frame borrows across a buffer you also need to mutate in between.
  • P3"For a real high-throughput parser reading many frames off a persistent connection, is a fresh Vec per read() call actually the right design?" — Usually not — the common real-world answer is a single reusable growable buffer (e.g. `bytes::BytesMut` from the `bytes` crate), read into repeatedly, with zero-copy frames sliced out via cheap, refcounted `Bytes::slice` views rather than borrows tied to a stack lifetime — trading the compiler-enforced &'a [u8] coupling shown here for a refcounted buffer that can outlive the specific read() call that produced it, which matters once frames need to be handed off to another task or thread asynchronously.
🎯 Senior angle
This is directly the shape of real network protocol parsers — HTTP chunked bodies, gRPC frames, Redis RESP, custom binary RPC. The trio of "parse into borrowed slices, validate lengths defensively before indexing, never copy the payload unnecessarily" is the actual, non-negotiable skillset behind that work, not a toy exercise — a candidate who claims backend or network experience should walk through this without hesitation.

// Write Exercise 41 · 20 min
W41 · Vec<u8> Buffer Building — Capacity Planning vs. Naive Push
Vec::with_capacity extend_from_slice to_le_bytes / from_le_bytes Medium
Prompt
"Implement fn serialize(items: &[u32]) -> Vec<u8>, encoding a u32 count prefix followed by each item as 4 little-endian bytes, matching the layout the paired fn deserialize(buf: &[u8]) -> Vec<u32> expects. Write serialize so the returned Vec allocates its backing buffer exactly once, no matter how many items are in items — as opposed to a naive version that repeatedly .push()es individual bytes into a Vec::new()."
Starter code to hand to candidate
fn serialize(items: &[u32]) -> Vec<u8> { todo!() }

fn deserialize(buf: &[u8]) -> Vec<u32> { todo!() }

fn main() {
    let items = vec![10u32, 20, 30, 4_000_000_000];
    let bytes = serialize(&items);
    assert_eq!(bytes.capacity(), 4 + items.len() * 4);  // exactly one allocation, no over-allocation from growth
    assert_eq!(deserialize(&bytes), items);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
fn serialize(items: &[u32]) -> Vec<u8> {
    let capacity = 4 + items.len() * 4;  // 4-byte count prefix + 4 bytes per item — computed exactly, not guessed
    let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(capacity);  // single allocation for the whole buffer, sized upfront
    out.extend_from_slice(&(items.len() as u32).to_le_bytes());
    for item in items {
        out.extend_from_slice(&item.to_le_bytes());  // bulk memcpy-backed append, not a byte-by-byte push loop
    }
    out
}

fn deserialize(buf: &[u8]) -> Vec<u32> {
    let count = u32::from_le_bytes(buf[0..4].try_into().unwrap()) as usize;
    (0..count)
        .map(|i| {
            let start = 4 + i * 4;
            u32::from_le_bytes(buf[start..start + 4].try_into().unwrap())  // idiomatic slice→array conversion, not manual byte shifting
        })
        .collect()
}

fn main() {
    let items = vec![10u32, 20, 30, 4_000_000_000];
    let bytes = serialize(&items);
    assert_eq!(bytes.capacity(), 4 + items.len() * 4);  // exactly one allocation, no over-allocation from growth
    assert_eq!(deserialize(&bytes), items);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Computes the exact required capacity upfront and passes it to Vec::with_capacity, rather than Vec::new() followed by pushes/extends that force geometric-growth reallocation — each of which copies every already-written byte into a newly, larger allocation.
  • ★★★Uses extend_from_slice (one bulk, memcpy-backed call per item) rather than a for byte in item.to_le_bytes() { out.push(byte) } loop — a meaningfully tighter inner loop, and the natural pairing with a pre-reserved with_capacity buffer.
  • ★★Explicitly picks and consistently applies one endianness convention (to_le_bytes/from_le_bytes) — recognizing this is an arbitrary-but-fixed wire-format decision, not something to leave to the platform's native in-memory representation, which is not guaranteed portable across machines.
  • ★deserialize uses .try_into().unwrap() to convert a &[u8] slice into a fixed-size [u8; 4] array for from_le_bytes, rather than manually shifting and OR-ing four bytes together by hand.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Why does capacity matter here at all — won't Vec::push handle growth automatically either way?" — Correctness-wise, yes, push always works regardless of starting capacity. The issue is pure performance: an empty Vec growing to N bytes via repeated pushes typically reallocates O(log N) times as it grows geometrically, and each reallocation copies every byte written so far into the new buffer — wasted work a single, correctly-sized upfront allocation avoids entirely. For a serialization path called frequently, this is a measurable difference, not a micro-optimization.
  • P2"What would you need to change if items.len() could be enormous — is items.len() * 4 always safe?" — items.len() * 4 could in principle overflow a usize on a target where that product exceeds usize::MAX (practically only relevant on 32-bit targets with very large inputs) — in a debug build, standard multiplication panics on overflow; in release, it silently wraps, computing a wrong, too-small capacity. A hardened version would use checked_mul/saturating_mul, or simply accept that with_capacity itself will fail loudly for a genuinely enormous, legitimate request rather than silently wrapping around to a small number first.
  • P3"Real wire formats (protobuf, bincode) usually use variable-length integers instead of a fixed 4-byte count — why?" — A fixed-width u32 count wastes up to 3 bytes for any count under 256, whereas a varint encoding (e.g. LEB128) uses a single byte for small values and grows only as needed — a meaningful size difference at scale for protocols with many small messages. The trade-off is a few more lines of branchy encode/decode logic than one to_le_bytes call — this exercise's fixed-width version is the right default for a first pass, but naming the varint alternative unprompted is a good signal of broader wire-format awareness.
🎯 Senior angle
Ask a candidate to justify with_capacity's argument by doing the arithmetic explicitly, rather than guessing or over-allocating "to be safe." Off-by-one capacity math (forgetting the 4-byte count prefix, or using items.len() instead of items.len() * 4) is a very easy, very common mistake — and catching it via a capacity assertion in the test itself (as main() does above), rather than only checking the output bytes, is worth calling out as a good testing habit in its own right.

The Long Ones
These are deliberately bigger than W1–W41 — each forces a candidate to combine several pillars at once (generics + trait bounds + closures + iterator chains + Result/Option + a real algorithmic core) rather than demonstrating one feature in isolation. Use one of these as the centerpiece of a 60–90 minute onsite round instead of three small exercises; the transitions between sub-parts are where the real signal lives.

Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::cmp::Reverse;
use std::collections::{BinaryHeap, HashMap};

struct Graph {
    adj: HashMap<usize, Vec<(usize, u32)>>,
}

impl Graph {
    fn new() -> Self { Self { adj: HashMap::new() } }

    fn add_edge(&mut self, from: usize, to: usize, weight: u32) {
        self.adj.entry(from).or_default().push((to, weight));  // entry API — one lookup, not check-then-insert
        self.adj.entry(to).or_default().push((from, weight));
    }

    fn dijkstra(&self, source: usize) -> HashMap<usize, u32> {
        let mut dist: HashMap<usize, u32> = HashMap::new();
        let mut heap: BinaryHeap<Reverse<(u32, usize)>> = BinaryHeap::new();  // Reverse flips Ord — smallest distance pops first

        dist.insert(source, 0);
        heap.push(Reverse((0, source)));

        while let Some(Reverse((d, node))) = heap.pop() {
            if d > *dist.get(&node).unwrap_or(&u32::MAX) { continue; }  // stale heap entry — a shorter path to `node` was already found
            if let Some(neighbors) = self.adj.get(&node) {
                for &(next, weight) in neighbors {
                    let candidate = d + weight;
                    if candidate < *dist.get(&next).unwrap_or(&u32::MAX) {
                        dist.insert(next, candidate);
                        heap.push(Reverse((candidate, next)));  // old, now-stale entries for `next` are left in the heap — cheaper than removing them
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        dist
    }

    fn shortest_path(&self, source: usize, target: usize) -> Option<(u32, Vec<usize>)> {
        let mut dist: HashMap<usize, u32> = HashMap::new();
        let mut prev: HashMap<usize, usize> = HashMap::new();  // breadcrumb trail for path reconstruction
        let mut heap: BinaryHeap<Reverse<(u32, usize)>> = BinaryHeap::new();

        dist.insert(source, 0);
        heap.push(Reverse((0, source)));

        while let Some(Reverse((d, node))) = heap.pop() {
            if node == target {  // early exit the moment target is POPPED — heap guarantees this is its final shortest distance
                let mut path = vec![target];
                let mut cur = target;
                while let Some(&p) = prev.get(&cur) { path.push(p); cur = p; }  // walk breadcrumbs back to source
                path.reverse();
                return Some((d, path));
            }
            if d > *dist.get(&node).unwrap_or(&u32::MAX) { continue; }
            if let Some(neighbors) = self.adj.get(&node) {
                for &(next, weight) in neighbors {
                    let candidate = d + weight;
                    if candidate < *dist.get(&next).unwrap_or(&u32::MAX) {
                        dist.insert(next, candidate);
                        prev.insert(next, node);
                        heap.push(Reverse((candidate, next)));
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        None  // heap ran dry without ever popping target — unreachable
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut g = Graph::new();
    g.add_edge(0, 1, 4);
    g.add_edge(0, 2, 1);
    g.add_edge(2, 1, 2);
    g.add_edge(1, 3, 1);
    g.add_edge(2, 3, 5);

    let dist = g.dijkstra(0);
    assert_eq!(dist[&3], 4);  // 0 -> 2 (1) -> 1 (2) -> 3 (1) = 4, beats the direct 0->1->3 path of 5

    let (cost, path) = g.shortest_path(0, 3).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(cost, 4);
    assert_eq!(path, vec![0, 2, 1, 3]);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Wraps the heap entries in Reverse without being reminded that BinaryHeap is a max-heap — this is exactly the Q8 gotcha from the std-library topic, and Dijkstra is the canonical place it bites people who haven't internalised it.
  • ★★★Handles stale heap entries correctly — recognizes that a node can be pushed onto the heap multiple times with different distances (since we never remove/decrease-key the old entry), and guards with if d > dist[node] { continue } rather than assuming every popped entry is fresh.
  • ★★Uses entry().or_default() when building the adjacency list rather than a manual contains_key/insert dance.
  • ★Early-exits the moment the target is popped in shortest_path, rather than running the algorithm to completion and looking up the target's distance afterward — functionally equivalent but shows understanding of why a popped node's distance is final.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Why is it safe to just leave stale entries in the heap instead of removing or updating them?" — Because the `if d > dist[node] { continue }` guard makes stale entries free to skip — they just cost a wasted pop-and-check, which is cheap (O(log n)) compared to implementing a proper decrease-key operation (which BinaryHeap doesn't support natively). This is the standard, pragmatic "lazy deletion" trick for Dijkstra with std's BinaryHeap.
  • P2"What breaks if an edge weight can be negative?" — Dijkstra's core assumption is that once a node is popped, its distance is final — but a later negative-weight edge could produce an even shorter path to an already-finalized node, silently producing a wrong (too-large) answer with no error or panic. Negative weights require Bellman-Ford instead, which is O(V·E) but correctly handles them (and can detect negative cycles, which have no well-defined shortest path at all).
  • P3"How would you make Graph generic over the node ID type instead of hardcoding usize?" — Add a type parameter `N: Eq + Hash + Copy` and make the HashMap keyed on N instead of usize — the algorithm's logic doesn't care what a node identifier actually is, only that it can be hashed, compared for equality, and cheaply copied, which is exactly the minimal bound needed.
🎯 Senior angle
This exercise deliberately punishes anyone who memorized Dijkstra from a language with a built-in decrease-key priority queue — Rust's BinaryHeap doesn't have one, and the "lazy deletion via a staleness check" pattern shown here is the idiomatic Rust answer, not a workaround. A candidate who reaches for it immediately, rather than trying to implement a custom heap with decrease-key support from scratch, is demonstrating real judgement about when std's simpler tool is sufficient.
