W51 · Write-Ahead Log With Crash Recovery — Framing, Checksums, Torn Writes
length-prefixed framing CRC32 checksum sync_data (fsync) graceful truncated-record handling Hard
Prompt
"Implement a minimal write-ahead log: append(&mut self, payload: &[u8]) -> io::Result<()> frames each record as [u32 length][u32 crc32][payload] and fsyncs before returning, so a caller is never told a write succeeded before it's actually durable. Then implement replay(path) -> io::Result<Vec<Vec<u8>>> that reads every valid record back — but critically, it must handle a file that ends mid-record (simulating a crash during write_all) by silently stopping at the last fully-valid record, not returning an error for the whole file. Prove it: intentionally truncate a record mid-write and show replay still recovers everything before it, cleanly."
Starter code to hand to candidate
struct WriteAheadLog { file: File }

// TODO: impl WriteAheadLog — open(path), append(&mut self, &[u8]) -> io::Result
//       record layout: [u32 len][u32 crc32][payload], fsync after every append
// TODO: fn replay(path: &Path) -> io::Result>> — must stop cleanly at a torn/corrupt record
// TODO: fn crc32(data: &[u8]) -> u32 — no external crate

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let path = std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("wal_test_{}.log", std::process::id()));
    let _cleanup = Cleanup(path.clone());

    {
        let mut wal = WriteAheadLog::open(&path)?;
        wal.append(b"insert user:1")?;
        wal.append(b"insert user:2")?;
        wal.append(b"update user:1 set active=false")?;
    }

    let records = replay(&path)?;
    assert_eq!(records.len(), 3);

    {  // simulate a crash: write a 4th record's header + HALF its payload, then stop —
       // exactly what a power loss mid-write_all looks like on disk
        let mut file = OpenOptions::new().append(true).open(&path)?;
        let full_payload = b"delete user:2";
        let crc = crc32(full_payload);
        file.write_all(&(full_payload.len() as u32).to_le_bytes())?;
        file.write_all(&crc.to_le_bytes())?;
        file.write_all(&full_payload[..5])?;  // only half the payload actually landed
        file.sync_data()?;
    }

    let records_after_crash = replay(&path)?;
    assert_eq!(records_after_crash.len(), 3);  // the torn 4th record is dropped — no error, no corruption of the first 3
    assert_eq!(records_after_crash, records);

    {  // a fully healthy record appended AFTER the torn bytes must NOT become reachable —
       // replay must stop at the FIRST torn record, never resync past corruption looking for more
        let mut wal = WriteAheadLog::open(&path)?;
        wal.append(b"this record is unreachable")?;
    }
    let records_final = replay(&path)?;
    assert_eq!(records_final.len(), 3);

    Ok(())
}

struct Cleanup(std::path::PathBuf);
impl Drop for Cleanup {
    fn drop(&mut self) { let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&self.0); }
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::fs::{File, OpenOptions};
use std::io::{self, Read, Write};
use std::path::Path;

struct WriteAheadLog { file: File }

impl WriteAheadLog {
    fn open(path: &Path) -> io::Result<Self> {
        let file = OpenOptions::new().create(true).append(true).open(path)?;
        Ok(Self { file })
    }

    fn append(&mut self, payload: &[u8]) -> io::Result<()> {
        let len = payload.len() as u32;
        let crc = crc32(payload);

        let mut record = Vec::with_capacity(4 + 4 + payload.len());
        record.extend_from_slice(&len.to_le_bytes());
        record.extend_from_slice(&crc.to_le_bytes());
        record.extend_from_slice(payload);

        self.file.write_all(&record)?;
        self.file.sync_data()?;  // durability point — the record is only "committed" after THIS returns, not after write_all
        Ok(())
    }
}

// Replays every valid record from the start of the file. Stops cleanly — no error — the
// moment it hits a truncated or checksum-mismatched record: that's the expected shape of a
// crash mid-append, not a corruption bug, and a real WAL reader must tolerate exactly this.
fn replay(path: &Path) -> io::Result<Vec<Vec<u8>>> {
    let mut file = File::open(path)?;
    let mut bytes = Vec::new();
    file.read_to_end(&mut bytes)?;

    let mut records = Vec::new();
    let mut cursor = 0usize;

    loop {
        if cursor + 8 > bytes.len() {
            break;  // not even a full header left — a torn write at the tail, stop here
        }
        let len = u32::from_le_bytes(bytes[cursor..cursor + 4].try_into().unwrap()) as usize;
        let crc = u32::from_le_bytes(bytes[cursor + 4..cursor + 8].try_into().unwrap());

        let payload_start = cursor + 8;
        let payload_end = payload_start + len;
        if payload_end > bytes.len() {
            break;  // header claims more payload than the file actually has — torn write, stop here
        }

        let payload = &bytes[payload_start..payload_end];
        if crc32(payload) != crc {
            break;  // checksum mismatch — treat as the tail of a torn/corrupted write, not a hard error
        }

        records.push(payload.to_vec());
        cursor = payload_end;
    }
    Ok(records)
}

// Textbook bit-by-bit CRC-32 (IEEE 802.3 polynomial), no lookup table — clarity over
// throughput, since the point here is framing/checksum SEMANTICS, not raw speed.
fn crc32(data: &[u8]) -> u32 {
    const POLY: u32 = 0xEDB88320;
    let mut crc: u32 = 0xFFFF_FFFF;
    for &byte in data {
        crc ^= byte as u32;
        for _ in 0..8 {
            let mask = 0u32.wrapping_sub(crc & 1);  // branchless "if low bit set, XOR the polynomial in"
            crc = (crc >> 1) ^ (POLY & mask);
        }
    }
    !crc
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let path = std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("wal_test_{}.log", std::process::id()));
    let _cleanup = Cleanup(path.clone());

    {
        let mut wal = WriteAheadLog::open(&path)?;
        wal.append(b"insert user:1")?;
        wal.append(b"insert user:2")?;
        wal.append(b"update user:1 set active=false")?;
    }

    let records = replay(&path)?;
    assert_eq!(records.len(), 3);

    {  // simulate a crash: write a 4th record's header + HALF its payload, then stop —
       // exactly what a power loss mid-write_all looks like on disk
        let mut file = OpenOptions::new().append(true).open(&path)?;
        let full_payload = b"delete user:2";
        let crc = crc32(full_payload);
        file.write_all(&(full_payload.len() as u32).to_le_bytes())?;
        file.write_all(&crc.to_le_bytes())?;
        file.write_all(&full_payload[..5])?;  // only half the payload actually landed
        file.sync_data()?;
    }

    let records_after_crash = replay(&path)?;
    assert_eq!(records_after_crash.len(), 3);  // the torn 4th record is dropped — no error, no corruption of the first 3
    assert_eq!(records_after_crash, records);

    {  // a fully healthy record appended AFTER the torn bytes must NOT become reachable —
       // replay must stop at the FIRST torn record, never resync past corruption looking for more
        let mut wal = WriteAheadLog::open(&path)?;
        wal.append(b"this record is unreachable")?;
    }
    let records_final = replay(&path)?;
    assert_eq!(records_final.len(), 3);

    Ok(())
}

struct Cleanup(std::path::PathBuf);
impl Drop for Cleanup {
    fn drop(&mut self) { let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&self.0); }
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Makes replay stop silently at the first torn/corrupt record instead of returning Err for the whole file — this is the single most important correctness property of the exercise: a real WAL's tail is EXPECTED to sometimes be a half-written record after a crash, and treating that as a fatal error would make the database refuse to start after every unclean shutdown.
  • ★★★Calls sync_data() (or sync_all()) after every write_all, inside append itself — recognizing that write_all returning Ok only means the bytes reached the OS's page cache, not the physical disk; without an explicit fsync, a power loss immediately after a "successful" append can lose data the caller was told was durable.
  • ★★Checks the checksum, not just the length, before trusting a record — a torn write can in principle leave a record whose length prefix happens to still look plausible (e.g. if the crash landed exactly on a byte boundary that coincidentally reads as a smaller, "complete" record) — the checksum is the real guard against silently accepting corrupted-but-well-shaped bytes.
  • ★Frames each record with an explicit length prefix rather than a delimiter byte (like a newline) — a length prefix handles arbitrary binary payloads (including ones that happen to contain the delimiter byte) with no escaping logic needed at all.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"fsync-ing after EVERY single append is a real throughput bottleneck — how do production systems (Postgres, Kafka) get around this without giving up durability?" — Group commit: batch multiple pending appends together and fsync once for the whole batch, amortizing the fsync cost across many records — callers whose writes land in the same batch all become durable together. The trade-off is added latency for individual writers (they must wait for the batch to close) in exchange for dramatically higher aggregate throughput — exactly the kind of throughput/latency trade-off senior infra roles are expected to reason about explicitly, not just implement blindly.
  • P2"This WAL grows forever — what's the real-world mechanism for reclaiming space, and why can't you just delete old records directly?" — Once a WAL's records have been applied to the actual data structure they're protecting (e.g. flushed into an LSM-tree's SSTables, as in W56) they're no longer needed for crash recovery — the standard mechanism is periodic CHECKPOINTING: record a marker (or roll over to a brand-new WAL file) once you know everything before a certain point is safely persisted elsewhere, then the old WAL segment can be deleted or archived wholesale, rather than editing/compacting the log file itself.
  • P3"What if a crash corrupts a record in the MIDDLE of the file, not at the tail — does this replay implementation handle that?" — No, and this is a real, worth-naming limitation: this implementation assumes corruption only ever happens at the tail (the natural consequence of a torn LAST write) and stops there permanently. Mid-file corruption (from a bad disk sector, a bit flip, or a bug that overwrote already-committed bytes) would be silently treated as "the end of valid data," discarding every subsequent GOOD record after it. Production WALs often add a per-record magic number/version byte and, in higher-assurance systems, treat mid-file checksum failures as a hard integrity error requiring operator intervention rather than silently truncating history.
🎯 Senior angle
The entire exercise hinges on one design decision: what does replay do when it finds a bad record? Candidates who reflexively return Err for any checksum mismatch — treating "corrupt" and "incomplete-due-to-crash" as the same failure mode — are missing the central insight of durability engineering: a WAL's tail being torn after an unclean shutdown isn't corruption, it's the expected, designed-for steady state, and the recovery code's entire job is to draw a clean, correct line between "committed" and "never happened."

    // Parent exercise still holds after the harden change:
    let path = std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("wal_test_{}.log", std::process::id()));
    let _cleanup = Cleanup(path.clone());

    {
        let mut wal = WriteAheadLog::open(&path)?;
        wal.append(b"insert user:1")?;
        wal.append(b"insert user:2")?;
        wal.append(b"update user:1 set active=false")?;
    }

    let records = replay(&path)?;
    assert_eq!(records.len(), 3);

    {  // simulate a crash: write a 4th record's header + HALF its payload, then stop —
       // exactly what a power loss mid-write_all looks like on disk
        let mut file = OpenOptions::new().append(true).open(&path)?;
        let full_payload = b"delete user:2";
        let crc = crc32(full_payload);
        file.write_all(&(full_payload.len() as u32).to_le_bytes())?;
        file.write_all(&crc.to_le_bytes())?;
        file.write_all(&full_payload[..5])?;  // only half the payload actually landed
        file.sync_data()?;
    }

    let records_after_crash = replay(&path)?;
    assert_eq!(records_after_crash.len(), 3);  // the torn 4th record is dropped — no error, no corruption of the first 3
    assert_eq!(records_after_crash, records);

    {  // a fully healthy record appended AFTER the torn bytes must NOT become reachable —
       // replay must stop at the FIRST torn record, never resync past corruption looking for more
        let mut wal = WriteAheadLog::open(&path)?;
        wal.append(b"this record is unreachable")?;
    }
    let records_final = replay(&path)?;
    assert_eq!(records_final.len(), 3);

    Ok(())
}

struct Cleanup(std::path::PathBuf);
impl Drop for Cleanup {
    fn drop(&mut self) { let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&self.0); }
}

// Systems Exercise 52 · 75 min
W52 · Generic B-Tree — Node Splitting, the Index Structure Behind Every Real Database
minimum-degree split algorithm Vec::split_off upsert semantics recursive in-order traversal Hard
Prompt
"Implement a generic BTree<K: Ord, V> — the actual on-disk index structure behind Postgres, MySQL/InnoDB, and SQLite. Minimum degree t = 2 (so each node holds up to 3 keys and 4 children). Implement insert (proactively splitting full nodes on the way down, so a single pass never has to backtrack), search, and in_order for verification. Get the split logic exactly right: a full node's median key must be promoted into its parent, and its remaining keys divided evenly into two siblings — this is the part almost everyone gets subtly wrong on the first try."
Starter code to hand to candidate
const T: usize = 2; // minimum degree — max keys = 2T-1 = 3, max children = 2T = 4

struct Node<K, V> { keys: Vec<K>, values: Vec<V>, children: Vec<Box<Node<K, V>>> }

pub struct BTree<K, V> { root: Node<K, V> }

// TODO: impl BTree — new(), search(&K) -> Option, insert(K, V) upsert,
//       in_order() -> Vec, len(), height()
// TODO: split_child(parent, i) — the median-promotion algorithm

fn main() {
    let mut tree: BTree<i32, String> = BTree::new();
    let inserted = [50,30,70,20,40,60,80,10,25,35,45,55,65,75,85,5,15,90,100,1];
    for &i in &inserted { tree.insert(i, format!("v{i}")); }

    let mut expected: Vec<i32> = inserted.to_vec();
    expected.sort_unstable();
    let collected: Vec<i32> = tree.in_order().into_iter().map(|(k, _)| *k).collect();
    assert_eq!(collected, expected);

    assert_eq!(tree.search(&40), Some(&"v40".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(tree.search(&999), None);
    assert!(tree.height() > 1);  // 20 insertions into a min-degree-2 tree must have forced at least one split

    tree.insert(40, "updated".to_string());  // upsert, not a duplicate
    assert_eq!(tree.search(&40), Some(&"updated".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(tree.len(), inserted.len());  // upsert must not change the key count
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
const T: usize = 2;

struct Node<K, V> {
    keys: Vec<K>,
    values: Vec<V>,
    children: Vec<Box<Node<K, V>>>,  // empty <=> leaf
}

impl<K: Ord, V> Node<K, V> {
    fn leaf() -> Self { Self { keys: Vec::new(), values: Vec::new(), children: Vec::new() } }
    fn is_leaf(&self) -> bool { self.children.is_empty() }
    fn is_full(&self) -> bool { self.keys.len() == 2 * T - 1 }
}

pub struct BTree<K, V> { root: Node<K, V> }

impl<K: Ord, V> BTree<K, V> {
    pub fn new() -> Self { Self { root: Node::leaf() } }

    pub fn search(&self, key: &K) -> Option<&V> { Self::search_node(&self.root, key) }

    fn search_node<'a>(node: &'a Node<K, V>, key: &K) -> Option<&'a V> {
        let pos = node.keys.partition_point(|k| k < key);  // binary search for the first key >= our target
        if pos < node.keys.len() && &node.keys[pos] == key {
            return Some(&node.values[pos]);
        }
        if node.is_leaf() { return None; }
        Self::search_node(&node.children[pos], key)
    }

    /// Insert, or overwrite the value if `key` already exists (upsert semantics).
    pub fn insert(&mut self, key: K, value: V) {
        if self.root.is_full() {
            // root is full — the tree can only grow taller by splitting the root FIRST,
            // unconditionally, before descending to insert (this is what keeps insert O(log n)
            // single-pass: we never have to backtrack up after finding a full node below).
            let old_root = std::mem::replace(&mut self.root, Node::leaf());
            let mut new_root = Node::leaf();
            new_root.children.push(Box::new(old_root));
            Self::split_child(&mut new_root, 0);
            self.root = new_root;
        }
        Self::insert_non_full(&mut self.root, key, value);
    }

    /// Splits `parent.children[i]`, which must be full, into two nodes of T-1 keys each,
    /// promoting its median key/value up into `parent` at index `i`.
    fn split_child(parent: &mut Node<K, V>, i: usize) {
        let child = &mut parent.children[i];

        let right_keys = child.keys.split_off(T);   // child keeps keys[0..T), right_keys takes keys[T..2T-1)
        let right_values = child.values.split_off(T);
        let median_key = child.keys.pop().unwrap();     // the last of child's remaining T keys IS the median
        let median_value = child.values.pop().unwrap();

        let right_children = if child.is_leaf() { Vec::new() } else { child.children.split_off(T) };
        let right_node = Node { keys: right_keys, values: right_values, children: right_children };

        parent.keys.insert(i, median_key);
        parent.values.insert(i, median_value);
        parent.children.insert(i + 1, Box::new(right_node));
    }

    fn insert_non_full(node: &mut Node<K, V>, key: K, value: V) {
        if node.is_leaf() {
            match node.keys.binary_search(&key) {
                Ok(existing) => node.values[existing] = value,  // upsert
                Err(pos) => { node.keys.insert(pos, key); node.values.insert(pos, value); }
            }
            return;
        }

        let mut pos = node.keys.partition_point(|k| k < &key);
        if pos < node.keys.len() && node.keys[pos] == key {
            node.values[pos] = value;  // key already lives at THIS internal level — upsert in place
            return;
        }

        if node.children[pos].is_full() {
            Self::split_child(node, pos);
            match key.cmp(&node.keys[pos]) {  // the just-promoted median might BE `key` itself
                std::cmp::Ordering::Equal => { node.values[pos] = value; return; }
                std::cmp::Ordering::Greater => pos += 1,
                std::cmp::Ordering::Less => {}
            }
        }
        Self::insert_non_full(&mut node.children[pos], key, value);
    }

    pub fn in_order(&self) -> Vec<(&K, &V)> {
        let mut out = Vec::new();
        Self::in_order_node(&self.root, &mut out);
        out
    }
    fn in_order_node<'a>(node: &'a Node<K, V>, out: &mut Vec<(&'a K, &'a V)>) {
        if node.is_leaf() {
            for i in 0..node.keys.len() { out.push((&node.keys[i], &node.values[i])); }
            return;
        }
        for i in 0..node.keys.len() {  // interleave: child[0], key[0], child[1], key[1], ... child[n]
            Self::in_order_node(&node.children[i], out);
            out.push((&node.keys[i], &node.values[i]));
        }
        Self::in_order_node(&node.children[node.keys.len()], out);
    }

    pub fn len(&self) -> usize { Self::len_node(&self.root) }
    fn len_node(node: &Node<K, V>) -> usize {
        node.keys.len() + node.children.iter().map(|c| Self::len_node(c)).sum::<usize>()
    }

    pub fn height(&self) -> usize { Self::height_node(&self.root) }
    fn height_node(node: &Node<K, V>) -> usize {
        if node.is_leaf() { 1 } else { 1 + Self::height_node(&node.children[0]) }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut tree: BTree<i32, String> = BTree::new();
    let inserted = [50,30,70,20,40,60,80,10,25,35,45,55,65,75,85,5,15,90,100,1];
    for &i in &inserted { tree.insert(i, format!("v{i}")); }

    let mut expected: Vec<i32> = inserted.to_vec();
    expected.sort_unstable();
    let collected: Vec<i32> = tree.in_order().into_iter().map(|(k, _)| *k).collect();
    assert_eq!(collected, expected);

    assert_eq!(tree.search(&40), Some(&"v40".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(tree.search(&999), None);
    assert!(tree.height() > 1);  // 20 insertions into a min-degree-2 tree must have forced at least one split

    tree.insert(40, "updated".to_string());  // upsert, not a duplicate
    assert_eq!(tree.search(&40), Some(&"updated".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(tree.len(), inserted.len());  // upsert must not change the key count
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Splits full nodes proactively on the way DOWN — checking and splitting node.children[pos] before recursing into it, rather than descending first and trying to split/rebalance on the way back up. This "pre-emptive split" is what makes a single top-down pass sufficient — a candidate who instead writes (or attempts) a post-order rebalancing pass has built something far more complex than necessary, and it's worth asking directly why they didn't split on the way down.
  • ★★★Handles the root-is-full case as a special, separate step in insert — recognizing that the root is the ONLY node allowed to be split without an existing parent to promote a median into, which requires manufacturing a brand-new root above it (the one way a B-tree's height ever increases).
  • ★★Uses Vec::split_off for the split rather than manually copying elements into a new Vec with a loop — recognizing this is exactly the operation split_off exists for, and it correctly moves ownership of the tail elements rather than cloning them.
  • ★Treats a duplicate key as an upsert (overwrite the value) rather than either silently ignoring it or inserting a genuine duplicate — and checks for this at EVERY internal level visited during descent, not just once at the final leaf, since B-tree keys can legitimately live at any internal level, not only in leaves.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Real databases use B+ trees, not plain B-trees like this one — what's the actual difference, and why does it matter for a disk-backed index?" — A B+ tree keeps ALL values only in the leaves (internal nodes store keys purely for routing, no values), and additionally links leaves together in a sorted linked list. This matters enormously for range scans (`WHERE x BETWEEN a AND b`): once you've found the starting leaf, you walk the leaf-level linked list directly instead of re-traversing from the root for each subsequent key — and since internal nodes carry no value payload, more keys fit per disk page, meaning a shallower tree and fewer disk reads to reach any leaf.
  • P2"This exercise never deletes anything — what makes B-tree deletion harder than insertion?" — Insertion only ever needs to SPLIT nodes that get too full, which composes cleanly on the way down. Deletion needs the mirror-image operation — MERGING or borrowing from a sibling when a node drops below the minimum key count (T-1) — and unlike splitting, merging requires looking at a node's siblings (not just itself), and if the key being deleted lives in an internal node rather than a leaf, you first need to find its in-order predecessor or successor to replace it with (the exact same idea as BST deletion in W43, but now interacting with the min-degree invariant on top).
  • P3"Why is a B-tree the right shape for a DISK-backed index, when a balanced binary tree (like your W43 BST) already gives O(log n) search?" — The real cost model for disk-backed structures isn't comparisons, it's DISK SEEKS — each node visited during a traversal is potentially a separate disk read, and disk latency dwarfs in-memory comparison cost by orders of magnitude. A binary tree with n keys has height ~log₂(n); a B-tree with branching factor ~100+ (sized to fill one disk page/block) has height ~log₁₀₀(n) — for a billion keys that's roughly 30 levels vs 5, a 6x reduction in disk seeks for the exact same dataset. The whole point of a high branching factor is minimizing tree HEIGHT, not minimizing comparisons.
🎯 Senior angle
The split algorithm is the entire exercise — everything else is bookkeeping around it. Have the candidate draw the tree on a whiteboard as they insert values, and watch what happens the moment a node hits its third key: do they split proactively before the NEXT insert would overflow it (correct), or do they try to insert into an already-full node and patch things up after the fact (a much harder, backtracking-heavy design that most people who "remember B-trees vaguely" gravitate toward)? That single decision point is the clearest signal in the whole problem.

Starter code to hand to candidate

Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
enum Token { Num(f64), Plus, Minus, Star, Slash, LParen, RParen, Eof }

#[derive(Debug)]
enum LexError { UnexpectedChar(char), BadNumber(String) }

impl std::fmt::Display for LexError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
        match self {
            LexError::UnexpectedChar(c) => write!(f, "unexpected character '{c}'"),
            LexError::BadNumber(raw) => write!(f, "invalid number literal '{raw}'"),
        }
    }
}

fn lex(input: &str) -> Result<Vec<Token>, LexError> {
    let mut chars = input.chars().peekable();
    let mut tokens = Vec::new();

    while let Some(&c) = chars.peek() {
        match c {
            ' ' | '\t' => { chars.next(); }
            '+' => { tokens.push(Token::Plus); chars.next(); }
            '-' => { tokens.push(Token::Minus); chars.next(); }
            '*' => { tokens.push(Token::Star); chars.next(); }
            '/' => { tokens.push(Token::Slash); chars.next(); }
            '(' => { tokens.push(Token::LParen); chars.next(); }
            ')' => { tokens.push(Token::RParen); chars.next(); }
            c if c.is_ascii_digit() || c == '.' => {
                let mut raw = String::new();
                while let Some(&c) = chars.peek() {
                    if c.is_ascii_digit() || c == '.' { raw.push(c); chars.next(); } else { break; }  // greedily consume the whole numeric literal
                }
                let value: f64 = raw.parse().map_err(|_| LexError::BadNumber(raw.clone()))?;
                tokens.push(Token::Num(value));
            }
            other => return Err(LexError::UnexpectedChar(other)),
        }
    }
    tokens.push(Token::Eof);
    Ok(tokens)
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
enum Op { Add, Sub, Mul, Div }

enum Expr { Num(f64), BinOp(Box<Expr>, Op, Box<Expr>) }

impl Expr {
    fn eval(&self) -> f64 {
        match self {
            Expr::Num(n) => *n,
            Expr::BinOp(l, op, r) => {
                let (lv, rv) = (l.eval(), r.eval());
                match op {
                    Op::Add => lv + rv, Op::Sub => lv - rv,
                    Op::Mul => lv * rv, Op::Div => lv / rv,
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

#[derive(Debug)]
enum ParseError { UnexpectedToken(Token) }

impl std::fmt::Display for ParseError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
        match self {
            ParseError::UnexpectedToken(t) => write!(f, "unexpected token {t:?}"),
        }
    }
}

struct Parser { tokens: Vec<Token>, pos: usize }

impl Parser {
    fn new(tokens: Vec<Token>) -> Self { Self { tokens, pos: 0 } }
    fn peek(&self) -> &Token { &self.tokens[self.pos] }
    fn advance(&mut self) -> Token { let t = self.tokens[self.pos].clone(); self.pos += 1; t }

    // expr := term (('+' | '-') term)*  — LOWEST precedence level, called first
    fn parse_expr(&mut self) -> Result<Expr, ParseError> {
        let mut left = self.parse_term()?;
        loop {
            let op = match self.peek() {
                Token::Plus => Op::Add, Token::Minus => Op::Sub, _ => break,
            };
            self.advance();
            let right = self.parse_term()?;
            left = Expr::BinOp(Box::new(left), op, Box::new(right));
        }
        Ok(left)
    }

    // term := factor (('*' | '/') factor)*  — HIGHER precedence, called FROM parse_expr,
    // which is exactly how "* binds tighter than +" falls out of the grammar's LAYERING
    // rather than any explicit precedence table or number.
    fn parse_term(&mut self) -> Result<Expr, ParseError> {
        let mut left = self.parse_factor()?;
        loop {
            let op = match self.peek() {
                Token::Star => Op::Mul, Token::Slash => Op::Div, _ => break,
            };
            self.advance();
            let right = self.parse_factor()?;
            left = Expr::BinOp(Box::new(left), op, Box::new(right));
        }
        Ok(left)
    }

    // factor := NUM | '(' expr ')' | '-' factor  — HIGHEST precedence, the recursion's base case
    fn parse_factor(&mut self) -> Result<Expr, ParseError> {
        match self.advance() {
            Token::Num(n) => Ok(Expr::Num(n)),
            Token::LParen => {
                let e = self.parse_expr()?;  // jump back to the LOWEST precedence level inside parens — resets precedence
                match self.advance() {
                    Token::RParen => Ok(e),
                    other => Err(ParseError::UnexpectedToken(other)),
                }
            }
            Token::Minus => {  // unary minus desugars to `0 - f`, reusing BinOp instead of a new AST node
                let f = self.parse_factor()?;
                Ok(Expr::BinOp(Box::new(Expr::Num(0.0)), Op::Sub, Box::new(f)))
            }
            other => Err(ParseError::UnexpectedToken(other)),
        }
    }
}

fn parse(input: &str) -> Result<Expr, String> {
    let tokens = lex(input).map_err(|e| format!("lex error: {e}"))?;
    let mut parser = Parser::new(tokens);
    let expr = parser.parse_expr().map_err(|e| format!("parse error: {e}"))?;
    if *parser.peek() != Token::Eof {  // grammar only consumes ONE full expression — leftover tokens mean a malformed input
        return Err(format!("trailing tokens starting at {:?}", parser.peek()));
    }
    Ok(expr)
}

fn main() {
    assert_eq!(parse("3 + 4 * 2").unwrap().eval(), 11.0);       // precedence: * before +
    assert_eq!(parse("(3 + 4) * 2").unwrap().eval(), 14.0);   // parens override precedence
    assert_eq!(parse("-5 + 3").unwrap().eval(), -2.0);        // unary minus
    assert_eq!(parse("2 * (3 + (4 - 1))").unwrap().eval(), 12.0); // nested parens

    assert!(parse("3 + ").is_err());
    assert!(parse("3 + + 4").is_err());
    assert!(parse("(3 + 4").is_err());
    assert!(parse("3 4").is_err());  // two numbers with no operator — caught by the trailing-tokens check, not the grammar itself
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Encodes precedence purely through which function calls which (parse_expr calls parse_term calls parse_factor) rather than through an explicit numeric precedence table or a Pratt-parser-style precedence-climbing loop — for a small, fixed grammar like arithmetic, layered recursive-descent functions ARE the standard, correct idiom, and a candidate reaching for a generic operator-precedence table here is over-engineering relative to the problem size (though it's the right call for a grammar with many more operators — worth asking about as a follow-up).
  • ★★★Checks for leftover tokens after parsing (if *parser.peek() != Token::Eof) — a very common bug is a parser that happily parses just the FIRST valid expression prefix of a malformed input and silently ignores everything after it (e.g. "3 4" would otherwise parse "3" successfully and never notice the trailing "4").
  • ★★Desugars unary minus into a binary 0 - x BinOp rather than adding a dedicated Expr::Neg AST variant — a legitimate, minimal-AST design choice worth stating explicitly (fewer variants to handle everywhere Expr is matched on, at the cost of a slightly less "obvious" AST shape for later compiler passes like constant folding).
  • ★Uses Peekable<Chars> in the lexer rather than indexing into a Vec<char> by position — peek()/next() on a peekable iterator is the idiomatic way to implement "look at the next character without consuming it yet," which every multi-character token (numbers, in this case) fundamentally needs.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"How would you add exponentiation (^) with the correct precedence AND right-associativity (2^3^2 should be 2^(3^2)=512, not (2^3)^2=64)?" — Add a new grammar level between term and factor (e.g. `parse_power`) called from parse_term's factor slot. For right-associativity specifically, the loop pattern used here (`left = BinOp(left, op, right)` repeatedly, which is naturally LEFT-associative) must be inverted to RECURSE on the right-hand side instead of looping: `fn parse_power(&mut self) -> Result { let base = self.parse_factor()?; if self.peek() == &Token::Caret { self.advance(); let exp = self.parse_power()?; /* recurse, not loop */ Ok(Expr::BinOp(Box::new(base), Op::Pow, Box::new(exp))) } else { Ok(base) } }` — recursing into itself for the right operand, rather than looping, is exactly what flips the associativity.
  • P2"Right now a lex error and a parse error are both just formatted into a String — what would you change for a real compiler that needs to report line/column numbers?" — Track a source position (line, column, or a byte offset) alongside each Token during lexing, then carry that position through into ParseError/LexError variants instead of discarding it — real compilers additionally track SPANS (start and end position) so error messages can underline the exact problematic substring, not just point at a single location.
  • P3"This parser bails out with Err on the very first problem it finds — what's the downside of that for a real compiler's user experience, and how do production compilers (rustc, clang) do better?" — Stopping at the first error means a file with 10 mistakes requires 10 separate compile-fix-recompile cycles to discover them all. Production compilers implement ERROR RECOVERY: after reporting an error, the parser tries to resynchronize (commonly by skipping tokens until it finds a likely statement/expression boundary) and keep parsing, so it can report multiple independent errors from a single pass — at the cost of significantly more complex parser logic, since a recovery heuristic can itself produce confusing cascading errors if it resynchronizes at the wrong point.
🎯 Senior angle
Ask the candidate to trace, by hand, exactly why 3 + 4 * 2 evaluates to 11 rather than 14 by walking through which function calls which — the precedence isn't encoded anywhere as data (no numbers, no table), it's encoded structurally in the call graph between parse_expr/parse_term/ parse_factor. A candidate who can explain that clearly, and can correctly predict what breaks if you swapped which function calls which, understands recursive descent at a level that transfers directly to reading real compiler front-ends (rustc's own parser is structured exactly this way).

// Compiler Exercise 54 · 45 min
W54 · Stack-Based Bytecode VM — Compiling an AST to a Linear Instruction Stream
post-order AST compilation stack machine execution disassembler well-formedness invariant checking Medium–Hard
Prompt
"Pairing with W53's front-end: compile an Expr AST into a flat Vec<OpCode> bytecode stream (PushConst, Add, Sub, Mul, Div, Neg), then implement a stack-based Vm that executes it. The VM must detect and report — not panic on — a malformed program: popping from an empty stack, dividing by zero, or a program that doesn't leave exactly one value on the stack when it finishes. Bonus: a disassemble function that pretty-prints the bytecode for debugging."
Starter code to hand to candidate
enum OpCode { PushConst(f64), Add, Sub, Mul, Div, Neg }
enum Expr { Num(f64), Add(Box<Expr>,Box<Expr>), Sub(..), Mul(..), Div(..), Neg(Box<Expr>) }

// TODO: fn compile(expr: &Expr, out: &mut Vec) — post-order walk
// TODO: struct Vm { stack: Vec } — fn run(&mut self, &[OpCode]) -> Result
// TODO: enum VmError { StackUnderflow, DivisionByZero, StackNotSingleValueAtEnd(usize) }

fn main() {
    // (3 + 4) * -2  =  -14
    let ast = Expr::Mul(
        Box::new(Expr::Add(Box::new(Expr::Num(3.0)), Box::new(Expr::Num(4.0)))),
        Box::new(Expr::Neg(Box::new(Expr::Num(2.0)))),
    );
    let mut bytecode = Vec::new();
    compile(&ast, &mut bytecode);
    assert_eq!(Vm::new().run(&bytecode).unwrap(), -14.0);
    println!("{}", disassemble(&bytecode));

    // (10 - 4) / 3 = 2 — also exercises Sub/Div, unused by the -14.0 case above
    let ast2 = Expr::Div(
        Box::new(Expr::Sub(Box::new(Expr::Num(10.0)), Box::new(Expr::Num(4.0)))),
        Box::new(Expr::Num(3.0)),
    );
    let mut bytecode2 = Vec::new();
    compile(&ast2, &mut bytecode2);
    assert_eq!(Vm::new().run(&bytecode2).unwrap(), 2.0);

    let div_by_zero = vec![OpCode::PushConst(1.0), OpCode::PushConst(0.0), OpCode::Div];
    assert_eq!(Vm::new().run(&div_by_zero), Err(VmError::DivisionByZero));

    let underflow = vec![OpCode::Add];
    assert_eq!(Vm::new().run(&underflow), Err(VmError::StackUnderflow));

    let malformed = vec![OpCode::PushConst(1.0), OpCode::PushConst(2.0)];  // leaves TWO values on the stack — invalid
    assert_eq!(Vm::new().run(&malformed), Err(VmError::StackNotSingleValueAtEnd(2)));

    assert_eq!(Vm::new().run(&bytecode).unwrap(), Vm::new().run(&bytecode).unwrap());  // bytecode is immutable data — all mutable state lives in the Vm, so re-running is deterministic

Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
enum OpCode { PushConst(f64), Add, Sub, Mul, Div, Neg }

enum Expr {
    Num(f64),
    Add(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>), Sub(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>),
    Mul(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>), Div(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>),
    Neg(Box<Expr>),
}

/// Post-order walk: each operand's bytecode is pushed BEFORE the operator that consumes
/// it, so by the time the VM executes e.g. `Add`, both operands are already on the stack.
fn compile(expr: &Expr, out: &mut Vec<OpCode>) {
    match expr {
        Expr::Num(n) => out.push(OpCode::PushConst(*n)),
        Expr::Add(l, r) => { compile(l, out); compile(r, out); out.push(OpCode::Add); }
        Expr::Sub(l, r) => { compile(l, out); compile(r, out); out.push(OpCode::Sub); }
        Expr::Mul(l, r) => { compile(l, out); compile(r, out); out.push(OpCode::Mul); }
        Expr::Div(l, r) => { compile(l, out); compile(r, out); out.push(OpCode::Div); }
        Expr::Neg(e) => { compile(e, out); out.push(OpCode::Neg); }
    }
}

fn disassemble(program: &[OpCode]) -> String {
    program.iter().enumerate()
        .map(|(i, op)| format!("{i:04}  {op:?}"))
        .collect::<Vec<_>>().join("\n")
}

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
enum VmError {
    StackUnderflow,
    DivisionByZero,
    StackNotSingleValueAtEnd(usize),  // a well-formed program must leave EXACTLY one value behind
}

struct Vm { stack: Vec<f64> }

impl Vm {
    fn new() -> Self { Self { stack: Vec::new() } }

    fn run(&mut self, program: &[OpCode]) -> Result<f64, VmError> {
        for &op in program {
            match op {
                OpCode::PushConst(n) => self.stack.push(n),
                OpCode::Add => self.binary(|a, b| Ok(a + b))?,
                OpCode::Sub => self.binary(|a, b| Ok(a - b))?,
                OpCode::Mul => self.binary(|a, b| Ok(a * b))?,
                OpCode::Div => self.binary(|a, b| if b == 0.0 { Err(VmError::DivisionByZero) } else { Ok(a / b) })?,
                OpCode::Neg => {
                    let v = self.stack.pop().ok_or(VmError::StackUnderflow)?;
                    self.stack.push(-v);
                }
            }
        }
        match self.stack.len() {
            1 => Ok(self.stack[0]),
            n => Err(VmError::StackNotSingleValueAtEnd(n)),
        }
    }

    fn binary(&mut self, f: impl FnOnce(f64, f64) -> Result<f64, VmError>) -> Result<(), VmError> {
        let b = self.stack.pop().ok_or(VmError::StackUnderflow)?;  // right operand was pushed LAST, so it pops FIRST
        let a = self.stack.pop().ok_or(VmError::StackUnderflow)?;
        self.stack.push(f(a, b)?);
        Ok(())
    }
}

fn main() {
    // (3 + 4) * -2  =  -14
    let ast = Expr::Mul(
        Box::new(Expr::Add(Box::new(Expr::Num(3.0)), Box::new(Expr::Num(4.0)))),
        Box::new(Expr::Neg(Box::new(Expr::Num(2.0)))),
    );
    let mut bytecode = Vec::new();
    compile(&ast, &mut bytecode);
    assert_eq!(Vm::new().run(&bytecode).unwrap(), -14.0);
    println!("{}", disassemble(&bytecode));

    // (10 - 4) / 3 = 2 — also exercises Sub/Div, unused by the -14.0 case above
    let ast2 = Expr::Div(
        Box::new(Expr::Sub(Box::new(Expr::Num(10.0)), Box::new(Expr::Num(4.0)))),
        Box::new(Expr::Num(3.0)),
    );
    let mut bytecode2 = Vec::new();
    compile(&ast2, &mut bytecode2);
    assert_eq!(Vm::new().run(&bytecode2).unwrap(), 2.0);

    let div_by_zero = vec![OpCode::PushConst(1.0), OpCode::PushConst(0.0), OpCode::Div];
    assert_eq!(Vm::new().run(&div_by_zero), Err(VmError::DivisionByZero));

    let underflow = vec![OpCode::Add];
    assert_eq!(Vm::new().run(&underflow), Err(VmError::StackUnderflow));

    let malformed = vec![OpCode::PushConst(1.0), OpCode::PushConst(2.0)];  // leaves TWO values on the stack — invalid
    assert_eq!(Vm::new().run(&malformed), Err(VmError::StackNotSingleValueAtEnd(2)));

    assert_eq!(Vm::new().run(&bytecode).unwrap(), Vm::new().run(&bytecode).unwrap());  // bytecode is immutable data — all mutable state lives in the Vm, so re-running is deterministic
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Pops operands in the correct order for non-commutative operators — for Sub/Div, the RIGHT operand was pushed last (so it pops FIRST); a candidate who writes a - b using whichever pop happens first without thinking about push order will get subtraction and division backwards, and it's an easy bug to miss since Add/Mul being commutative would still pass their tests.
  • ★★★Cleanly separates the VM's error cases (StackUnderflow, DivisionByZero, StackNotSingleValueAtEnd) into a real enum returned via Result, rather than panicking on a malformed program — a VM executing untrusted or buggy compiler output needs to fail predictably, not crash the host process.
  • ★★Checks the final stack has EXACTLY one value, not just "at least one" — a program that leaves two or more values behind is just as malformed as one that underflows, and silently returning only stack[0] or stack.last() would mask a real compiler bug rather than surface it.
  • ★Factors the four binary operators through one shared binary() helper taking a closure, rather than duplicating the "pop b, pop a, check underflow twice, push result" sequence four times — DRY-ing out identical stack-manipulation boilerplate while keeping the actual arithmetic (and division's special zero-check) distinct per call site.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"How would you add variables (like `x`) to this language — what changes in both the compiler and the VM?" — The VM needs actual mutable state beyond the stack: a `Vec` (or `HashMap`) of variable slots, plus new opcodes `LoadVar(usize)` (push a variable's current value) and `StoreVar(usize)` (pop the top of stack into a variable). The compiler needs a symbol table mapping variable names to slot indices at compile time — this is genuinely the first step toward a real bytecode language rather than a pure calculator, and it's where "compile-time name resolution" as a concept first becomes necessary.
  • P2"Real VMs (the JVM, CPython) do constant folding and other optimizations on bytecode — could you fold `PushConst(3), PushConst(4), Add` into a single `PushConst(7)` as a post-compile pass, and does it need to inspect the AST or the bytecode?" — It can be done as a peephole optimization purely on the flat bytecode stream itself: scan for the pattern `[PushConst(a), PushConst(b), ]` and replace it in-place with `[PushConst(folded_result)]` — no need to go back to the AST at all, since by this point the bytecode already fully captures the computation. This is a good moment to see if a candidate recognizes bytecode-level peephole optimization as a DISTINCT technique from AST-level constant folding (which would instead pattern-match `Expr::Add(Expr::Num(a), Expr::Num(b))` before compilation ever happens).
  • P3"This VM uses a Vec as an operand stack with dynamic push/pop — how would a register-based VM (like Lua's actual bytecode) differ, and why might it be faster?" — A register-based VM has instructions reference explicit "register" slots (a fixed-size local array) directly, e.g. `Add r0, r1, r2` meaning "r0 = r1 + r2", rather than implicitly operating on whatever's on top of a stack. This eliminates a large fraction of PushConst/pop traffic for intermediate values — fewer total instructions need to execute for the same computation — at the cost of a more complex compiler that must do register allocation (deciding which register holds which intermediate value) instead of just emitting a linear post-order walk.
🎯 Senior angle
Have the candidate compile 10 - 3 by hand and trace exactly which value pops first inside binary(). This one detail — right-operand-pops-first, because it was pushed last — is where a stack-machine implementation silently breaks for every non-commutative operator if you get it backwards, and it's exactly the kind of "obviously correct until you actually trace it" bug that only shows up when someone has genuinely built (not just read about) a stack-based VM before.

W55 · Generational Arena — Safe, Stale-Handle-Proof Typed Indices
free-list recycling generation counter 100% safe Rust ABA-bug prevention Medium–Hard
Prompt
"Implement a generational arena — the pattern behind every game engine's entity system, most graph/AST node storage in compilers, and slotmap-style crates: Arena<T> with insert(&mut self, T) -> Handle, get(&self, Handle) -> Option<&T>, get_mut, and remove(&mut self, Handle) -> Option<T>. Removed slots must be recycled for future inserts (not just left empty forever), but a Handle captured before a removal must never resolve to whatever new value later reuses that slot's index — entirely with safe code, no Rc/RefCell, no unsafe."
Starter code to hand to candidate
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub struct Handle { index: usize, generation: u32 }

// TODO: enum Slot { Occupied { value: T, generation: u32 }, Vacant { generation: u32, next_free: Option } }
// TODO: struct Arena { slots: Vec>, free_head: Option, len: usize }
// TODO: impl Arena — insert, get, get_mut, remove, len — free-list based slot reuse

fn main() {
    let mut arena: Arena<String> = Arena::new();
    let h1 = arena.insert("alice".to_string());
    let h2 = arena.insert("bob".to_string());

    arena.remove(h1);
    assert_eq!(arena.get(h1), None);  // removed handle correctly resolves to None
    assert_eq!(arena.remove(h1), None);  // double-remove is a safe no-op, not a panic

    let h3 = arena.insert("carol".to_string());  // reuses h1's freed slot INDEX
    assert_eq!(h3.index, h1.index);
    assert_ne!(h3.generation, h1.generation);  // but the generation is bumped

    // the crux of the whole pattern: h1 is stale now, but its INDEX has been physically
    // reused by h3 — without the generation check this would incorrectly resolve to "carol"
    assert_eq!(arena.get(h1), None);
    assert_eq!(arena.get(h3).unwrap(), "carol");
    assert_eq!(arena.get(h2).unwrap(), "bob");  // unrelated live handle unaffected by h1's churn

    if let Some(v) = arena.get_mut(h2) { v.push_str("!"); }
    assert_eq!(arena.get(h2).unwrap(), "bob!");
    assert_eq!(arena.len(), 2);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub struct Handle { index: usize, generation: u32 }

enum Slot<T> {
    Occupied { value: T, generation: u32 },
    Vacant { generation: u32, next_free: Option<usize> },  // next_free chains vacant slots into a singly-linked free list
}

/// A Vec-backed pool of `T`s addressed by Handle instead of raw indices or pointers. Every
/// slot carries a generation counter that bumps on removal, so a stale Handle captured
/// before a remove() can never accidentally resolve to whatever unrelated value later
/// reuses that same slot index — the classic "ABA" bug, closed off entirely with safe code.
pub struct Arena<T> { slots: Vec<Slot<T>>, free_head: Option<usize>, len: usize }

impl<T> Arena<T> {
    pub fn new() -> Self { Self { slots: Vec::new(), free_head: None, len: 0 } }

    pub fn insert(&mut self, value: T) -> Handle {
        match self.free_head {
            Some(index) => {
                let generation = match self.slots[index] {  // pop the head of the free list
                    Slot::Vacant { generation, next_free } => { self.free_head = next_free; generation }
                    Slot::Occupied { .. } => unreachable!("free list pointed at an occupied slot"),
                };
                self.slots[index] = Slot::Occupied { value, generation };
                self.len += 1;
                Handle { index, generation }
            }
            None => {
                let index = self.slots.len();
                self.slots.push(Slot::Occupied { value, generation: 0 });  // no free slots — grow the backing Vec
                self.len += 1;
                Handle { index, generation: 0 }
            }
        }
    }

    pub fn get(&self, handle: Handle) -> Option<&T> {
        match self.slots.get(handle.index)? {
            Slot::Occupied { value, generation } if *generation == handle.generation => Some(value),  // generation MUST match — the entire safety property lives on this one line
            _ => None,
        }
    }

    pub fn get_mut(&mut self, handle: Handle) -> Option<&mut T> {
        match self.slots.get_mut(handle.index)? {
            Slot::Occupied { value, generation } if *generation == handle.generation => Some(value),
            _ => None,
        }
    }

    pub fn remove(&mut self, handle: Handle) -> Option<T> {
        match self.slots.get(handle.index) {
            Some(Slot::Occupied { generation, .. }) if *generation == handle.generation => {
                let next_generation = handle.generation.wrapping_add(1);  // bump so ANY handle captured before this remove() is now permanently stale
                let old = std::mem::replace(
                    &mut self.slots[handle.index],
                    Slot::Vacant { generation: next_generation, next_free: self.free_head },
                );
                self.free_head = Some(handle.index);
                self.len -= 1;
                match old { Slot::Occupied { value, .. } => Some(value), Slot::Vacant { .. } => unreachable!() }
            }
            _ => None,
        }
    }

    pub fn len(&self) -> usize { self.len }
}

fn main() {
    let mut arena: Arena<String> = Arena::new();
    let h1 = arena.insert("alice".to_string());
    let h2 = arena.insert("bob".to_string());

    arena.remove(h1);
    assert_eq!(arena.get(h1), None);  // removed handle correctly resolves to None
    assert_eq!(arena.remove(h1), None);  // double-remove is a safe no-op, not a panic

    let h3 = arena.insert("carol".to_string());  // reuses h1's freed slot INDEX
    assert_eq!(h3.index, h1.index);
    assert_ne!(h3.generation, h1.generation);  // but the generation is bumped

    // the crux of the whole pattern: h1 is stale now, but its INDEX has been physically
    // reused by h3 — without the generation check this would incorrectly resolve to "carol"
    assert_eq!(arena.get(h1), None);
    assert_eq!(arena.get(h3).unwrap(), "carol");
    assert_eq!(arena.get(h2).unwrap(), "bob");  // unrelated live handle unaffected by h1's churn

    if let Some(v) = arena.get_mut(h2) { v.push_str("!"); }
    assert_eq!(arena.get(h2).unwrap(), "bob!");
    assert_eq!(arena.len(), 2);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Bumps the generation counter on remove, not on insert — the generation must live in the VACANT slot state and travel forward with it, so that the NEXT occupant of that index starts at the bumped value, which is what makes every handle issued before the removal permanently unable to match again.
  • ★★★Threads a free list through the vacant slots themselves (next_free: Option<usize> inside Slot::Vacant) rather than maintaining a separate Vec<usize> of free indices — reusing the already-allocated vacant slot's own memory to store the linked-list pointer costs zero extra allocation.
  • ★★Guards every accessor (get/get_mut/remove) with the exact same generation-match condition, not just get — a common half-finished version checks the generation on read but forgets to gate remove the same way, which would let a stale handle incorrectly remove whatever NEW value now occupies its old slot.
  • ★Solves this with zero unsafe, zero Rc/RefCell — recognizing that the generation-counter technique achieves memory safety and use-after-free prevention through pure data modeling (an extra integer comparison), not through runtime reference counting or borrow-checking bypass.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"generation is a u32 — what happens after 4 billion insert/remove cycles on the SAME slot index wrap it back to a value a still-live old handle happens to match?" — Technically possible (`wrapping_add` explicitly allows the wraparound rather than panicking), but astronomically unlikely in practice for any realistic workload — 4 billion churns of one specific slot is an enormous number even for a very hot slot in a long-running process. Production slotmap-style crates typically accept this same theoretical risk rather than paying for a wider (u64) generation counter, though using u64 instead would be a legitimate, simple hardening if the risk profile genuinely warranted it — the key signal is recognizing this as a real, nameable (if negligible) edge case rather than either dismissing it as impossible or treating it as an urgent bug.
  • P2"How does this compare to just using Vec> with plain usize indices instead of Handle?" — Vec> with raw usize indices has EXACTLY the ABA vulnerability this design closes: remove index 5, insert something new, and it lands at index 5 again — any old usize "handle" a caller held onto now silently, incorrectly resolves to the new value with no way to detect the mistake. The generation counter is the entire difference, and it's a nearly-free addition (one extra u32 per slot, one integer comparison per access) for a real safety guarantee.
  • P3"Where would you actually reach for this pattern over Rc> in a real codebase — what's the concrete trade-off?" — Generational arenas shine for large, homogeneous COLLECTIONS of similar objects with complex, changing relationships between them (ECS entity/component systems, a compiler's AST/IR nodes referencing each other by ID, a graph's nodes and edges) — you get cheap Copy handles instead of reference-counted pointers, no runtime borrow-checking panics from RefCell, and everything lives in one contiguous, cache-friendlier allocation. Rc> remains the better fit for a small number of genuinely individually-owned objects with organic, tree-like or ad-hoc sharing patterns that don't naturally form a single homogeneous pool.
🎯 Senior angle
This is a great complement to W17's raw bump allocator: both solve a "how do you manage a pool of objects efficiently" problem, but this one does it with zero unsafe and zero reference counting — purely through data design (an extra integer per slot). Ask a candidate who's only ever reached for Rc<RefCell<T>> to solve "objects that reference each other" whether this pattern could replace it in a specific scenario you describe (an AST, a scene graph) — recognizing when a generational index is the more appropriate tool is a genuine architectural judgement call, not just a syntax exercise.

// Database Exercise 56 · 75 min
W56 · LSM-Tree — Memtable, SSTables, Tombstones & Compaction
BTreeMap memtable immutable sorted SSTables tombstone deletes newest-wins compaction merge Hard
Prompt
"Implement an LSM-tree — the write-optimized storage engine behind Cassandra, RocksDB, and LevelDB. put/delete go into an in-memory memtable (a BTreeMap); once it hits a size limit, flush it into a new immutable, sorted SSTable. get must check the memtable first, then SSTables newest-to-oldest, stopping at the first match. Deletes are tombstones (a marker, not an actual removal) so they can correctly mask an older value that lives in an older, already-flushed SSTable. Finally, implement compact: merge all SSTables into one, keeping only the newest version of each key, and only NOW discard tombstones for good."
Starter code to hand to candidate
enum Value { Present(String), Tombstone }
struct SSTable { entries: Vec<(String, Value)> }  // sorted, immutable once created

struct LsmTree {
    memtable: BTreeMap<String, Value>,
    memtable_limit: usize,
    sstables: Vec<SSTable>,  // oldest first, newest LAST
}

// TODO: impl LsmTree — put, delete, get (memtable -> sstables newest-first), flush, compact

fn main() {
    let mut db = LsmTree::new(3);  // tiny limit on purpose — forces multiple SSTable flushes

    db.put("a".into(), "1".into());
    db.put("b".into(), "2".into());
    db.put("c".into(), "3".into());  // flush #1 -> sstable [a=1, b=2, c=3]

    db.put("a".into(), "10".into());  // newer value for "a" — still sitting in the memtable
    db.put("d".into(), "4".into());
    db.delete("b".into());  // flush #2 -> sstable [a=10, b=tombstone, d=4]

    assert_eq!(db.sstables.len(), 2);
    assert_eq!(db.get("a"), Some("10".to_string()));  // newer sstable wins over the older one
    assert_eq!(db.get("b"), None);  // tombstone in the newer sstable masks the older, still-present value
    assert_eq!(db.get("c"), Some("3".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(db.get("d"), Some("4".to_string()));

    db.compact();
    assert_eq!(db.sstables.len(), 1);  // merged down to a single table
    assert_eq!(db.get("a"), Some("10".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(db.get("b"), None);  // still reads as deleted after the tombstone ITSELF is gone

    assert!(!db.sstables[0].entries.iter().any(|(k, _)| k == "b"));  // verify the tombstone was actually DROPPED, not merely masked
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::collections::BTreeMap;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
enum Value {
    Present(String),
    Tombstone,  // marks a deletion so it can outlive the memtable flush that recorded it
}

/// An immutable, key-sorted snapshot of a flushed memtable. Once created it is never
/// mutated — exactly like a real SSTable on disk, only ever superseded or merged away.
struct SSTable { entries: Vec<(String, Value)> }

impl SSTable {
    fn from_memtable(memtable: &BTreeMap<String, Value>) -> Self {
        Self { entries: memtable.iter().map(|(k, v)| (k.clone(), v.clone())).collect() }
    }
    fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<&Value> {
        self.entries.binary_search_by(|(k, _)| k.as_str().cmp(key)).ok().map(|i| &self.entries[i].1)
    }
}

struct LsmTree {
    memtable: BTreeMap<String, Value>,
    memtable_limit: usize,
    sstables: Vec<SSTable>,  // oldest first, newest LAST
}

impl LsmTree {
    fn new(memtable_limit: usize) -> Self {
        Self { memtable: BTreeMap::new(), memtable_limit, sstables: Vec::new() }
    }

    fn put(&mut self, key: String, value: String) {
        self.memtable.insert(key, Value::Present(value));
        self.maybe_flush();
    }
    fn delete(&mut self, key: String) {
        self.memtable.insert(key, Value::Tombstone);
        self.maybe_flush();
    }
    fn maybe_flush(&mut self) {
        if self.memtable.len() >= self.memtable_limit { self.flush(); }
    }
    fn flush(&mut self) {
        if self.memtable.is_empty() { return; }
        let table = SSTable::from_memtable(&self.memtable);
        self.memtable.clear();
        self.sstables.push(table);
    }

    /// Lookup order matters: memtable is always freshest, then SSTables newest-first — the
    /// first Value found for `key`, anywhere in that order, is authoritative.
    fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<String> {
        if let Some(v) = self.memtable.get(key) { return Self::unwrap_value(v); }
        for table in self.sstables.iter().rev() {
            if let Some(v) = table.get(key) { return Self::unwrap_value(v); }
        }
        None
    }
    fn unwrap_value(v: &Value) -> Option<String> {
        match v { Value::Present(s) => Some(s.clone()), Value::Tombstone => None }
    }

    /// Merges every SSTable (oldest -> newest, so later writes correctly overwrite earlier
    /// ones for the same key) into a single table, dropping tombstones for good — once a
    /// compaction has merged away every older version of a key, the tombstone has done its
    /// job and can finally be discarded instead of taking up space forever.
    fn compact(&mut self) {
        self.flush();
        if self.sstables.len() <= 1 { return; }

        let mut merged: BTreeMap<String, Value> = BTreeMap::new();
        for table in self.sstables.drain(..) {
            for (k, v) in table.entries { merged.insert(k, v); }  // oldest -> newest order means the LAST insert per key wins, matching real recency
        }
        merged.retain(|_, v| !matches!(v, Value::Tombstone));  // NOW it's safe to drop tombstones — every older version they masked is gone too

        if !merged.is_empty() {
            self.sstables.push(SSTable { entries: merged.into_iter().collect() });
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut db = LsmTree::new(3);  // tiny limit on purpose — forces multiple SSTable flushes

    db.put("a".into(), "1".into());
    db.put("b".into(), "2".into());
    db.put("c".into(), "3".into());  // flush #1 -> sstable [a=1, b=2, c=3]

    db.put("a".into(), "10".into());  // newer value for "a" — still sitting in the memtable
    db.put("d".into(), "4".into());
    db.delete("b".into());  // flush #2 -> sstable [a=10, b=tombstone, d=4]

    assert_eq!(db.sstables.len(), 2);
    assert_eq!(db.get("a"), Some("10".to_string()));  // newer sstable wins over the older one
    assert_eq!(db.get("b"), None);  // tombstone in the newer sstable masks the older, still-present value
    assert_eq!(db.get("c"), Some("3".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(db.get("d"), Some("4".to_string()));

    db.compact();
    assert_eq!(db.sstables.len(), 1);  // merged down to a single table
    assert_eq!(db.get("a"), Some("10".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(db.get("b"), None);  // still reads as deleted after the tombstone ITSELF is gone

    assert!(!db.sstables[0].entries.iter().any(|(k, _)| k == "b"));  // verify the tombstone was actually DROPPED, not merely masked
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Uses a tombstone marker for deletes, not an actual removal from the memtable — if delete just removed the key from the memtable outright, a subsequent get would fall through to an OLDER SSTable and incorrectly resurrect a value that was supposed to be deleted. The tombstone has to be a real, first-class value that positively masks older data, exactly like a "present" value does.
  • ★★★Searches SSTables newest-to-oldest and stops at the first match (.iter().rev(), early return) — reflecting the fundamental LSM invariant that more-recently-flushed data is always more authoritative for a given key, and a candidate who searches oldest-to-first (or scans all of them and picks... something) has the recency model backwards.
  • ★★Only drops tombstones during compact, never during an ordinary flush — a tombstone that got discarded prematurely (say, during a routine flush rather than a full compaction that's actually merged away every older version) would let an older SSTable's stale value silently resurface on the next get.
  • ★Keeps each SSTable genuinely immutable once created (no method mutates entries after construction) — compaction always builds a brand-new merged table and discards the old ones wholesale via drain, mirroring how a real LSM engine never edits an on-disk SSTable file in place.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"get() here scans EVERY SSTable in the worst case — how do real LSM engines (RocksDB, Cassandra) avoid that for a key that doesn't exist at all?" — Bloom filters: a small, probabilistic, per-SSTable structure that can say "definitely not present" (skip this SSTable entirely, no disk read needed) or "maybe present" (worth actually checking) — false positives are possible (occasionally checking a table that doesn't actually have the key) but false negatives are not, so a Bloom filter can only ever save work, never cause an incorrect miss. This is one of the single highest-leverage optimizations in real LSM-tree implementations specifically because most point lookups in a large database are for keys that DON'T exist in most SSTables.
  • P2"This design keeps compacting into fewer, bigger tables — what's the actual trade-off LSM-trees make that a plain B-tree (W52) doesn't, and why would anyone choose this?" — LSM-trees trade READ amplification (a point lookup might have to check several SSTables) and periodic COMPACTION overhead (background CPU/IO work merging tables) for dramatically cheaper, purely-sequential WRITES (every write just appends to an in-memory memtable and, eventually, a new immutable file — no in-place random-access disk seeks to update an existing B-tree node). This makes LSM-trees the right choice for write-heavy workloads (time-series data, logging, high-ingest analytics) while B-trees remain better for read-heavy, point-lookup-dominated workloads where you want the fewest possible disk seeks per read.
  • P3"Real systems don't just merge ALL sstables into one giant table every time — what's 'leveled' vs 'size-tiered' compaction, and why does the strategy matter?" — Size-tiered compaction merges similarly-SIZED sstables together as they accumulate (simple, but read amplification stays roughly proportional to the number of sstables, and compactions can temporarily need up to 2x the disk space). Leveled compaction organizes sstables into levels of exponentially increasing size, where each level (past the first) has non-overlapping key ranges — bounding worst-case read amplification much more tightly at the cost of more total compaction I/O over time. Naming this trade-off (write amplification vs read amplification vs space amplification — the "RUM conjecture" territory) is a strong senior-database-systems signal.
🎯 Senior angle
Ask the candidate to explain, without looking at their own code, exactly what would go wrong if delete simply removed the key from the memtable instead of writing a tombstone — most candidates who've never actually built a storage engine will need a moment to realize the bug (a stale value resurfacing from an older SSTable) rather than seeing it immediately. That gap between "the tombstone pattern" as vocabulary and as internalized, load-bearing understanding is exactly the signal this exercise is designed to surface.

fn main() {
    // Harden · get() here scans EVERY SSTable in the worst case — how do real LSM en…
    harden_w56_1();
    // Parent exercise still holds after the harden change:
    let mut db = LsmTree::new(3);  // tiny limit on purpose — forces multiple SSTable flushes

    db.put("a".into(), "1".into());
    db.put("b".into(), "2".into());
    db.put("c".into(), "3".into());  // flush #1 -> sstable [a=1, b=2, c=3]

    db.put("a".into(), "10".into());  // newer value for "a" — still sitting in the memtable
    db.put("d".into(), "4".into());
    db.delete("b".into());  // flush #2 -> sstable [a=10, b=tombstone, d=4]

    assert_eq!(db.sstables.len(), 2);
    assert_eq!(db.get("a"), Some("10".to_string()));  // newer sstable wins over the older one
    assert_eq!(db.get("b"), None);  // tombstone in the newer sstable masks the older, still-present value
    assert_eq!(db.get("c"), Some("3".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(db.get("d"), Some("4".to_string()));

    db.compact();
    assert_eq!(db.sstables.len(), 1);  // merged down to a single table
    assert_eq!(db.get("a"), Some("10".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(db.get("b"), None);  // still reads as deleted after the tombstone ITSELF is gone

    assert!(!db.sstables[0].entries.iter().any(|(k, _)| k == "b"));  // verify the tombstone was actually DROPPED, not merely masked
}
