W57 · Generic Blocking Connection Pool — Condvar, RAII, Timeouts
Mutex + Condvar RAII guard via Deref/Drop wait_timeout generic factory closure Hard
Prompt
"Implement a generic, thread-safe Pool<T: Connection> with a bounded max_size: acquire(&self, timeout: Duration) -> Option<PooledConn<T>> blocks (parked on a Condvar, not spinning) until either an idle healthy connection is available, a new one can be created under the cap, or the timeout elapses. PooledConn must be an RAII guard — dropping it automatically returns the connection to the pool, so callers can never forget to release one. Discard unhealthy idle connections instead of ever handing them back out."
Starter code to hand to candidate
trait Connection: Send { fn is_healthy(&self) -> bool; }

struct PoolInner<T> { idle: Vec<T>, total: usize, max_size: usize }
struct Pool<T> { inner: Mutex<PoolInner<T>>, cond: Condvar, factory: Box<dyn Fn() -> T + Send + Sync> }

// TODO: struct PooledConn — Deref/DerefMut/Drop returning the conn to the pool
// TODO: impl Pool — new(max_size, factory), acquire(timeout), release(conn)

fn main() {
    use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
    use std::thread;

    struct SimpleConn { id: u32, healthy: bool }
    impl Connection for SimpleConn { fn is_healthy(&self) -> bool { self.healthy } }

    let next_id = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let next_id_for_factory = next_id.clone();
    let pool: Arc<Pool<SimpleConn>> = Arc::new(Pool::new(2, move || {
        let id = next_id_for_factory.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst) as u32;
        SimpleConn { id, healthy: true }
    }));

    let concurrent = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let max_concurrent = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..6 {
        let (pool, concurrent, max_concurrent) = (pool.clone(), concurrent.clone(), max_concurrent.clone());
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            let conn = pool.acquire(Duration::from_secs(2)).expect("generous timeout");
            let now = concurrent.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst) + 1;
            max_concurrent.fetch_max(now, Ordering::SeqCst);
            thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(30));
            concurrent.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
            assert!(conn.id < 2);  // pool should never construct more than max_size distinct connections
            drop(conn);  // RAII — returns the connection to the pool right here
        }));
    }
    for h in handles { h.join().unwrap(); }

    assert!(max_concurrent.load(Ordering::SeqCst) <= 2);  // pool never exceeded max_size checked-out connections
    assert_eq!(next_id.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 2);  // exactly max_size connections ever constructed, reused after that

    // Timeout path: exhaust the pool deliberately, confirm acquire() respects the timeout
    let g1 = pool.acquire(Duration::from_millis(100)).unwrap();
    let g2 = pool.acquire(Duration::from_millis(100)).unwrap();
    let start = Instant::now();
    let g3 = pool.acquire(Duration::from_millis(100));
    assert!(g3.is_none());  // pool exhausted — must time out, not block forever
    assert!(start.elapsed() >= Duration::from_millis(90));
    drop(g1); drop(g2);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::sync::{Arc, Condvar, Mutex};
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

trait Connection: Send { fn is_healthy(&self) -> bool; }

struct PoolInner<T> { idle: Vec<T>, total: usize, max_size: usize }

struct Pool<T> {
    inner: Mutex<PoolInner<T>>,
    cond: Condvar,
    factory: Box<dyn Fn() -> T + Send + Sync>,
}

/// RAII guard — returns its connection to the pool automatically on drop, so callers can
/// never forget to release one back (the classic connection-leak bug class).
struct PooledConn<'a, T: Connection> { pool: &'a Pool<T>, conn: Option<T> }

impl<T: Connection> std::ops::Deref for PooledConn<'_, T> {
    type Target = T;
    fn deref(&self) -> &T { self.conn.as_ref().unwrap() }
}
impl<T: Connection> std::ops::DerefMut for PooledConn<'_, T> {
    fn deref_mut(&mut self) -> &mut T { self.conn.as_mut().unwrap() }
}
impl<T: Connection> Drop for PooledConn<'_, T> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        if let Some(conn) = self.conn.take() { self.pool.release(conn); }
    }
}

impl<T: Connection> Pool<T> {
    fn new(max_size: usize, factory: impl Fn() -> T + Send + Sync + 'static) -> Self {
        Self { inner: Mutex::new(PoolInner { idle: Vec::new(), total: 0, max_size }), cond: Condvar::new(), factory: Box::new(factory) }
    }

    /// Blocks (parked on a Condvar, NOT spinning) until an idle+healthy connection exists,
    /// a brand-new one can be built under max_size, or `timeout` elapses — whichever first.
    fn acquire(&self, timeout: Duration) -> Option<PooledConn<'_, T>> {
        let deadline = Instant::now() + timeout;
        let mut guard = self.inner.lock().unwrap();

        loop {
            while let Some(conn) = guard.idle.pop() {
                if conn.is_healthy() {
                    return Some(PooledConn { pool: self, conn: Some(conn) });
                }
                guard.total -= 1;  // discard unhealthy connections instead of ever handing them out
            }

            if guard.total < guard.max_size {
                guard.total += 1;
                let conn = (self.factory)();
                return Some(PooledConn { pool: self, conn: Some(conn) });
            }

            let now = Instant::now();
            if now >= deadline { return None; }
            let (g, wait_result) = self.cond.wait_timeout(guard, deadline - now).unwrap();  // releases the lock while parked, reacquires it on wake
            guard = g;
            if wait_result.timed_out() { return None; }
            // spurious wakeup or a real notify_one() — either way, loop back and re-check state
        }
    }

    fn release(&self, conn: T) {
        let mut guard = self.inner.lock().unwrap();
        guard.idle.push(conn);
        drop(guard);  // release the lock BEFORE notifying — avoids waking a thread that immediately blocks again on the same mutex
        self.cond.notify_one();
    }
}

fn main() {
    use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
    use std::thread;

    struct SimpleConn { id: u32, healthy: bool }
    impl Connection for SimpleConn { fn is_healthy(&self) -> bool { self.healthy } }

    let next_id = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let next_id_for_factory = next_id.clone();
    let pool: Arc<Pool<SimpleConn>> = Arc::new(Pool::new(2, move || {
        let id = next_id_for_factory.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst) as u32;
        SimpleConn { id, healthy: true }
    }));

    let concurrent = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let max_concurrent = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..6 {
        let (pool, concurrent, max_concurrent) = (pool.clone(), concurrent.clone(), max_concurrent.clone());
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            let conn = pool.acquire(Duration::from_secs(2)).expect("generous timeout");
            let now = concurrent.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst) + 1;
            max_concurrent.fetch_max(now, Ordering::SeqCst);
            thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(30));
            concurrent.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
            assert!(conn.id < 2);  // pool should never construct more than max_size distinct connections
            drop(conn);  // RAII — returns the connection to the pool right here
        }));
    }
    for h in handles { h.join().unwrap(); }

    assert!(max_concurrent.load(Ordering::SeqCst) <= 2);  // pool never exceeded max_size checked-out connections
    assert_eq!(next_id.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 2);  // exactly max_size connections ever constructed, reused after that

    // Timeout path: exhaust the pool deliberately, confirm acquire() respects the timeout
    let g1 = pool.acquire(Duration::from_millis(100)).unwrap();
    let g2 = pool.acquire(Duration::from_millis(100)).unwrap();
    let start = Instant::now();
    let g3 = pool.acquire(Duration::from_millis(100));
    assert!(g3.is_none());  // pool exhausted — must time out, not block forever
    assert!(start.elapsed() >= Duration::from_millis(90));
    drop(g1); drop(g2);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Blocks on a Condvar rather than busy-polling — a pool is a "wait for a resource that some OTHER thread will free" problem, which is precisely what condition variables exist for; a candidate who reaches for a sleep-and-retry loop instead is burning CPU for no reason and adding needless latency between a connection becoming free and a waiter noticing.
  • ★★★Makes PooledConn's Drop return the connection automatically rather than requiring callers to call an explicit pool.release(conn) — this closes off an entire, extremely common bug class (a caller that forgets to release, or forgets on an early-return/panic path) purely through RAII, with zero cooperation required from callers.
  • ★★★Discovers (or is told, and correctly applies) that a Drop impl's bounds must exactly match its type's declared bounds — impl<T> Drop for PooledConn<'_, T> will NOT compile if PooledConn itself only requires T: Connection in some impls but not on the struct definition; Rust requires the Drop impl's generic bounds to match the type's own bounds exactly (E0367) — a genuinely easy-to-hit, slightly obscure compiler rule worth probing directly if the candidate doesn't hit it organically.
  • ★★Drops the lock BEFORE calling notify_one() in release — notifying while still holding the mutex risks the classic "thundering herd into an immediate re-block" inefficiency, where the woken thread immediately contends for a lock the notifier is still holding; releasing first lets the woken thread proceed without that extra bounce.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"wait_timeout can wake up spuriously — does this code correctly handle a spurious wakeup, and how do you know?" — Yes: the entire wait sits inside a `loop`, so a spurious (or even a legitimate but now-stale) wakeup just re-enters the loop and re-checks the actual condition (idle connections available, or room under max_size) rather than assuming the wakeup itself means "the resource is definitely ready now." This "always re-check the condition in a loop after waking, never trust the wakeup alone" pattern is THE standard, mandatory idiom for condition variables in every language that has them, not a Rust-specific quirk.
  • P2"Real connection pools (e.g. for a database) also need periodic health-checking of IDLE connections that might go stale while just sitting there unused — how would you add that without blocking acquire() callers?" — A background thread (or async task) that periodically takes the lock, walks `idle`, calls `is_healthy()` (or actively pings) each connection, and evicts/replaces failures — entirely decoupled from `acquire()`'s hot path, which should stay minimal and fast. This also surfaces a real trade-off: how often to check (checking too rarely leaves stale connections handed out between checks; checking too often adds background load) — worth asking a candidate to at least name the trade-off even without implementing the background thread live.
  • P3"This pool is synchronous/blocking — what would have to change for an async version usable inside a tokio application, and why can't you just sprinkle .await on the current code?" — A blocking `Mutex`/`Condvar` combo would block an entire async executor THREAD (potentially stalling many unrelated tasks multiplexed onto it) rather than just the one logical task waiting — the async equivalent needs an async-aware mutex (e.g. `tokio::sync::Mutex`) and, in place of `Condvar::wait_timeout`, either an async notification primitive (`tokio::sync::Notify`) or a bounded channel-based semaphore pattern, so a waiting task yields control back to the executor instead of parking an OS thread. This distinction — blocking a THREAD vs. yielding a TASK — is one of the most important async-Rust mental models to check for explicitly.
🎯 Senior angle
The Drop-bound-matching compiler error (E0367) that this exercise's PooledConn naturally runs into is a great, low-stakes way to see how a candidate reacts to an unfamiliar, slightly obscure compiler error: do they read the message, understand it names a real Rust rule (a type's Drop impl bounds must match its own declared bounds), and fix the struct definition — or do they start randomly adding/removing bounds hoping something sticks? That diagnostic instinct generalizes far beyond this one error.

fn main() {
    // Harden · Real connection pools (e.g. for a database) also need periodic health…
    harden_w57_2();
    // Parent exercise still holds after the harden change:
    use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
    use std::thread;

    struct SimpleConn { id: u32, healthy: bool }
    impl Connection for SimpleConn { fn is_healthy(&self) -> bool { self.healthy } }

    let next_id = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let next_id_for_factory = next_id.clone();
    let pool: Arc<Pool<SimpleConn>> = Arc::new(Pool::new(2, move || {
        let id = next_id_for_factory.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst) as u32;
        SimpleConn { id, healthy: true }
    }));

    let concurrent = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let max_concurrent = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..6 {
        let (pool, concurrent, max_concurrent) = (pool.clone(), concurrent.clone(), max_concurrent.clone());
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            let conn = pool.acquire(Duration::from_secs(2)).expect("generous timeout");
            let now = concurrent.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst) + 1;
            max_concurrent.fetch_max(now, Ordering::SeqCst);
            thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(30));
            concurrent.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
            assert!(conn.id < 2);  // pool should never construct more than max_size distinct connections
            drop(conn);  // RAII — returns the connection to the pool right here
        }));
    }
    for h in handles { h.join().unwrap(); }

    assert!(max_concurrent.load(Ordering::SeqCst) <= 2);  // pool never exceeded max_size checked-out connections
    assert_eq!(next_id.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 2);  // exactly max_size connections ever constructed, reused after that

    // Timeout path: exhaust the pool deliberately, confirm acquire() respects the timeout
    let g1 = pool.acquire(Duration::from_millis(100)).unwrap();
    let g2 = pool.acquire(Duration::from_millis(100)).unwrap();
    let start = Instant::now();
    let g3 = pool.acquire(Duration::from_millis(100));
    assert!(g3.is_none());  // pool exhausted — must time out, not block forever
    assert!(start.elapsed() >= Duration::from_millis(90));
    drop(g1); drop(g2);
}

W58 · Single-Threaded Event Loop — the Reactor Pattern Behind epoll/kqueue
reactor pattern level-triggered semantics trait-object callbacks HashMap-based registration table Medium–Hard
Prompt
"Implement the core loop of a reactor — the pattern underneath epoll (Linux), kqueue (BSD/macOS), and ultimately every async runtime's I/O driver: a single-threaded EventLoop<T: Pollable> that lets you register a source with a callback, then repeatedly tick() — each tick checks which registered sources are currently 'ready' and dispatches their callback exactly once, batched the way a real epoll_wait() returns a batch of ready file descriptors rather than a live, constantly-changing view. Semantics must be level-triggered: a source that's still ready after its callback runs must simply fire again on the next tick, with no separate re-arm step."
Starter code to hand to candidate
trait Pollable { fn is_ready(&self) -> bool; }
type Token = usize;

struct EventLoop<T: Pollable> { registrations: HashMap<Token, Registration<T>>, next_token: Token }

// TODO: struct Registration { source: T, callback: Box }
// TODO: impl EventLoop — register, deregister, tick() -> usize (fired count), run_until_idle

fn main() {
    let mut reactor: EventLoop<MockSocket> = EventLoop::new();

    let sock_a = MockSocket { buffer: VecDeque::from(vec![1,2,3,4,5]), received: Vec::new() };
    let sock_b = MockSocket { buffer: VecDeque::from(vec![10,20]), received: Vec::new() };

    let token_a = reactor.register(sock_a, |sock: &mut MockSocket| {  // simulates a non-blocking read draining only a SMALL chunk per call
        for _ in 0..2 {
            match sock.buffer.pop_front() { Some(b) => sock.received.push(b), None => break }
        }
    });
    let token_b = reactor.register(sock_b, |sock: &mut MockSocket| {  // drains fully in a single callback invocation
        while let Some(b) = sock.buffer.pop_front() { sock.received.push(b); }
    });

    let ticks = reactor.run_until_idle(20);

    assert_eq!(reactor.registrations[&token_a].source.received, vec![1,2,3,4,5]);
    assert_eq!(reactor.registrations[&token_b].source.received, vec![10,20]);
    assert!(ticks >= 3);  // socket A only reads 2 bytes/tick, so draining 5 bytes needs multiple ticks

    assert!(reactor.deregister(token_a));
    assert!(!reactor.deregister(token_a));  // already gone — must report false, not panic

    // a source that never becomes ready again must simply stop firing — no error, no hang
    let idle_sock = MockSocket { buffer: VecDeque::new(), received: Vec::new() };
    reactor.register(idle_sock, |_| panic!("callback for a never-ready source must never run"));
    let idle_ticks = reactor.run_until_idle(5);
    assert_eq!(idle_ticks, 1);  // recognizes nothing is ready and stops after a single empty tick
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::collections::{HashMap, VecDeque};

/// Stand-in for "an OS-level readiness check" (a real reactor asks the kernel via
/// epoll_wait/kqueue; here we ask the mock source directly) — the loop itself doesn't
/// care HOW readiness is determined, only that it can be asked cheaply and often.
trait Pollable { fn is_ready(&self) -> bool; }

type Token = usize;

struct Registration<T: Pollable> { source: T, callback: Box<dyn FnMut(&mut T)> }

/// A single-threaded, level-triggered event loop: one tick() is the moral equivalent of
/// one epoll_wait() call followed by dispatching every ready fd's callback — the reactor
/// pattern that lets one thread multiplex thousands of slow, independent I/O sources
/// without spawning a thread per connection.
struct EventLoop<T: Pollable> { registrations: HashMap<Token, Registration<T>>, next_token: Token }

impl<T: Pollable> EventLoop<T> {
    fn new() -> Self { Self { registrations: HashMap::new(), next_token: 0 } }

    fn register(&mut self, source: T, callback: impl FnMut(&mut T) + 'static) -> Token {
        let token = self.next_token;
        self.next_token += 1;
        self.registrations.insert(token, Registration { source, callback: Box::new(callback) });
        token
    }

    fn deregister(&mut self, token: Token) -> bool { self.registrations.remove(&token).is_some() }

    /// One iteration: snapshot which sources are ready right now, then dispatch each one's
    /// callback exactly once — mirroring how epoll_wait() returns a FIXED batch of ready fds
    /// rather than a live, ever-changing view while you're still processing it. LEVEL-triggered:
    /// a source still ready after its callback runs simply gets reported ready again NEXT tick —
    /// no separate re-arm step, unlike edge-triggered epoll.
    fn tick(&mut self) -> usize {
        let ready: Vec<Token> = self.registrations.iter()
            .filter(|(_, reg)| reg.source.is_ready())
            .map(|(&token, _)| token)
            .collect();

        let mut fired = 0;
        for token in ready {
            if let Some(reg) = self.registrations.get_mut(&token) {
                (reg.callback)(&mut reg.source);
                fired += 1;
            }
        }
        fired
    }

    fn run_until_idle(&mut self, max_ticks: usize) -> usize {
        let mut ticks = 0;
        while ticks < max_ticks {
            let fired = self.tick();
            ticks += 1;
            if fired == 0 { break; }
        }
        ticks
    }
}

struct MockSocket { buffer: VecDeque<u8>, received: Vec<u8> }
impl Pollable for MockSocket { fn is_ready(&self) -> bool { !self.buffer.is_empty() } }

fn main() {
    let mut reactor: EventLoop<MockSocket> = EventLoop::new();

    let sock_a = MockSocket { buffer: VecDeque::from(vec![1,2,3,4,5]), received: Vec::new() };
    let sock_b = MockSocket { buffer: VecDeque::from(vec![10,20]), received: Vec::new() };

    let token_a = reactor.register(sock_a, |sock: &mut MockSocket| {  // simulates a non-blocking read draining only a SMALL chunk per call
        for _ in 0..2 {
            match sock.buffer.pop_front() { Some(b) => sock.received.push(b), None => break }
        }
    });
    let token_b = reactor.register(sock_b, |sock: &mut MockSocket| {  // drains fully in a single callback invocation
        while let Some(b) = sock.buffer.pop_front() { sock.received.push(b); }
    });

    let ticks = reactor.run_until_idle(20);

    assert_eq!(reactor.registrations[&token_a].source.received, vec![1,2,3,4,5]);
    assert_eq!(reactor.registrations[&token_b].source.received, vec![10,20]);
    assert!(ticks >= 3);  // socket A only reads 2 bytes/tick, so draining 5 bytes needs multiple ticks

    assert!(reactor.deregister(token_a));
    assert!(!reactor.deregister(token_a));  // already gone — must report false, not panic

    // a source that never becomes ready again must simply stop firing — no error, no hang
    let idle_sock = MockSocket { buffer: VecDeque::new(), received: Vec::new() };
    reactor.register(idle_sock, |_| panic!("callback for a never-ready source must never run"));
    let idle_ticks = reactor.run_until_idle(5);
    assert_eq!(idle_ticks, 1);  // recognizes nothing is ready and stops after a single empty tick
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Snapshots the ready set into a Vec before dispatching any callbacks, rather than trying to iterate self.registrations directly while also mutating it inside the loop — the latter is either a borrow-checker error (mutably borrowing a HashMap you're also iterating) or, if worked around carelessly, a source of confusing behavior if a callback's side effects change what "currently ready" means mid-dispatch. Taking a fixed batch upfront mirrors exactly how a real epoll_wait() call returns a fixed-size batch of events.
  • ★★★Correctly implements level-triggered semantics with NO special re-arm logic — a source that only got partially drained by its callback simply gets checked again (and re-fires) on the very next tick(), entirely for free, because readiness is recomputed fresh every tick rather than cached or requiring an explicit "re-register interest" call.
  • ★★Uses Box<dyn FnMut(&mut T)> for the callback — recognizing that different registrations need DIFFERENT closures (each capturing its own state), which can't be stored as a single concrete generic type parameter on the whole EventLoop; type erasure via a trait object is the correct tool here, exactly as with the polymorphic-shapes pattern from earlier exercises.
  • ★run_until_idle terminates the moment a tick fires zero callbacks, rather than always running the full max_ticks — recognizing "nothing fired" as the natural, correct signal that the loop has reached a quiescent state, not just an arbitrary iteration budget.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"This EventLoop is generic over ONE Pollable type T — a real epoll multiplexes sockets, timers, and files all at once, wildly different types. How would you support that?" — This is the design's most important real limitation, worth naming even unprompted: replace the generic `T` with a trait object, `Registration { source: Box, callback: Box }` (or similar), so a single `EventLoop` can hold heterogeneous source types behind one shared vtable-dispatched interface — at the cost of an extra layer of indirection (a heap allocation and dynamic dispatch per source) compared to the generic, monomorphized version, which only works for one concrete type at a time.
  • P2"is_ready() here is called synchronously and cheaply on every single registered source, every single tick — what does REAL epoll do differently that makes it scale to tens of thousands of connections without burning CPU doing exactly that?" — Real epoll's registration is push-based, not poll-based: you register interest once, and the KERNEL itself tracks readiness (updated as network packets etc. arrive) and `epoll_wait()` blocks the calling thread using ZERO CPU until at least one registered fd actually becomes ready, then returns just that small ready subset directly — it never has to linearly scan every registered fd to find out. This toy reactor's linear `is_ready()` scan over every registration each tick is a perfectly fine teaching simplification but would not scale to a real, large connection count the way genuine OS-level readiness notification does.
  • P3"What's the actual difference between level-triggered and edge-triggered epoll, and why would anyone choose the more complicated edge-triggered mode?" — Level-triggered (this exercise's behavior) reports a source as ready EVERY time you check as long as data remains — simple to reason about, but can mean redundant wakeups if a consumer only partially drains a source each time, as W58's socket A demonstrates. Edge-triggered only reports readiness ONCE, at the moment of the state TRANSITION from not-ready to ready — after that, the application must keep reading/writing until it gets an explicit EWOULDBLOCK/EAGAIN, or it will never be told again even if more data remains. Edge-triggered can reduce the number of wakeup notifications delivered under high load, at the cost of requiring every consumer to correctly drain-until-EAGAIN every time, since epoll won't remind you to keep trying.
🎯 Senior angle
Push on the "one `Pollable` type" limitation directly — a candidate who volunteers, unprompted, that this design couldn't multiplex a socket and a timer in the same loop (and can sketch the Box<dyn Pollable> fix) is demonstrating the kind of self-critical architectural awareness that separates "I can implement the pattern you described" from "I understand the pattern well enough to know where this toy version diverges from a real one." That gap is exactly what a senior infra interview is trying to surface.

Every one of these mirrors a component that actually exists inside a production database engine, not a toy abstraction of one.

fn main() {
    // Harden · is_ready() here is called synchronously and cheaply on every single r…
    harden_w58_2();
    // Parent exercise still holds after the harden change:
    let mut reactor: EventLoop<MockSocket> = EventLoop::new();

    let sock_a = MockSocket { buffer: VecDeque::from(vec![1,2,3,4,5]), received: Vec::new() };
    let sock_b = MockSocket { buffer: VecDeque::from(vec![10,20]), received: Vec::new() };

    let token_a = reactor.register(sock_a, |sock: &mut MockSocket| {  // simulates a non-blocking read draining only a SMALL chunk per call
        for _ in 0..2 {

    });

    assert_eq!(reactor.registrations[&token_a].source.received, vec![1,2,3,4,5]);

    let idle_sock = MockSocket { buffer: VecDeque::new(), received: Vec::new() };
    reactor.register(idle_sock, |_| panic!("callback for a never-ready source must never run"));
    let idle_ticks = reactor.run_until_idle(5);
    assert_eq!(idle_ticks, 1);  // recognizes nothing is ready and stops after a single empty tick
}

// Database Engineering Exercise 59 · 45 min
W59 · LRU-K Cache Replacement Policy
backward K-distance per-page VecDeque<u64> buffer-pool eviction Medium
Prompt
"Implement the LRU-K page-replacement algorithm used in real buffer pool managers (an alternative to PostgreSQL's clock-sweep, classically described in the 1993 O'Neil et al. paper). Unlike plain LRU, which only tracks a page's single most recent access, LRU-K tracks the timestamp of each page's K-th-most-recent access. On eviction, pick the page whose K-th-most-recent access is furthest in the past — i.e. has the maximum backward K-distance. Pages with fewer than K total accesses so far must be treated as infinitely far back, given eviction priority over any page that already has a full K-length history — otherwise a page touched only once would accidentally be protected from eviction the way plain LRU lets it be. Support record_access(page_id) and evict() -> Option<page_id>; hardcoding page_id as usize is fine."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::collections::{HashMap, VecDeque};

struct LruK {
    k: usize,
    history: HashMap<usize, VecDeque<u64>>,
    clock: u64,
}

impl LruK {
    fn new(k: usize) -> Self {
        Self { k, history: HashMap::new(), clock: 0 }
    }

    // TODO: record_access(&mut self, page_id: usize) -- append a new timestamp for this page,
    //       and cap its history at the most recent `k` timestamps.
    // TODO: evict(&mut self) -> Option<usize> -- remove and return the page with the largest
    //       backward-K-distance; a page with FEWER than k accesses so far must be considered
    //       infinitely far back and evicted before ANY page with a full k-length history.
}

fn main() {
    let mut cache = LruK::new(2);

    cache.record_access(1);  // page 1: 1 access -> cold
    cache.record_access(2);  // page 2: 1 access -> cold
    cache.record_access(2);  // page 2: 2 accesses -> now hot, has a full K-length history

    assert_eq!(cache.backward_k_distance(1), None);       // fewer than K accesses -> no finite distance defined
    assert!(cache.backward_k_distance(2).is_some());  // page 2 has K accesses -> finite distance defined

    // Drive many more accesses to a third page so the global clock advances a long way while
    // page 2 (hot) is never touched again -- its backward-K-distance grows huge -- yet page 1
    // (touched only once, ever) must STILL be evicted first. This is THE most commonly gotten
    // wrong detail of LRU-K: "fewer than K accesses" outranks any finite distance, period.
    for _ in 0..20 {
        cache.record_access(3);  // page 3 stays hot with a small, constantly-refreshed distance
    }

    let big_distance = cache.backward_k_distance(2).unwrap();
    assert!(big_distance > 15);  // page 2's backward-distance is now large purely from disuse

    let victim = cache.evict();
    assert_eq!(victim, Some(1));  // cold page (1 access) evicted before hot page 2, despite page 2's huge distance
    assert!(!cache.history.contains_key(&1));  // page 1 fully removed from tracking now

    // With the only cold page gone, eviction must fall back to comparing finite backward-K-distances
    // among the remaining hot pages: page 2 (distance ~21, untouched since early on) vastly exceeds
    // page 3 (distance ~1, touched on nearly every tick), so page 2 must be evicted next.
    let dist_2 = cache.backward_k_distance(2).unwrap();
    let dist_3 = cache.backward_k_distance(3).unwrap();
    assert!(dist_2 > dist_3);  // correct backward-K-distance comparison between two hot pages
    let victim2 = cache.evict();
    assert_eq!(victim2, Some(2));

    // A fresh page with a single access is still cold and must outrank the sole remaining hot page.
    cache.record_access(4);
    let victim3 = cache.evict();
    assert_eq!(victim3, Some(4));  // single-access page beats page 3 despite page 3's long survival

    // Deque never grows past K entries even after many repeated accesses to the same page.
    let mut solo = LruK::new(3);
    for _ in 0..50 { solo.record_access(99); }
    assert_eq!(solo.history[&99].len(), 3);

    println!("W59 LRU-K cache: all assertions passed.");
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::collections::{HashMap, VecDeque};

struct LruK {
    k: usize,
    history: HashMap<usize, VecDeque<u64>>,
    clock: u64,
}

impl LruK {
    fn new(k: usize) -> Self {
        assert!(k >= 1, "k must be at least 1");
        Self { k, history: HashMap::new(), clock: 0 }
    }

    fn record_access(&mut self, page_id: usize) {
        self.clock += 1;
        let now = self.clock;
        let deque = self.history.entry(page_id).or_insert_with(VecDeque::new);
        deque.push_back(now);
        if deque.len() > self.k { deque.pop_front(); }  // only the K most recent timestamps ever survive
    }

    /// (category, magnitude) key where category 1 ("cold", fewer than k accesses) always
    /// outranks category 0 ("hot", exactly k accesses) for eviction purposes, REGARDLESS of
    /// magnitude -- this tuple ordering is the entire "fewer than K beats infinite distance" rule.
    fn eviction_key(&self, page_id: usize) -> (u8, u64) {
        let deque = &self.history[&page_id];
        if deque.len() < self.k {
            let last_access = *deque.back().unwrap();
            (1, u64::MAX - last_access)  // category 1 = cold; always > any category-0 key below
        } else {
            let kth_most_recent = *deque.front().unwrap();  // oldest of the K stored = the K-th-most-recent access
            let backward_distance = self.clock - kth_most_recent;
            (0, backward_distance)
        }
    }

    fn backward_k_distance(&self, page_id: usize) -> Option<u64> {
        let deque = self.history.get(&page_id)?;
        if deque.len() < self.k { None } else { Some(self.clock - *deque.front().unwrap()) }
    }

    fn evict(&mut self) -> Option<usize> {
        let victim = self.history.keys().copied().max_by_key(|&pid| self.eviction_key(pid))?;
        self.history.remove(&victim);
        Some(victim)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut cache = LruK::new(2);

    cache.record_access(1);  // page 1: 1 access -> cold
    cache.record_access(2);  // page 2: 1 access -> cold
    cache.record_access(2);  // page 2: 2 accesses -> now hot, has a full K-length history

    assert_eq!(cache.backward_k_distance(1), None);       // fewer than K accesses -> no finite distance defined
    assert!(cache.backward_k_distance(2).is_some());  // page 2 has K accesses -> finite distance defined

    // Drive many more accesses to a third page so the global clock advances a long way while
    // page 2 (hot) is never touched again -- its backward-K-distance grows huge -- yet page 1
    // (touched only once, ever) must STILL be evicted first. This is THE most commonly gotten
    // wrong detail of LRU-K: "fewer than K accesses" outranks any finite distance, period.
    for _ in 0..20 {
        cache.record_access(3);  // page 3 stays hot with a small, constantly-refreshed distance
    }

    let big_distance = cache.backward_k_distance(2).unwrap();
    assert!(big_distance > 15);  // page 2's backward-distance is now large purely from disuse

    let victim = cache.evict();
    assert_eq!(victim, Some(1));  // cold page (1 access) evicted before hot page 2, despite page 2's huge distance
    assert!(!cache.history.contains_key(&1));  // page 1 fully removed from tracking now

    // With the only cold page gone, eviction must fall back to comparing finite backward-K-distances
    // among the remaining hot pages: page 2 (distance ~21, untouched since early on) vastly exceeds
    // page 3 (distance ~1, touched on nearly every tick), so page 2 must be evicted next.
    let dist_2 = cache.backward_k_distance(2).unwrap();
    let dist_3 = cache.backward_k_distance(3).unwrap();
    assert!(dist_2 > dist_3);  // correct backward-K-distance comparison between two hot pages
    let victim2 = cache.evict();
    assert_eq!(victim2, Some(2));

    // A fresh page with a single access is still cold and must outrank the sole remaining hot page.
    cache.record_access(4);
    let victim3 = cache.evict();
    assert_eq!(victim3, Some(4));  // single-access page beats page 3 despite page 3's long survival

    // Deque never grows past K entries even after many repeated accesses to the same page.
    let mut solo = LruK::new(3);
    for _ in 0..50 { solo.record_access(99); }
    assert_eq!(solo.history[&99].len(), 3);

    println!("W59 LRU-K cache: all assertions passed.");
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Encodes "fewer than K accesses" as a strictly higher-priority category, not a large-but-finite number — the most common bug is representing "infinite distance" as something like u64::MAX mixed directly into the same numeric comparison as real distances; if enough real distances accumulate (or the candidate off-by-ones the sentinel), a long-lived hot page can spuriously "win" against a cold page. A two-level key (category, then magnitude) closes this off structurally instead of relying on a magic number staying big enough forever.
  • ★★★Correctly identifies the K-th-most-recent access as the oldest entry in a K-length window, not the newest — a candidate who reads deque.back() (the most recent access) instead of deque.front() (the K-th-most-recent, once the deque is full) has silently reimplemented plain LRU with extra bookkeeping, which defeats the entire point of LRU-K.
  • ★★Caps each page's history deque at exactly k entries on every access, not just occasionally — an unbounded deque is an unbounded per-page memory leak in a real buffer pool that may see millions of accesses to a single hot page over its lifetime.
  • ★Uses a monotonic logical clock, not wall-clock time, for timestamps — a logical counter is deterministic, immune to clock skew/adjustment, and trivially testable, whereas Instant::now() introduces non-determinism that makes exact backward-distance assertions in tests fragile.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Why does the original LRU-K paper bother with K greater than 2 at all — what does K=2 already buy you over plain LRU (K=1), and what would K=3 additionally buy?" — Plain LRU (effectively K=1) is fooled by a single access: one scan through a table that's read once and never again can evict genuinely hot pages purely because that one-off scan happened most recently. K=2 already fixes the classic "one-time sequential scan pollutes the cache" problem, because a page needs to be accessed twice before its recency is trusted at all. Larger K values make the algorithm increasingly resistant to bursty-but-not-actually-hot access patterns (e.g. a page touched 3 times in a tight loop then abandoned) at the cost of more per-page memory and slightly slower convergence for genuinely newly-hot pages — K=2 is the overwhelmingly common choice in practice precisely because it captures most of the benefit for the least bookkeeping.
  • P2"The reference implementation scans every page's history on every evict() call — how would you avoid an O(n) scan on every eviction in a buffer pool with millions of pages?" — Maintain a priority queue (e.g. a min-heap or an ordered structure like a BTreeMap) keyed by each page's current backward-K-distance (with cold pages given a dedicated always-first bucket), and update a page's position in that structure whenever its distance changes on record_access. This turns eviction into an O(log n) heap-pop instead of an O(n) linear scan, at the cost of needing to support efficient key-updates (a plain BinaryHeap can't update an existing entry's priority in place, so real implementations either use a heap with lazy deletion + a "is this still valid" generation check, or an indexed/intrusive priority queue).
  • P3"LRU-K's original paper also proposes a 'correlated reference period' — what problem does that solve that this implementation doesn't handle?" — A single logical operation (e.g. a multi-row join, or a B-tree traversal walking through several levels) can touch the same page multiple times in rapid succession as pure side effects of that one operation, not because the page is independently "hot." Without a correlated-reference filter, those rapid repeated touches inside one operation can artificially inflate a page's reference count and make it look K-accessed sooner than it deserves. The paper's fix ignores repeated accesses to the same page that fall within a short correlated-reference window, only counting the first access to a page within that window toward its K-history — a real buffer pool manager would combine this exercise's core mechanism with that filter.
🎯 Senior angle
Anyone can write "evict the least-recently-used page." A senior candidate reasons explicitly about why plain LRU is exploitable — a single cold sequential scan can evict pages that are genuinely hot in the workload's steady state — and can articulate LRU-K's fix in terms of that failure mode, not just recite the algorithm's mechanics. Watch for whether they treat the "fewer than K beats infinite distance" rule as an arbitrary spec detail to satisfy, versus recognizing it as the load-bearing piece that makes newly-touched pages evictable again immediately, which is exactly what prevents cold scans from polluting the cache in the first place.

    cache.record_access(2);  // page 2: 1 access -> cold
    cache.record_access(2);  // page 2: 2 accesses -> now hot, has a full K-length history

    assert_eq!(cache.backward_k_distance(1), None);       // fewer than K accesses -> no finite distance defined
    assert!(cache.backward_k_distance(2).is_some());  // page 2 has K accesses -> finite distance defined

    // Drive many more accesses to a third page so the global clock advances a long way while
    // page 2 (hot) is never touched again -- its backward-K-distance grows huge -- yet page 1
    // (touched only once, ever) must STILL be evicted first. This is THE most commonly gotten
    // wrong detail of LRU-K: "fewer than K accesses" outranks any finite distance, period.
    for _ in 0..20 {
        cache.record_access(3);  // page 3 stays hot with a small, constantly-refreshed distance
    }

    let big_distance = cache.backward_k_distance(2).unwrap();
    assert!(big_distance > 15);  // page 2's backward-distance is now large purely from disuse

    let victim = cache.evict();
    assert_eq!(victim, Some(1));  // cold page (1 access) evicted before hot page 2, despite page 2's huge distance
    assert!(!cache.history.contains_key(&1));  // page 1 fully removed from tracking now

    // With the only cold page gone, eviction must fall back to comparing finite backward-K-distances
    // among the remaining hot pages: page 2 (distance ~21, untouched since early on) vastly exceeds
    // page 3 (distance ~1, touched on nearly every tick), so page 2 must be evicted next.
    let dist_2 = cache.backward_k_distance(2).unwrap();
    let dist_3 = cache.backward_k_distance(3).unwrap();
    assert!(dist_2 > dist_3);  // correct backward-K-distance comparison between two hot pages
    let victim2 = cache.evict();
    assert_eq!(victim2, Some(2));

    // A fresh page with a single access is still cold and must outrank the sole remaining hot page.
    cache.record_access(4);
    let victim3 = cache.evict();
    assert_eq!(victim3, Some(4));  // single-access page beats page 3 despite page 3's long survival

    // Deque never grows past K entries even after many repeated accesses to the same page.
    let mut solo = LruK::new(3);
    for _ in 0..50 { solo.record_access(99); }
    assert_eq!(solo.history[&99].len(), 3);

    println!("W59 LRU-K cache: all assertions passed.");
}

W60 · Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC) with Arena-Backed Storage
T1/T2/B1/B2 four-list ARC adaptive target size p arena / slab allocator free-list slot reuse Hard
Prompt
"Implement ARC (Adaptive Replacement Cache, the IBM/ZFS algorithm). Maintain four lists: T1 (recent real entries — "recency"), T2 (frequent real entries — "frequency"), B1 (ghost keys recently evicted from T1), and B2 (ghost keys recently evicted from T2) — plus an adaptive target size p for T1 that shifts based on which ghost list a re-access lands in: a hit in B1 increases p (favor recency), a hit in B2 decreases p (favor frequency). Separately: back the actual cached values with a simple arena / slab allocator — a Vec<Option<V>> of slots plus a free-list of reclaimed indices — instead of storing values directly in a HashMap<K, V>, so evicting an entry returns its slot to the free-list for reuse rather than triggering a fresh heap dealloc/realloc on every insert, mirroring how a real storage engine backs a cache with a fixed-size buffer pool instead of ad-hoc per-entry heap allocations."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::collections::{HashMap, VecDeque};
use std::hash::Hash;

struct Arena<V> { slots: Vec<Option<V>>, free_list: Vec<usize> }

// TODO: impl<V> Arena<V> -- insert(value) -> usize (reuse a free_list slot if one exists,
//       else grow), remove(idx) -> Option<V> (take the value, push idx onto free_list),
//       get(idx) -> Option<&V>, allocated()/live() for introspection.

struct ArcCache<K, V> {
    capacity: usize,
    p: usize,                       // adaptive target size for T1
    t1: VecDeque<K>, t2: VecDeque<K>,     // real entries: recency, frequency
    b1: VecDeque<K>, b2: VecDeque<K>,     // ghosts: keys only, evicted from T1 / T2
    slots: HashMap<K, usize>,             // key -> arena slot, only while in T1/T2
    arena: Arena<V>,
}

// TODO: impl<K: Eq + Hash + Clone, V> ArcCache<K, V> --
//   get(&mut self, key: &K, loader: impl FnOnce() -> V) -> &V, implementing all four ARC cases:
//     Case I:   key in T1 or T2       -> cache hit, move to MRU of T2
//     Case II:  key in B1             -> ghost hit, p = min(c, p + max(1, |B2|/|B1|)), then insert to T2
//     Case III: key in B2             -> ghost hit, p = max(0, p - max(1, |B1|/|B2|)), then insert to T2
//     Case IV:  key nowhere           -> true miss, evict room if needed, insert to T1
//   replace(&mut self, hint_in_b2: bool) -- evict T1 or T2's LRU into the matching ghost list
//     based on whether |T1| > p (evict T1) or not (evict T2), freeing the arena slot either way.

fn main() {
    let mut cache: ArcCache<char, i32> = ArcCache::new(4);

    cache.get(&'A', || 100);
    cache.get(&'B', || 200);
    let b_slot_before_eviction = cache.slot_of(&'B').unwrap();
    cache.get(&'A', || 999);  // hit -> promotes A into T2
    cache.get(&'C', || 300);
    cache.get(&'D', || 400);
    assert_eq!(cache.real_size(), 4);  // T1={B,C,D}, T2={A} -> cache exactly full, never over capacity

    // Miss on E forces REPLACE(): T1's LRU (B) is evicted into the B1 ghost list, freeing its slot.
    cache.get(&'E', || 500);
    assert!(cache.b1.contains(&'B'));
    assert_eq!(cache.real_size(), 4);
    assert_eq!(cache.slot_of(&'E'), Some(b_slot_before_eviction));  // arena reused B's exact freed slot for E

    // --- Deliberate B1 ghost-hit scenario: re-touching a key that's currently only a ghost in
    // B1 must shift the adaptive target p toward recency (p increases). ---
    let p_before_b1_hit = cache.p;
    cache.get(&'B', || 111);  // B is in B1 right now -> Case II ghost hit
    assert!(cache.p > p_before_b1_hit);  // p must have grown -- the core adaptive behavior of ARC
    assert!(!cache.b1.contains(&'B'));
    assert!(cache.t2.contains(&'B'));

    cache.get(&'F', || 600);
    cache.get(&'A', || 222);  // T2 hit, just reorders MRU within T2
    cache.get(&'G', || 700);
    cache.get(&'H', || 800);
    cache.get(&'I', || 900);
    assert_eq!(cache.real_size(), cache.capacity);  // still bounded exactly at capacity, never exceeded

    // Push p up further via another B1 ghost hit until T1's live length is <= p, which forces
    // REPLACE() to evict from T2 (not T1) -- manufacturing a real B2 ghost entry.
    assert!(cache.b1.contains(&'F'));
    let p_before_second_b1_hit = cache.p;
    cache.get(&'F', || 601);
    assert!(cache.p > p_before_second_b1_hit);
    assert!(cache.b2.len() >= 1);  // REPLACE() was forced to evict from T2 this time

    // --- Deliberate B2 ghost-hit scenario: re-touching a key that's currently a ghost in B2
    // must shift p back toward frequency (p decreases). ---
    let ghost_in_b2 = cache.b2.front().copied().unwrap();
    let p_before_b2_hit = cache.p;
    cache.get(&ghost_in_b2, || 601);
    assert!(cache.p < p_before_b2_hit);  // p must have shrunk -- symmetric adaptive behavior confirmed
    assert!(!cache.b2.contains(&ghost_in_b2));
    assert!(cache.t2.contains(&ghost_in_b2));

    assert_eq!(cache.real_size(), cache.capacity);  // still exactly at capacity, never over, after all this churn

    // The arena never grew past `capacity` live slots despite far more than `capacity` distinct
    // keys having passed through the cache -- proof the free-list is actually being reused.
    assert_eq!(cache.arena.allocated(), cache.capacity);
    assert_eq!(cache.arena.live(), cache.real_size());

    println!("W60 ARC cache with arena-backed storage: all assertions passed.");
}

use std::collections::{HashMap, VecDeque};
use std::hash::Hash;

/// Slab allocator: `Vec<Option<V>>` slots plus a free-list of reclaimed indices, so evicting
/// a cached value reuses its slot on the next insert instead of paying a fresh heap alloc/dealloc.
struct Arena<V> {
    slots: Vec<Option<V>>,
    free_list: Vec<usize>,
}

impl<V> Arena<V> {
    fn new() -> Self { Self { slots: Vec::new(), free_list: Vec::new() } }

    fn insert(&mut self, value: V) -> usize {
        if let Some(idx) = self.free_list.pop() {
            self.slots[idx] = Some(value);  // reuse a reclaimed slot -- no Vec growth, no fresh allocation
            idx
        } else {
            self.slots.push(Some(value));
            self.slots.len() - 1
        }
    }

    fn remove(&mut self, idx: usize) -> Option<V> {
        let v = self.slots[idx].take();
        self.free_list.push(idx);
        v
    }

    fn get(&self, idx: usize) -> Option<&V> { self.slots.get(idx).and_then(|s| s.as_ref()) }
    fn allocated(&self) -> usize { self.slots.len() }
    fn live(&self) -> usize { self.slots.len() - self.free_list.len() }
}

struct ArcCache<K, V> {
    capacity: usize,
    p: usize,
    t1: VecDeque<K>, // recency list: real entries seen exactly once recently
    t2: VecDeque<K>, // frequency list: real entries seen more than once
    b1: VecDeque<K>, // ghost list: keys recently evicted from T1 (no values, key-only)
    b2: VecDeque<K>, // ghost list: keys recently evicted from T2 (no values, key-only)
    slots: HashMap<K, usize>, // key -> arena slot, only for keys currently in T1 or T2
    arena: Arena<V>,
}

impl<K: Eq + Hash + Clone, V> ArcCache<K, V> {
    fn new(capacity: usize) -> Self {
        assert!(capacity > 0, "capacity must be positive");
        Self {
            capacity, p: 0,
            t1: VecDeque::new(), t2: VecDeque::new(),
            b1: VecDeque::new(), b2: VecDeque::new(),
            slots: HashMap::new(), arena: Arena::new(),
        }
    }

    fn remove_from(list: &mut VecDeque<K>, key: &K) -> bool {
        if let Some(pos) = list.iter().position(|k| k == key) { list.remove(pos); true } else { false }
    }

    /// REPLACE(): evicts one real cache entry (from T1 or T2's LRU end) into the matching
    /// ghost list, freeing its arena slot for reuse. `hint_in_b2` is the paper's "x in B2"
    /// tie-break clause, only relevant on a B2 ghost hit that lands exactly on the T1/T2
    /// boundary (`|T1| == p`).
    fn replace(&mut self, hint_in_b2: bool) {
        let evict_from_t1 = !self.t1.is_empty()
            && (self.t1.len() > self.p || (hint_in_b2 && self.t1.len() == self.p));  // the adaptive rule, literally
        if evict_from_t1 {
            let victim = self.t1.pop_front().unwrap();
            let idx = self.slots.remove(&victim).unwrap();
            self.arena.remove(idx);  // slot goes back to the free-list here, NOT deallocated
            self.b1.push_back(victim);
        } else {
            let victim = self.t2.pop_front().unwrap();
            let idx = self.slots.remove(&victim).unwrap();
            self.arena.remove(idx);
            self.b2.push_back(victim);
        }
    }

    /// One ARC step for `key`: cache hit (Case I), ghost hit in B1/B2 (Cases II/III, each of
    /// which adapts `p`), or a true miss (Case IV). `loader` is only ever called on a miss or
    /// a ghost hit, mirroring "go fetch this from disk" in a real buffer pool.
    fn get(&mut self, key: &K, loader: impl FnOnce() -> V) -> &V {
        let c = self.capacity;

        if let Some(&idx) = self.slots.get(key) {
            if Self::remove_from(&mut self.t1, key) {
                self.t2.push_back(key.clone());
            } else {
                Self::remove_from(&mut self.t2, key);
                self.t2.push_back(key.clone());
            }
            return self.arena.get(idx).unwrap();  // Case I: plain cache hit, no p change
        }

        if self.b1.contains(key) {
            let delta = std::cmp::max(1, self.b2.len() / self.b1.len());
            self.p = std::cmp::min(c, self.p + delta); // ghost hit in B1 -> favor recency, grow p
            Self::remove_from(&mut self.b1, key);
            if self.t1.len() + self.t2.len() == c { self.replace(false); }
            let idx = self.arena.insert(loader());
            self.slots.insert(key.clone(), idx);
            self.t2.push_back(key.clone());  // promoted straight into T2 (frequency), never T1
            return self.arena.get(idx).unwrap();
        }

        if self.b2.contains(key) {
            let delta = std::cmp::max(1, self.b1.len() / self.b2.len());
            self.p = self.p.saturating_sub(delta); // ghost hit in B2 -> favor frequency, shrink p
            Self::remove_from(&mut self.b2, key);
            if self.t1.len() + self.t2.len() == c { self.replace(true); }
            let idx = self.arena.insert(loader());
            self.slots.insert(key.clone(), idx);
            self.t2.push_back(key.clone());
            return self.arena.get(idx).unwrap();
        }

        // Case IV: true miss, key is in none of T1/T2/B1/B2.
        if self.t1.len() + self.b1.len() == c {
            if self.t1.len() < c {
                self.b1.pop_front();
                if self.t1.len() + self.t2.len() == c { self.replace(false); }
            } else {
                // T1 alone already fills the whole cache; drop its LRU outright, no ghost room.
                let victim = self.t1.pop_front().unwrap();
                let idx = self.slots.remove(&victim).unwrap();
                self.arena.remove(idx);
            }
        } else {
            let total = self.t1.len() + self.t2.len() + self.b1.len() + self.b2.len();
            if total >= c {
                if total == 2 * c { self.b2.pop_front(); } // cap the combined directory at 2c
                if self.t1.len() + self.t2.len() == c { self.replace(false); }
            }
        }
        let idx = self.arena.insert(loader());
        self.slots.insert(key.clone(), idx);
        self.t1.push_back(key.clone());
        self.arena.get(idx).unwrap()
    }

    fn real_size(&self) -> usize { self.t1.len() + self.t2.len() }
    fn slot_of(&self, key: &K) -> Option<usize> { self.slots.get(key).copied() }
}

fn main() {
    let mut cache: ArcCache<char, i32> = ArcCache::new(4);

    cache.get(&'A', || 100);
    cache.get(&'B', || 200);
    let b_slot_before_eviction = cache.slot_of(&'B').unwrap();
    cache.get(&'A', || 999);  // hit -> promotes A into T2
    cache.get(&'C', || 300);
    cache.get(&'D', || 400);
    assert_eq!(cache.real_size(), 4);  // T1={B,C,D}, T2={A} -> cache exactly full, never over capacity

    // Miss on E forces REPLACE(): T1's LRU (B) is evicted into the B1 ghost list, freeing its slot.
    cache.get(&'E', || 500);
    assert!(cache.b1.contains(&'B'));
    assert_eq!(cache.real_size(), 4);
    assert_eq!(cache.slot_of(&'E'), Some(b_slot_before_eviction));  // arena reused B's exact freed slot for E

    // --- Deliberate B1 ghost-hit scenario: re-touching a key that's currently only a ghost in
    // B1 must shift the adaptive target p toward recency (p increases). ---
    let p_before_b1_hit = cache.p;
    cache.get(&'B', || 111);  // B is in B1 right now -> Case II ghost hit
    assert!(cache.p > p_before_b1_hit);  // p must have grown -- the core adaptive behavior of ARC
    assert!(!cache.b1.contains(&'B'));
    assert!(cache.t2.contains(&'B'));

    cache.get(&'F', || 600);
    cache.get(&'A', || 222);  // T2 hit, just reorders MRU within T2
    cache.get(&'G', || 700);
    cache.get(&'H', || 800);
    cache.get(&'I', || 900);
    assert_eq!(cache.real_size(), cache.capacity);  // still bounded exactly at capacity, never exceeded

    // Push p up further via another B1 ghost hit until T1's live length is <= p, which forces
    // REPLACE() to evict from T2 (not T1) -- manufacturing a real B2 ghost entry.
    assert!(cache.b1.contains(&'F'));
    let p_before_second_b1_hit = cache.p;
    cache.get(&'F', || 601);
    assert!(cache.p > p_before_second_b1_hit);
    assert!(cache.b2.len() >= 1);  // REPLACE() was forced to evict from T2 this time

    // --- Deliberate B2 ghost-hit scenario: re-touching a key that's currently a ghost in B2
    // must shift p back toward frequency (p decreases). ---
    let ghost_in_b2 = cache.b2.front().copied().unwrap();
    let p_before_b2_hit = cache.p;
    cache.get(&ghost_in_b2, || 601);
    assert!(cache.p < p_before_b2_hit);  // p must have shrunk -- symmetric adaptive behavior confirmed
    assert!(!cache.b2.contains(&ghost_in_b2));
    assert!(cache.t2.contains(&ghost_in_b2));

    assert_eq!(cache.real_size(), cache.capacity);  // still exactly at capacity, never over, after all this churn

    // The arena never grew past `capacity` live slots despite far more than `capacity` distinct
    // keys having passed through the cache -- proof the free-list is actually being reused.
    assert_eq!(cache.arena.allocated(), cache.capacity);
    assert_eq!(cache.arena.live(), cache.real_size());

    println!("W60 ARC cache with arena-backed storage: all assertions passed.");
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Computes the B1/B2 adaptation ratio using the ghost list sizes at the moment of the hit — including the entry being hit — a subtle spec detail: max(1, |B2|/|B1|) must be computed before removing the hit key from B1, since that key's own presence is part of |B1|'s size in the paper's formula. Getting this order backwards under-counts the denominator and makes p swing slightly too aggressively — a real but easy-to-miss correctness bug that a careful candidate catches by re-reading the paper's pseudocode rather than "close enough" approximating it.
  • ★★★Never lets the arena's live slot count exceed capacity — the entire point of the exercise's arena half is that a cache holding at most capacity real entries should never allocate more than capacity value slots, no matter how many thousands of distinct keys eventually pass through it over the cache's lifetime; a candidate who inserts into the arena unconditionally on every miss/ghost-hit without first freeing the evicted slot defeats this property silently (the arena just grows forever, indistinguishable from a plain Vec::push).
  • ★★Correctly decides, inside REPLACE(), whether to evict from T1 or T2 based on |T1| vs. p — not some simpler proxy like "whichever list is longer." This is the exact mechanism by which the adaptive target actually takes effect on real cache behavior; getting it wrong makes p a number that changes but has zero effect on eviction decisions, silently degrading ARC into either plain LRU or plain LFU depending on the bug.
  • ★Clamps p to [0, capacity] on every adaptation (min on the B1 branch, saturating_sub or an explicit max(0, ...) on the B2 branch) — without both clamps, a long run of one-sided ghost hits can push p outside the valid range for a usize target size, either overflowing/panicking on subtraction or producing a target larger than the cache itself.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Why does ARC need TWO ghost lists instead of just tracking 'recently evicted keys' as one combined set?" — Because the whole self-tuning mechanism depends on knowing which side of the cache a ghost hit is correcting for. A hit in B1 specifically means "a page we evicted for being merely recent (not yet proven frequent) turned out to still be wanted" — evidence the cache is currently too frequency-biased, so p should grow to give recency more room. A hit in B2 means the opposite: a page evicted for lacking sustained frequency is being re-referenced, meaning the cache is too recency-biased. Collapsing both into one undifferentiated "recently evicted" set would throw away exactly the signal ARC needs to decide which direction to adapt.
  • P2"This implementation's arena has O(n) worst-case behavior nowhere in the hot path, but what would you change if V were large (e.g. a full 8KB database page) and cloned on every access?" — The current design already avoids cloning V itself (only K is cloned, since keys move between the four lists as plain values while the arena holds the real payload by reference-free ownership), so the main remaining risk is Vec<Option<V>> doing a large memcpy when the backing Vec reallocates and grows past its current capacity. For large, rarely-resized V, pre-allocating Arena::with_capacity(pool_size) up front (since ARC's arena never needs more than capacity live slots anyway) avoids ever reallocating the slots Vec after startup — turning an occasional O(capacity) copy into a one-time cost.
  • P3"ZFS's actual ARC implementation is famous for being tunable in production and has additional knobs beyond this exercise's core algorithm — name one, and why production systems need it." — ZFS's ARC adds a minimum/maximum size for the whole cache (arc_c_min/arc_c_max) so the algorithm can shrink under system memory pressure and grow back when memory frees up, rather than the fixed capacity this exercise assumes. A textbook ARC's four-list invariants (like |T1|+|T2|+|B1|+|B2| <= 2c) are derived assuming c is constant — dynamically resizing c at runtime while under load, without violating those invariants or thrashing the adaptive p value, is a genuinely hard production concern that the paper's original algorithm doesn't have to address at all.
🎯 Senior angle
ARC's real trick isn't the four lists — it's that p adapts using evidence the cache itself already has for free (which ghost list a re-reference lands in), with zero external tuning or workload classification required. A senior candidate should be able to say, unprompted, that this is what makes ARC "self-tuning" versus a fixed hybrid like "80% LRU + 20% LFU" — and should notice that the arena half of this exercise is testing an entirely separate, equally real skill: recognizing that a cache's *metadata* churn (evictions, reinsertions) shouldn't force allocator churn on the *payload* it's caching, which is exactly why production buffer pools use fixed slabs instead of a bare HashMap<K, V>.
