    assert!(cache.t2.contains(&ghost_in_b2));

    assert_eq!(cache.real_size(), cache.capacity);  // still exactly at capacity, never over, after all this churn

    // The arena never grew past `capacity` live slots despite far more than `capacity` distinct
    // keys having passed through the cache -- proof the free-list is actually being reused.
    assert_eq!(cache.arena.allocated(), cache.capacity);
    assert_eq!(cache.arena.live(), cache.real_size());

    println!("W60 ARC cache with arena-backed storage: all assertions passed.");
}
// Database Engineering Exercise 61 · 90 min
W61 · Buffer Pool Manager — Pinning, Dirty Flags, Clock Eviction
page table + frame slots pin counts, never evict pinned clock / second-chance sweep RAII guard, Drop unpins Hard
Prompt
"Implement the core of a database buffer pool manager — the component sitting between a query executor and disk, as in PostgreSQL's shared_buffers or CMU 15-445's Project 1. You need: a fixed-size pool of frame_id -> Option<Page> slots; a page table (HashMap<page_id, frame_id>); a pin count per frame — a frame with pin_count > 0 must NEVER be evicted; a dirty flag per frame; and a MockDiskManager that "reads"/"writes" pages by id (a HashMap-backed stand-in is fine — no real disk I/O). Required API: fetch_page(page_id) -> Option<Guard> (increments pin count; on a cache miss, loads from "disk" via the mock disk manager, choosing a victim frame via LRU-K or clock-replacement among unpinned frames when the pool is full); and a guard type that decrements pin count on Drop and marks the frame dirty if the caller wrote through it. Flushing a dirty victim page back to the mock disk manager before reusing its frame is mandatory."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::rc::Rc;

type PageId = u64;
type FrameId = usize;

#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
struct Page { data: Vec<u8> }

struct MockDiskManager { storage: HashMap<PageId, Vec<u8>> }
// TODO: impl MockDiskManager -- read_page(id) -> Page (zeroed default if never written),
//       write_page(id, &Page) -- just a HashMap read/insert, no real I/O.

struct Frame {
    page_id: Option<PageId>,
    page: Option<Page>,
    pin_count: usize,
    dirty: bool,
    ref_bit: bool,  // for clock/second-chance eviction among unpinned frames
}

// TODO: struct BufferPoolManager { frames: Vec<Frame>, page_table: HashMap<PageId, FrameId>,
//       free_list: Vec<FrameId>, clock_hand: usize, disk: MockDiskManager } -- wrap in
//       Rc<RefCell<...>> so a PageGuard can hold a shared handle back to it for Drop.
// TODO: struct PageGuard { ..., frame_id: FrameId } -- read()/write() accessors, and a Drop
//       impl that decrements pin_count (write() marks the frame dirty, NOT Drop itself).
// TODO: fetch_page(&self, page_id) -> Option<PageGuard> -- hit: pin++, return guard on the
//       existing frame. Miss: take a free frame, or evict an UNPINNED victim via a clock sweep
//       (flushing it to disk first if dirty). Return None if every frame is pinned.

fn main() {
    let bpm = BufferPoolManager::new(2);

    // Fetching the same page twice must return the SAME frame with pin count 2, not two copies.
    let g1 = bpm.fetch_page(1).unwrap();
    let g2 = bpm.fetch_page(1).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(g1.frame_id(), g2.frame_id());
    assert_eq!(bpm.pin_count_of(g1.frame_id()), 2);
    assert_eq!(g1.page_id(), 1);
    assert_eq!(g1.read(), vec![0u8; 8]);  // freshly "read from disk" page defaults to zeroed bytes

    g1.write(vec![9u8; 8]);
    assert_eq!(bpm.disk_bytes(1), None);  // NOT yet flushed -- writes only hit the frame, not disk
    drop(g2);  // pin 2 -> 1
    assert_eq!(bpm.pin_count_of(g1.frame_id()), 1);
    drop(g1);  // pin 1 -> 0, frame1 now unpinned but still dirty

    let g3 = bpm.fetch_page(2).unwrap();  // pool has one free frame left -> no eviction needed yet
    let frame1 = 1 - g3.frame_id();  // the other frame, still holding dirty page 1

    // Force the "never evict a pinned frame" scenario explicitly: keep g3 pinned on frame for
    // page 2, and make frame1 (page 1, unpinned+dirty) the ONLY eligible victim, even though a
    // pinned frame could otherwise look just as cold to a naive scan.
    let g4 = bpm.fetch_page(4).expect("must evict the unpinned dirty frame, not the pinned one");
    assert_eq!(g4.frame_id(), frame1);  // victim was exactly the unpinned frame, never the pinned one
    assert_eq!(bpm.pin_count_of(g3.frame_id()), 1);  // page 2's frame was never touched by the sweep

    assert_eq!(bpm.disk_bytes(1), Some(vec![9u8; 8]));  // dirty page WAS flushed to disk before its frame got reused

    // Pool is now full and BOTH remaining frames are pinned (g3 on page 2, g4 on page 4) --
    // fetching anything new must return None, not panic or silently corrupt state.
    let g5 = bpm.fetch_page(5);
    assert!(g5.is_none());
    assert_eq!(bpm.pin_count_of(g3.frame_id()), 1);  // untouched by the failed fetch attempt
    assert_eq!(bpm.pin_count_of(g4.frame_id()), 1);

    drop(g3);
    drop(g4);
    // Now that both are unpinned, a fetch must succeed again (proves None wasn't a permanent wedge).
    let g6 = bpm.fetch_page(6);
    assert!(g6.is_some());

    println!("W61 buffer pool manager: all assertions passed.");
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::rc::Rc;

type PageId = u64;
type FrameId = usize;

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Page { data: Vec<u8> }

/// Stands in for real disk I/O: pages that were never written come back as zeroed defaults.
struct MockDiskManager { storage: HashMap<PageId, Vec<u8>> }

impl MockDiskManager {
    fn new() -> Self { Self { storage: HashMap::new() } }

    fn read_page(&self, page_id: PageId) -> Page {
        Page { data: self.storage.get(&page_id).cloned().unwrap_or_else(|| vec![0u8; 8]) }
    }

    fn write_page(&mut self, page_id: PageId, page: &Page) {
        self.storage.insert(page_id, page.data.clone());
    }
}

struct Frame {
    page_id: Option<PageId>,
    page: Option<Page>,
    pin_count: usize,
    dirty: bool,
    ref_bit: bool,  // clock/second-chance "recently used" bit, only meaningful while unpinned
}

impl Frame {
    fn empty() -> Self { Self { page_id: None, page: None, pin_count: 0, dirty: false, ref_bit: false } }
}

struct BpmInner {
    frames: Vec<Frame>,
    page_table: HashMap<PageId, FrameId>,
    free_list: Vec<FrameId>,
    clock_hand: usize,
    disk: MockDiskManager,
}

impl BpmInner {
    /// Clock (second-chance) sweep: skip pinned frames entirely, give unpinned-but-recently-used
    /// frames one free pass (clearing their ref bit), and evict the first unpinned frame the
    /// hand finds with its ref bit already false. Returns None if every frame is pinned.
    fn find_victim(&mut self) -> Option<FrameId> {
        let n = self.frames.len();
        let mut scanned = 0;
        loop {
            if scanned > 2 * n { return None; }  // a full sweep-and-a-half found nothing evictable -> all pinned
            let idx = self.clock_hand;
            self.clock_hand = (self.clock_hand + 1) % n;
            let frame = &mut self.frames[idx];
            if frame.pin_count > 0 { scanned += 1; continue; }  // pinned frames are NEVER eligible, full stop
            if frame.ref_bit {
                frame.ref_bit = false;  // second chance: downgrade instead of evicting immediately
                scanned += 1;
                continue;
            }
            if frame.dirty {
                let pid = frame.page_id.unwrap();
                let page = frame.page.clone().unwrap();
                self.disk.write_page(pid, &page);  // flush BEFORE the frame is handed to a new page
            }
            if let Some(pid) = frame.page_id.take() { self.page_table.remove(&pid); }
            return Some(idx);
        }
    }
}

struct BufferPoolManager { inner: Rc<RefCell<BpmInner>> }

/// RAII handle for a pinned page: `Drop` unpins it, and `write()` marks the frame dirty so a
/// later eviction knows to flush it back to the mock disk manager first.
struct PageGuard { inner: Rc<RefCell<BpmInner>>, frame_id: FrameId, page_id: PageId }

impl PageGuard {
    fn frame_id(&self) -> FrameId { self.frame_id }
    fn page_id(&self) -> PageId { self.page_id }

    fn read(&self) -> Vec<u8> { self.inner.borrow().frames[self.frame_id].page.as_ref().unwrap().data.clone() }

    fn write(&self, new_data: Vec<u8>) {
        let mut inner = self.inner.borrow_mut();
        let frame = &mut inner.frames[self.frame_id];
        frame.page.as_mut().unwrap().data = new_data;
        frame.dirty = true;  // the guard marks its own frame dirty the moment a caller writes through it
    }
}

impl Drop for PageGuard {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        let mut inner = self.inner.borrow_mut();
        let frame = &mut inner.frames[self.frame_id];
        frame.pin_count -= 1;
        frame.ref_bit = true;
    }
}

impl BufferPoolManager {
    fn new(pool_size: usize) -> Self {
        let frames: Vec<Frame> = (0..pool_size).map(|_| Frame::empty()).collect();
        Self { inner: Rc::new(RefCell::new(BpmInner {
            frames, page_table: HashMap::new(), free_list: (0..pool_size).collect(),
            clock_hand: 0, disk: MockDiskManager::new(),
        })) }
    }

    fn pin_count_of(&self, frame_id: FrameId) -> usize { self.inner.borrow().frames[frame_id].pin_count }
    fn disk_bytes(&self, page_id: PageId) -> Option<Vec<u8>> { self.inner.borrow().disk.storage.get(&page_id).cloned() }

    fn fetch_page(&self, page_id: PageId) -> Option<PageGuard> {
        let mut inner = self.inner.borrow_mut();

        if let Some(&frame_id) = inner.page_table.get(&page_id) {
            inner.frames[frame_id].pin_count += 1;  // second fetch of an already-resident page: SAME frame, pin count grows
            inner.frames[frame_id].ref_bit = true;
            drop(inner);
            return Some(PageGuard { inner: self.inner.clone(), frame_id, page_id });
        }

        let frame_id = if let Some(fid) = inner.free_list.pop() {
            fid
        } else {
            match inner.find_victim() {
                Some(fid) => fid,
                None => return None,  // pool full AND every frame pinned -- cannot evict, cannot fetch
            }
        };

        let page = inner.disk.read_page(page_id);
        inner.page_table.insert(page_id, frame_id);
        inner.frames[frame_id] = Frame { page_id: Some(page_id), page: Some(page), pin_count: 1, dirty: false, ref_bit: true };
        drop(inner);
        Some(PageGuard { inner: self.inner.clone(), frame_id, page_id })
    }
}

fn main() {
    let bpm = BufferPoolManager::new(2);

    // Fetching the same page twice must return the SAME frame with pin count 2, not two copies.
    let g1 = bpm.fetch_page(1).unwrap();
    let g2 = bpm.fetch_page(1).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(g1.frame_id(), g2.frame_id());
    assert_eq!(bpm.pin_count_of(g1.frame_id()), 2);
    assert_eq!(g1.page_id(), 1);
    assert_eq!(g1.read(), vec![0u8; 8]);  // freshly "read from disk" page defaults to zeroed bytes

    g1.write(vec![9u8; 8]);
    assert_eq!(bpm.disk_bytes(1), None);  // NOT yet flushed -- writes only hit the frame, not disk
    drop(g2);  // pin 2 -> 1
    assert_eq!(bpm.pin_count_of(g1.frame_id()), 1);
    drop(g1);  // pin 1 -> 0, frame1 now unpinned but still dirty

    let g3 = bpm.fetch_page(2).unwrap();  // pool has one free frame left -> no eviction needed yet
    let frame1 = 1 - g3.frame_id();  // the other frame, still holding dirty page 1

    // Force the "never evict a pinned frame" scenario explicitly: keep g3 pinned on frame for
    // page 2, and make frame1 (page 1, unpinned+dirty) the ONLY eligible victim, even though a
    // pinned frame could otherwise look just as cold to a naive scan.
    let g4 = bpm.fetch_page(4).expect("must evict the unpinned dirty frame, not the pinned one");
    assert_eq!(g4.frame_id(), frame1);  // victim was exactly the unpinned frame, never the pinned one
    assert_eq!(bpm.pin_count_of(g3.frame_id()), 1);  // page 2's frame was never touched by the sweep

    assert_eq!(bpm.disk_bytes(1), Some(vec![9u8; 8]));  // dirty page WAS flushed to disk before its frame got reused

    // Pool is now full and BOTH remaining frames are pinned (g3 on page 2, g4 on page 4) --
    // fetching anything new must return None, not panic or silently corrupt state.
    let g5 = bpm.fetch_page(5);
    assert!(g5.is_none());
    assert_eq!(bpm.pin_count_of(g3.frame_id()), 1);  // untouched by the failed fetch attempt
    assert_eq!(bpm.pin_count_of(g4.frame_id()), 1);

    drop(g3);
    drop(g4);
    // Now that both are unpinned, a fetch must succeed again (proves None wasn't a permanent wedge).
    let g6 = bpm.fetch_page(6);
    assert!(g6.is_some());

    println!("W61 buffer pool manager: all assertions passed.");
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Treats pin_count > 0 as an absolute veto on eviction, checked first, before any recency/frequency logic even runs — this is the single non-negotiable invariant of a real buffer pool manager: a page pinned by a query executor is actively in use by running code that holds a raw reference into that frame's memory, and evicting it out from under that reference would be a correctness bug (or a memory-safety bug, in a language without Rust's guard-based design), not just a performance one.
  • ★★★Flushes a dirty victim to the mock disk manager before overwriting its frame, not after — a candidate who reads the new page into the frame first and flushes "at some point" risks a bug where an early return, a panic, or simply the wrong ordering loses the previous page's uncommitted writes permanently, since nothing else in the system remembers that data once the frame's contents are overwritten.
  • ★★Fetching an already-resident page increments pin_count and returns the existing frame rather than re-reading from disk — this is the page table's entire reason for existing (an O(1) page_id → frame_id lookup); a candidate who forgets to check the page table first and always goes through the miss path will "work" in casual testing but silently double-load pages and desync pin counts under concurrent-style access patterns.
  • ★Returns None from fetch_page when the pool is full and every frame is pinned, instead of panicking or looping forever — a buffer pool exhausting all frames to concurrent pinned readers/writers is an expected, recoverable condition in a real system (the caller should back off and retry, or the query should abort cleanly), not something that should crash the whole process.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"This solution uses Rc<RefCell<...>> so a PageGuard can call back into the manager on Drop. What breaks if you tried to make this multi-threaded, and what would you change?" — Rc is not Send/Sync, so this exact type simply won't compile if you try to share a BufferPoolManager across threads; you'd swap to Arc<Mutex<BpmInner>> (or a lock-free/sharded design for less contention). But the deeper issue is the single global lock: every fetch_page call — hits and misses alike — currently serializes through one mutex, which is exactly the kind of central bottleneck real buffer pool managers work hard to avoid, typically via per-page-table-partition locks or an entirely lock-free page table with per-frame latches.
  • P2"Real buffer pool managers distinguish a shared (read) pin from an exclusive (write) pin — why does this matter, and what would you add to support it?" — This exercise's single pin_count only proves "someone is using this frame, don't evict it," but says nothing about whether concurrent readers can safely coexist. A real system needs latch semantics: many readers can hold a shared pin simultaneously and read the page concurrently, but a writer needs to know it has exclusive access before mutating page contents, or two threads racing to write the same page corrupt it. You'd extend the pin count into something like a reader-writer lock per frame (e.g. track separate shared/exclusive counts, or wrap the page itself in an RwLock), with the guard type recording which mode it acquired so Drop releases the correct one.
  • P3"You chose clock/second-chance for victim selection. What would change if you used LRU-K (from an earlier exercise) instead, and when would that trade-off matter?" — Clock is O(1) amortized per fetch and needs only one bit per frame, but it's an approximation of LRU that can occasionally evict a page that was touched somewhat recently if the hand happens to sweep past it during a busy period. LRU-K gives strictly better eviction decisions (resistant to one-off scans polluting the pool, as covered in this packet's LRU-K exercise) but costs more per-page bookkeeping (a K-length timestamp history per frame) and a more expensive victim-selection scan unless backed by a proper priority structure. PostgreSQL itself uses clock-sweep specifically because the buffer pool is touched on nearly every query and the per-access overhead has to stay minimal — a good candidate should frame this as "how expensive is a fetch versus how good does the eviction decision need to be," not "which algorithm is objectively best."
🎯 Senior angle
Every piece of this exercise — the page table, the pin counts, the dirty flag, the mandatory flush-before-reuse ordering — exists to answer one question a real database has to answer millions of times a second: "is it safe to reuse this piece of memory yet?" A senior candidate treats the RAII guard not as Rust idiom for its own sake but as the mechanism that makes "forgetting to unpin" structurally impossible, the same way a missing unlock() on an early-return path is a classic, expensive production bug in buffer pool managers written in C. Watch for whether they reason about what happens on a panicking write path — does the pin still get released, or does that frame leak pinned forever? — since that's precisely the failure class RAII is meant to close off.

    assert_eq!(g1.read(), vec![0u8; 8]);  // freshly "read from disk" page defaults to zeroed bytes

    g1.write(vec![9u8; 8]);
    assert_eq!(bpm.disk_bytes(1), None);  // NOT yet flushed -- writes only hit the frame, not disk
    drop(g2);  // pin 2 -> 1
    assert_eq!(bpm.pin_count_of(g1.frame_id()), 1);
    drop(g1);  // pin 1 -> 0, frame1 now unpinned but still dirty

    let g3 = bpm.fetch_page(2).unwrap();  // pool has one free frame left -> no eviction needed yet
    let frame1 = 1 - g3.frame_id();  // the other frame, still holding dirty page 1

    // Force the "never evict a pinned frame" scenario explicitly: keep g3 pinned on frame for
    // page 2, and make frame1 (page 1, unpinned+dirty) the ONLY eligible victim, even though a
    // pinned frame could otherwise look just as cold to a naive scan.
    let g4 = bpm.fetch_page(4).expect("must evict the unpinned dirty frame, not the pinned one");
    assert_eq!(g4.frame_id(), frame1);  // victim was exactly the unpinned frame, never the pinned one
    assert_eq!(bpm.pin_count_of(g3.frame_id()), 1);  // page 2's frame was never touched by the sweep

    assert_eq!(bpm.disk_bytes(1), Some(vec![9u8; 8]));  // dirty page WAS flushed to disk before its frame got reused

    // Pool is now full and BOTH remaining frames are pinned (g3 on page 2, g4 on page 4) --
    // fetching anything new must return None, not panic or silently corrupt state.
    let g5 = bpm.fetch_page(5);
    assert!(g5.is_none());
    assert_eq!(bpm.pin_count_of(g3.frame_id()), 1);  // untouched by the failed fetch attempt
    assert_eq!(bpm.pin_count_of(g4.frame_id()), 1);

    drop(g3);
    drop(g4);
    // Now that both are unpinned, a fetch must succeed again (proves None wasn't a permanent wedge).
    let g6 = bpm.fetch_page(6);
    assert!(g6.is_some());

    println!("W61 buffer pool manager: all assertions passed.");
}

// Database Engineering Exercise 62 · 75 min
W62 · Cost-Based Join Order Optimizer — System R Dynamic Programming
DP over table subsets bitmask-keyed plan table selectivity-based cardinality cartesian-join refusal Hard
Prompt
"Implement the classic System R-style dynamic-programming join-order optimizer. You're given N base tables, each with a known row-count/cardinality estimate, and a set of pairwise join-selectivity estimates — the fraction of the cross product between two specific tables that survives an actual join predicate connecting them. Find the join order — which pairs of intermediate results to join, and in what sequence — that minimizes total estimated intermediate-result cardinality (a simplified proxy for total query cost), by searching all 2^N - 1 non-empty subsets of tables via bottom-up dynamic programming over subsets: a bitmask-keyed HashMap<u32, BestPlan> where each BestPlan stores the subset's estimated cost and which two smaller sub-plans it was assembled from, so the optimal plan can be reconstructed afterward and printed as a join tree (left-deep or bushy — either is legal). Only consider joining two subsets if a selectivity estimate exists connecting some table in one subset to some table in the other — never cost a cartesian-product join when a real join predicate could instead connect the two sides. This constraint is the single most important realism detail in the whole exercise."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::collections::HashMap;

struct BestPlan {
    output_card: f64,  // estimated row count of this subset's join result
    total_cost: f64,   // cumulative sum of every intermediate join size in this subtree
    left: u32,         // bitmask of left child subset (0 == base table, no children)
    right: u32,        // bitmask of right child subset
}

struct Optimizer {
    n: usize,
    base_card: Vec<f64>,
    // selectivity[(i, j)] with i < j == fraction of cross(i, j) that survives the join predicate
    selectivity: HashMap<(usize, usize), f64>,
}

impl Optimizer {
    fn new(base_card: Vec<f64>) -> Self {
        Self { n: base_card.len(), base_card, selectivity: HashMap::new() }
    }

    fn add_join(&mut self, a: usize, b: usize, selectivity: f64) {
        let key = if a < b { (a, b) } else { (b, a) };
        self.selectivity.insert(key, selectivity);
    }

    // TODO: fn has_join_predicate(&self, left: u32, right: u32) -> bool
    //       -- true iff some table in `left` has a selectivity entry with some table in `right`

    // TODO: fn join_cardinality(&self, left: u32, left_card: f64, right: u32, right_card: f64) -> f64
    //       -- left_card * right_card * (product of every selectivity crossing leftright)

    // TODO: fn optimize(&self) -> HashMap  -- bottom-up DP over 2^n - 1 subsets
    // TODO: fn print_plan(&self, dp: &HashMap, mask: u32, names: &[&str]) -> String
}

fn main() {
    // Tables form a query-graph PATH: LineItems -- Orders -- Customers -- Nation.
    let base_card = vec![100_000.0, 1_000.0, 1_000_000.0, 20.0]; // Orders, Customers, LineItems, Nation
    let mut opt = Optimizer::new(base_card.clone());
    let names = ["Orders", "Customers", "LineItems", "Nation"];

    opt.add_join(0, 1, 0.01);       // Orders  Customers: loose FK fan-out
    opt.add_join(2, 0, 0.000_001);  // LineItems  Orders: very tight (~1 order per line item)
    opt.add_join(1, 3, 0.05);       // Customers  Nation: each customer in one of 20 nations
    // No predicate LineItemsCustomers or OrdersNation: joining either pair directly
    // would require a cartesian product.

    let dp = opt.optimize();
    let full = (1u32 << opt.n) - 1;
    let best = dp.get(&full).expect("a valid non-cartesian plan must exist for the full query");

    // -- Naive "obvious" left-to-right order 0,1,2,3 (Orders, Customers, LineItems, Nation) --
    let step1 = opt.join_cardinality(0b0001, base_card[0], 0b0010, base_card[1]); // Orders x Customers
    let step2 = opt.join_cardinality(0b0011, step1, 0b0100, base_card[2]);        // + LineItems
    let step3 = opt.join_cardinality(0b0111, step2, 0b1000, base_card[3]);        // + Nation
    let naive_total = step1 + step2 + step3;

    println!("DP optimal plan: {}", opt.print_plan(&dp, full, &names));
    println!("DP optimal total intermediate cardinality: {}", best.total_cost);
    println!("Naive left-to-right total intermediate cardinality: {}", naive_total);

    assert!(best.total_cost < naive_total);  // DP must strictly beat the "obvious" left-to-right order

    // The true global optimum here is a BUSHY plan, not left-deep: join LineItems with
    // Orders on one side (shrinking the 1,000,000-row table via its tight predicate) while
    // independently joining Customers with Nation, then combining the two small results
    // last. Assert the EXACT known-optimal total, not merely "some cost less than naive".
    let lineitems_orders = opt.join_cardinality(0b0100, base_card[2], 0b0001, base_card[0]);
    let customers_nation = opt.join_cardinality(0b0010, base_card[1], 0b1000, base_card[3]);
    let top_join = opt.join_cardinality(0b0101, lineitems_orders, 0b1010, customers_nation);
    let expected_optimal_total = lineitems_orders + customers_nation + top_join;

    assert_eq!(lineitems_orders, 100_000.0);
    assert_eq!(customers_nation, 1_000.0);
    assert_eq!(top_join, 1_000_000.0);
    assert_eq!(expected_optimal_total, 1_101_000.0);
    assert_eq!(best.total_cost, expected_optimal_total);
    assert_eq!(best.output_card, top_join);

    // The reconstructed plan tree really is the bushy shape, confirmed via the exact
    // child masks the DP stored.
    assert_eq!(best.left.min(best.right), 0b0101); // {LineItems, Orders}
    assert_eq!(best.left.max(best.right), 0b1010); // {Customers, Nation}

    // -- Cartesian-product refusal check --
    // Table A and B have a real predicate; table C is isolated (no predicate to A or B at
    // all). The optimizer must never bridge C in via a cartesian product.
    let mut opt2 = Optimizer::new(vec![10.0, 5.0, 1000.0]);
    opt2.add_join(0, 1, 0.5); // A-B: real predicate; no edge at all to isolated table C
    let dp2 = opt2.optimize();
    assert!(dp2.contains_key(&0b011), "A-B has a real predicate; must be reachable");
    assert!(!dp2.contains_key(&0b101), "A-C has no predicate; must be refused, not costed as cartesian");
    assert!(!dp2.contains_key(&0b110), "B-C has no predicate; must be refused, not costed as cartesian");
    assert!(
        !dp2.contains_key(&0b111),
        "full set requires a cartesian product to include isolated table C; must be refused"
    );

    println!("Cartesian-refusal check passed: isolated table correctly makes {{A,B,C}} unreachable.");
    println!("All assertions passed.");
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::collections::HashMap;

struct BestPlan {
    // Estimated row count of THIS subset's join result. Under the standard independence
    // assumption this value is the SAME no matter which internal join order produced it --
    // it depends only on which tables are in the subset and which selectivity edges lie
    // fully inside it -- so it's safe to reuse whenever this subset becomes someone's child.
    output_card: f64,
    // Sum of every intermediate join's output size inside this subtree. THIS -- not
    // output_card -- is the quantity join-order optimization actually minimizes: two
    // different orders producing the same subset have IDENTICAL final output_card but can
    // have wildly different total_cost, depending on how large the intermediates were.
    total_cost: f64,
    left: u32,  // bitmask of left sub-plan (0 = this is a base table, not a join)
    right: u32, // bitmask of right sub-plan
}

struct Optimizer {
    n: usize,
    base_card: Vec<f64>,
    // selectivity[(i, j)] with i < j = fraction of cross product i x j that survives the join predicate
    selectivity: HashMap<(usize, usize), f64>,
}

impl Optimizer {
    fn new(base_card: Vec<f64>) -> Self {
        Self { n: base_card.len(), base_card, selectivity: HashMap::new() }
    }

    fn add_join(&mut self, a: usize, b: usize, selectivity: f64) {
        let key = if a < b { (a, b) } else { (b, a) };
        self.selectivity.insert(key, selectivity);
    }

    /// True if at least one predicate connects some table in `left` to some table in `right`.
    /// Without this check the DP would happily cost a cartesian product exactly like a real
    /// join, which is the single most common mistake in a naive from-scratch implementation.
    fn has_join_predicate(&self, left: u32, right: u32) -> bool {
        for i in 0..self.n {
            if left & (1 << i) == 0 { continue; }
            for j in 0..self.n {
                if right & (1 << j) == 0 { continue; }
                let key = if i < j { (i, j) } else { (j, i) };
                if self.selectivity.contains_key(&key) { return true; }
            }
        }
        false
    }

    /// Estimated output cardinality of joining two subsets whose own estimated cardinalities
    /// are already known: cross product scaled down by the product of every selectivity that
    /// connects a table on the left to a table on the right (a pair only contributes once,
    /// and only if a predicate actually exists between that specific pair).
    fn join_cardinality(&self, left: u32, left_card: f64, right: u32, right_card: f64) -> f64 {
        let mut sel_product = 1.0;
        for i in 0..self.n {
            if left & (1 << i) == 0 { continue; }
            for j in 0..self.n {
                if right & (1 << j) == 0 { continue; }
                let key = if i < j { (i, j) } else { (j, i) };
                if let Some(&s) = self.selectivity.get(&key) { sel_product *= s; }
            }
        }
        left_card * right_card * sel_product
    }

    /// Classic System R bottom-up dynamic program over all 2^n - 1 non-empty subsets of
    /// tables, keyed by bitmask. dp[S] holds the cheapest way (by cumulative intermediate
    /// cost) to join every table in S, plus the two child masks it was assembled from so the
    /// plan tree can be reconstructed afterward.
    fn optimize(&self) -> HashMap<u32, BestPlan> {
        let mut dp: HashMap<u32, BestPlan> = HashMap::new();

        for i in 0..self.n {
            let mask = 1u32 << i;
            dp.insert(mask, BestPlan { output_card: self.base_card[i], total_cost: 0.0, left: 0, right: 0 });
        }

        let full = (1u32 << self.n) - 1;
        for size in 2..=self.n {
            for subset in 1..=full {
                if (subset.count_ones() as usize) != size { continue; }
                let mut best: Option<BestPlan> = None;

                // Enumerate every way to split `subset` into two non-empty, disjoint sub-masks
                // that together cover it exactly -- every such split is a candidate join order.
                let mut sub = (subset - 1) & subset;
                while sub > 0 {
                    let left = sub;
                    let right = subset & !sub;
                    if left != 0 && right != 0 {
                        if let (Some(lp), Some(rp)) = (dp.get(&left), dp.get(&right)) {
                            if self.has_join_predicate(left, right) {  // refuse every split with no real predicate
                                let join_card = self.join_cardinality(left, lp.output_card, right, rp.output_card);
                                let total_cost = join_card + lp.total_cost + rp.total_cost;  // cumulative, not just this join's own size
                                if best.as_ref().map_or(true, |b| total_cost < b.total_cost) {  // compare total_cost, NEVER output_card
                                    best = Some(BestPlan { output_card: join_card, total_cost, left, right });
                                }
                            }
                        }
                    }
                    sub = (sub - 1) & subset;
                }

                if let Some(plan) = best {
                    dp.insert(subset, plan);
                }
                // if `best` stays None, every split of this subset required a cartesian product --
                // it correctly stays permanently absent from the DP table, never silently costed.
            }
        }
        dp
    }

    fn print_plan(&self, dp: &HashMap<u32, BestPlan>, mask: u32, names: &[&str]) -> String {
        if mask.count_ones() == 1 {
            let idx = mask.trailing_zeros() as usize;
            return names[idx].to_string();
        }
        let plan = &dp[&mask];
        format!(
            "({} JOIN {})",
            self.print_plan(dp, plan.left, names),
            self.print_plan(dp, plan.right, names)
        )
    }
}

fn main() {
    // Tables form a query-graph PATH: LineItems -- Orders -- Customers -- Nation.
    let base_card = vec![100_000.0, 1_000.0, 1_000_000.0, 20.0]; // Orders, Customers, LineItems, Nation
    let mut opt = Optimizer::new(base_card.clone());
    let names = ["Orders", "Customers", "LineItems", "Nation"];

    opt.add_join(0, 1, 0.01);       // Orders <-> Customers: loose FK fan-out
    opt.add_join(2, 0, 0.000_001);  // LineItems <-> Orders: very tight (~1 order per line item)
    opt.add_join(1, 3, 0.05);       // Customers <-> Nation: each customer in one of 20 nations
    // No predicate LineItems<->Customers or Orders<->Nation: joining either pair directly
    // would require a cartesian product.

    let dp = opt.optimize();
    let full = (1u32 << opt.n) - 1;
    let best = dp.get(&full).expect("a valid non-cartesian plan must exist for the full query");

    // -- Naive "obvious" left-to-right order 0,1,2,3 (Orders, Customers, LineItems, Nation) --
    let step1 = opt.join_cardinality(0b0001, base_card[0], 0b0010, base_card[1]); // Orders x Customers
    let step2 = opt.join_cardinality(0b0011, step1, 0b0100, base_card[2]);        // + LineItems
    let step3 = opt.join_cardinality(0b0111, step2, 0b1000, base_card[3]);        // + Nation
    let naive_total = step1 + step2 + step3;

    println!("DP optimal plan: {}", opt.print_plan(&dp, full, &names));
    println!("DP optimal total intermediate cardinality: {}", best.total_cost);
    println!("Naive left-to-right total intermediate cardinality: {}", naive_total);

    assert!(best.total_cost < naive_total);  // DP must strictly beat the "obvious" left-to-right order

    // The true global optimum here is a BUSHY plan, not left-deep: join LineItems with
    // Orders on one side (shrinking the 1,000,000-row table via its tight predicate) while
    // independently joining Customers with Nation, then combining the two small results
    // last. Assert the EXACT known-optimal total, not merely "some cost less than naive".
    let lineitems_orders = opt.join_cardinality(0b0100, base_card[2], 0b0001, base_card[0]);
    let customers_nation = opt.join_cardinality(0b0010, base_card[1], 0b1000, base_card[3]);
    let top_join = opt.join_cardinality(0b0101, lineitems_orders, 0b1010, customers_nation);
    let expected_optimal_total = lineitems_orders + customers_nation + top_join;

    assert_eq!(lineitems_orders, 100_000.0);
    assert_eq!(customers_nation, 1_000.0);
    assert_eq!(top_join, 1_000_000.0);
    assert_eq!(expected_optimal_total, 1_101_000.0);
    assert_eq!(best.total_cost, expected_optimal_total);
    assert_eq!(best.output_card, top_join);

    // The reconstructed plan tree really is the bushy shape, confirmed via the exact
    // child masks the DP stored.
    assert_eq!(best.left.min(best.right), 0b0101); // {LineItems, Orders}
    assert_eq!(best.left.max(best.right), 0b1010); // {Customers, Nation}

    // -- Cartesian-product refusal check --
    // Table A and B have a real predicate; table C is isolated (no predicate to A or B at
    // all). The optimizer must never bridge C in via a cartesian product.
    let mut opt2 = Optimizer::new(vec![10.0, 5.0, 1000.0]);
    opt2.add_join(0, 1, 0.5); // A-B: real predicate; no edge at all to isolated table C
    let dp2 = opt2.optimize();
    assert!(dp2.contains_key(&0b011), "A-B has a real predicate; must be reachable");
    assert!(!dp2.contains_key(&0b101), "A-C has no predicate; must be refused, not costed as cartesian");
    assert!(!dp2.contains_key(&0b110), "B-C has no predicate; must be refused, not costed as cartesian");
    assert!(
        !dp2.contains_key(&0b111),
        "full set requires a cartesian product to include isolated table C; must be refused"
    );

    println!("Cartesian-refusal check passed: isolated table correctly makes {{A,B,C}} unreachable.");
    println!("All assertions passed.");
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Distinguishes a subset's output cardinality from its cumulative cost, and compares the right one in the DP — under the standard independence assumption, the estimated row count of joining a fixed set of tables is the same regardless of join order (it only depends on which tables and which selectivity edges are involved), but the SUM of intermediate sizes produced along the way absolutely does depend on order. A candidate who accidentally compares/minimizes output cardinality instead of cumulative cost will produce a DP that silently ties on every split of a given subset (since that value never varies) and picks whichever split happens to be enumerated first — a bug that runs, produces plausible-looking output, and is completely wrong.
  • ★★★Enforces the "must have a real predicate to combine two subsets" rule as a hard gate, not a cost penalty — a subset with no legal non-cartesian split must be genuinely unreachable in the DP table (absent, not merely expensive), because in this simplified model there is no finite selectivity that makes a cartesian product an acceptable substitute for a real join in the optimizer's search space.
  • ★★Considers bushy plans, not just left-deep chains — enumerating every non-empty proper submask of a subset (not just "the subset minus one table") is what allows the DP to discover that joining two independent pairs first and combining them last can beat any strictly incremental left-deep build order, exactly like this exercise's own optimal plan.
  • ★Reconstructs the actual plan tree from stored child masks rather than only reporting a final cost number — a query optimizer's real deliverable is the plan itself (what a downstream execution engine will run), not just a cost estimate.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"This DP is O(3^N) in the number of tables — real queries can have dozens of tables. How do production optimizers like Postgres or CockroachDB avoid blowing up?" — Postgres switches from exhaustive DP to a genetic algorithm (GEQO) once the join count passes a configurable threshold (geqo_threshold, default 12), trading optimality for tractable planning time. Many systems also restrict the search to left-deep (or "zig-zag") trees above some size to cut the branching factor, or apply heuristics to prune subsets unlikely to be useful (e.g. only keep the single best plan per subset under one cost metric, which is exactly what this exercise's DP already does — the real generalization is pruning WHICH subsets get explored at all, not just picking one plan per subset).
  • P2"Where would real selectivity estimates actually come from, and what happens when the independence assumption this exercise relies on is wrong?" — Real optimizers derive selectivities from per-column statistics: histograms, most-common-value lists, and distinct-value counts collected by ANALYZE-style commands, then combine multiple predicates by multiplying their individual selectivities together — which is precisely the independence assumption. When columns are correlated (e.g. city='NYC' AND zip_code='10001' are almost perfectly correlated, not independent), multiplying selectivities badly under-estimates the true result size, which is one of the most common real-world causes of a query optimizer picking a catastrophically bad plan; modern systems partially address this with multi-column statistics/extended statistics.
  • P3"This DP's cost model is pure row-count. What's missing to make it a real query optimizer's cost model?" — Real cost models fold in the PHYSICAL cost of each join algorithm (nested-loop vs. hash join vs. sort-merge join), each with different CPU/IO cost curves depending on whether inputs fit in memory, whether an index is available, and whether the output needs to preserve a particular sort order for a later operation (e.g. a merge join or a subsequent ORDER BY) — so the "best" plan for a subset often isn't a single number but a small set of Pareto-optimal candidates, one per useful output ordering/interesting property, all of which must be carried forward through the DP rather than collapsed to one number per subset.
🎯 Senior angle
The line between a mid-level and a senior answer here is almost entirely about that output-cardinality-vs-cumulative-cost distinction. A mid-level candidate will often write a DP that "works" on simple test cases (because with only two children, comparing either quantity coincidentally steers toward a locally-plausible plan) but silently degrades to "first split found" on any subset with more than one legal non-cartesian split — exactly the failure mode this exercise's own fixture was engineered to expose. Watching whether a candidate proves to themselves (with a concrete pen-and-paper counter-example, not just intuition) that final row count is order-invariant while total cost is not is a genuinely excellent signal of real query-optimization understanding versus pattern-matched DP syntax.

// Answer by code:
// This DP is O(3^N) in the number of tables — real queries can have dozens of tables. How do production optimizers like Postgres or CockroachDB avoid blowing up?
fn harden_w62_1() {
    // use: BestPlan, Optimizer
    todo!()
}

fn main() {
    // Harden · This DP is O(3^N) in the number of tables — real queries can have doz…
    harden_w62_1();
    // Parent exercise still holds after the harden change:
    // Tables form a query-graph PATH: LineItems -- Orders -- Customers -- Nation.
    let base_card = vec![100_000.0, 1_000.0, 1_000_000.0, 20.0]; // Orders, Customers, LineItems, Nation
    let mut opt = Optimizer::new(base_card.clone());
    let names = ["Orders", "Customers", "LineItems", "Nation"];

    opt.add_join(0, 1, 0.01);       // Orders  Customers: loose FK fan-out
    opt.add_join(2, 0, 0.000_001);  // LineItems  Orders: very tight (~1 order per line item)
    opt.add_join(1, 3, 0.05);       // Customers  Nation: each customer in one of 20 nations
    // No predicate LineItemsCustomers or OrdersNation: joining either pair directly
    // would require a cartesian product.

    let dp = opt.optimize();
    let full = (1u32 << opt.n) - 1;
    let best = dp.get(&full).expect("a valid non-cartesian plan must exist for the full query");

    // -- Naive "obvious" left-to-right order 0,1,2,3 (Orders, Customers, LineItems, Nation) --
    let step1 = opt.join_cardinality(0b0001, base_card[0], 0b0010, base_card[1]); // Orders x Customers
    let step2 = opt.join_cardinality(0b0011, step1, 0b0100, base_card[2]);        // + LineItems
    let step3 = opt.join_cardinality(0b0111, step2, 0b1000, base_card[3]);        // + Nation
    let naive_total = step1 + step2 + step3;

    println!("DP optimal plan: {}", opt.print_plan(&dp, full, &names));
    println!("DP optimal total intermediate cardinality: {}", best.total_cost);
    println!("Naive left-to-right total intermediate cardinality: {}", naive_total);

    assert!(best.total_cost < naive_total);  // DP must strictly beat the "obvious" left-to-right order

    // The true global optimum here is a BUSHY plan, not left-deep: join LineItems with
    // Orders on one side (shrinking the 1,000,000-row table via its tight predicate) while
    // independently joining Customers with Nation, then combining the two small results
    // last. Assert the EXACT known-optimal total, not merely "some cost less than naive".
    let lineitems_orders = opt.join_cardinality(0b0100, base_card[2], 0b0001, base_card[0]);
    let customers_nation = opt.join_cardinality(0b0010, base_card[1], 0b1000, base_card[3]);
    let top_join = opt.join_cardinality(0b0101, lineitems_orders, 0b1010, customers_nation);
    let expected_optimal_total = lineitems_orders + customers_nation + top_join;

    assert_eq!(lineitems_orders, 100_000.0);
    assert_eq!(customers_nation, 1_000.0);
    assert_eq!(top_join, 1_000_000.0);
    assert_eq!(expected_optimal_total, 1_101_000.0);
    assert_eq!(best.total_cost, expected_optimal_total);
    assert_eq!(best.output_card, top_join);

    // The reconstructed plan tree really is the bushy shape, confirmed via the exact
    // child masks the DP stored.
    assert_eq!(best.left.min(best.right), 0b0101); // {LineItems, Orders}
    assert_eq!(best.left.max(best.right), 0b1010); // {Customers, Nation}

    // -- Cartesian-product refusal check --
    // Table A and B have a real predicate; table C is isolated (no predicate to A or B at
    // all). The optimizer must never bridge C in via a cartesian product.
    let mut opt2 = Optimizer::new(vec![10.0, 5.0, 1000.0]);
    opt2.add_join(0, 1, 0.5); // A-B: real predicate; no edge at all to isolated table C
    let dp2 = opt2.optimize();
    assert!(dp2.contains_key(&0b011), "A-B has a real predicate; must be reachable");
    assert!(!dp2.contains_key(&0b101), "A-C has no predicate; must be refused, not costed as cartesian");
    assert!(!dp2.contains_key(&0b110), "B-C has no predicate; must be refused, not costed as cartesian");
    assert!(
        !dp2.contains_key(&0b111),
        "full set requires a cartesian product to include isolated table C; must be refused"
    );

    println!("Cartesian-refusal check passed: isolated table correctly makes {{A,B,C}} unreachable.");
    println!("All assertions passed.");
}

    let lineitems_orders = opt.join_cardinality(0b0100, base_card[2], 0b0001, base_card[0]);
    let customers_nation = opt.join_cardinality(0b0010, base_card[1], 0b1000, base_card[3]);
    let top_join = opt.join_cardinality(0b0101, lineitems_orders, 0b1010, customers_nation);
    let expected_optimal_total = lineitems_orders + customers_nation + top_join;

    assert_eq!(lineitems_orders, 100_000.0);
    assert_eq!(customers_nation, 1_000.0);
    assert_eq!(top_join, 1_000_000.0);
    assert_eq!(expected_optimal_total, 1_101_000.0);
    assert_eq!(best.total_cost, expected_optimal_total);
    assert_eq!(best.output_card, top_join);

    // The reconstructed plan tree really is the bushy shape, confirmed via the exact
    // child masks the DP stored.
    assert_eq!(best.left.min(best.right), 0b0101); // {LineItems, Orders}
    assert_eq!(best.left.max(best.right), 0b1010); // {Customers, Nation}

    // -- Cartesian-product refusal check --
    // Table A and B have a real predicate; table C is isolated (no predicate to A or B at
    // all). The optimizer must never bridge C in via a cartesian product.
    let mut opt2 = Optimizer::new(vec![10.0, 5.0, 1000.0]);
    opt2.add_join(0, 1, 0.5); // A-B: real predicate; no edge at all to isolated table C
    let dp2 = opt2.optimize();
    assert!(dp2.contains_key(&0b011), "A-B has a real predicate; must be reachable");
    assert!(!dp2.contains_key(&0b101), "A-C has no predicate; must be refused, not costed as cartesian");
    assert!(!dp2.contains_key(&0b110), "B-C has no predicate; must be refused, not costed as cartesian");
    assert!(
        !dp2.contains_key(&0b111),
        "full set requires a cartesian product to include isolated table C; must be refused"
    );

    println!("Cartesian-refusal check passed: isolated table correctly makes {{A,B,C}} unreachable.");
    println!("All assertions passed.");
}

use std::fmt;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
enum Token {
    Select, From, Join, On, Where, And, Or,
    Ident(String), Number(i64), Str(String),
    Comma, Dot, LParen, RParen,
    Eq, Ne, Lt, Gt, Le, Ge, Eof,
}

impl fmt::Display for Token {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        match self {
            Token::Select => write!(f, "SELECT"),
            Token::From => write!(f, "FROM"),
            Token::Join => write!(f, "JOIN"),
            Token::On => write!(f, "ON"),
            Token::Where => write!(f, "WHERE"),
            Token::And => write!(f, "AND"),
            Token::Or => write!(f, "OR"),
            Token::Ident(s) => write!(f, "identifier `{}`", s),
            Token::Number(n) => write!(f, "number `{}`", n),
            Token::Str(s) => write!(f, "string '{}'", s),
            Token::Comma => write!(f, "','"),
            Token::Dot => write!(f, "'.'"),
            Token::LParen => write!(f, "'('"),
            Token::RParen => write!(f, "')'"),
            Token::Eq => write!(f, "'='"),
            Token::Ne => write!(f, "'!='"),
            Token::Lt => write!(f, "'<'"),
            Token::Gt => write!(f, "'>'"),
            Token::Le => write!(f, "'<='"),
            Token::Ge => write!(f, "'>='"),
            Token::Eof => write!(f, "end of input"),
        }
    }
}

#[derive(Debug)]
enum LexError { UnterminatedString, UnexpectedChar(char) }

impl fmt::Display for LexError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        match self {
            LexError::UnterminatedString => write!(f, "unterminated string literal"),
            LexError::UnexpectedChar(c) => write!(f, "unexpected character '{}'", c),
        }
    }
}

fn tokenize(src: &str) -> Result<Vec<Token>, LexError> {
    let chars: Vec<char> = src.chars().collect();
    let mut i = 0;
    let mut tokens = Vec::new();

    while i < chars.len() {
        let c = chars[i];
        if c.is_whitespace() { i += 1; continue; }
        match c {
            ',' => { tokens.push(Token::Comma); i += 1; }
            '.' => { tokens.push(Token::Dot); i += 1; }
            '(' => { tokens.push(Token::LParen); i += 1; }
            ')' => { tokens.push(Token::RParen); i += 1; }
            '=' => { tokens.push(Token::Eq); i += 1; }
            '!' if chars.get(i + 1) == Some(&'=') => { tokens.push(Token::Ne); i += 2; }
            '<' if chars.get(i + 1) == Some(&'=') => { tokens.push(Token::Le); i += 2; }
            '>' if chars.get(i + 1) == Some(&'=') => { tokens.push(Token::Ge); i += 2; }
            '<' => { tokens.push(Token::Lt); i += 1; }
            '>' => { tokens.push(Token::Gt); i += 1; }
            '\'' => {
                let start = i + 1;
                let mut j = start;
                while j < chars.len() && chars[j] != '\'' { j += 1; }  // scan to the CLOSING quote
                if j >= chars.len() { return Err(LexError::UnterminatedString); }
                tokens.push(Token::Str(chars[start..j].iter().collect()));
                i = j + 1;
            }
            _ if c.is_ascii_digit() => {
                let start = i;
                while i < chars.len() && chars[i].is_ascii_digit() { i += 1; }
                let text: String = chars[start..i].iter().collect();
                tokens.push(Token::Number(text.parse().expect("digit-only scan always parses")));
            }
            _ if c.is_alphabetic() || c == '_' => {
                let start = i;
                while i < chars.len() && (chars[i].is_alphanumeric() || chars[i] == '_') { i += 1; }
                let text: String = chars[start..i].iter().collect();
                tokens.push(match text.to_ascii_uppercase().as_str() {  // case-insensitive keyword match
                    "SELECT" => Token::Select,
                    "FROM" => Token::From,
                    "JOIN" => Token::Join,
                    "ON" => Token::On,
                    "WHERE" => Token::Where,
                    "AND" => Token::And,
                    "OR" => Token::Or,
                    _ => Token::Ident(text),
                });
            }
            other => return Err(LexError::UnexpectedChar(other)),
        }
    }
    tokens.push(Token::Eof);
    Ok(tokens)
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
struct ColRef { table: Option<String>, column: String }

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
enum CompareOp { Eq, Ne, Lt, Gt, Le, Ge }

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
enum Value { Int(i64), Str(String), Column(ColRef) }

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
enum Expr {
    Compare(ColRef, CompareOp, Value),
    And(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>),
    Or(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>),
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
struct JoinClause { table: String, left: ColRef, right: ColRef }

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
struct SelectStmt {
    columns: Vec<ColRef>,
    from: String,
    join: Option<JoinClause>,
    where_clause: Option<Expr>,
}

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
enum ParseError {
    UnexpectedToken { expected: &'static str, found: String },
    UnexpectedEof { expected: &'static str },
    LexFailure(String),
}

impl fmt::Display for ParseError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        match self {
            ParseError::UnexpectedToken { expected, found } => write!(f, "expected {} but found {}", expected, found),
            ParseError::UnexpectedEof { expected } => write!(f, "expected {} but reached end of input", expected),
            ParseError::LexFailure(msg) => write!(f, "lex error: {}", msg),
        }
    }
}

struct Parser { tokens: Vec<Token>, pos: usize }

impl Parser {
    fn new(tokens: Vec<Token>) -> Self { Self { tokens, pos: 0 } }

    fn peek(&self) -> &Token { &self.tokens[self.pos] }

    fn advance(&mut self) -> Token {
        let t = self.tokens[self.pos].clone();
        if self.pos + 1 < self.tokens.len() { self.pos += 1; }
        t
    }

    fn expect(&mut self, expected: &Token, name: &'static str) -> Result<(), ParseError> {
        if self.peek() == expected {
            self.advance();
            Ok(())
        } else if self.peek() == &Token::Eof {
            Err(ParseError::UnexpectedEof { expected: name })
        } else {
            Err(ParseError::UnexpectedToken { expected: name, found: self.peek().to_string() })
        }
    }

    fn expect_ident(&mut self, name: &'static str) -> Result<String, ParseError> {
        match self.peek().clone() {
            Token::Ident(s) => { self.advance(); Ok(s) }
            Token::Eof => Err(ParseError::UnexpectedEof { expected: name }),
            other => Err(ParseError::UnexpectedToken { expected: name, found: other.to_string() }),
        }
    }

    fn parse_col_ref(&mut self) -> Result<ColRef, ParseError> {
        let first = self.expect_ident("column or table.column reference")?;
        if self.peek() == &Token::Dot {
            self.advance();
            let column = self.expect_ident("column name after '.'")?;
            Ok(ColRef { table: Some(first), column })
        } else {
            Ok(ColRef { table: None, column: first })
        }
    }

    fn parse_compare_op(&mut self) -> Result<CompareOp, ParseError> {
        let op = match self.peek() {
            Token::Eq => CompareOp::Eq,
            Token::Ne => CompareOp::Ne,
            Token::Lt => CompareOp::Lt,
            Token::Gt => CompareOp::Gt,
            Token::Le => CompareOp::Le,
            Token::Ge => CompareOp::Ge,
            Token::Eof => return Err(ParseError::UnexpectedEof { expected: "comparison operator" }),
            other => return Err(ParseError::UnexpectedToken { expected: "comparison operator", found: other.to_string() }),
        };
        self.advance();
        Ok(op)
    }

    fn parse_value(&mut self) -> Result<Value, ParseError> {
        match self.peek().clone() {
            Token::Number(n) => { self.advance(); Ok(Value::Int(n)) }
            Token::Str(s) => { self.advance(); Ok(Value::Str(s)) }
            Token::Ident(_) => Ok(Value::Column(self.parse_col_ref()?)),
            Token::Eof => Err(ParseError::UnexpectedEof { expected: "a value (number, string, or column reference)" }),
            other => Err(ParseError::UnexpectedToken { expected: "a value (number, string, or column reference)", found: other.to_string() }),
        }
    }

    fn parse_comparison(&mut self) -> Result<Expr, ParseError> {
        let left = self.parse_col_ref()?;
        let op = self.parse_compare_op()?;
        let right = self.parse_value()?;
        Ok(Expr::Compare(left, op, right))
    }

    fn parse_primary(&mut self) -> Result<Expr, ParseError> {
        if self.peek() == &Token::LParen {
            self.advance();
            let inner = self.parse_or_expr()?;
            self.expect(&Token::RParen, "')'")?;
            Ok(inner)
        } else {
            self.parse_comparison()
        }
    }

    // AND binds tighter than OR: parse_and_expr consumes a whole run of ANDs before
    // parse_or_expr ever gets to combine anything with OR, so `a OR b AND c` becomes
    // Or(a, And(b, c)) rather than the wrong And(Or(a, b), c).
    fn parse_and_expr(&mut self) -> Result<Expr, ParseError> {
        let mut left = self.parse_primary()?;
        while self.peek() == &Token::And {
            self.advance();
            let right = self.parse_primary()?;
            left = Expr::And(Box::new(left), Box::new(right));
        }
        Ok(left)
    }

    fn parse_or_expr(&mut self) -> Result<Expr, ParseError> {
        let mut left = self.parse_and_expr()?;  // each side of an OR is itself a full AND-chain
        while self.peek() == &Token::Or {
            self.advance();
            let right = self.parse_and_expr()?;
            left = Expr::Or(Box::new(left), Box::new(right));
        }
        Ok(left)
    }

    fn parse_select(&mut self) -> Result<SelectStmt, ParseError> {
        self.expect(&Token::Select, "SELECT")?;

        let mut columns = vec![self.parse_col_ref()?];
        while self.peek() == &Token::Comma {
            self.advance();
            columns.push(self.parse_col_ref()?);
        }

        self.expect(&Token::From, "FROM")?;
        let from = self.expect_ident("table name after FROM")?;

        let join = if self.peek() == &Token::Join {
            self.advance();
            let table = self.expect_ident("table name after JOIN")?;
            self.expect(&Token::On, "ON")?;
            let left = self.parse_col_ref()?;
            self.expect(&Token::Eq, "'=' in JOIN ON clause")?;
            let right = self.parse_col_ref()?;
            Some(JoinClause { table, left, right })
        } else {
            None
        };

        let where_clause = if self.peek() == &Token::Where {
            self.advance();
            Some(self.parse_or_expr()?)
        } else {
            None
        };

        self.expect(&Token::Eof, "end of statement")?;
        Ok(SelectStmt { columns, from, join, where_clause })
    }
}

fn parse_sql(src: &str) -> Result<SelectStmt, ParseError> {
    let tokens = tokenize(src).map_err(|e| ParseError::LexFailure(e.to_string()))?;
    Parser::new(tokens).parse_select()
}

fn col(table: Option<&str>, column: &str) -> ColRef {
    ColRef { table: table.map(String::from), column: column.to_string() }
}

fn main() {
    // -- 1. Full query: JOIN + WHERE combining AND/OR/parens -- assert the EXACT AST shape --
    let sql = "SELECT o.id, c.name FROM orders JOIN customers ON orders.cust_id = customers.id \
               WHERE (o.total > 100 AND c.active = 1) OR c.vip = 1";
    let stmt = parse_sql(sql).expect("well-formed query must parse");

    let expected = SelectStmt {
        columns: vec![col(Some("o"), "id"), col(Some("c"), "name")],
        from: "orders".to_string(),
        join: Some(JoinClause {
            table: "customers".to_string(),
            left: col(Some("orders"), "cust_id"),
            right: col(Some("customers"), "id"),
        }),
        where_clause: Some(Expr::Or(
            Box::new(Expr::And(
                Box::new(Expr::Compare(col(Some("o"), "total"), CompareOp::Gt, Value::Int(100))),
                Box::new(Expr::Compare(col(Some("c"), "active"), CompareOp::Eq, Value::Int(1))),
            )),
            Box::new(Expr::Compare(col(Some("c"), "vip"), CompareOp::Eq, Value::Int(1))),
        )),
    };
    assert_eq!(stmt, expected, "full JOIN+WHERE query must parse into the exact expected AST");

    // -- 2. Precedence: AND binds tighter than OR, WITHOUT parens forcing it --
    let stmt2 = parse_sql("SELECT x FROM t WHERE a = 1 OR b = 2 AND c = 3").unwrap();
    let precedence_expected = Expr::Or(

        Box::new(Expr::And(

    // -- 3. String literal + all six comparison operators + bare column (no table prefix) --

            Box::new(Expr::Compare(col(None, "status"), CompareOp::Ne, Value::Str("inactive".to_string()))),
            Box::new(Expr::Compare(col(None, "age"), CompareOp::Ge, Value::Int(18))),

    // -- 4. Column-to-column comparison in WHERE (not just column-to-literal) --
    let stmt4 = parse_sql("SELECT a FROM t1 WHERE t1.x = t1.y").unwrap();
    assert_eq!(
        stmt4.where_clause,

    );

    // -- 5. No JOIN, no WHERE -- both are genuinely optional --
    let stmt5 = parse_sql("SELECT a, b FROM t").unwrap();
    assert!(stmt5.join.is_none());
    assert!(stmt5.where_clause.is_none());
    assert_eq!(stmt5.columns, vec![col(None, "a"), col(None, "b")]);

    // -- 6. Malformed #1: missing FROM entirely -> UnexpectedToken (WHERE found instead) --
    let err1 = parse_sql("SELECT a, b WHERE a = 1").unwrap_err();
    match &err1 {
        ParseError::UnexpectedToken { expected, found } => {
            assert_eq!(*expected, "FROM");
            assert_eq!(found, "WHERE");
        }
        other => panic!("expected UnexpectedToken variant, got {:?}", other),
    }
    assert_eq!(err1.to_string(), "expected FROM but found WHERE");

    // -- 7. Malformed #2: unterminated parenthesis in WHERE -> a DIFFERENT error variant --
    let err2 = parse_sql("SELECT a FROM t WHERE (a = 1 AND b = 2").unwrap_err();

        other => panic!("expected UnexpectedEof variant, got {:?}", other),
    }

    let err3 = parse_sql("SELECT a, FROM t").unwrap_err();

        }
        other => panic!("expected UnexpectedToken variant, got {:?}", other),
    }

    println!("All assertions passed.");
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Structures the grammar itself so AND binds tighter than OR, rather than parsing a flat list of tokens and trying to fix precedence after the fact — the standard recursive-descent trick is layering: parse_or_expr calls parse_and_expr as its unit, and parse_and_expr calls parse_primary as ITS unit, so a run of ANDs is always fully consumed and combined before an enclosing OR ever gets a chance to grab one side of it. A candidate who instead parses left-to-right and combines whichever operator comes next will get the precedence backwards on exactly the kind of unparenthesized mixed expression this exercise tests for.
  • ★★★Produces genuinely useful, position-aware error messages (naming what was expected AND what was actually found) instead of a generic "parse failed" — this is the difference between a parser a candidate could imagine shipping and a toy one; it also forces correctly threading Result with ? through every recursive call rather than panicking on the first malformed token.
  • ★★Cleanly separates lexing from parsing — tokenizing first into a flat Vec<Token> (handling whitespace, keyword case-insensitivity, and multi-character operators like <= in one dedicated pass) lets the recursive-descent parser reason purely about token TYPES via peek/advance, instead of re-deriving lexical rules (like "is this `=` part of `>=`?") deep inside grammar logic where they don't belong.
  • ★Derives PartialEq on every AST node specifically so tests can assert on exact tree shape with assert_eq! rather than manually walking the tree or only checking that parsing didn't error — this is a strong signal that a candidate actually thinks about how their own code will be tested and verified, not just how it will be written.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Real SQL also has NOT, IN, BETWEEN, and IS NULL. Where would each fit into this grammar's precedence hierarchy, and does anything here need to change structurally?" — NOT is a prefix unary operator that binds tighter than AND (standard SQL precedence is NOT > AND > OR), so it would slot in as a new layer between parse_and_expr and parse_primary: parse_not_expr checks for a leading NOT token and wraps the result of parse_primary in an Expr::Not(Box<Expr>) variant. IN, BETWEEN, and IS NULL are all really just alternate FORMS of comparison (same precedence level as =/</etc.), so they'd extend parse_comparison's dispatch on the operator token rather than requiring a new precedence layer at all.
  • P2"This parser rejects a query the instant it hits one error. A real SQL client or IDE often wants to report MULTIPLE errors from one bad query, or recover and keep parsing. How would you change this?" — This requires moving from "fail-fast on first Err" to "error recovery": on a parse failure, instead of immediately propagating via ?, the parser records the error and then skips forward to a known synchronization point (e.g. the next ,, the next clause keyword like WHERE/JOIN, or end of statement) before resuming — the classic technique is called "panic-mode recovery," borrowed directly from compiler construction, and it requires the parser to track a list of accumulated errors rather than short-circuiting on the first one.
  • P3"This grammar hard-codes exactly one optional JOIN. How would you extend it to support an arbitrary chain of JOINs, and what does that change about the AST shape?" — join: Option<JoinClause> becomes joins: Vec<JoinClause>, and parse_select's single if peek == JOIN check becomes a while peek == JOIN loop appending to that vector — each `JoinClause` already fully specifies its own table and ON condition, so the grammar change is almost mechanical. The more interesting follow-up is semantic, not syntactic: once there are multiple joins, a query PLANNER (not this parser) has to decide their execution order, which is precisely the join-order-optimization problem, independent of how the AST represents the request.
🎯 Senior angle
Anyone can chain if/else checks against a token stream and eventually produce SOMETHING for a simple query. What separates a senior answer is treating precedence as a STRUCTURAL property of the grammar (which function calls which, in which order) rather than something to patch in with extra logic after the fact — and being able to articulate, unprompted, why layering parse_or_expr over parse_and_expr over parse_primary is sufficient to get precedence right for free, with zero explicit "if this operator has higher precedence than that one" comparisons anywhere in the code.
