// Database Engineering Exercise 64 · 45 min
W64 · K-Way External Merge Sort — BinaryHeap Merge Phase
BinaryHeap + Reverse O(N log K), not O(N log N) O(K) heap space, not O(N) Medium
Prompt
"Implement the MERGE phase of external sort — as used to sort data too large for memory, or to merge sorted SSTable-style runs in a database storage engine. You're given K already individually-sorted "runs" (each a Vec<i32>, standing in for sorted chunks that in a real system would each be a temp file on disk). Merge all K of them into a single fully-sorted output using a BinaryHeap (with std::cmp::Reverse for min-heap behavior) that holds at most K elements at any time — one "next candidate" per still-non-exhausted run — NOT by concatenating everything and re-sorting, which is the wrong-but-tempting approach a weak candidate might reach for. Track and report total comparisons / heap-pops performed, to make the O(N log K) behavior — versus O(N log N) for the naive concatenate-and-sort approach — concretely demonstrable, not just asymptotically claimed."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::cmp::Reverse;
use std::collections::BinaryHeap;

struct MergeStats {
    comparisons: usize,
    heap_pops: usize,
    max_heap_size: usize,
}

// TODO: fn k_way_merge(runs: &[Vec]) -> (Vec, MergeStats)
//   - use a BinaryHeap> holding at most one pending candidate per non-exhausted run
//   - never hold more than runs.len() elements in the heap at once
//   - must correctly handle an empty run without panicking
//   - must report how many elements the heap held at its largest point (max_heap_size)

fn main() {
    // -- 1. Correctness, including runs of very different lengths AND one empty run --
    let runs: Vec<Vec<i32>> = vec![
        vec![1, 4, 9, 15, 15, 42],
        vec![],                          // empty run -- must be handled, not panic
        vec![-3, 0, 2],
        vec![100],
        vec![5, 5, 5, 20, 21, 22, 23, 50],
    ];
    let k = runs.len();
    let total: usize = runs.iter().map(|r| r.len()).sum();

    let mut expected: Vec<i32> = runs.iter().flatten().copied().collect();
    expected.sort();

    let (merged, stats) = k_way_merge(&runs);
    assert_eq!(merged, expected, "k-way merge must equal sorting the full concatenation");
    assert_eq!(stats.heap_pops, total, "exactly one heap pop per output element");
    assert!(stats.max_heap_size <= k, "heap held {} elements at once, exceeding K={}", stats.max_heap_size, k);
    println!(
        "Small test: N={}, K={}, comparisons={}, heap_pops={}, max_heap_size={}",
        total, k, stats.comparisons, stats.heap_pops, stats.max_heap_size
    );

    // -- 2. All-empty-except-one-run edge case: heap must still never exceed K (trivially 1) --
    let single_run: Vec<Vec<i32>> = vec![vec![], vec![], vec![7, 7, 8], vec![]];
    let (merged2, stats2) = k_way_merge(&single_run);
    assert_eq!(merged2, vec![7, 7, 8]);
    assert!(stats2.max_heap_size <= single_run.len());
    assert_eq!(stats2.max_heap_size, 1); // only ever one non-exhausted run at a time here

    // -- 3. Scale test: K=16 sorted-but-heavily-overlapping runs, N in the tens of thousands --
    // Demonstrates the actual O(N log K) vs O(N log N) gap empirically, not just asymptotically:
    // k-way merge should need strictly fewer real comparisons than concatenate-and-sort once
    // K is meaningfully smaller than N, because each heap op costs O(log K), not O(log N).
    let mut seed: u32 = 0x1234_5678;
    let big_k = 16;
    let mut big_runs: Vec<Vec<i32>> = Vec::with_capacity(big_k);
    let mut big_total = 0usize;
    for i in 0..big_k {
        let len = 1_000 + (i * 137) % 600; // deliberately uneven run lengths
        let mut run: Vec<i32> = (0..len).map(|_| (xorshift32(&mut seed) % 2_000_000) as i32).collect();
        run.sort();
        big_total += run.len();
        big_runs.push(run);
    }

    let mut big_expected: Vec<i32> = big_runs.iter().flatten().copied().collect();
    big_expected.sort();

    let (big_merged, big_stats) = k_way_merge(&big_runs);
    assert_eq!(big_merged, big_expected);
    assert_eq!(big_stats.heap_pops, big_total);
    assert!(big_stats.max_heap_size <= big_k, "heap exceeded K={} at some point", big_k);

    let (naive_result, naive_comparisons) = naive_concatenate_and_sort(&big_runs, &mut seed);
    assert_eq!(naive_result, big_expected);
    assert!(
        big_stats.comparisons < naive_comparisons,
        "k-way merge ({} comparisons) should need fewer comparisons than concatenate-and-sort ({}) once K << N",
        big_stats.comparisons,
        naive_comparisons
    );

    println!(
        "Scale test: N={}, K={}, k-way comparisons={}, naive-sort comparisons={} ({:.1}x fewer)",
        big_total, big_k, big_stats.comparisons, naive_comparisons,
        naive_comparisons as f64 / big_stats.comparisons as f64
    );
    println!("max_heap_size_seen across every test: never exceeded its own K -- confirmed O(K) space, not O(N).");
    println!("All assertions passed.");
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::cell::Cell;
use std::cmp::{Ordering, Reverse};
use std::collections::BinaryHeap;
use std::rc::Rc;

#[derive(Clone)]
struct Counter(Rc<Cell<usize>>);
impl Counter {
    fn new() -> Self { Counter(Rc::new(Cell::new(0))) }
    fn bump(&self) { self.0.set(self.0.get() + 1); }
    fn get(&self) -> usize { self.0.get() }
}

/// Wraps one "next candidate" value from a run, plus a shared counter that ticks up on every
/// comparison the heap performs against it -- this is how we get an honest, empirical count
/// of comparisons done by BinaryHeap's internal sift-up/sift-down, not a hand-waved estimate.
struct Candidate { value: i32, run_idx: usize, counter: Counter }

impl PartialEq for Candidate {
    fn eq(&self, other: &Self) -> bool { self.value == other.value && self.run_idx == other.run_idx }
}
impl Eq for Candidate {}
impl PartialOrd for Candidate {
    fn partial_cmp(&self, other: &Self) -> Option<Ordering> { Some(self.cmp(other)) }
}
impl Ord for Candidate {
    fn cmp(&self, other: &Self) -> Ordering {
        self.counter.bump();  // every single heap comparison ticks this -- the empirical O(log K) proof
        self.value.cmp(&other.value).then_with(|| self.run_idx.cmp(&other.run_idx))
    }
}

struct MergeStats { comparisons: usize, heap_pops: usize, max_heap_size: usize }

/// Merges K already-sorted runs using a heap that holds at most one live candidate per
/// still-non-exhausted run (so at most K elements total) -- NOT by concatenating everything
/// and calling a general sort, which is the wrong-but-tempting O(N log N) shortcut.
fn k_way_merge(runs: &[Vec<i32>]) -> (Vec<i32>, MergeStats) {
    let counter = Counter::new();
    let mut heap: BinaryHeap<Reverse<Candidate>> = BinaryHeap::new();
    let mut cursors = vec![0usize; runs.len()];
    let mut max_heap_size = 0;

    for (run_idx, run) in runs.iter().enumerate() {  // seed the heap with ONE candidate per non-empty run
        if let Some(&value) = run.first() {
            heap.push(Reverse(Candidate { value, run_idx, counter: counter.clone() }));
        }
        // an empty run simply contributes nothing here -- no panic, no special-case branch needed
    }
    max_heap_size = max_heap_size.max(heap.len());

    let total: usize = runs.iter().map(|r| r.len()).sum();
    let mut output = Vec::with_capacity(total);
    let mut heap_pops = 0;

    while let Some(Reverse(top)) = heap.pop() {
        heap_pops += 1;
        output.push(top.value);
        cursors[top.run_idx] += 1;
        if let Some(&next_value) = runs[top.run_idx].get(cursors[top.run_idx]) {  // pull the NEXT element from that SAME run only
            heap.push(Reverse(Candidate { value: next_value, run_idx: top.run_idx, counter: counter.clone() }));
            max_heap_size = max_heap_size.max(heap.len());
        }
        // heap.len() here is always <= (number of runs not yet fully exhausted) <= K --
        // we never hold more than one pending candidate per run, no matter how many total
        // elements N are still left to produce.
    }

    (output, MergeStats { comparisons: counter.get(), heap_pops, max_heap_size })
}

/// The "wrong but tempting" baseline: concatenate everything and run a general sort. The
/// concatenation is shuffled first -- a real `Vec::sort` has no idea (and shouldn't rely on
/// the idea) that its input happens to be K pre-sorted chunks back to back, so leaving it in
/// that order would let an adaptive sort unfairly detect the existing runs and cheat its way
/// to a speed that has nothing to do with the general O(N log N) comparison-sort behavior
/// we're actually contrasting against O(N log K). The comparator is instrumented with the
/// same kind of counter so both approaches' real comparison counts are measured fairly.
fn naive_concatenate_and_sort(runs: &[Vec<i32>], shuffle_seed: &mut u32) -> (Vec<i32>, usize) {
    let mut all: Vec<i32> = runs.iter().flatten().copied().collect();
    for i in (1..all.len()).rev() {
        let j = (xorshift32(shuffle_seed) as usize) % (i + 1);
        all.swap(i, j);
    }
    let counter = Counter::new();
    let counter_for_closure = counter.clone();
    all.sort_by(move |a, b| {
        counter_for_closure.bump();
        a.cmp(b)
    });
    (all, counter.get())
}

fn xorshift32(state: &mut u32) -> u32 {
    let mut x = *state;
    x ^= x << 13;
    x ^= x >> 17;
    x ^= x << 5;
    *state = x;
    x
}

fn main() {
    // -- 1. Correctness, including runs of very different lengths AND one empty run --
    let runs: Vec<Vec<i32>> = vec![
        vec![1, 4, 9, 15, 15, 42],
        vec![],                          // empty run -- must be handled, not panic
        vec![-3, 0, 2],
        vec![100],
        vec![5, 5, 5, 20, 21, 22, 23, 50],
    ];
    let k = runs.len();
    let total: usize = runs.iter().map(|r| r.len()).sum();

    let mut expected: Vec<i32> = runs.iter().flatten().copied().collect();
    expected.sort();

    let (merged, stats) = k_way_merge(&runs);
    assert_eq!(merged, expected, "k-way merge must equal sorting the full concatenation");
    assert_eq!(stats.heap_pops, total, "exactly one heap pop per output element");
    assert!(stats.max_heap_size <= k, "heap held {} elements at once, exceeding K={}", stats.max_heap_size, k);
    println!(
        "Small test: N={}, K={}, comparisons={}, heap_pops={}, max_heap_size={}",
        total, k, stats.comparisons, stats.heap_pops, stats.max_heap_size
    );

    // -- 2. All-empty-except-one-run edge case: heap must still never exceed K (trivially 1) --
    let single_run: Vec<Vec<i32>> = vec![vec![], vec![], vec![7, 7, 8], vec![]];
    let (merged2, stats2) = k_way_merge(&single_run);
    assert_eq!(merged2, vec![7, 7, 8]);
    assert!(stats2.max_heap_size <= single_run.len());
    assert_eq!(stats2.max_heap_size, 1); // only ever one non-exhausted run at a time here

    // -- 3. Scale test: K=16 sorted-but-heavily-overlapping runs, N in the tens of thousands --
    // Demonstrates the actual O(N log K) vs O(N log N) gap empirically, not just asymptotically:
    // k-way merge should need strictly fewer real comparisons than concatenate-and-sort once
    // K is meaningfully smaller than N, because each heap op costs O(log K), not O(log N).
    let mut seed: u32 = 0x1234_5678;
    let big_k = 16;
    let mut big_runs: Vec<Vec<i32>> = Vec::with_capacity(big_k);
    let mut big_total = 0usize;
    for i in 0..big_k {
        let len = 1_000 + (i * 137) % 600; // deliberately uneven run lengths
        let mut run: Vec<i32> = (0..len).map(|_| (xorshift32(&mut seed) % 2_000_000) as i32).collect();
        run.sort();
        big_total += run.len();
        big_runs.push(run);
    }

    let mut big_expected: Vec<i32> = big_runs.iter().flatten().copied().collect();
    big_expected.sort();

    let (big_merged, big_stats) = k_way_merge(&big_runs);
    assert_eq!(big_merged, big_expected);
    assert_eq!(big_stats.heap_pops, big_total);
    assert!(big_stats.max_heap_size <= big_k, "heap exceeded K={} at some point", big_k);

    let (naive_result, naive_comparisons) = naive_concatenate_and_sort(&big_runs, &mut seed);
    assert_eq!(naive_result, big_expected);
    assert!(
        big_stats.comparisons < naive_comparisons,
        "k-way merge ({} comparisons) should need fewer comparisons than concatenate-and-sort ({}) once K << N",
        big_stats.comparisons,
        naive_comparisons
    );

    println!(
        "Scale test: N={}, K={}, k-way comparisons={}, naive-sort comparisons={} ({:.1}x fewer)",
        big_total, big_k, big_stats.comparisons, naive_comparisons,
        naive_comparisons as f64 / big_stats.comparisons as f64
    );
    println!("max_heap_size_seen across every test: never exceeded its own K -- confirmed O(K) space, not O(N).");
    println!("All assertions passed.");
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Reaches for a heap holding one candidate per run, not "concatenate then sort" — this is precisely the distinction the exercise exists to test. A candidate who writes runs.concat(); result.sort() gets a correct answer that completely defeats the point of external merge sort: the whole reason it exists is that you often CANNOT hold all N elements in memory at once, only K (one buffered page per input run), so any solution that materializes the full concatenation has silently reintroduced the exact memory constraint the algorithm is designed to avoid.
  • ★★★Actually instruments and asserts max_heap_size <= K rather than just trusting the design — this is the one test in the whole exercise that would catch a subtle bug like accidentally pushing a run's ENTIRE remaining slice into the heap instead of just its next single element, which would still often produce a correctly-sorted final answer while silently violating the space bound that is the entire point of the exercise.
  • ★★Handles the empty-run edge case as a natural consequence of the algorithm's structure (an empty run simply never gets a candidate pushed for it) rather than as a bolted-on special case with an explicit if run.is_empty() { continue } guard bracketed around otherwise-different logic — the cleanest solutions treat "this run has no more elements" and "this run started with zero elements" as literally the same code path.
  • ★Recognizes that Reverse is needed because BinaryHeap is a max-heap by default — and can explain WHY: for a MIN-heap-style pop order (always emitting the globally smallest remaining candidate next, which is what a correct ascending merge requires), you either wrap elements in std::cmp::Reverse or write a custom, deliberately-inverted Ord impl; forgetting this produces a heap that confidently pops the LARGEST candidate first, which very obviously does not merge sorted runs into ascending order.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"In a real database or file-based external sort, each 'run' is actually a temp file on disk. What changes about this code if K gets large — say, merging 10,000 SSTables at once — and why do real systems cap K instead of letting it grow unbounded?" — Each run needs an open file handle and an I/O read buffer, so the true resource cost per run isn't just "one heap slot," it's a file descriptor plus a page of buffered I/O; most operating systems and storage engines cap concurrently-open file descriptors far below 10,000, and even where that's not the limit, each heap comparison and I/O read still costs real CPU/syscall time per pop. This is exactly why real systems (e.g. LSM-tree compaction in RocksDB/LevelDB) perform merges in BOUNDED-fan-in tiers — merging a manageable K files at a time, repeatedly, into progressively larger runs — rather than one giant K=10,000 merge.
  • P2"This assumes each run already fits comfortably as an in-memory Vec. What if a single run itself is too large to fully load into memory?" — Replace each run's `Vec` with a buffered, lazily-advancing iterator over the underlying file (reading one block/page at a time, refilling a small in-memory buffer as it's consumed) — the heap's contract doesn't change at all (it still only ever needs to know each run's CURRENT smallest remaining value), only how "get the next value from this run" is implemented underneath. This buffered-iterator swap is exactly the seam between this exercise's simplified in-memory version and a real external-sort implementation.
  • P3"Why would total heap_pops always exactly equal N, the total number of elements across all runs — and what would it mean if that assertion ever failed?" — Every element from every run gets pushed into the heap exactly once (as either an initial seed candidate or as the "next" candidate pushed right after its predecessor from the same run gets popped) and popped exactly once when it's chosen as the next output element, so `heap_pops` is mechanically forced to equal the total input size. If that assertion ever failed, it would mean the merge either dropped elements (a run's cursor advanced past values that were never pushed) or double-counted them (a candidate got pushed more than once) — a `heap_pops != N` mismatch is actually one of the fastest possible smoke tests for a broken merge, well before checking full output correctness.
🎯 Senior angle
Almost every candidate can eventually produce a correctly sorted list. The signal that actually matters here is whether they treat the SPACE bound — one candidate per run, O(K) total, never O(N) — as a hard correctness requirement of "did you build external merge sort" rather than a minor implementation detail, and whether they instrument for it unprompted. That instinct (measure the resource the algorithm exists to conserve, not just the output it produces) is exactly the same instinct that separates someone who can explain a database's LSM-compaction or buffer-pool behavior from someone who can only recite that it "uses a heap."

    assert_eq!(merged2, vec![7, 7, 8]);
    assert!(stats2.max_heap_size <= single_run.len());
    assert_eq!(stats2.max_heap_size, 1); // only ever one non-exhausted run at a time here

    // -- 3. Scale test: K=16 sorted-but-heavily-overlapping runs, N in the tens of thousands --
    // Demonstrates the actual O(N log K) vs O(N log N) gap empirically, not just asymptotically:
    // k-way merge should need strictly fewer real comparisons than concatenate-and-sort once
    // K is meaningfully smaller than N, because each heap op costs O(log K), not O(log N).
    let mut seed: u32 = 0x1234_5678;
    let big_k = 16;
    let mut big_runs: Vec<Vec<i32>> = Vec::with_capacity(big_k);
    let mut big_total = 0usize;
    for i in 0..big_k {
        let len = 1_000 + (i * 137) % 600; // deliberately uneven run lengths
        let mut run: Vec<i32> = (0..len).map(|_| (xorshift32(&mut seed) % 2_000_000) as i32).collect();
        run.sort();
        big_total += run.len();
        big_runs.push(run);
    }

    let mut big_expected: Vec<i32> = big_runs.iter().flatten().copied().collect();
    big_expected.sort();

    let (big_merged, big_stats) = k_way_merge(&big_runs);
    assert_eq!(big_merged, big_expected);
    assert_eq!(big_stats.heap_pops, big_total);
    assert!(big_stats.max_heap_size <= big_k, "heap exceeded K={} at some point", big_k);

    let (naive_result, naive_comparisons) = naive_concatenate_and_sort(&big_runs, &mut seed);
    assert_eq!(naive_result, big_expected);
    assert!(
        big_stats.comparisons < naive_comparisons,
        "k-way merge ({} comparisons) should need fewer comparisons than concatenate-and-sort ({}) once K << N",
        big_stats.comparisons,
        naive_comparisons
    );

    println!(
        "Scale test: N={}, K={}, k-way comparisons={}, naive-sort comparisons={} ({:.1}x fewer)",
        big_total, big_k, big_stats.comparisons, naive_comparisons,
        naive_comparisons as f64 / big_stats.comparisons as f64
    );
    println!("max_heap_size_seen across every test: never exceeded its own K -- confirmed O(K) space, not O(N).");
    println!("All assertions passed.");
}

Prompt
"Implement a Pratt parser (a.k.a. precedence-climbing / top-down operator-precedence parsing — the technique rustc's own expression parser uses, and structurally different from a classic recursive-descent parser with one function per precedence level) for arithmetic expressions: binary + - * / at standard precedence, a right-associative ^ (exponentiation), a prefix unary minus, and a postfix ! (factorial). The defining structural requirement: implement it via explicit fn binding_power(op) -> (left_bp, right_bp) functions that a single generic loop consults — not a giant if/else precedence-level cascade or one function per precedence tier."

    let e1 = parse("2 + 3 * 4");

    let e7 = parse("10 - 3 - 2");
    assert_eq!(eval(&e7), 5.0, "- must be left-associative: (10-3)-2, not 10-(3-2)=9");

    // Chained factorial + power together to stress binding-power interplay.
    let e8 = parse("2 ^ 2!");
    assert_eq!(eval(&e8), 4.0, "2! = 2, then 2^2 = 4 (postfix binds tighter than ^)");

    println!("all Pratt parser assertions passed: {} {} {} {}", e1, e2, e3, e4);

use std::fmt;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
enum Token {
    Num(f64),
    Plus,
    Minus,
    Star,
    Slash,
    Caret,
    Bang,
    LParen,
    RParen,
    Eof,
}

fn lex(src: &str) -> Vec<Token> {
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    let chars: Vec<char> = src.chars().collect();
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < chars.len() {
        let c = chars[i];
        match c {
            ' ' | '\t' => { i += 1; }
            '+' => { out.push(Token::Plus); i += 1; }
            '-' => { out.push(Token::Minus); i += 1; }
            '*' => { out.push(Token::Star); i += 1; }
            '/' => { out.push(Token::Slash); i += 1; }
            '^' => { out.push(Token::Caret); i += 1; }
            '!' => { out.push(Token::Bang); i += 1; }
            '(' => { out.push(Token::LParen); i += 1; }
            ')' => { out.push(Token::RParen); i += 1; }
            d if d.is_ascii_digit() => {
                let start = i;
                while i < chars.len() && (chars[i].is_ascii_digit() || chars[i] == '.') {
                    i += 1;
                }
                let s: String = chars[start..i].iter().collect();
                out.push(Token::Num(s.parse().unwrap()));
            }
            _ => panic!("unexpected character: {}", c),
        }
    }
    out.push(Token::Eof);
    out
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
enum Expr {
    Num(f64),
    Neg(Box<Expr>),
    Fact(Box<Expr>),
    Bin(char, Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>),
}

impl fmt::Display for Expr {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        match self {
            Expr::Num(n) => write!(f, "{}", n),
            Expr::Neg(e) => write!(f, "(-{})", e),
            Expr::Fact(e) => write!(f, "({}!)", e),
            Expr::Bin(op, l, r) => write!(f, "({} {} {})", l, op, r),
        }
    }
}

/// Binding power for INFIX operators: (left_bp, right_bp). Equal-ish pairs like
/// (1, 2) give LEFT associativity -- a following same-precedence op binds weaker on
/// the left than the currently-open right slot, so it's swallowed by the CALLER.
/// `^`'s pair is (6, 5) -- right_bp < left_bp -- which flips that: a following `^`
/// binds MORE strongly than the caller's minimum, so it's swallowed into the current
/// node's right side instead. That single swap is the entire associativity mechanism.
fn infix_binding_power(op: char) -> Option<(u8, u8)> {
    match op {
        '+' | '-' => Some((1, 2)),
        '*' | '/' => Some((3, 4)),
        '^' => Some((6, 5)),  // right-associative: right_bp < left_bp
        _ => None,
    }
}

/// PREFIX unary minus: only a right side, since nothing sits to its left. Chosen
/// HIGHER than `*` `/` but LOWER than `^`, so `-2 ^ 2` parses as `-(2 ^ 2)` = -4
/// (documented convention: exponentiation binds tighter than unary minus, matching
/// mathematical convention and languages like Python).
fn prefix_binding_power(op: char) -> Option<u8> {
    match op {
        '-' => Some(5),
        _ => None,
    }
}

/// POSTFIX factorial: only a left side. Chosen higher than everything else so
/// `3! + 1` = 7 -- factorial always grabs its operand immediately.
fn postfix_binding_power(op: char) -> Option<u8> {
    match op {
        '!' => Some(7),
        _ => None,
    }
}

struct Parser { tokens: Vec<Token>, pos: usize }

impl Parser {
    fn new(tokens: Vec<Token>) -> Self { Parser { tokens, pos: 0 } }

    fn peek(&self) -> &Token { &self.tokens[self.pos] }

    fn advance(&mut self) -> Token {
        let t = self.tokens[self.pos].clone();
        self.pos += 1;
        t
    }

    fn token_as_op(t: &Token) -> Option<char> {
        match t {
            Token::Plus => Some('+'),
            Token::Minus => Some('-'),
            Token::Star => Some('*'),
            Token::Slash => Some('/'),
            Token::Caret => Some('^'),
            Token::Bang => Some('!'),
            _ => None,
        }
    }

    /// The heart of a Pratt parser: parse an expression that binds no looser than
    /// `min_bp`. Every loop iteration checks the NEXT operator's binding power against
    /// `min_bp` before consuming it -- that single comparison replaces the entire
    /// cascade of parse_term/parse_factor/parse_power mutually-recursive functions a
    /// classic recursive-descent parser would need.
    fn parse_expr(&mut self, min_bp: u8) -> Expr {
        let mut lhs = match self.advance() {
            Token::Num(n) => Expr::Num(n),
            Token::LParen => {
                let inner = self.parse_expr(0);
                assert_eq!(self.advance(), Token::RParen, "expected closing paren");
                inner
            }
            Token::Minus => {
                let bp = prefix_binding_power('-').unwrap();
                let rhs = self.parse_expr(bp);
                Expr::Neg(Box::new(rhs))
            }
            t => panic!("unexpected token in operand position: {:?}", t),
        };

        loop {
            let op = match Self::token_as_op(self.peek()) {
                Some(op) => op,
                None => break,
            };

            if let Some(l_bp) = postfix_binding_power(op) {
                if l_bp < min_bp { break; }
                self.advance();
                lhs = Expr::Fact(Box::new(lhs));
                continue;
            }

            if let Some((l_bp, r_bp)) = infix_binding_power(op) {
                if l_bp < min_bp { break; }  // this op binds too loosely for our caller -- stop, let them consume it
                self.advance();
                let rhs = self.parse_expr(r_bp);  // recurse with r_bp as the new min -- THIS is where associativity is decided
                lhs = Expr::Bin(op, Box::new(lhs), Box::new(rhs));
                continue;
            }

            break;
        }

        lhs
    }
}

fn eval(e: &Expr) -> f64 {
    match e {
        Expr::Num(n) => *n,
        Expr::Neg(inner) => -eval(inner),
        Expr::Fact(inner) => {
            let n = eval(inner) as u64;
            (1..=n).product::<u64>() as f64
        }
        Expr::Bin(op, l, r) => {
            let (lv, rv) = (eval(l), eval(r));
            match op {
                '+' => lv + rv,
                '-' => lv - rv,
                '*' => lv * rv,
                '/' => lv / rv,
                '^' => lv.powf(rv),
                _ => panic!("unknown op {}", op),
            }
        }
    }
}

fn parse(src: &str) -> Expr {
    let tokens = lex(src);
    let mut p = Parser::new(tokens);
    let e = p.parse_expr(0);
    assert_eq!(*p.peek(), Token::Eof, "trailing tokens after expression");
    e
}

fn main() {
    // Precedence: * binds tighter than +.
    let e1 = parse("2 + 3 * 4");
    assert_eq!(eval(&e1), 14.0);

    // Right-associativity: 2 ^ (3 ^ 2) = 2 ^ 9 = 512, NOT (2 ^ 3) ^ 2 = 64.
    let e2 = parse("2 ^ 3 ^ 2");
    assert_eq!(eval(&e2), 512.0, "^ must be right-associative");
    assert_ne!(eval(&e2), 64.0, "512 != the WRONG left-associative answer of 64");

    // Documented convention: unary minus binds LOWER than ^, so -2 ^ 2 == -(2^2) == -4.
    let e3 = parse("-2 ^ 2");
    assert_eq!(eval(&e3), -4.0, "prefix - binds looser than ^ per documented convention");
    assert_eq!(format!("{}", e3), "(-(2 ^ 2))");

    // Postfix factorial.
    let e4 = parse("3!");
    assert_eq!(eval(&e4), 6.0);

    // Mixed: postfix binds tighter than +, parens override everything.
    let e5 = parse("3! + 1");
    assert_eq!(eval(&e5), 7.0);
    let e6 = parse("(2 + 3) * 4");
    assert_eq!(eval(&e6), 20.0);

    // Left-associativity of + and - (the "normal" case, contrasted with ^ above).
    let e7 = parse("10 - 3 - 2");
    assert_eq!(eval(&e7), 5.0, "- must be left-associative: (10-3)-2, not 10-(3-2)=9");

    // Chained factorial + power together to stress binding-power interplay.
    let e8 = parse("2 ^ 2!");
    assert_eq!(eval(&e8), 4.0, "2! = 2, then 2^2 = 4 (postfix binds tighter than ^)");

    println!("all Pratt parser assertions passed: {} {} {} {}", e1, e2, e3, e4);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Implements binding power as data (a function returning a tuple), not as control flow — the entire structural point of a Pratt parser is that parse_expr is a SINGLE generic function consulting a lookup table, rather than rustc-style layered functions (parse_term → parse_factor → ...). A candidate who writes binding_power() but then still hand-codes a per-precedence-level cascade around it hasn't actually understood what makes this technique different — probe for this explicitly if the code looks suspicious.
  • ★★★Gets right-associativity via an asymmetric (left_bp, right_bp) pair for ^ rather than a special-cased "if op is caret, recurse instead of loop" branch — the whole point of binding power is that associativity is just a data choice (which of the pair is smaller), fully unified with the rest of the precedence logic, not a separate code path bolted on.
  • ★★Handles the prefix/postfix cases inside the same min_bp framework as infix operators (rather than as totally separate, ad hoc parsing paths) — real Pratt parsers unify prefix ("null denotation") and infix/postfix ("left denotation") handling under the identical binding-power comparison, which is exactly why the technique scales cleanly to grammars with many mixed operator kinds.
  • ★States their prefix-vs-power precedence choice explicitly and tests it — -2 ^ 2 is genuinely ambiguous across real languages (Python: -(2**2) = -4; many hand-written calculators: (-2)^2 = 4), so a candidate who picks a convention, documents it, and asserts on it is showing the same rigor a language spec author needs, rather than leaving the behavior as an accidental side effect of code order.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"How would you add a ternary `a ? b : c` operator to this parser without restructuring the loop?" — Ternary is a great stress-test for Pratt parsers because it's neither purely prefix, infix, nor postfix: on seeing `?`, if its left binding power clears `min_bp`, consume it, recursively parse the "then" branch with binding power 0 (a fresh sub-expression, since `:` acts like a closing delimiter), then require and consume the `:`, then recurse for the "else" branch using the ternary's own right binding power (very low, since `?:` is famously right-associative in most languages: `a ? b : c ? d : e` means `a ? b : (c ? d : e)`). This is exactly the kind of "operator with more than 2 slots" case that shows whether a candidate understands binding power as a general mechanism versus having memorized a binary-operator-only recipe.
  • P2"Real production Pratt parsers (like rustc's) don't return values with 0-min_bp calls scattered everywhere — how do they usually organize the entry points?" — They typically expose `parse_expr()` as a thin public wrapper calling `parse_expr_bp(0)` internally, and additionally expose a `parse_expr_no_struct_literal()` or similar variant with a DIFFERENT starting min_bp/context flag for places in the grammar where certain constructs are ambiguous or disallowed (rustc famously disables struct-literal parsing inside `if`/`while`/`match` scrutinee position for exactly this reason) — the same binding-power engine handles both by varying the starting parameters and a small amount of contextual state, not by writing a second parser.
  • P3"This parser panics on malformed input. What's the minimal change to make it return `Result` instead, and does that complicate the binding-power logic itself?" — Swap every `panic!`/`unwrap`/`assert_eq!` for a `Result`-returning equivalent and thread `?` through `parse_expr`'s recursive calls — critically, the binding-power comparisons and the loop structure itself don't change AT ALL, since error handling is orthogonal to precedence logic. This separation (precedence mechanism vs. error reporting) is itself a signal: a parser design where switching error-handling strategy requires touching the precedence logic is a sign the two concerns were tangled together in the first place.
🎯 Senior angle
A mid-level answer gets the three test cases to pass, possibly by special-casing ^'s associativity as an if-branch bolted onto otherwise-symmetric logic. A senior answer recognizes that binding power is a unifying abstraction — precedence, associativity, and even prefix/postfix "arity" are all just numbers a single loop compares — and can explain, unprompted, why that generality is exactly what lets real compilers extend their expression grammar (ternaries, range operators, cast expressions) without a parser rewrite, whereas each new operator kind in a recursive-descent-with-levels design demands touching the function-call chain itself.

// Database Engineering Exercise 66 · 90 min
W66 · ACID Transactions via MVCC Snapshot Isolation
append-only version chains snapshot = committed-set at BEGIN first-committer-wins Hard
Prompt
"Implement a tiny in-memory key-value store providing snapshot-isolation transactions via MVCC (multi-version concurrency control) — the mechanism Postgres and CockroachCB actually use. Every write creates a new versioned entry (key, value, created_txn_id, deleted_txn_id: Option<u64>) rather than overwriting in place. Each transaction gets a monotonically-increasing txn_id and records a snapshot — the set of txns already committed at BEGIN time. A read must only see versions created by a txn visible in its snapshot (or by itself), and must not see versions deleted by anyone visible in its snapshot. commit() must detect a write-write conflict (first-committer-wins: if this txn wrote a key some OTHER txn also wrote and committed after this txn's snapshot began, abort with a conflict error), and rollback() must discard all of this txn's uncommitted versions."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::sync::Mutex;

type TxnId = u64;

struct Version { value: String, created_txn: TxnId, deleted_txn: Option<TxnId> }

struct Store {
    versions: Mutex<HashMap<String, Vec<Version>>>,
    next_txn_id: Mutex<TxnId>,
    committed: Mutex<Vec<TxnId>>,  // txn ids that have committed, in commit order
}

struct Txn<'a> {
    store: &'a Store,
    id: TxnId,
    snapshot: Vec<TxnId>,  // committed-txn-ids visible as of BEGIN
    writes: HashMap<String, String>,   // staged, uncommitted
    deletes: HashMap<String, ()>,
}

// TODO: impl Store { fn begin(&self) -> Txn }
// TODO: impl Txn {
//   fn visible(&self, v: &Version) -> bool  -- creator visible in snapshot (or self),
//                                              AND not deleted by anyone visible
//   fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option  -- own writes first, then newest visible version
//   fn set(&mut self, key: &str, value: &str) / fn delete(&mut self, key: &str)
//   fn commit(self) -> Result  -- first-committer-wins conflict check
//   fn rollback(self)
// }

fn main() {
    let store = Store::new();

    // --- Snapshot isolation: B must not see A's uncommitted write. ---
    let mut txn_a = store.begin();
    txn_a.set("x", "from_a");
    let txn_b = store.begin();  // later snapshot, but A hasn't committed yet
    assert_eq!(txn_b.get("x"), None, "B must not see A's uncommitted write");

    txn_a.commit().expect("A should commit cleanly");

    // B's snapshot predates A's commit, so B must STILL not see it even after commit.
    assert_eq!(
        txn_b.get("x"),
        None,
        "B's snapshot predates A's commit -- must remain stable for B's whole lifetime"
    );

    // A fresh txn C begun AFTER A's commit must see it.
    let txn_c = store.begin();
    assert_eq!(txn_c.get("x"), Some("from_a".to_string()));
    txn_c.commit().expect("C is read-only, trivially commits");
    txn_b.rollback();

    // --- Write-write conflict: two concurrent txns write the same key. ---
    let mut txn_d = store.begin();
    let mut txn_e = store.begin();
    txn_d.set("y", "from_d");
    txn_e.set("y", "from_e");
    txn_d.commit().expect("D commits first, no conflict yet");
    let e_result = txn_e.commit();
    assert!(
        matches!(e_result, Err(TxnError::Conflict(ref k)) if k == "y"),
        "E must be rejected: D committed a conflicting write to 'y' after E's snapshot began"
    );

    // Confirm D's write actually stuck (E's rejected write must not have applied).
    let txn_f = store.begin();
    assert_eq!(txn_f.get("y"), Some("from_d".to_string()));
    txn_f.commit().unwrap();

    // --- Delete visibility: a delete must behave like a tombstone under MVCC. ---
    let mut txn_g = store.begin();
    txn_g.set("z", "temp");
    txn_g.commit().unwrap();
    let mut txn_h = store.begin();
    txn_h.delete("z");
    let txn_i = store.begin();  // began before H's commit
    txn_h.commit().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(txn_i.get("z"), Some("temp".to_string()), "I's snapshot predates H's delete");
    let txn_j = store.begin();
    assert_eq!(txn_j.get("z"), None, "J begins after H's commit, must see the tombstone");
    txn_i.rollback();
    txn_j.rollback();

    println!("all MVCC snapshot-isolation assertions passed");
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::sync::Mutex;

type TxnId = u64;

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct Version {
    value: String,
    created_txn: TxnId,
    deleted_txn: Option<TxnId>,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
enum TxnError {
    Conflict(String),
}

impl std::fmt::Display for TxnError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
        match self {
            TxnError::Conflict(k) => write!(f, "write-write conflict on key {:?}", k),
        }
    }
}

/// Global store: append-only version chains per key, plus which txns have committed
/// (and in what order) -- this list, sliced at BEGIN time, IS a transaction's snapshot.
struct Store {
    versions: Mutex<HashMap<String, Vec<Version>>>,
    next_txn_id: Mutex<TxnId>,
    committed: Mutex<Vec<TxnId>>,
}

impl Store {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Store {
            versions: Mutex::new(HashMap::new()),
            next_txn_id: Mutex::new(1),
            committed: Mutex::new(Vec::new()),
        }
    }

    fn begin(&self) -> Txn<'_> {
        let mut next = self.next_txn_id.lock().unwrap();
        let id = *next;
        *next += 1;
        let snapshot: Vec<TxnId> = self.committed.lock().unwrap().clone();  // the entire snapshot IS this frozen list
        Txn { store: self, id, snapshot, writes: HashMap::new(), deletes: HashMap::new(), done: false }
    }
}

struct Txn<'a> {
    store: &'a Store,
    id: TxnId,
    snapshot: Vec<TxnId>,
    writes: HashMap<String, String>,
    deletes: HashMap<String, ()>,
    done: bool,
}

impl<'a> Txn<'a> {
    fn visible(&self, v: &Version) -> bool {
        let creator_visible = v.created_txn == self.id || self.snapshot.contains(&v.created_txn);
        if !creator_visible { return false; }  // can't see a version from a txn outside our snapshot, committed or not
        match v.deleted_txn {
            None => true,
            Some(d) => !(d == self.id || self.snapshot.contains(&d)),
        }
    }

    /// Reads check own uncommitted writes first, then the newest chain entry visible
    /// under the snapshot -- never anything from a txn outside the snapshot.
    fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<String> {
        if self.deletes.contains_key(key) { return None; }
        if let Some(v) = self.writes.get(key) { return Some(v.clone()); }
        let versions = self.store.versions.lock().unwrap();
        versions
            .get(key)
            .and_then(|chain| chain.iter().rev().find(|v| self.visible(v)))
            .map(|v| v.value.clone())
    }

    fn set(&mut self, key: &str, value: &str) {
        self.deletes.remove(key);
        self.writes.insert(key.to_string(), value.to_string());
    }

    fn delete(&mut self, key: &str) {
        self.writes.remove(key);
        self.deletes.insert(key.to_string(), ());
    }

    /// First-committer-wins: for every key this txn touched, check whether some OTHER
    /// txn created a version NOT visible in our snapshot (i.e. it committed concurrently,
    /// after our snapshot was taken) -- if so, abort rather than silently overwrite it.
    fn commit(mut self) -> Result<(), TxnError> {
        let mut versions = self.store.versions.lock().unwrap();
        let mut committed = self.store.committed.lock().unwrap();

        let touched: Vec<String> = self.writes.keys().cloned()
            .chain(self.deletes.keys().cloned())
            .collect();

        for key in &touched {
            if let Some(chain) = versions.get(key) {
                for v in chain {
                    let concurrent_writer = v.created_txn != self.id && !self.snapshot.contains(&v.created_txn);
                    if concurrent_writer {
                        self.done = true;
                        return Err(TxnError::Conflict(key.clone()));
                    }
                }
            }
        }

        for (key, value) in self.writes.drain() {
            let chain = versions.entry(key).or_insert_with(Vec::new);
            chain.push(Version { value, created_txn: self.id, deleted_txn: None });
        }
        for (key, _) in self.deletes.drain() {
            if let Some(chain) = versions.get_mut(&key) {
                if let Some(latest) = chain.iter_mut().rev().find(|v| v.deleted_txn.is_none()) {
                    latest.deleted_txn = Some(self.id);
                }
            }
        }

        committed.push(self.id);
        self.done = true;
        Ok(())
    }

    /// Writes are only ever staged in local maps until commit() flushes them into the
    /// shared version chains -- so rollback is just "discard the staged maps."
    fn rollback(mut self) {
        self.writes.clear();
        self.deletes.clear();
        self.done = true;
    }
}

impl<'a> Drop for Txn<'a> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        if !self.done {
            // A txn dropped without explicit commit/rollback behaves like an implicit
            // rollback -- its staged writes simply vanish since they never touched the
            // shared version chains.
            self.done = true;
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let store = Store::new();

    // --- Snapshot isolation: B must not see A's uncommitted write. ---
    let mut txn_a = store.begin();
    txn_a.set("x", "from_a");
    let txn_b = store.begin();  // later snapshot, but A hasn't committed yet
    assert_eq!(txn_b.get("x"), None, "B must not see A's uncommitted write");

    txn_a.commit().expect("A should commit cleanly");

    // B's snapshot predates A's commit, so B must STILL not see it even after commit.
    assert_eq!(
        txn_b.get("x"),
        None,
        "B's snapshot predates A's commit -- must remain stable for B's whole lifetime"
    );

    // A fresh txn C begun AFTER A's commit must see it.
    let txn_c = store.begin();
    assert_eq!(txn_c.get("x"), Some("from_a".to_string()));
    txn_c.commit().expect("C is read-only, trivially commits");
    txn_b.rollback();

    // --- Write-write conflict: two concurrent txns write the same key. ---
    let mut txn_d = store.begin();
    let mut txn_e = store.begin();
    txn_d.set("y", "from_d");
    txn_e.set("y", "from_e");
    txn_d.commit().expect("D commits first, no conflict yet");
    let e_result = txn_e.commit();
    assert!(
        matches!(e_result, Err(TxnError::Conflict(ref k)) if k == "y"),
        "E must be rejected: D committed a conflicting write to 'y' after E's snapshot began"
    );

    // Confirm D's write actually stuck (E's rejected write must not have applied).
    let txn_f = store.begin();
    assert_eq!(txn_f.get("y"), Some("from_d".to_string()));
    txn_f.commit().unwrap();

    // --- Delete visibility: a delete must behave like a tombstone under MVCC. ---
    let mut txn_g = store.begin();
    txn_g.set("z", "temp");
    txn_g.commit().unwrap();
    let mut txn_h = store.begin();
    txn_h.delete("z");
    let txn_i = store.begin();  // began before H's commit
    txn_h.commit().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(txn_i.get("z"), Some("temp".to_string()), "I's snapshot predates H's delete");
    let txn_j = store.begin();
    assert_eq!(txn_j.get("z"), None, "J begins after H's commit, must see the tombstone");
    txn_i.rollback();
    txn_j.rollback();

    println!("all MVCC snapshot-isolation assertions passed");
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Freezes the snapshot at BEGIN, not at first read — a subtle but critical bug is computing "what's visible" lazily on every get() call using the CURRENT committed set instead of a snapshot captured once at transaction start; that would silently give REPEATABLE READ's weaker cousin or even READ COMMITTED semantics instead of true snapshot isolation, where every read within one transaction must see the exact same frozen point in time.
  • ★★★Checks visibility on the version's CREATOR independently from its DELETER — a version is visible only if both (a) its creator is visible in the snapshot and (b) it has no visible deleter; conflating these (e.g. treating "has a deleted_txn at all" as "invisible," regardless of whether that deleting txn is itself visible to us) breaks the exact "I might not see a delete that happened after my snapshot" case the exercise specifically tests.
  • ★★★Implements first-committer-wins by checking for a competing COMMITTED write, not just a competing in-progress one — the conflict check must scan the actual persisted version chain for entries created by txns outside this txn's snapshot, not merely check "is some other Txn struct currently alive holding this key" (which would be closer to pessimistic locking and wouldn't generalize to a real multi-process database).
  • ★★Never mutates a Version in place — every write, including a delete, is expressed as either a brand-new Version appended to the chain or a tombstone field set on an existing one, never as an in-place value overwrite; this append-only discipline is precisely what lets older transactions keep reading a consistent past state while newer ones write concurrently, without any read ever needing a lock.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Snapshot isolation is famous for still allowing one specific anomaly that serializability forbids — what is it, and does this implementation permit it?" — Write skew: two transactions each read an overlapping set of rows, each writes to a DIFFERENT key based on what it read, and both commit successfully because first-committer-wins only checks for conflicts on keys actually WRITTEN, not keys merely READ — so two txns can each independently decide "the invariant still holds" based on a stale read of the other's not-yet-committed change, and together violate an invariant neither one individually broke. This exact gap is why Postgres's true SERIALIZABLE isolation level needs additional read-set tracking (SSI, serializable snapshot isolation) beyond what plain snapshot isolation (their REPEATABLE READ) provides.
  • P2"This version chain grows forever — how would a real MVCC database like Postgres reclaim space from old versions, and what's the trade-off?" — VACUUM (Postgres's term) periodically scans for versions whose deleter (or superseding version) is visible to EVERY currently-open transaction's snapshot — i.e. no live transaction could possibly still need to see the old version — and physically removes them. The trade-off: a single old, long-running transaction holding an ancient snapshot open prevents vacuuming ANY version newer than its snapshot for the whole store, which is exactly why long-idle transactions are a notorious operational hazard in real MVCC databases (unbounded table bloat, "transaction ID wraparound" in Postgres's specific case).
  • P3"Right now conflict detection scans the whole version chain per touched key at commit time — how would this need to change to stay fast with millions of versions per key?" — Track, per key, just the LATEST version's creating txn id (or better, its commit sequence number) rather than scanning the full chain — since only the most recent committed write to a key can possibly be "the conflicting one" under first-committer-wins (anything older was necessarily visible to everyone still alive), an O(1) check against that single cached value replaces an O(chain length) scan, which is exactly the kind of "maintain a denormalized summary instead of rescanning history" trick real storage engines rely on.
🎯 Senior angle
A mid-level answer implements the happy-path version chain and gets the three required scenarios to pass. A senior answer can immediately name write skew as the anomaly snapshot isolation still permits (and explain it's a read-set problem, not a write-set one, so no amount of tweaking first-committer-wins on writes alone fixes it) — and can connect that gap directly to why Postgres calls its snapshot-isolation level "REPEATABLE READ" rather than "SERIALIZABLE," reserving the latter name for the strictly stronger SSI algorithm. That distinction between "looks correct because the tests pass" and "understands the exact theoretical boundary of what this technique guarantees" is the tell.

fn harden_w66_1() {

fn main() {
    // Harden · Snapshot isolation is famous for still allowing one specific anomaly …
    harden_w66_1();
    // Parent exercise still holds after the harden change:
    let store = Store::new();

    // --- Snapshot isolation: B must not see A's uncommitted write. ---
    let mut txn_a = store.begin();
    txn_a.set("x", "from_a");
    let txn_b = store.begin();  // later snapshot, but A hasn't committed yet
    assert_eq!(txn_b.get("x"), None, "B must not see A's uncommitted write");

    txn_a.commit().expect("A should commit cleanly");

    // B's snapshot predates A's commit, so B must STILL not see it even after commit.
    assert_eq!(
        txn_b.get("x"),
        None,
        "B's snapshot predates A's commit -- must remain stable for B's whole lifetime"
    );

    // A fresh txn C begun AFTER A's commit must see it.
    let txn_c = store.begin();
    assert_eq!(txn_c.get("x"), Some("from_a".to_string()));
    txn_c.commit().expect("C is read-only, trivially commits");
    txn_b.rollback();

    // --- Write-write conflict: two concurrent txns write the same key. ---
    let mut txn_d = store.begin();
    let mut txn_e = store.begin();
    txn_d.set("y", "from_d");
    txn_e.set("y", "from_e");
    txn_d.commit().expect("D commits first, no conflict yet");
    let e_result = txn_e.commit();
    assert!(
        matches!(e_result, Err(TxnError::Conflict(ref k)) if k == "y"),
        "E must be rejected: D committed a conflicting write to 'y' after E's snapshot began"
    );

    // Confirm D's write actually stuck (E's rejected write must not have applied).
    let txn_f = store.begin();
    assert_eq!(txn_f.get("y"), Some("from_d".to_string()));
    txn_f.commit().unwrap();

    // --- Delete visibility: a delete must behave like a tombstone under MVCC. ---
    let mut txn_g = store.begin();
    txn_g.set("z", "temp");
    txn_g.commit().unwrap();
    let mut txn_h = store.begin();
    txn_h.delete("z");
    let txn_i = store.begin();  // began before H's commit
    txn_h.commit().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(txn_i.get("z"), Some("temp".to_string()), "I's snapshot predates H's delete");
    let txn_j = store.begin();
    assert_eq!(txn_j.get("z"), None, "J begins after H's commit, must see the tombstone");
    txn_i.rollback();
    txn_j.rollback();

    println!("all MVCC snapshot-isolation assertions passed");
}

// Database Engineering Exercise 67 · 90 min
W67 · ARIES-Style Crash Recovery — Analysis / Redo / Undo
3-phase ARIES dirty-page table + recLSN CLRs for idempotent undo Hard
Prompt
"Implement the three-phase ARIES recovery algorithm over a write-ahead log of typed records — Begin(txn), Update(txn, page_id, lsn, before, after), Commit(txn), Abort(txn), and CLR(txn, page_id, undo_next_lsn) (compensation log records) — each carrying a monotonic LSN. On restart after a crash, run: (1) ANALYSIS — scan forward to rebuild the transaction table and dirty-page table (earliest-dirtying LSN per page); (2) REDO — scan forward from the earliest relevant LSN, re-applying every update whose LSN is ≥ a page's on-disk LSN, including updates from transactions that will later be undone; (3) UNDO — scan backward, rolling back every transaction still active at crash time, writing a CLR for each undone update so a second crash mid-undo can't redo-then-undo the same change twice."
Starter code to hand to candidate
type Lsn = u64;
type TxnId = u64;

enum LogRecordKind {
    Begin { txn: TxnId },
    Update { txn: TxnId, page_id: String, before: i64, after: i64, prev_lsn: Option<Lsn> },
    Commit { txn: TxnId },
    Abort { txn: TxnId },
    /// undo_next_lsn: the NEXT (earlier) LSN of this txn still needing undo
    Clr { txn: TxnId, page_id: String, undo_next_lsn: Option<Lsn>, after: i64 },
}

struct Wal { records: Vec<LogRecordKind>, next_lsn: Lsn }
struct PageOnDisk { value: i64, page_lsn: Lsn }

// TODO: fn analysis(wal: &Wal) -> (transaction_table, dirty_page_table)
//   forward scan: Begin -> insert Active; Update/CLR -> dirty_page_table.entry(page)
//   .or_insert(lsn) [EARLIEST lsn wins]; Commit/Abort -> update status
// TODO: fn redo(wal: &Wal, dirty_page_table, disk) -> pages
//   start at min(dirty_page_table.values()); reapply EVERY Update/CLR with
//   lsn >= page's current on-disk lsn -- even for txns that will be undone next
// TODO: fn undo(wal: &mut Wal, transaction_table, pages)
//   for each txn still Active: walk backward via each record's own prev_lsn chain,
//   restore before-image, append a CLR pointing at the next-earlier lsn to undo

fn main() {
    let mut wal = Wal::new();
    let (t1, t2, t3) = (1u64, 2u64, 3u64);

    // T1: a normal transaction that commits cleanly before the crash.
    wal.begin(t1);
    wal.update(t1, "A", 0, 100);
    wal.commit(t1);

    // T2: begins, writes, then the crash happens while it's still active/uncommitted.
    let b2 = wal.begin(t2);
    wal.update(t2, "B", 0, 999);

    // T3: aborts NORMALLY before the crash -- its own runtime rollback already wrote a
    // CLR for its one update, so recovery must recognize it as resolved and leave it alone.
    let b3 = wal.begin(t3);
    wal.update(t3, "C", 5, 50);
    wal.clr(t3, "C", Some(b3), 5);
    wal.abort(t3);

    // What actually reached durable storage before the crash: nothing was flushed, so
    // every page's on-disk LSN is 0 and every logged action since must be redone.
    let mut disk = HashMap::new();
    disk.insert("A".to_string(), PageOnDisk { value: 0, page_lsn: 0 });
    disk.insert("B".to_string(), PageOnDisk { value: 0, page_lsn: 0 });
    disk.insert("C".to_string(), PageOnDisk { value: 5, page_lsn: 0 });

    let pre_crash_len = wal.records.len();
    let final_pages = recover(&mut wal, &disk);

    assert_eq!(final_pages.get("A"), Some(&100), "T1 committed -- REDO must make its effect durable");
    assert_eq!(final_pages.get("B"), Some(&0), "T2 never committed -- UNDO must roll it back to its before-image");
    assert_eq!(final_pages.get("C"), Some(&5), "T3 already self-aborted pre-crash -- REDO replays its own CLR back to 5");

    // Prove the "redo everything, even doomed work, THEN undo" ordering was honored, by
    // asserting on the LOG's contents post-recovery rather than only the final data state:
    // UNDO only emits a CLR for a record it actually processed, so a CLR for T2 existing
    // at all proves T2's doomed update really was redone and then rolled back afterward.
    let new_records = &wal.records[pre_crash_len..];
    let t2_clrs: Vec<&LogRecord> = new_records.iter()
        .filter(|r| matches!(&r.kind, LogRecordKind::Clr { txn, .. } if *txn == t2))
        .collect();
    assert_eq!(t2_clrs.len(), 1, "UNDO must write exactly one CLR for T2's single update");
    match &t2_clrs[0].kind {
        LogRecordKind::Clr { page_id, undo_next_lsn, after, .. } => {
            assert_eq!(page_id, "B");
            assert_eq!(*undo_next_lsn, Some(b2), "CLR must point back at T2's Begin -- nothing earlier left to undo");
            assert_eq!(*after, 0, "CLR's redo-value must be the original update's before-image");
        }
        _ => unreachable!(),
    }

    // No spurious CLRs for a committed txn or for one that had already resolved itself.
    let t1_new_clrs = new_records.iter().filter(|r| matches!(&r.kind, LogRecordKind::Clr { txn, .. } if *txn == t1)).count();
    let t3_new_clrs = new_records.iter().filter(|r| matches!(&r.kind, LogRecordKind::Clr { txn, .. } if *txn == t3)).count();
    assert_eq!(t1_new_clrs, 0, "T1 committed -- must never be undone");
    assert_eq!(t3_new_clrs, 0, "T3 was already fully rolled back before the crash -- must not be re-undone");

    println!("all ARIES recovery assertions passed");
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::collections::HashMap;

type Lsn = u64;
type TxnId = u64;

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
enum LogRecordKind {
    Begin { txn: TxnId },
    Update { txn: TxnId, page_id: String, before: i64, after: i64, prev_lsn: Option<Lsn> },
    Commit { txn: TxnId },
    Abort { txn: TxnId },
    /// Compensation Log Record: written while undoing `txn`'s update to `page_id`.
    /// `undo_next_lsn` points to the NEXT (earlier) LSN of this txn still needing undo,
    /// so a SECOND crash mid-rollback resumes from there instead of redoing this undo
    /// and then undoing it again. `after` is the value a redo of the CLR itself applies
    /// (i.e. the original update's before-image).
    Clr { txn: TxnId, page_id: String, undo_next_lsn: Option<Lsn>, after: i64 },
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct LogRecord { lsn: Lsn, kind: LogRecordKind }

/// The write-ahead log itself: an append-only sequence of monotonically-numbered records.
struct Wal {
    records: Vec<LogRecord>,
    next_lsn: Lsn,
    last_lsn_by_txn: HashMap<TxnId, Lsn>,
}

impl Wal {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Wal { records: Vec::new(), next_lsn: 1, last_lsn_by_txn: HashMap::new() }
    }

    fn append(&mut self, txn: TxnId, kind: LogRecordKind) -> Lsn {
        let lsn = self.next_lsn;
        self.next_lsn += 1;
        self.records.push(LogRecord { lsn, kind });
        self.last_lsn_by_txn.insert(txn, lsn);
        lsn
    }

    fn begin(&mut self, txn: TxnId) -> Lsn { self.append(txn, LogRecordKind::Begin { txn }) }

    /// `prev_lsn` is looked up from this txn's last log record -- the exact chain ARIES
    /// uses so UNDO can walk a txn's actions backward without rescanning the whole log.
    fn update(&mut self, txn: TxnId, page_id: &str, before: i64, after: i64) -> Lsn {
        let prev_lsn = self.last_lsn_by_txn.get(&txn).copied();
        self.append(txn, LogRecordKind::Update {
            txn, page_id: page_id.to_string(), before, after, prev_lsn,
        })
    }

    fn commit(&mut self, txn: TxnId) -> Lsn { self.append(txn, LogRecordKind::Commit { txn }) }
    fn abort(&mut self, txn: TxnId) -> Lsn { self.append(txn, LogRecordKind::Abort { txn }) }

    fn clr(&mut self, txn: TxnId, page_id: &str, undo_next_lsn: Option<Lsn>, after: i64) -> Lsn {
        self.append(txn, LogRecordKind::Clr { txn, page_id: page_id.to_string(), undo_next_lsn, after })
    }

    fn get(&self, lsn: Lsn) -> &LogRecord { &self.records[(lsn - 1) as usize] }
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct PageOnDisk { value: i64, page_lsn: Lsn }

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
enum TxnStatus { Active, Committed, Aborted }

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct TxnTableEntry { last_lsn: Lsn, status: TxnStatus }

/// PHASE 1 -- ANALYSIS: scan forward (from the last checkpoint, which this toy log has
/// none of, so we scan from the start) to rebuild exactly the in-memory state lost in
/// the crash: which transactions were in flight, and which pages have updates not yet
/// known to be durable (the dirty-page table, keyed by each page's recLSN -- the
/// EARLIEST log record that could have dirtied it since its last flush).
fn analysis(wal: &Wal) -> (HashMap<TxnId, TxnTableEntry>, HashMap<String, Lsn>) {
    let mut txn_table: HashMap<TxnId, TxnTableEntry> = HashMap::new();
    let mut dirty_page_table: HashMap<String, Lsn> = HashMap::new();

    for rec in &wal.records {
        match &rec.kind {
            LogRecordKind::Begin { txn } => {
                txn_table.insert(*txn, TxnTableEntry { last_lsn: rec.lsn, status: TxnStatus::Active });
            }
            LogRecordKind::Update { txn, page_id, .. } => {
                dirty_page_table.entry(page_id.clone()).or_insert(rec.lsn);  // only the FIRST (earliest) dirtying lsn is kept
                if let Some(e) = txn_table.get_mut(txn) { e.last_lsn = rec.lsn; }
            }
            LogRecordKind::Commit { txn } => {
                if let Some(e) = txn_table.get_mut(txn) { e.status = TxnStatus::Committed; e.last_lsn = rec.lsn; }
            }
            LogRecordKind::Abort { txn } => {
                if let Some(e) = txn_table.get_mut(txn) { e.status = TxnStatus::Aborted; e.last_lsn = rec.lsn; }
            }
            LogRecordKind::Clr { txn, page_id, .. } => {
                dirty_page_table.entry(page_id.clone()).or_insert(rec.lsn);
                if let Some(e) = txn_table.get_mut(txn) { e.last_lsn = rec.lsn; }
            }
        }
    }

    (txn_table, dirty_page_table)
}

/// PHASE 2 -- REDO: replay history forward from the earliest recLSN in the dirty-page
/// table, reapplying EVERY logged update whose LSN is >= that page's on-disk LSN.
/// Crucially this includes updates from transactions that UNDO will later roll back --
/// ARIES always restores the exact pre-crash state first and only THEN runs undo,
/// rather than trying to cleverly skip "doomed" work during redo. Skipping it here is
/// the single most commonly-missed ARIES detail.
fn redo(
    wal: &Wal,
    dirty_page_table: &HashMap<String, Lsn>,
    disk: &HashMap<String, PageOnDisk>,
) -> HashMap<String, (i64, Lsn)> {
    let mut pages: HashMap<String, (i64, Lsn)> =
        disk.iter().map(|(k, v)| (k.clone(), (v.value, v.page_lsn))).collect();

    let start_lsn = match dirty_page_table.values().min() {
        Some(lsn) => *lsn,
        None => return pages,
    };

    for rec in wal.records.iter().filter(|r| r.lsn >= start_lsn) {
        let (page_id, redo_value) = match &rec.kind {
            LogRecordKind::Update { page_id, after, .. } => (page_id, *after),
            LogRecordKind::Clr { page_id, after, .. } => (page_id, *after),
            _ => continue,
        };
        let entry = pages.entry(page_id.clone()).or_insert((0, 0));
        if entry.1 < rec.lsn {  // idempotency: never re-apply a record already reflected on the page
            entry.0 = redo_value;
            entry.1 = rec.lsn;
        }
    }

    pages
}

/// PHASE 3 -- UNDO: for every transaction still Active after analysis (never
/// committed nor aborted before the crash), walk its updates backward via each
/// record's own prev_lsn chain, restore each before-image, and log a CLR per undone
/// update pointing at the next-earlier LSN to undo -- so a second crash mid-undo can
/// resume correctly instead of re-undoing (or redoing) the same action twice.
fn undo(wal: &mut Wal, txn_table: &HashMap<TxnId, TxnTableEntry>, pages: &mut HashMap<String, (i64, Lsn)>) {
    let active_txns: Vec<TxnId> = txn_table
        .iter()
        .filter(|(_, e)| e.status == TxnStatus::Active)
        .map(|(txn, _)| *txn)
        .collect();

    for txn in active_txns {
        let mut cursor = Some(txn_table[&txn].last_lsn);
        while let Some(lsn) = cursor {
            let (page_id, before_val, prev_lsn) = {
                let record = wal.get(lsn);
                match &record.kind {
                    LogRecordKind::Update { page_id, before, prev_lsn, .. } => (page_id.clone(), *before, *prev_lsn),
                    _ => break,  // reached this txn's Begin (or a non-update record) -- fully undone
                }
            };

            let entry = pages.entry(page_id.clone()).or_insert((0, 0));
            entry.0 = before_val;
            let clr_lsn = wal.clr(txn, &page_id, prev_lsn, before_val);  // log the undo itself -- this IS the "log the undo too" ARIES rule
            entry.1 = clr_lsn;

            cursor = prev_lsn;
        }
    }
}

fn recover(wal: &mut Wal, disk: &HashMap<String, PageOnDisk>) -> HashMap<String, i64> {
    let (txn_table, dirty_page_table) = analysis(wal);
    let mut pages = redo(wal, &dirty_page_table, disk);
    undo(wal, &txn_table, &mut pages);
    pages.into_iter().map(|(k, (v, _))| (k, v)).collect()
}

fn main() {
    let mut wal = Wal::new();
    let (t1, t2, t3) = (1u64, 2u64, 3u64);

    // T1: a normal transaction that commits cleanly before the crash.
    wal.begin(t1);
    wal.update(t1, "A", 0, 100);
    wal.commit(t1);

    // T2: begins, writes, then the crash happens while it's still active/uncommitted.
    let b2 = wal.begin(t2);
    wal.update(t2, "B", 0, 999);

    // T3: aborts NORMALLY before the crash -- its own runtime rollback already wrote a
    // CLR for its one update, so recovery must recognize it as resolved and leave it alone.
    let b3 = wal.begin(t3);
    wal.update(t3, "C", 5, 50);
    wal.clr(t3, "C", Some(b3), 5);
    wal.abort(t3);

    // What actually reached durable storage before the crash: nothing was flushed, so
    // every page's on-disk LSN is 0 and every logged action since must be redone.
    let mut disk = HashMap::new();
    disk.insert("A".to_string(), PageOnDisk { value: 0, page_lsn: 0 });
    disk.insert("B".to_string(), PageOnDisk { value: 0, page_lsn: 0 });
    disk.insert("C".to_string(), PageOnDisk { value: 5, page_lsn: 0 });

    let pre_crash_len = wal.records.len();
    let final_pages = recover(&mut wal, &disk);

    assert_eq!(final_pages.get("A"), Some(&100), "T1 committed -- REDO must make its effect durable");
    assert_eq!(final_pages.get("B"), Some(&0), "T2 never committed -- UNDO must roll it back to its before-image");
    assert_eq!(final_pages.get("C"), Some(&5), "T3 already self-aborted pre-crash -- REDO replays its own CLR back to 5");

    // Prove the "redo everything, even doomed work, THEN undo" ordering was honored, by
    // asserting on the LOG's contents post-recovery rather than only the final data state:
    // UNDO only emits a CLR for a record it actually processed, so a CLR for T2 existing
    // at all proves T2's doomed update really was redone and then rolled back afterward.
    let new_records = &wal.records[pre_crash_len..];
    let t2_clrs: Vec<&LogRecord> = new_records.iter()
        .filter(|r| matches!(&r.kind, LogRecordKind::Clr { txn, .. } if *txn == t2))
        .collect();
    assert_eq!(t2_clrs.len(), 1, "UNDO must write exactly one CLR for T2's single update");
    match &t2_clrs[0].kind {
        LogRecordKind::Clr { page_id, undo_next_lsn, after, .. } => {
            assert_eq!(page_id, "B");
            assert_eq!(*undo_next_lsn, Some(b2), "CLR must point back at T2's Begin -- nothing earlier left to undo");
            assert_eq!(*after, 0, "CLR's redo-value must be the original update's before-image");
        }
        _ => unreachable!(),
    }

    // No spurious CLRs for a committed txn or for one that had already resolved itself.
    let t1_new_clrs = new_records.iter().filter(|r| matches!(&r.kind, LogRecordKind::Clr { txn, .. } if *txn == t1)).count();
    let t3_new_clrs = new_records.iter().filter(|r| matches!(&r.kind, LogRecordKind::Clr { txn, .. } if *txn == t3)).count();
    assert_eq!(t1_new_clrs, 0, "T1 committed -- must never be undone");
    assert_eq!(t3_new_clrs, 0, "T3 was already fully rolled back before the crash -- must not be re-undone");

    println!("all ARIES recovery assertions passed");
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Redoes a doomed transaction's updates anyway — the single most commonly-missed ARIES rule. A candidate who "optimizes" by consulting the transaction table during REDO and skipping updates from transactions ANALYSIS already knows are uncommitted has silently reinvented a subtly wrong recovery algorithm: REDO's whole point is to deterministically reconstruct the exact pre-crash state first, using ONLY per-page LSN comparisons, completely independent of any transaction's eventual fate — UNDO is the only phase allowed to consult transaction outcomes.
  • ★★★Writes a CLR for every undone action, not just a raw before-image restore — skipping the CLR is the second most common ARIES bug, and it's catastrophic specifically on a SECOND crash: without a durable record of "this action was already undone," a subsequent recovery pass would REDO the original update (since its LSN is still in the log and still ≥ the page's on-disk LSN) and then have no way to know to UNDO it again, permanently losing the rollback.
  • ★★★Uses per-page LSN comparison for REDO idempotency (if page_lsn < record.lsn) rather than blindly replaying every update in order — this is what makes REDO safe to re-run against a partially-flushed disk image where some pages already reflect later writes than others; without it, replaying an old update over a page that's already ahead would silently corrupt data by reverting it.
  • ★★Recognizes that a self-aborted transaction (T3) needs no further UNDO work at recovery time — its own pre-crash rollback already wrote the CLR; ANALYSIS should classify it by its LAST log record (the Abort), not by "did it ever have an active status at some point," so recovery doesn't waste effort (or worse, double-undo) work that already completed before the crash.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"This recovery scans the ENTIRE log from the beginning during Analysis — how does a checkpoint let a real database avoid that on a system that's been running for months?" — A checkpoint periodically writes a special log record capturing a snapshot of the CURRENT transaction table and dirty-page table (a "fuzzy checkpoint" in ARIES doesn't even need to pause activity to take it), plus a pointer to the earliest LSN still needed. Analysis then starts from that checkpoint's begin_lsn instead of LSN 1, using its embedded tables as the starting point rather than rebuilding them from empty — turning an O(entire log history) scan into an O(log since last checkpoint) scan, which is the entire reason checkpoints exist.
  • P2"Why does ARIES insist on redoing history before undoing anything, instead of just undoing uncommitted transactions directly from the crash-time page state?" — Because the crash-time in-memory page state is GONE — all we have on disk is some inconsistent mix of flushed and unflushed pages, each possibly reflecting a different point in history. REDO's job is to first deterministically reconstruct ONE consistent, fully-caught-up state (as if the crash never paused anything mid-flush) so that UNDO has a well-defined, guaranteed-consistent starting point to roll transactions back FROM — trying to undo directly from an inconsistent, partially-flushed disk image has no reliable "before" image to reason from in general.
  • P3"How would you extend the dirty-page table concept to avoid flushing every page on every commit, while still guaranteeing durability?" — This is exactly what the dirty-page table already enables: as long as the WAL record for an update is durably flushed BEFORE the update's effect on the page needs to be considered committed (the actual "write-ahead" rule), the in-memory page itself can stay dirty and get flushed later, lazily, by a background process — REDO from the dirty-page table's recLSNs is precisely the mechanism that makes it safe to defer page flushes arbitrarily, since recovery can always reconstruct any unflushed page's correct state from the log.
🎯 Senior angle
A mid-level answer can describe ARIES's three phases from memory. A senior answer, when handed this exact scenario, will proactively ask "wait — should T2's update actually land on the page during REDO if it's going to be undone anyway?" and then answer their own question correctly: yes, unconditionally, because REDO must be a pure function of LSNs and on-disk page state, with zero knowledge of transaction outcomes — mixing that knowledge in is the classic way an ARIES implementation looks fine in the common case but silently diverges from a real crash-recovery guarantee the one time REDO and UNDO interact in a subtle order-dependent way (e.g. a second crash mid-recovery). Asking to see it fail before believing it's correct is the real signal here, not reciting the phase names.

    let new_records = &wal.records[pre_crash_len..];
    let t2_clrs: Vec<&LogRecord> = new_records.iter()
        .filter(|r| matches!(&r.kind, LogRecordKind::Clr { txn, .. } if *txn == t2))
        .collect();
    assert_eq!(t2_clrs.len(), 1, "UNDO must write exactly one CLR for T2's single update");
    match &t2_clrs[0].kind {
        LogRecordKind::Clr { page_id, undo_next_lsn, after, .. } => {
            assert_eq!(page_id, "B");
            assert_eq!(*undo_next_lsn, Some(b2), "CLR must point back at T2's Begin -- nothing earlier left to undo");
            assert_eq!(*after, 0, "CLR's redo-value must be the original update's before-image");
        }
        _ => unreachable!(),
    }

    // No spurious CLRs for a committed txn or for one that had already resolved itself.
    let t1_new_clrs = new_records.iter().filter(|r| matches!(&r.kind, LogRecordKind::Clr { txn, .. } if *txn == t1)).count();
    let t3_new_clrs = new_records.iter().filter(|r| matches!(&r.kind, LogRecordKind::Clr { txn, .. } if *txn == t3)).count();
    assert_eq!(t1_new_clrs, 0, "T1 committed -- must never be undone");
    assert_eq!(t3_new_clrs, 0, "T3 was already fully rolled back before the crash -- must not be re-undone");

    println!("all ARIES recovery assertions passed");
}
