// Database Engineering Exercise 68 · 75 min
W68 · Copy-on-Write Persistent B-Tree — Structural Sharing Across Versions
path copying, O(log n) nodes touched Rc-shared siblings old root handles stay valid forever Hard
Prompt
"Implement a persistent (in the functional-data-structure sense, as used by LMDB and Datomic-style databases — old versions remain accessible) copy-on-write B-tree: insert(key, value) -> NewRootHandle must never mutate any existing node in place. Instead, copy only the O(log n) nodes along the path from root to the modified leaf, rewiring the copied ancestors' child pointers to point at the copies, while every unchanged sibling subtree is shared — via Rc<Node> — between the old and new tree versions rather than duplicated. After N inserts, looking up the tree exactly as it existed after insert K (for any K ≤ N) must still work, using the root handle that insert K returned."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::rc::Rc;

const MAX_KEYS: usize = 3;

/// Unified node shape (classic B-tree): children.is_empty() means leaf, otherwise
/// children.len() == keys.len() + 1. Nothing here is ever mutated once built.
struct Node { keys: Vec<i64>, values: Vec<String>, children: Vec<Rc<Node>> }

type Tree = Rc<Node>;

enum InsertResult {
    Updated(Rc<Node>),
    /// This subtree overflowed and split: (new_left, median_key, median_value, new_right)
    Split(Rc<Node>, i64, String, Rc<Node>),
}

// TODO: fn insert_into(node: &Rc, key: i64, value: String) -> InsertResult
//   leaf: copy keys/values, splice in the new entry, split if over MAX_KEYS
//   internal: recurse into ONE child; every OTHER child is `node.children.clone()`
//   (an Rc clone, i.e. a cheap refcount bump, NOT a deep copy) -- this line is the
//   entire structural-sharing mechanism. Splice in a promoted median if the child split.
// TODO: fn insert(tree: &Tree, key: i64, value: &str) -> Tree  -- handle a root split
// TODO: fn get(tree: &Tree, key: i64) -> Option

fn main() {
    let mut v0 = empty();
    for (k, v) in [(10, "v10"), (20, "v20"), (30, "v30")] {
        v0 = insert(&v0, k, v);
    }
    // This 4th insert overflows the root leaf (3 keys is the max) and forces the first
    // split, so V1's root becomes an internal node with two leaf children.
    let v1 = insert(&v0, 40, "v40");
    assert_eq!(v1.children.len(), 2, "root should have split into an internal node with two children");
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 10), Some("v10".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 40), Some("v40".to_string()));

    // Insert 50 to build V2. 50 belongs in the RIGHT child's range, so the LEFT child
    // ([10, 20]) is never visited by this insert at all.
    let v2 = insert(&v1, 50, "v50");

    // V1's root handle must still resolve to exactly V1's data -- untouched by V2's insert.
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 10), Some("v10".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 20), Some("v20".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 30), Some("v30".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 40), Some("v40".to_string()));

    // A key added only in V2 must be absent when looked up via V1's root handle.
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 50), None, "50 was only ever inserted into V2 -- must not leak into V1");
    assert_eq!(get(&v2, 50), Some("v50".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(get(&v2, 10), Some("v10".to_string()), "V2 must still see everything V1 had (persistence, not just isolation)");

    // Structural-sharing proof #1: pointer identity. The left child was never on the
    // insertion path for 50, so V1 and V2 must reference the literal same allocation.
    assert!(Rc::ptr_eq(&v1.children[0], &v2.children[0]), "untouched sibling subtree must be shared, not copied");

    // Structural-sharing proof #2: refcount. Exactly two owners exist for that shared
    // leaf -- V1's root and V2's root -- proving no hidden extra copy was ever made.
    assert_eq!(Rc::strong_count(&v1.children[0]), 2, "exactly two owners of the untouched subtree: v1 and v2's roots");

    // Contrast case: the RIGHT child WAS on the insertion path (50 landed there), so it
    // must NOT be shared -- confirming the sharing above isn't accidental/blanket sharing.
    assert!(!Rc::ptr_eq(&v1.children[1], &v2.children[1]), "the modified child must be a fresh copy, not shared with the old version");

    println!("all copy-on-write persistent B-tree assertions passed");
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::rc::Rc;

/// Order-4 B-tree: at most 3 keys per node, overflowing at 4 forces a split.
const MAX_KEYS: usize = 3;

/// A single unified node shape (classic B-tree, not B+tree): `children.is_empty()`
/// means leaf, otherwise `children.len() == keys.len() + 1`. Every field is immutable
/// once built -- `insert` never mutates a `Node` in place, only ever builds brand-new ones.
struct Node {
    keys: Vec<i64>,
    values: Vec<String>,
    children: Vec<Rc<Node>>,
}

/// A tree "version" is just a handle to its root -- cheap to keep any number of these
/// around simultaneously, since old versions share every node they didn't need to copy.
type Tree = Rc<Node>;

fn empty() -> Tree {
    Rc::new(Node { keys: Vec::new(), values: Vec::new(), children: Vec::new() })
}

enum InsertResult {
    /// This subtree was rebuilt without overflowing -- here's its new root.
    Updated(Rc<Node>),
    /// This subtree overflowed and had to split: (new_left, median_key, median_value, new_right).
    /// The caller is responsible for inserting the median into itself as a separator.
    Split(Rc<Node>, i64, String, Rc<Node>),
}

fn split_leaf(keys: Vec<i64>, values: Vec<String>) -> InsertResult {
    let mid = keys.len() / 2;
    let left = Rc::new(Node { keys: keys[..mid].to_vec(), values: values[..mid].to_vec(), children: vec![] });
    let right = Rc::new(Node { keys: keys[mid + 1..].to_vec(), values: values[mid + 1..].to_vec(), children: vec![] });
    InsertResult::Split(left, keys[mid], values[mid].clone(), right)
}

fn split_internal(keys: Vec<i64>, values: Vec<String>, children: Vec<Rc<Node>>) -> InsertResult {
    let mid = keys.len() / 2;
    let left = Rc::new(Node {
        keys: keys[..mid].to_vec(), values: values[..mid].to_vec(), children: children[..=mid].to_vec(),
    });
    let right = Rc::new(Node {
        keys: keys[mid + 1..].to_vec(), values: values[mid + 1..].to_vec(), children: children[mid + 1..].to_vec(),
    });
    InsertResult::Split(left, keys[mid], values[mid].clone(), right)
}

/// The core of the whole exercise: copies ONLY the nodes on the path from `node` down
/// to wherever `key` belongs, and reuses every sibling subtree the path doesn't pass
/// through by cloning its `Rc` (a cheap refcount bump), never its contents.
fn insert_into(node: &Rc<Node>, key: i64, value: String) -> InsertResult {
    let pos = node.keys.partition_point(|&k| k < key);
    let exact_match = pos < node.keys.len() && node.keys[pos] == key;

    if exact_match {
        let mut new_keys = node.keys.clone();
        let mut new_values = node.values.clone();
        new_keys[pos] = key;
        new_values[pos] = value;
        return InsertResult::Updated(Rc::new(Node { keys: new_keys, values: new_values, children: node.children.clone() }));
    }

    if node.children.is_empty() {
        let mut new_keys = node.keys.clone();
        let mut new_values = node.values.clone();
        new_keys.insert(pos, key);
        new_values.insert(pos, value);
        if new_keys.len() <= MAX_KEYS {
            InsertResult::Updated(Rc::new(Node { keys: new_keys, values: new_values, children: vec![] }))
        } else {
            split_leaf(new_keys, new_values)
        }
    } else {
        match insert_into(&node.children[pos], key, value) {  // recurse into exactly ONE child
            InsertResult::Updated(new_child) => {
                let mut new_children = node.children.clone();  // Rc clone: EVERY other child is shared, not copied
                new_children[pos] = new_child;
                InsertResult::Updated(Rc::new(Node { keys: node.keys.clone(), values: node.values.clone(), children: new_children }))
            }
            InsertResult::Split(left, mid_key, mid_value, right) => {
                let mut new_keys = node.keys.clone();
                let mut new_values = node.values.clone();
                let mut new_children = node.children.clone();
                new_keys.insert(pos, mid_key);
                new_values.insert(pos, mid_value);
                new_children[pos] = left;
                new_children.insert(pos + 1, right);
                if new_keys.len() <= MAX_KEYS {
                    InsertResult::Updated(Rc::new(Node { keys: new_keys, values: new_values, children: new_children }))
                } else {
                    split_internal(new_keys, new_values, new_children)
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

/// Returns a brand-new root handle; `tree` (and everything reachable from it) is left
/// completely untouched and remains a perfectly valid, independently queryable version.
fn insert(tree: &Tree, key: i64, value: &str) -> Tree {
    match insert_into(tree, key, value.to_string()) {
        InsertResult::Updated(new_root) => new_root,
        InsertResult::Split(left, mid_key, mid_value, right) => {
            Rc::new(Node { keys: vec![mid_key], values: vec![mid_value], children: vec![left, right] })
        }
    }
}

fn get(tree: &Tree, key: i64) -> Option<String> {
    let mut node = tree;
    loop {
        let pos = node.keys.partition_point(|&k| k < key);
        if pos < node.keys.len() && node.keys[pos] == key {
            return Some(node.values[pos].clone());
        }
        if node.children.is_empty() { return None; }
        node = &node.children[pos];
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut v0 = empty();
    for (k, v) in [(10, "v10"), (20, "v20"), (30, "v30")] {
        v0 = insert(&v0, k, v);
    }
    // This 4th insert overflows the root leaf (3 keys is the max) and forces the first
    // split, so V1's root becomes an internal node with two leaf children.
    let v1 = insert(&v0, 40, "v40");
    assert_eq!(v1.children.len(), 2, "root should have split into an internal node with two children");
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 10), Some("v10".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 40), Some("v40".to_string()));

    // Insert 50 to build V2. 50 belongs in the RIGHT child's range, so the LEFT child
    // ([10, 20]) is never visited by this insert at all.
    let v2 = insert(&v1, 50, "v50");

    // V1's root handle must still resolve to exactly V1's data -- untouched by V2's insert.
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 10), Some("v10".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 20), Some("v20".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 30), Some("v30".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 40), Some("v40".to_string()));

    // A key added only in V2 must be absent when looked up via V1's root handle.
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 50), None, "50 was only ever inserted into V2 -- must not leak into V1");
    assert_eq!(get(&v2, 50), Some("v50".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(get(&v2, 10), Some("v10".to_string()), "V2 must still see everything V1 had (persistence, not just isolation)");

    // Structural-sharing proof #1: pointer identity. The left child was never on the
    // insertion path for 50, so V1 and V2 must reference the literal same allocation.
    assert!(Rc::ptr_eq(&v1.children[0], &v2.children[0]), "untouched sibling subtree must be shared, not copied");

    // Structural-sharing proof #2: refcount. Exactly two owners exist for that shared
    // leaf -- V1's root and V2's root -- proving no hidden extra copy was ever made.
    assert_eq!(Rc::strong_count(&v1.children[0]), 2, "exactly two owners of the untouched subtree: v1 and v2's roots");

    // Contrast case: the RIGHT child WAS on the insertion path (50 landed there), so it
    // must NOT be shared -- confirming the sharing above isn't accidental/blanket sharing.
    assert!(!Rc::ptr_eq(&v1.children[1], &v2.children[1]), "the modified child must be a fresh copy, not shared with the old version");

    println!("all copy-on-write persistent B-tree assertions passed");
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Clones the children Vec<Rc<Node>>, not the nodes it contains — node.children.clone() clones the vector's spine (a `Vec` of pointer-sized `Rc`s) while bumping each contained `Rc`'s refcount, which is O(fanout), not O(subtree size); a candidate who instead recursively deep-clones every child node "to be safe" has silently turned an O(log n) persistent structure into an O(n) full-copy-per-insert structure while still superficially compiling and passing correctness tests that don't check sharing.
  • ★★★Never calls Rc::get_mut / Rc::make_mut to "sneak" a mutation into a node — the entire exercise is void if a candidate reaches for interior mutability or `Rc::get_mut` to tweak an existing node instead of building a fresh one; watch specifically for whether they reach for `RefCell` here out of habit — it would work for single-threaded read/write but fundamentally violates "never mutate a node in place," breaking every old version silently.
  • ★★Handles a root split by allocating a brand-new root node, not by trying to mutate the existing root's arity — since the root has no parent to notify, the top-level insert function itself must special-case InsertResult::Split at the very top and build one new level; missing this case means the tree silently stops growing in height once the root's `MAX_KEYS` is reached even as more keys are inserted.
  • ★Proves sharing quantitatively (Rc::strong_count / Rc::ptr_eq), not just "trust me, get() returns the right values" — a candidate who only tests correctness of lookups across versions hasn't actually verified the STRUCTURAL SHARING claim at all (a naive full-deep-copy-per-insert implementation would pass every one of those lookup tests too); the refcount/pointer-identity assertions are the only way to distinguish "genuinely persistent" from "just versioned by accident via full copies."
Follow-up probes
  • P1"This is single-threaded — what breaks if two threads call insert() on the SAME root handle concurrently, and what's the minimal fix?" — Nothing breaks from a memory-safety standpoint (each `insert` call only ever READS the shared `tree` argument and builds entirely new nodes), but `Rc` itself is `!Send`/`!Sync` — its refcount increments/decrements are not atomic, so sharing an `Rc` across threads is a data race on the refcount, not on tree contents. The fix is purely mechanical: swap `Rc` for `Arc` everywhere (atomic refcounting), which costs a little performance on refcount operations but requires ZERO changes to the actual COW/path-copying algorithm — a nice illustration that this design was already "thread-safe" in spirit, modulo the refcounting primitive's own thread-safety.
  • P2"Real systems like LMDB don't keep every historical root forever — how would you let old versions eventually get garbage collected while keeping recent ones alive?" — This falls out almost for free from `Rc`'s own reference counting: once the LAST `Tree` handle referencing a given root is dropped, that root's refcount (and transitively, every node ONLY reachable through it and not shared with a still-live version) drops to zero and Rust deallocates it automatically — a real system just needs an explicit policy for which historical roots to keep alive at all (e.g. "keep the last N committed versions," or "keep whatever the oldest still-open reader transaction needs," directly analogous to MVCC vacuum in W66) rather than any new mechanism in the tree itself.
  • P3"This B-tree only grows — how would you implement a persistent DELETE while preserving the same sharing guarantees, and what's the extra wrinkle versus insert?" — Delete follows the identical path-copying shape (copy the path from root to the key, share every untouched sibling) but adds underflow handling instead of overflow handling: if removing a key drops a node below the minimum required key count, you must either borrow a key from an adjacent sibling (which, notably, ALSO forces that sibling to be copied rather than shared, since its contents change) or merge two nodes together — meaning delete's sharing "footprint" is less predictable than insert's clean O(log n), since an underflow can ripple into touching more nodes than the direct root-to-leaf path alone.
🎯 Senior angle
A mid-level answer builds a correct-looking versioned tree where every version happens to return the right values — including, unnoticed, one that deep-copies the entire tree on every insert and still passes all the lookup assertions. A senior answer treats the Rc::strong_count / Rc::ptr_eq checks as the actual spec, not an afterthought, because "old versions are still correct" and "old versions are cheap to keep around" are two completely different claims — real systems like LMDB adopt copy-on-write specifically for the second property (O(log n) writes, O(1)-ish space-amortized snapshots), and an implementation that only satisfies the first has quietly failed the actual engineering goal while looking identical from the outside.

The Concurrency & Async Track
Goes past "can you use a Mutex" into the mechanisms underneath: a writer-preferring reader-writer lock built from raw primitives, real fork-join parallelism with scoped threads, a hand-rolled Future + Waker pair (the exact machinery every async runtime is built on), why Pin exists and what breaks without it, manually desugaring an "async trait method" to its object-safe boxed form, and the Tokio-specific traps — cancellation safety, backpressure, and the Send rules that decide whether a future can be spawned at all.

// Answer by code:
// This is single-threaded — what breaks if two threads call insert() on the SAME root handle concurrently, and what's the minimal fix?
fn harden_w68_1() {
    // use: Node
    todo!()

fn main() {
    // Harden · This is single-threaded — what breaks if two threads call insert() on…
    harden_w68_1();
    // Parent exercise still holds after the harden change:
    let mut v0 = empty();
    for (k, v) in [(10, "v10"), (20, "v20"), (30, "v30")] {
        v0 = insert(&v0, k, v);
    }
    // This 4th insert overflows the root leaf (3 keys is the max) and forces the first
    // split, so V1's root becomes an internal node with two leaf children.
    let v1 = insert(&v0, 40, "v40");
    assert_eq!(v1.children.len(), 2, "root should have split into an internal node with two children");
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 10), Some("v10".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 40), Some("v40".to_string()));

    // Insert 50 to build V2. 50 belongs in the RIGHT child's range, so the LEFT child
    // ([10, 20]) is never visited by this insert at all.
    let v2 = insert(&v1, 50, "v50");

    // V1's root handle must still resolve to exactly V1's data -- untouched by V2's insert.
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 10), Some("v10".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 20), Some("v20".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 30), Some("v30".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 40), Some("v40".to_string()));

    // A key added only in V2 must be absent when looked up via V1's root handle.
    assert_eq!(get(&v1, 50), None, "50 was only ever inserted into V2 -- must not leak into V1");
    assert_eq!(get(&v2, 50), Some("v50".to_string()));
    assert_eq!(get(&v2, 10), Some("v10".to_string()), "V2 must still see everything V1 had (persistence, not just isolation)");

    // Structural-sharing proof #1: pointer identity. The left child was never on the
    // insertion path for 50, so V1 and V2 must reference the literal same allocation.
    assert!(Rc::ptr_eq(&v1.children[0], &v2.children[0]), "untouched sibling subtree must be shared, not copied");

    // Structural-sharing proof #2: refcount. Exactly two owners exist for that shared
    // leaf -- V1's root and V2's root -- proving no hidden extra copy was ever made.
    assert_eq!(Rc::strong_count(&v1.children[0]), 2, "exactly two owners of the untouched subtree: v1 and v2's roots");

    // Contrast case: the RIGHT child WAS on the insertion path (50 landed there), so it
    // must NOT be shared -- confirming the sharing above isn't accidental/blanket sharing.
    assert!(!Rc::ptr_eq(&v1.children[1], &v2.children[1]), "the modified child must be a fresh copy, not shared with the old version");

    println!("all copy-on-write persistent B-tree assertions passed");
}

// Concurrency & Async Exercise 69 · 60 min
W69 · Custom RwLock From Scratch — Atomics + Condvar, Writer-Preferring
Mutex + Condvar RAII guards via Deref/DerefMut/Drop writer-preferring fairness UnsafeCell interior mutability Hard
Prompt
"Implement a reader-writer lock from scratch using Mutex<State> + Condvar, where State tracks the number of active readers, whether a writer is currently active, and the number of writers currently WAITING. Expose read(&self) -> ReadGuard and write(&self) -> WriteGuard RAII guards (Deref/DerefMut/Drop). Critically, make it writer-preferring: once a writer is waiting, no NEW reader may acquire the lock even if it's currently read-locked by others and would otherwise admit more readers — new readers must queue behind the waiting writer, preventing writer starvation under a continuous stream of readers (the classic 'naive RwLock' bug). Readers already holding the lock when a writer starts waiting may finish normally; only new/incoming reader acquisitions are blocked."
Starter code to hand to candidate
struct State { readers: usize, writer_active: bool, writers_waiting: usize }

struct RwLock<T> { state: Mutex<State>, cond: Condvar, data: UnsafeCell<T> }

// TODO: unsafe impl<T: Send> Sync for RwLock<T> {} — data is only ever exposed through guards
// TODO: struct ReadGuard<'a, T> / WriteGuard<'a, T> — Deref (+DerefMut for Write) + Drop
// TODO: impl<T> RwLock<T> — new(value), read(&self) -> ReadGuard, write(&self) -> WriteGuard
//       write() must be WRITER-PREFERRING: once writers_waiting > 0, no NEW reader may proceed,
//       even if readers == 0 and no writer is currently active

fn main() {
    let lock = Arc::new(RwLock::new(Counters { a: 0, b: 0 }));

    // --- Property 1: multiple readers can hold the lock simultaneously ---
    let concurrent_readers = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let max_concurrent_readers = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..8 {
        let lock = lock.clone();
        let concurrent_readers = concurrent_readers.clone();
        let max_concurrent_readers = max_concurrent_readers.clone();
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            let guard = lock.read();
            let now = concurrent_readers.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst) + 1;
            max_concurrent_readers.fetch_max(now, Ordering::SeqCst);
            thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(40));
            concurrent_readers.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
            assert_eq!(guard.a, guard.b);
        }));
    }
    for h in handles { h.join().unwrap(); }
    assert!(max_concurrent_readers.load(Ordering::SeqCst) > 1);  // real concurrent reader admission, not accidental serialization

    // --- Property 2: a writer never runs concurrently with any reader ---
    let writer_running = Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(false));
    let readers_running = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let violations = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..4 {
        let (lock, writer_running, readers_running, violations) =
            (lock.clone(), writer_running.clone(), readers_running.clone(), violations.clone());
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            for _ in 0..40 {
                let guard = lock.read();
                readers_running.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
                if writer_running.load(Ordering::SeqCst) {
                    violations.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);  // a writer must NEVER be active while we hold a read guard
                }
                assert_eq!(guard.a, guard.b);
                readers_running.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
            }
        }));
    }
    for _ in 0..4 {
        let (lock, writer_running, readers_running, violations) =
            (lock.clone(), writer_running.clone(), readers_running.clone(), violations.clone());
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            for _ in 0..40 {
                let mut guard = lock.write();
                writer_running.store(true, Ordering::SeqCst);
                if readers_running.load(Ordering::SeqCst) > 0 {
                    violations.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);  // impossible state: writer active AND reader count > 0
                }
                guard.a += 1;
                guard.b += 1;
                writer_running.store(false, Ordering::SeqCst);
            }
        }));
    }
    for h in handles { h.join().unwrap(); }
    assert_eq!(violations.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 0);  // mutual exclusion held under real contention, verified externally

    // --- Property 3: writer preference — no starvation under a continuous reader flood ---
    let stop = Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(false));
    let reader_iterations = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let mut reader_handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..6 {
        let (lock, stop, reader_iterations) = (lock.clone(), stop.clone(), reader_iterations.clone());
        reader_handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            while !stop.load(Ordering::Relaxed) {
                let guard = lock.read();
                assert_eq!(guard.a, guard.b);
                drop(guard);
                reader_iterations.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);  // no sleep: fire acquisitions as fast as possible
            }
        }));
    }
    thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(20));  // let the reader flood get going before the writer even tries

    let writer_lock = lock.clone();
    let start = Instant::now();
    let writer_handle = thread::spawn(move || {
        let mut guard = writer_lock.write();
        guard.a += 1;
        guard.b += 1;
    });
    writer_handle.join().unwrap();
    let elapsed = start.elapsed();
    stop.store(true, Ordering::Relaxed);
    for h in reader_handles { h.join().unwrap(); }

    assert!(reader_iterations.load(Ordering::Relaxed) > 200);  // the reader stream really was continuous and fast
    assert!(elapsed < Duration::from_secs(2));  // writer still got in within a bounded time — no starvation

    println!("max_concurrent_readers={} violations={} writer_wait={:?} reader_iterations={}",
        max_concurrent_readers.load(Ordering::SeqCst), violations.load(Ordering::SeqCst), elapsed, reader_iterations.load(Ordering::Relaxed));
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::cell::UnsafeCell;
use std::ops::{Deref, DerefMut};
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, AtomicUsize, Ordering};
use std::sync::{Arc, Condvar, Mutex};
use std::thread;
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

struct State {
    readers: usize,
    writer_active: bool,
    writers_waiting: usize,
}

struct RwLock<T> {
    state: Mutex<State>,
    cond: Condvar,
    data: UnsafeCell<T>,
}

// SAFETY: `data` is only ever reached through a ReadGuard/WriteGuard, whose existence proves
// the internal State already enforces exclusive/shared access rules — same contract std's own RwLock uses.
unsafe impl<T: Send> Sync for RwLock<T> {}
unsafe impl<T: Send> Send for RwLock<T> {}

struct ReadGuard<'a, T> { lock: &'a RwLock<T> }
struct WriteGuard<'a, T> { lock: &'a RwLock<T> }

impl<T> RwLock<T> {
    fn new(value: T) -> Self {
        Self {
            state: Mutex::new(State { readers: 0, writer_active: false, writers_waiting: 0 }),
            cond: Condvar::new(),
            data: UnsafeCell::new(value),
        }
    }

    // Writer-preferring: block NEW readers whenever a writer is active OR merely WAITING —
    // even though `readers == 0` alone would otherwise happily admit us. This is the one line
    // that separates this from the classic starvation-prone "naive" RwLock.
    fn read(&self) -> ReadGuard<'_, T> {
        let mut st = self.state.lock().unwrap();
        while st.writer_active || st.writers_waiting > 0 {
            st = self.cond.wait(st).unwrap();
        }
        st.readers += 1;
        ReadGuard { lock: self }
    }

    fn write(&self) -> WriteGuard<'_, T> {
        let mut st = self.state.lock().unwrap();
        st.writers_waiting += 1;  // register intent FIRST — any reader arriving after this instant queues behind us
        while st.writer_active || st.readers > 0 {
            st = self.cond.wait(st).unwrap();
        }
        st.writers_waiting -= 1;
        st.writer_active = true;
        WriteGuard { lock: self }
    }
}

impl<'a, T> Deref for ReadGuard<'a, T> {
    type Target = T;
    fn deref(&self) -> &T { unsafe { &*self.lock.data.get() } }
}

impl<'a, T> Drop for ReadGuard<'a, T> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        let mut st = self.lock.state.lock().unwrap();
        st.readers -= 1;
        let should_notify = st.readers == 0;
        drop(st);
        if should_notify { self.lock.cond.notify_all(); }  // last reader out — wake a waiting writer
    }
}

impl<'a, T> Deref for WriteGuard<'a, T> {
    type Target = T;
    fn deref(&self) -> &T { unsafe { &*self.lock.data.get() } }
}
impl<'a, T> DerefMut for WriteGuard<'a, T> {
    fn deref_mut(&mut self) -> &mut T { unsafe { &mut *self.lock.data.get() } }
}
impl<'a, T> Drop for WriteGuard<'a, T> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        let mut st = self.lock.state.lock().unwrap();
        st.writer_active = false;
        drop(st);
        self.lock.cond.notify_all();  // wake both waiting readers AND waiting writers to re-check state
    }
}

struct Counters { a: u64, b: u64 }

fn main() {
    let lock = Arc::new(RwLock::new(Counters { a: 0, b: 0 }));

    // --- Property 1: multiple readers can hold the lock simultaneously ---
    let concurrent_readers = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let max_concurrent_readers = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..8 {
        let lock = lock.clone();
        let concurrent_readers = concurrent_readers.clone();
        let max_concurrent_readers = max_concurrent_readers.clone();
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            let guard = lock.read();
            let now = concurrent_readers.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst) + 1;
            max_concurrent_readers.fetch_max(now, Ordering::SeqCst);
            thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(40));
            concurrent_readers.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
            assert_eq!(guard.a, guard.b);
        }));
    }
    for h in handles { h.join().unwrap(); }
    assert!(max_concurrent_readers.load(Ordering::SeqCst) > 1);  // real concurrent reader admission, not accidental serialization

    // --- Property 2: a writer never runs concurrently with any reader ---
    let writer_running = Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(false));
    let readers_running = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let violations = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..4 {
        let (lock, writer_running, readers_running, violations) =
            (lock.clone(), writer_running.clone(), readers_running.clone(), violations.clone());
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            for _ in 0..40 {
                let guard = lock.read();
                readers_running.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
                if writer_running.load(Ordering::SeqCst) {
                    violations.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);  // a writer must NEVER be active while we hold a read guard
                }
                assert_eq!(guard.a, guard.b);
                readers_running.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
            }
        }));
    }
    for _ in 0..4 {
        let (lock, writer_running, readers_running, violations) =
            (lock.clone(), writer_running.clone(), readers_running.clone(), violations.clone());
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            for _ in 0..40 {
                let mut guard = lock.write();
                writer_running.store(true, Ordering::SeqCst);
                if readers_running.load(Ordering::SeqCst) > 0 {
                    violations.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);  // impossible state: writer active AND reader count > 0
                }
                guard.a += 1;
                guard.b += 1;
                writer_running.store(false, Ordering::SeqCst);
            }
        }));
    }
    for h in handles { h.join().unwrap(); }
    assert_eq!(violations.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 0);  // mutual exclusion held under real contention, verified externally

    // --- Property 3: writer preference — no starvation under a continuous reader flood ---
    let stop = Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(false));
    let reader_iterations = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let mut reader_handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..6 {
        let (lock, stop, reader_iterations) = (lock.clone(), stop.clone(), reader_iterations.clone());
        reader_handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            while !stop.load(Ordering::Relaxed) {
                let guard = lock.read();
                assert_eq!(guard.a, guard.b);
                drop(guard);
                reader_iterations.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);  // no sleep: fire acquisitions as fast as possible
            }
        }));
    }
    thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(20));  // let the reader flood get going before the writer even tries

    let writer_lock = lock.clone();
    let start = Instant::now();
    let writer_handle = thread::spawn(move || {
        let mut guard = writer_lock.write();
        guard.a += 1;
        guard.b += 1;
    });
    writer_handle.join().unwrap();
    let elapsed = start.elapsed();
    stop.store(true, Ordering::Relaxed);
    for h in reader_handles { h.join().unwrap(); }

    assert!(reader_iterations.load(Ordering::Relaxed) > 200);  // the reader stream really was continuous and fast
    assert!(elapsed < Duration::from_secs(2));  // writer still got in within a bounded time — no starvation

    println!("max_concurrent_readers={} violations={} writer_wait={:?} reader_iterations={}",
        max_concurrent_readers.load(Ordering::SeqCst), violations.load(Ordering::SeqCst), elapsed, reader_iterations.load(Ordering::Relaxed));
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Checks writers_waiting > 0 in the reader's admission condition, not just writer_active — this is the entire exercise. A candidate who writes while st.writer_active { wait } for readers has built the textbook "naive" RwLock that starves writers forever under a continuous reader stream, because a new reader can always sneak in the instant the previous reader count hits a gap. Watch for whether they realize this failure mode unprompted or only after being shown the starvation test fail.
  • ★★★Increments writers_waiting BEFORE blocking in write(), not after — if a writer only marks itself "waiting" after successfully acquiring exclusivity, the flag is useless for turning away concurrent new readers during the writer's own wait window, defeating the entire writer-preference mechanism.
  • ★★★Wraps every Condvar::wait call in a while loop that re-checks the full condition (not an if) — spurious wakeups are real and permitted by the OS/Condvar contract, and here specifically, a reader woken after a writer finishes must re-check that ANOTHER writer isn't now also waiting before proceeding.
  • ★★Uses UnsafeCell + a manual unsafe impl Sync with a written-out safety justification rather than reaching for a RefCell (which isn't Sync at all and wouldn't compile across threads) or accidentally requiring T: Sync on the data itself (unnecessary — the RwLock's own locking is what provides the synchronization, so only T: Send should be required).
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Your writer-preferring design can now starve READERS instead, under a continuous stream of writers — is that acceptable, and how would a production lock (like Rust's own `parking_lot::RwLock` or a database's latch manager) actually handle this trade-off?" — Pure writer-preference and pure reader-preference are both starvation-prone in the opposite direction; real implementations typically use a fair, ticket-based or FIFO-queue approach where readers and writers are served roughly in arrival order (e.g. a single wait queue where a batch of consecutive readers can proceed together, but a writer in the queue blocks any READER that arrived after it, not before) — this is essentially what `std::sync::RwLock`'s poison-free "fairness is unspecified" disclaimer is dodging, and why serious systems build their own.
  • P2"Why does a plain `AtomicUsize` reader-count with compare-and-swap loops not suffice here, and why did we reach for Mutex+Condvar instead?" — A lock-free CAS-loop approach can track counts (and even encode a "writer waiting" bit in spare bits of one atomic) but has no way to BLOCK a thread efficiently while a condition is false — it would have to spin, burning CPU, or you'd need to bolt on a separate parking mechanism, which is exactly what `Condvar` already provides atomically with the state check via the mutex. Real high-performance RwLocks (`parking_lot`) DO use atomics as the fast path and only fall back to OS-level parking on contention — a hybrid worth mentioning to a strong candidate.
  • P3"What happens to this RwLock if a thread panics while holding a WriteGuard?" — Unlike `std::sync::Mutex`, which "poisons" itself on a panicking guard drop (subsequent `.lock()` calls return an `Err` by default), this hand-rolled version's `Drop` for `WriteGuard` just unconditionally clears `writer_active` and notifies — a panic mid-write leaves `T` in a possibly-inconsistent state with NO signal to future acquirers, silently propagating corruption. A senior candidate should recognize this gap unprompted and at least discuss how they'd add poisoning (a `poisoned: AtomicBool` checked on every acquire, set in a `Drop` guarded by `std::thread::panicking()`).
🎯 Senior angle
The single line that matters most here — readers checking writers_waiting > 0, not just writer_active — is exactly the kind of subtlety that separates "I can use a Condvar" from "I understand the fairness trade-offs Condvars force you to make explicit." A senior candidate should also proactively volunteer that writer-preference just moves the starvation problem onto readers, without being asked — showing they think in terms of trade-offs rather than "correct vs. incorrect."

// Concurrency & Async Exercise 70 · 45 min
W70 · Fork-Join Parallel Merge Sort with Scoped Threads
std::thread::scope split_at_mut fork-join no Arc/Mutex/unsafe sequential-fallback threshold Medium
Prompt
"Implement a parallel merge sort using std::thread::scope (stable scoped threads — NOT Arc + 'static thread::spawn) that recursively splits a &mut [T] slice in half, sorts each half in a separate scoped thread when the slice is above some size threshold, and falls back to sequential slice::sort_unstable below the threshold (thread-spawn overhead is absurd on tiny slices) — then merges the two sorted halves back together in the parent. The entire point is that thread::scope lets you safely borrow non-'static slice data across threads (each recursive call borrows a disjoint mutable sub-slice via split_at_mut) without any Arc/Mutex/unsafe — demonstrate that clearly."
Starter code to hand to candidate
const SEQUENTIAL_THRESHOLD: usize = 2_000;

// TODO: fn parallel_merge_sort<T: Ord + Copy + Send>(slice: &mut [T], threads_spawned: &AtomicUsize)
//   - below SEQUENTIAL_THRESHOLD: fall back to slice.sort_unstable()
//   - above: split_at_mut, thread::scope { spawn one half, recurse on the other half HERE },
//     then merge the two now-sorted halves back into `slice`
// TODO: fn merge_in_place<T: Ord + Copy>(slice: &mut [T], mid: usize)

fn main() {
    let mut rng_state: u64 = 0x2545_F491_4F6C_DD1D;
    let mut next_rand = move || {
        rng_state ^= rng_state << 13;
        rng_state ^= rng_state >> 7;
        rng_state ^= rng_state << 17;
        rng_state
    };

    // --- Correctness on a decent-sized randomly shuffled vector ---
    let n = 200_000;
    let mut data = make_shuffled(n, &mut next_rand);
    let mut reference = data.clone();
    reference.sort();

    let threads_spawned = AtomicUsize::new(0);
    let start = Instant::now();
    parallel_merge_sort(&mut data, &threads_spawned);
    let elapsed = start.elapsed();

    assert_eq!(data, reference);  // matches std's own trusted sort exactly
    assert!(threads_spawned.load(Ordering::Relaxed) > 0);  // proves real parallel recursion, not an accidentally-sequential impl
    println!("sorted {} elements in {:?} using {} spawned threads", n, elapsed, threads_spawned.load(Ordering::Relaxed));

    // --- Sequential-fallback threshold boundary: just below and just above ---
    let mut below = make_shuffled(SEQUENTIAL_THRESHOLD - 1, &mut next_rand);
    let mut below_ref = below.clone();
    below_ref.sort();
    let below_counter = AtomicUsize::new(0);
    parallel_merge_sort(&mut below, &below_counter);
    assert_eq!(below, below_ref);
    assert_eq!(below_counter.load(Ordering::Relaxed), 0);  // at/under threshold: must take the sequential fallback, zero threads spawned

    let mut above = make_shuffled(SEQUENTIAL_THRESHOLD + 1, &mut next_rand);
    let mut above_ref = above.clone();
    above_ref.sort();
    let above_counter = AtomicUsize::new(0);
    parallel_merge_sort(&mut above, &above_counter);
    assert_eq!(above, above_ref);
    assert!(above_counter.load(Ordering::Relaxed) > 0);  // just above threshold: must actually spawn at least one thread

    // --- Trivial edge inputs ---
    let mut empty: Vec<i32> = vec![];
    parallel_merge_sort(&mut empty, &AtomicUsize::new(0));
    assert!(empty.is_empty());

    let mut single = vec![42];
    parallel_merge_sort(&mut single, &AtomicUsize::new(0));
    assert_eq!(single, vec![42]);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
use std::thread;
use std::time::Instant;

const SEQUENTIAL_THRESHOLD: usize = 2_000;  // below this, thread-spawn overhead isn't worth it

fn parallel_merge_sort<T: Ord + Copy + Send>(slice: &mut [T], threads_spawned: &AtomicUsize) {
    if slice.len() <= SEQUENTIAL_THRESHOLD {
        slice.sort_unstable();
        return;
    }
    let mid = slice.len() / 2;
    let (left, right) = slice.split_at_mut(mid);  // disjoint mutable borrows of ONE slice — no Arc/Mutex/unsafe needed

    thread::scope(|s| {
        threads_spawned.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
        let handle = s.spawn(|| parallel_merge_sort(left, threads_spawned));  // borrows `left`, non-'static, sound only inside `scope`
        parallel_merge_sort(right, threads_spawned);  // sort the OTHER half on this thread while the child works in parallel
        handle.join().unwrap();
    });  // thread::scope also guarantees the child is joined here even without the explicit join() above

    merge_in_place(slice, mid);
}

fn merge_in_place<T: Ord + Copy>(slice: &mut [T], mid: usize) {
    let mut merged = Vec::with_capacity(slice.len());
    let (left, right) = slice.split_at(mid);
    let (mut i, mut j) = (0, 0);
    while i < left.len() && j < right.len() {
        if left[i] <= right[j] {
            merged.push(left[i]);
            i += 1;
        } else {
            merged.push(right[j]);
            j += 1;
        }
    }
    merged.extend_from_slice(&left[i..]);
    merged.extend_from_slice(&right[j..]);
    slice.copy_from_slice(&merged);
}

fn make_shuffled(n: usize, rng: &mut impl FnMut() -> u64) -> Vec<i64> {
    (0..n).map(|_| (rng() % 1_000_000) as i64).collect()
}

fn main() {
    let mut rng_state: u64 = 0x2545_F491_4F6C_DD1D;
    let mut next_rand = move || {
        rng_state ^= rng_state << 13;
        rng_state ^= rng_state >> 7;
        rng_state ^= rng_state << 17;
        rng_state
    };

    // --- Correctness on a decent-sized randomly shuffled vector ---
    let n = 200_000;
    let mut data = make_shuffled(n, &mut next_rand);
    let mut reference = data.clone();
    reference.sort();

    let threads_spawned = AtomicUsize::new(0);
    let start = Instant::now();
    parallel_merge_sort(&mut data, &threads_spawned);
    let elapsed = start.elapsed();

    assert_eq!(data, reference);  // matches std's own trusted sort exactly
    assert!(threads_spawned.load(Ordering::Relaxed) > 0);  // proves real parallel recursion, not an accidentally-sequential impl
    println!("sorted {} elements in {:?} using {} spawned threads", n, elapsed, threads_spawned.load(Ordering::Relaxed));

    // --- Sequential-fallback threshold boundary: just below and just above ---
    let mut below = make_shuffled(SEQUENTIAL_THRESHOLD - 1, &mut next_rand);
    let mut below_ref = below.clone();
    below_ref.sort();
    let below_counter = AtomicUsize::new(0);
    parallel_merge_sort(&mut below, &below_counter);
    assert_eq!(below, below_ref);
    assert_eq!(below_counter.load(Ordering::Relaxed), 0);  // at/under threshold: must take the sequential fallback, zero threads spawned

    let mut above = make_shuffled(SEQUENTIAL_THRESHOLD + 1, &mut next_rand);
    let mut above_ref = above.clone();
    above_ref.sort();
    let above_counter = AtomicUsize::new(0);
    parallel_merge_sort(&mut above, &above_counter);
    assert_eq!(above, above_ref);
    assert!(above_counter.load(Ordering::Relaxed) > 0);  // just above threshold: must actually spawn at least one thread

    // --- Trivial edge inputs ---
    let mut empty: Vec<i32> = vec![];
    parallel_merge_sort(&mut empty, &AtomicUsize::new(0));
    assert!(empty.is_empty());

    let mut single = vec![42];
    parallel_merge_sort(&mut single, &AtomicUsize::new(0));
    assert_eq!(single, vec![42]);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Reaches for thread::scope + split_at_mut instead of Arc<Mutex<Vec<T>>> — this is the entire point of the exercise. A candidate who wraps the slice in an Arc<Mutex<_>> to "make the borrow checker happy" has missed that scoped threads exist specifically to let the compiler PROVE two disjoint mutable sub-slices can't alias, with zero runtime locking overhead.
  • ★★★Has an actual sequential fallback threshold, not naive recursion all the way to length-1 sub-slices — spawning an OS thread per recursive call down to single elements would be catastrophically slower than a plain sequential sort due to thread-spawn overhead dwarfing the O(1) work being parallelized at the leaves.
  • ★★Merges into a temporary buffer rather than attempting an in-place merge directly over the aliased sub-slices — the two sorted halves physically live in adjacent memory within the same original slice, so merging "in place" without a scratch buffer requires nontrivial shifting logic; using a `Vec` scratch buffer and copying back is the standard, correct, and interview-reasonable approach.
  • ★★Bounds the generic with `Send` (and typically `Copy` or at least a cheap `Clone`) — `thread::scope`'s spawned closures require their captured data to be `Send` to cross a thread boundary, and a candidate should know to add this bound rather than being surprised by a compiler error.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Before `thread::scope` was stabilized in Rust 1.63, how would you have written safe parallel recursion over disjoint mutable sub-slices?" — Either `crossbeam::scope` (a third-party crate providing the same guarantee before std had it), or `Arc>>` with index-range locking (much clumsier and with real runtime overhead), or genuinely `unsafe` raw-pointer splitting with a manually-argued safety proof (fragile and easy to get wrong). `std::thread::scope`'s stabilization was a big deal specifically because it moved this pattern from "needs a crate or `unsafe`" to "safe std API," which is worth a candidate knowing as context.
  • P2"This spawns a fresh thread at every level of recursion above the threshold — for very large inputs, could that create an unreasonable number of OS threads, and how would you fix it?" — Yes: recursion depth is `O(log(n/threshold))`, and total threads spawned across the whole call tree is `O(n/threshold)` in the worst case, which for a huge array and a small threshold could spawn thousands of OS threads, each with real kernel overhead. Production fork-join systems (Rayon's work-stealing thread pool being the canonical Rust example) instead maintain a FIXED-size pool of worker threads and submit "tasks" that get stolen and executed by idle workers, amortizing thread-creation cost to near zero regardless of recursion depth.
  • P3"Why is `sort_unstable` an acceptable fallback here instead of a stable sort, given merge sort is normally described as a STABLE sorting algorithm?" — Stability only matters when there are multiple elements that compare `Ord`-equal but are otherwise distinguishable (e.g. sorting `(key, original_index)` pairs) — nothing in this exercise's contract promises stability for equal keys, so using the faster, allocation-free `sort_unstable` at the leaves is a legitimate optimization; if stability WERE required, you'd swap in `slice::sort` (which itself is a hybrid merge sort, TimSort-derived) at the leaves and keep the same fork-join structure above the threshold.
🎯 Senior angle
The interesting engineering judgment call isn't "can you write fork-join recursion" — it's picking a sane SEQUENTIAL_THRESHOLD and being able to articulate WHY it exists at all (thread creation is microseconds of real OS overhead, dwarfing the sort work on tiny slices) without being told. Bonus points for a candidate who spontaneously mentions that this whole approach is what Rayon's par_sort does under the hood, just with a work-stealing pool instead of raw thread::spawn per level.

// Concurrency & Async Exercise 71 · 75 min
W71 · Hand-Rolled Future + Waker — a Manual Timer
manual Future::poll Arc<Mutex<Option<Waker>>> std::task::Wake + thread::park/unpark no tokio — pure std executor Hard
Prompt
"Implement a Timer type that implements std::future::Future<Output = ()> manually (no async fn sugar for the timer itself) by spawning a background OS thread that sleeps for the requested Duration and then calls cx.waker().clone().wake(). Timer::poll must return Poll::Pending and store the waker (in an Arc<Mutex<Option<Waker>>> shared with the background thread) the first time it's polled before the duration elapses, and Poll::Ready(()) once the background thread has signaled completion. Then write a minimal hand-rolled single-threaded executor (no tokio) that drives one or more Timer futures to completion by repeatedly polling and parking the current thread (std::thread::park) between polls, woken by a Waker built from a custom Wake impl (via std::task::Wake + Arc::new(...).into()) that calls Thread::unpark on the executor's thread. This is the real Waker/Context/poll state machine underneath every async runtime — implement it directly."
Starter code to hand to candidate
struct SharedState { completed: bool, waker: Option<Waker> }
struct Timer { shared: Arc<Mutex<SharedState>>, poll_count: Arc<AtomicUsize> }

// TODO: impl Timer::new(duration, poll_count) — spawn a background thread that sleeps then
//       sets completed=true and wakes the stored Waker, if any
// TODO: impl Future for Timer — poll() must store cx.waker().clone() before returning Pending,
//       and return Ready(()) once the background thread has signaled completion
// TODO: struct ThreadWaker(std::thread::Thread) + impl std::task::Wake — wake() unparks it
// TODO: fn block_on<F: Future + Unpin>(future: F) -> F::Output — minimal executor: poll, then
//       thread::park() while Pending, looping until Ready

fn main() {
    // --- A single Timer resolves after roughly its requested duration ---
    let poll_count = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let single_start = Instant::now();
    block_on(Timer::new(Duration::from_millis(150), poll_count.clone()));
    let single_elapsed = single_start.elapsed();
    assert!(single_elapsed >= Duration::from_millis(140));  // didn't return instantly / wasn't a fake no-op
    assert!(single_elapsed < Duration::from_millis(800));   // didn't hang forever

    // --- poll() is genuinely called more than once: Pending was returned, not spun on ---
    assert!(poll_count.load(Ordering::SeqCst) >= 2);  // at least one Pending poll, then the final Ready poll

    // --- Two timers with different durations complete independently ---
    let short_polls = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let long_polls = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let join_start = Instant::now();
    block_on(JoinTimers {
        a: Some(Timer::new(Duration::from_millis(60), short_polls.clone())),
        b: Some(Timer::new(Duration::from_millis(220), long_polls.clone())),
    });
    let join_elapsed = join_start.elapsed();
    assert!(join_elapsed >= Duration::from_millis(210));  // join completes only once the LONGER timer also fires
    assert!(join_elapsed < Duration::from_millis(900));
    assert!(short_polls.load(Ordering::SeqCst) >= 2);  // short timer: Pending at least once, then Ready
    assert!(long_polls.load(Ordering::SeqCst) >= 2);   // long timer polled independently, of its own accord

    println!("single timer elapsed={:?} poll_count={} | join elapsed={:?} short_polls={} long_polls={}",
        single_elapsed, poll_count.load(Ordering::SeqCst), join_elapsed, short_polls.load(Ordering::SeqCst), long_polls.load(Ordering::SeqCst));
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::task::{Context, Poll, Wake, Waker};
use std::thread;
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

struct SharedState {
    completed: bool,
    waker: Option<Waker>,
}

struct Timer {
    shared: Arc<Mutex<SharedState>>,
    poll_count: Arc<AtomicUsize>,
}

impl Timer {
    fn new(duration: Duration, poll_count: Arc<AtomicUsize>) -> Self {
        let shared = Arc::new(Mutex::new(SharedState { completed: false, waker: None }));
        let bg_shared = shared.clone();
        thread::spawn(move || {
            thread::sleep(duration);
            let mut state = bg_shared.lock().unwrap();
            state.completed = true;
            if let Some(waker) = state.waker.take() {
                waker.wake();  // consumes the Waker and schedules the executor to re-poll us
            }
        });
        Timer { shared, poll_count }
    }
}

impl Future for Timer {
    type Output = ();
    fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<()> {
        self.poll_count.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
        let mut state = self.shared.lock().unwrap();
        if state.completed {
            Poll::Ready(())
        } else {
            state.waker = Some(cx.waker().clone());  // store the waker so the background thread can wake us later
            Poll::Pending
        }
    }
}

/// A join of two Timers — Ready only once BOTH children are Ready, but each child
/// is polled (and can independently return Ready) on every wake, regardless of the other.
struct JoinTimers { a: Option<Timer>, b: Option<Timer> }

impl Future for JoinTimers {
    type Output = ();
    fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<()> {
        let this = self.get_mut();  // JoinTimers is Unpin: both fields are plain Unpin Timers
        if let Some(timer) = this.a.as_mut() {
            if Pin::new(timer).poll(cx).is_ready() { this.a = None; }
        }
        if let Some(timer) = this.b.as_mut() {
            if Pin::new(timer).poll(cx).is_ready() { this.b = None; }
        }
        if this.a.is_none() && this.b.is_none() { Poll::Ready(()) } else { Poll::Pending }
    }
}

/// Wakes the executor's OS thread by unparking it — the bridge between the abstract
/// Waker/Context machinery and a concrete blocking single-threaded executor.
struct ThreadWaker(thread::Thread);

impl Wake for ThreadWaker {
    fn wake(self: Arc<Self>) { self.0.unpark(); }
    fn wake_by_ref(self: &Arc<Self>) { self.0.unpark(); }
}

/// A minimal single-threaded executor: poll, and if Pending, park until woken.
fn block_on<F: Future + Unpin>(mut future: F) -> F::Output {
    let waker: Waker = Arc::new(ThreadWaker(thread::current())).into();
    let mut cx = Context::from_waker(&waker);
    let mut future = Pin::new(&mut future);  // Timer/JoinTimers are Unpin — safe to pin on the stack directly
    loop {
        match future.as_mut().poll(&mut cx) {
            Poll::Ready(output) => return output,
            Poll::Pending => thread::park(),  // sleeps until ThreadWaker::wake() unparks us — no busy-polling
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    // --- A single Timer resolves after roughly its requested duration ---
    let poll_count = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let single_start = Instant::now();
    block_on(Timer::new(Duration::from_millis(150), poll_count.clone()));
    let single_elapsed = single_start.elapsed();
    assert!(single_elapsed >= Duration::from_millis(140));  // didn't return instantly / wasn't a fake no-op
    assert!(single_elapsed < Duration::from_millis(800));   // didn't hang forever

    // --- poll() is genuinely called more than once: Pending was returned, not spun on ---
    assert!(poll_count.load(Ordering::SeqCst) >= 2);  // at least one Pending poll, then the final Ready poll

    // --- Two timers with different durations complete independently ---
    let short_polls = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let long_polls = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let join_start = Instant::now();
    block_on(JoinTimers {
        a: Some(Timer::new(Duration::from_millis(60), short_polls.clone())),
        b: Some(Timer::new(Duration::from_millis(220), long_polls.clone())),
    });
    let join_elapsed = join_start.elapsed();
    assert!(join_elapsed >= Duration::from_millis(210));  // join completes only once the LONGER timer also fires
    assert!(join_elapsed < Duration::from_millis(900));
    assert!(short_polls.load(Ordering::SeqCst) >= 2);  // short timer: Pending at least once, then Ready
    assert!(long_polls.load(Ordering::SeqCst) >= 2);   // long timer polled independently, of its own accord

    println!("single timer elapsed={:?} poll_count={} | join elapsed={:?} short_polls={} long_polls={}",
        single_elapsed, poll_count.load(Ordering::SeqCst), join_elapsed, short_polls.load(Ordering::SeqCst), long_polls.load(Ordering::SeqCst));
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Stores cx.waker().clone() — not the Context itself and not a raw reference — a Context borrows for a specific poll call's lifetime and cannot outlive it, so the only thing safe to persist past `poll()` returning is an owned, cloned `Waker`. A candidate who tries to stash the `&mut Context` or `&Context` will hit a lifetime wall immediately and should recognize why.
  • ★★★Parks the executor thread instead of busy-spinning on `poll()` in a tight loop — the whole design of `Poll::Pending` + `Waker` exists so an executor can go fully idle (zero CPU) between a task becoming un-runnable and something making it runnable again; a `loop { poll(); }` with no `park()` defeats the entire point of the Waker mechanism even though it would still "work" and pass a loose test.
  • ★★★Correctly implements `JoinTimers` so BOTH children get polled on every wake, not just re-polling whichever timer's background thread happened to call `wake()` — a real executor has no way to know WHICH future woke it when multiple tasks share one `Waker`/thread, so the safe, standard approach (and what this exercise is really testing) is to re-poll everything not-yet-ready on every wake, exactly like a real join combinator or a real multi-task executor's run loop.
  • ★★Uses `std::task::Wake` (object-safe, `Arc`-based) rather than hand-rolling a `RawWaker`/`RawWakerVTable` — both are valid, but `Wake` was stabilized specifically to make this exact pattern (a `Send + Sync` wake target wrapped in `Arc`) far less error-prone than manually writing vtable function pointers and getting the clone/drop reference-counting exactly right by hand.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What's actually inside a `std::task::Waker`, mechanically, and why does `Context` even need to exist as a separate type from `Waker`?" — Under the hood a `Waker` wraps a `RawWaker`, which is just a type-erased data pointer plus a vtable of four function pointers (`clone`, `wake`, `wake_by_ref`, `drop`) — this is how `Future::poll` can be a plain, non-generic, dyn-compatible method signature without knowing anything about the concrete executor type. `Context` exists as a separate, deliberately extensible wrapper around `&Waker` specifically so future Rust versions can add MORE per-poll data to it (task-local values, etc.) without breaking every `Future` implementation's `poll` signature.
  • P2"This Timer spawns a brand-new OS thread per timer — real async runtimes obviously don't do that for potentially millions of timers. How do they actually implement efficient timers?" — Production executors (tokio, async-std) maintain a single centralized timer wheel or a sorted min-heap of deadlines, driven by ONE background thread (or integrated into the I/O reactor's poll/epoll/kqueue wait timeout) that wakes the relevant tasks' Wakers as deadlines expire — turning O(n) background threads into O(1), with O(log n) or better insert/expire cost per timer.
  • P3"Is there a race between the background thread checking `completed`/calling `wake()` and the polling thread checking `completed`/storing the waker? Walk through the interleaving." — No, and the reason is the shared `Mutex`: both the poll-side check-and-maybe-store-waker and the background-thread's set-completed-and-take-waker happen while holding the SAME mutex, so they're strictly ordered relative to each other. The only "racy-looking" interleaving that matters — background thread finishes and calls `wake()` on a waker BEFORE `poll()` has stored one — literally cannot manufacture a lost wakeup here because setting `completed = true` happens under the same lock `poll()` checks first; if `poll()` sees `completed == false` and stores a waker, the background thread hasn't taken the lock yet to finish, so it will see the freshly-stored waker when it does.
🎯 Senior angle
Most candidates who've only ever used async/await via tokio have never once had to think about what a Waker actually IS. This exercise forces that confrontation directly, and the JoinTimers combinator is the real tell for seniority: does the candidate understand that a shared executor thread has no idea which of N pending tasks woke it, and so the only correct design is "re-poll everything not-yet-done on every wake" — the exact same principle every real multi-task executor's run loop relies on?

// Concurrency & Async Exercise 72 · 75 min
W72 · Pin Deep-Dive — Why a Self-Referential Async State Machine Needs It
self-referential struct PhantomPinned / !Unpin Pin<Box<Self>> + get_unchecked_mut sound "what breaks" demo, no UB Hard
Prompt
"By hand — not via async fn — build a small self-referential state machine struct that mimics what the compiler generates for an async fn containing a let x = ...; foo(&x).await; pattern: a struct holding both an owned String field AND a raw pointer field that points into that same struct's own storage, plus a state: usize discriminant. Implement Future for it manually such that the self-reference is only valid/initialized on the SECOND poll onward. Demonstrate concretely, with actual code, why this type must be !Unpin and can only be soundly polled through Pin<&mut Self>/Pin<Box<Self>> — show what breaks (the pointer becomes stale) if the struct is moved after the self-reference is established, by writing a version that DOES move it via mem::swap, in a way that's safely observable (numeric address comparison only — never a dereference of dangling memory) — then show the fixed, Pin-based version that cannot be moved once pinned, using PhantomPinned and a safe poll() that only ever receives Pin<&mut Self>."
Starter code to hand to candidate
struct SelfRef {
    value: String,
    self_ptr: *const String,
    state: usize,
    _pin: PhantomPinned,
}

// TODO: impl Future for SelfRef — poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, ..) must, via
//       unsafe { self.get_unchecked_mut() }: on state 0, set self_ptr = &this.value and
//       return Pending; on state 1, dereference self_ptr and return Ready(clone)
// TODO: struct BrokenNotPinned (same shape, NO PhantomPinned) + a function that
//       mem::swaps it after the self-reference is set, then compares self_ptr's raw
//       numeric address against &moved.value's CURRENT address (no dereference!)

fn main() {
    // --- The CORRECT, Pin-based version polls to completion and produces the right output ---
    let waker: Waker = Arc::new(NoopWaker).into();
    let mut cx = Context::from_waker(&waker);

    let mut fut = Box::pin(SelfRef::new("pinned and sound"));  // Box::pin: the only safe way to pin a !Unpin value we want to keep around
    let mut polls = 0;
    let result = loop {
        polls += 1;
        match fut.as_mut().poll(&mut cx) {
            Poll::Ready(v) => break v,
            Poll::Pending => continue,
        }
    };
    assert_eq!(result, "pinned and sound");
    assert_eq!(polls, 2);  // state 0 (establish self-ref) -> Pending, state 1 (dereference it) -> Ready

    // --- Demonstrate SelfRef is !Unpin: proven by what compiles and what does not ---
    //
    // The following does NOT compile (verified with `rustc --edition 2021`, real error
    // reproduced below) — included here only as a comment, since this file must compile clean:
    //
    //     let mut instance = SelfRef::new("stack");
    //     let _p = Pin::new(&mut instance);
    //
    //     error[E0277]: `PhantomPinned` cannot be unpinned
    //        --> src.rs:23:23
    //         |
    //      23 |     let _p = Pin::new(&mut instance);
    //         |              -------- ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ within `SelfRef`, the trait `Unpin` is
    //         |                                       not implemented for `PhantomPinned`
    //         |              |
    //         |              required by a bound introduced by this call
    //         = note: consider using the `pin!` macro
    //                 consider using `Box::pin` if you need to access the pinned value
    //                 outside of the current scope
    //
    // `Pin::new` requires `Ptr::Target: Unpin` at COMPILE TIME (see `impl<Ptr: Deref<Target:
    // Unpin>> Pin<Ptr>` in core::pin) — there is no runtime check to bypass it. A !Unpin
    // type can ONLY be pinned via Box::pin (heap, used above) or the std::pin::pin! macro
    // (stack, but the resulting Pin<&mut T> can never be moved out of again).
    let _boxed_ok: Pin<Box<SelfRef>> = Box::pin(SelfRef::new("this compiles: heap + Box::pin"));
    drop(_boxed_ok);  // the positive half of the proof: Box::pin is the sanctioned way to pin a !Unpin value

    // --- Show, concretely, what breaks when the pattern is used WITHOUT Pin ---
    demonstrate_move_danger();
}

use std::future::Future;
use std::marker::PhantomPinned;
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::ptr;
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::task::{Context, Poll, Wake, Waker};

/// Mimics what rustc generates for `async fn f() { let x = String::from(..); foo(&x).await; }`:
/// the generator holds BOTH the owned String (`value`) AND a pointer that, from state 1
/// onward, points at the `value` FIELD'S OWN ADDRESS (i.e. `&value as *const String`) — the
/// same thing `&x` captures across the `.await` point. This is NOT a pointer into the
/// String's heap byte buffer (that heap allocation's address is stable across moves of the
/// 3-word String header) — it is a pointer to where the String STRUCT itself is stored,
/// which very much DOES move if the containing struct moves. That distinction is the entire
/// reason this needs Pin.
struct SelfRef {
    value: String,
    self_ptr: *const String,
    state: usize,
    _pin: PhantomPinned,  // opts SelfRef out of Unpin — see main() for what this buys us
}

impl SelfRef {
    fn new(text: &str) -> Self {
        SelfRef { value: text.to_string(), self_ptr: ptr::null(), state: 0, _pin: PhantomPinned }
    }
}

impl Future for SelfRef {
    type Output = String;
    fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, _cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<String> {
        // SAFETY: sound because we never move `*this` out (only mutate fields in place) —
        // `self` being Pin<&mut Self> is our caller-enforced guarantee it will never move again.
        let this = unsafe { self.get_unchecked_mut() };
        match this.state {
            0 => {
                this.self_ptr = &this.value as *const String;  // establish the self-reference — sound ONLY because `this` is pinned
                this.state = 1;
                Poll::Pending
            }
            1 => {
                // Sound ONLY because Pin guaranteed `value` has not moved since `self_ptr` was set.
                let s: &String = unsafe { &*this.self_ptr };
                this.state = 2;
                Poll::Ready(s.clone())
            }
            _ => panic!("polled after completion"),
        }
    }
}

/// The unpinned, unsafe twin of SelfRef — used ONLY to demonstrate what breaks. It has no
/// PhantomPinned, so nothing stops it from being moved after the self-reference exists.
struct BrokenNotPinned { value: String, self_ptr: *const String }

/// Moves a BrokenNotPinned AFTER its self-reference is established, then shows the pointer
/// is stale using ONLY a numeric address comparison — never a dereference of dangling memory.
fn demonstrate_move_danger() {
    let mut it = BrokenNotPinned { value: "hello".to_string(), self_ptr: ptr::null() };
    it.self_ptr = &it.value as *const String;  // self-reference established while `it` sits at its current address
    assert_eq!(it.self_ptr as usize, &it.value as *const String as usize);

    let mut swapped = BrokenNotPinned { value: String::new(), self_ptr: ptr::null() };
    std::mem::swap(&mut it, &mut swapped);  // moves BrokenNotPinned's bytes — nothing prevents this, unlike the Pin version
    let moved = swapped;  // `moved` now holds the ORIGINAL data, but at `swapped`'s old address

    // `moved.self_ptr` still holds the OLD address of `it.value` — but that address has since
    // been overwritten (by the swap) with the empty String that used to live in `swapped`. We
    // compare only raw ADDRESSES (never `unsafe { &*moved.self_ptr }`) — no UB anywhere here.
    let true_address_now = &moved.value as *const String as usize;
    assert_ne!(moved.self_ptr as usize, true_address_now);  // self-reference points at the WRONG place after the move
    println!("stale self_ptr = {:#x}, value's real (post-move) address = {:#x}", moved.self_ptr as usize, true_address_now);
}

struct NoopWaker;
impl Wake for NoopWaker {
    fn wake(self: Arc<Self>) {}
}

fn main() {
    // --- The CORRECT, Pin-based version polls to completion and produces the right output ---
    let waker: Waker = Arc::new(NoopWaker).into();
    let mut cx = Context::from_waker(&waker);

    let mut fut = Box::pin(SelfRef::new("pinned and sound"));  // Box::pin: the only safe way to pin a !Unpin value we want to keep around
    let mut polls = 0;
    let result = loop {
        polls += 1;
        match fut.as_mut().poll(&mut cx) {
            Poll::Ready(v) => break v,
            Poll::Pending => continue,
        }
    };
    assert_eq!(result, "pinned and sound");
    assert_eq!(polls, 2);  // state 0 (establish self-ref) -> Pending, state 1 (dereference it) -> Ready

    // --- Demonstrate SelfRef is !Unpin: proven by what compiles and what does not ---
    //
    // The following does NOT compile (verified with `rustc --edition 2021`, real error
    // reproduced below) — included here only as a comment, since this file must compile clean:
    //
    //     let mut instance = SelfRef::new("stack");
    //     let _p = Pin::new(&mut instance);
    //
    //     error[E0277]: `PhantomPinned` cannot be unpinned
    //        --> src.rs:23:23
    //         |
    //      23 |     let _p = Pin::new(&mut instance);
    //         |              -------- ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ within `SelfRef`, the trait `Unpin` is
    //         |                                       not implemented for `PhantomPinned`
    //         |              |
    //         |              required by a bound introduced by this call
    //         = note: consider using the `pin!` macro
    //                 consider using `Box::pin` if you need to access the pinned value
    //                 outside of the current scope
    //
    // `Pin::new` requires `Ptr::Target: Unpin` at COMPILE TIME (see `impl<Ptr: Deref<Target:
    // Unpin>> Pin<Ptr>` in core::pin) — there is no runtime check to bypass it. A !Unpin
    // type can ONLY be pinned via Box::pin (heap, used above) or the std::pin::pin! macro
    // (stack, but the resulting Pin<&mut T> can never be moved out of again).
    let _boxed_ok: Pin<Box<SelfRef>> = Box::pin(SelfRef::new("this compiles: heap + Box::pin"));
    drop(_boxed_ok);  // the positive half of the proof: Box::pin is the sanctioned way to pin a !Unpin value

    // --- Show, concretely, what breaks when the pattern is used WITHOUT Pin ---
    demonstrate_move_danger();
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Knows the self-reference points at the String` field's own storage address, not at its heap byte buffer — this is a genuinely common misconception even among candidates who use Pin daily: a `String`'s heap allocation address IS stable across moves of the owning struct (only the 3-word ptr/len/cap header moves), so a pointer into the heap bytes would NOT actually break here. What breaks is a pointer to the FIELD itself (`&self.value`), because that address changes when the containing struct's memory moves. A candidate who can articulate this distinction unprompted has genuine, not memorized, understanding.
  • ★★★Never dereferences the stale pointer to "prove" it's dangling — comparing `moved.self_ptr as usize` against the field's current address is perfectly sound (raw pointers are just integers for comparison purposes); actually writing `unsafe { &*moved.self_ptr }` on the swapped-out struct would be real, live undefined behavior, and a candidate reaching for that "to make the demo more convincing" is a serious red flag about their `unsafe` instincts.
  • ★★★Only ever calls `poll` on a `Pin<&mut Self>`/`Pin<Box<Self>>`, and specifically uses `Box::pin` (not `Pin::new`) for the `!Unpin` type — reaching for `Pin::new(&mut on_the_stack)` and being surprised it doesn't compile, then correctly diagnosing why via the `Unpin` bound rather than just adding `#[allow]` attributes to force it through, is exactly the diagnostic instinct this exercise is designed to surface.
  • ★★Writes a genuine safety comment justifying `get_unchecked_mut()` — specifically that the code never moves `*this` out of the pinned location, only mutates fields through the reference — rather than treating `unsafe` as a magic keyword that silences the compiler. This is the exact discipline real `Pin`-based code in the ecosystem (e.g. `pin-project`) automates precisely because humans get it wrong by hand.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Most Rust code that handles futures never writes `unsafe`, `get_unchecked_mut`, or `PhantomPinned` at all — why not, if this self-referential machinery is what's really going on underneath every `async fn`?" — Because the compiler generates the self-referential state machine's `poll` implementation FOR you when you write `async fn`/`async {}` blocks, and it does so correctly by construction (it knows exactly which locals are borrowed across which `.await` points and only self-references those) — ordinary users only ever touch the SAFE surface (`Future::poll` taking `Pin<&mut Self>`, `.await`, combinators like `join!`). Manually implementing a self-referential `Future` by hand, as this exercise does, is something you'd only do writing a runtime primitive or an FFI/embedded async shim — which is exactly why it's a strong interview signal rather than everyday code.
  • P2"Could you have avoided all of this `unsafe`/`Pin` machinery by just storing an `Option<usize>` OFFSET into `value` instead of a raw pointer, and computing the actual address only when needed?" — Yes, and this is precisely the standard, idiomatic, safe-Rust workaround for self-referential structs in practice: store an index/offset/range instead of a pointer/reference, and re-derive the actual reference from `&self.value` + the offset at the point of use. It sacrifices nothing for this use case and needs zero `unsafe`, `Pin`, or `PhantomPinned` — which is exactly why experienced Rust engineers avoid genuinely self-referential structs whenever an index-based alternative exists, reserving true self-reference for cases (like compiler-generated async state machines, or crates like `ouroboros`/`pin-project`) where there's no practical alternative.
  • P3"If `SelfRef` did NOT have `PhantomPinned` and did NOT opt out of `Unpin`, but you still wrote the same unsafe self-referential poll logic — would it compile, and would it be sound?" — It would compile (since every type is `Unpin` by default unless it contains a `!Unpin` field/marker or explicitly opts out), but it would NOT be sound: an `Unpin` type can be freely moved even from behind a `Pin`, via `Pin::get_mut()` + `mem::swap`, or trivially just never being pinned in the first place (`Pin::new` works on any `Unpin` type without ever proving immovability) — exactly the `BrokenNotPinned` scenario in this exercise, but now hiding behind a false promise of `Pin`-safety. `PhantomPinned` is not decorative; it's the ONLY thing making the compiler actually refuse to let this type be moved once pinned.
🎯 Senior angle
The single most telling moment in this exercise is whether a candidate can correctly explain WHY the self-reference points at the String field's own address rather than its heap bytes — most engineers who've merely read about Pin get this backwards, assuming (incorrectly) that moving a String around invalidates pointers into its heap data. Catching and correcting that exact misconception, unprompted, is a far stronger signal of real understanding than reciting "Pin prevents moves."

    //      23 |     let _p = Pin::new(&mut instance);
    //         |              -------- ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ within `SelfRef`, the trait `Unpin` is
    //         |                                       not implemented for `PhantomPinned`
    //         |              |
    //         |              required by a bound introduced by this call
    //         = note: consider using the `pin!` macro
    //                 consider using `Box::pin` if you need to access the pinned value
    //                 outside of the current scope
    //
    // `Pin::new` requires `Ptr::Target: Unpin` at COMPILE TIME (see `impl<Ptr: Deref<Target:
    // Unpin>> Pin<Ptr>` in core::pin) — there is no runtime check to bypass it. A !Unpin
    // type can ONLY be pinned via Box::pin (heap, used above) or the std::pin::pin! macro
    // (stack, but the resulting Pin<&mut T> can never be moved out of again).
    let _boxed_ok: Pin<Box<SelfRef>> = Box::pin(SelfRef::new("this compiles: heap + Box::pin"));
    drop(_boxed_ok);  // the positive half of the proof: Box::pin is the sanctioned way to pin a !Unpin value

    // --- Show, concretely, what breaks when the pattern is used WITHOUT Pin ---
    demonstrate_move_danger();
}
