Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

// Manually desugared "async trait method" — exactly what `async-trait` (and pre-2023
// stable Rust, before native async fn in traits) expands `async fn fetch(&self) -> String`
// into. The trait itself contains NO `async fn`; it's a plain method returning a boxed,
// pinned, Send future. This is the ONLY form that is object-safe.
trait AsyncFetcher: Send + Sync {
    fn fetch(&self) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = String> + Send + '_>>;
}

struct SlowFetcher { label: String, delay: Duration }

impl AsyncFetcher for SlowFetcher {
    fn fetch(&self) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = String> + Send + '_>> {
        // The method BODY is free to use ordinary `async {}` block syntax — it just gets
        // boxed and pinned before being handed back across the object-safe boundary.
        Box::pin(async move {
            tokio::time::sleep(self.delay).await;
            format!("slow:{}", self.label)
        })
    }
}

struct InstantFetcher { label: String }

impl AsyncFetcher for InstantFetcher {
    fn fetch(&self) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = String> + Send + '_>> {
        Box::pin(async move { format!("instant:{}", self.label) })
    }
}

// The entire reason this desugaring exists: taking `&dyn AsyncFetcher` as a genuine trait
// object. Native `async fn` in traits still cannot do this on stable Rust — the returned
// `impl Future` type is unnameable/unsized per-impl, so the trait as a whole isn't object
// safe unless you box the future by hand, which is exactly what we did above.
async fn fetch_via_object(fetcher: &dyn AsyncFetcher) -> String {
    fetcher.fetch().await
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let slow = SlowFetcher { label: "db".to_string(), delay: Duration::from_millis(60) };
    let instant = InstantFetcher { label: "cache".to_string() };

    let out = fetch_via_object(&slow).await;
    assert_eq!(out, "slow:db");
    let out = fetch_via_object(&instant).await;
    assert_eq!(out, "instant:cache");

    // A Vec> of heterogeneous implementors, iterated and awaited —
    // the payoff of object safety: one collection, many concrete future-producing types.
    let fetchers: Vec<Box<dyn AsyncFetcher>> = vec![
        Box::new(SlowFetcher { label: "a".to_string(), delay: Duration::from_millis(30) }),
        Box::new(InstantFetcher { label: "b".to_string() }),
        Box::new(SlowFetcher { label: "c".to_string(), delay: Duration::from_millis(30) }),
    ];

    let mut results = Vec::new();
    for f in &fetchers {
        results.push(f.fetch().await);
    }
    assert_eq!(results, vec!["slow:a", "instant:b", "slow:c"]);

    // Timing-sensitive proof: the sleep-based impl must measurably outlast the instant
    // one, confirming the boxed future actually runs a real await and isn't eager.
    let start = Instant::now();
    let _ = fetch_via_object(&instant).await;
    let instant_elapsed = start.elapsed();

    let start = Instant::now();
    let _ = fetch_via_object(&slow).await;
    let slow_elapsed = start.elapsed();

    assert!(
        slow_elapsed > instant_elapsed + Duration::from_millis(20),
        "expected slow fetcher ({:?}) to measurably outlast instant fetcher ({:?})",
        slow_elapsed, instant_elapsed
    );
    assert!(slow_elapsed >= Duration::from_millis(55));

    println!("W73 ok: instant={:?} slow={:?}", instant_elapsed, slow_elapsed);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Returns Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = String> + Send + '_>> from the trait method rather than trying to write async fn fetch(&self) directly in the trait — recognizing native async-fn-in-traits still isn't object-safe on stable Rust.
  • ★★★Actually calls the method through &dyn AsyncFetcher and it compiles and awaits correctly — proving they understand this pattern's entire reason for existing, not just reciting the boxed-future syntax.
  • ★★Boxes/pins an ordinary async move {} block inline inside each impl's method body rather than hand-writing a manual poll state machine — recognizing the boxed-async-block is the correct, pragmatic implementation technique here.
  • ★Adds a + Send bound to the returned future type so it can safely cross into tokio::spawn or other multi-threaded contexts later.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Native async fn in traits is stable now — why can't it just replace this pattern entirely?" — Each impl of an async fn trait method produces a DIFFERENT, anonymous, unnameable future type (like impl Trait) — the trait's vtable would need a single fixed size/type for that return value at the call site, which is fundamentally incompatible with dynamic dispatch. Erasing to Box<dyn Future>, as this exercise does, is still required whenever you need `dyn Trait` object safety.
  • P2"This boxes a brand-new future on every single call to fetch() — what's the actual runtime cost, and is there a way to avoid it?" — Every call heap-allocates the boxed future (the same cost the async-trait macro pays). If you don't actually need dynamic dispatch — e.g. you always know the concrete type at each call site — generic static dispatch (monomorphized per type, no boxing) avoids the allocation entirely, at the cost of losing the ability to store heterogeneous implementors in one collection.
  • P3"What if two different implementors capture wildly different amounts of state in their futures — does this design handle that?" — Yes, that's the entire point of boxing: erasing to a common Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output=...>>> trait object regardless of the underlying concrete future's size or captured-state layout, at the cost of one heap allocation and one virtual dispatch per call.
🎯 Senior angle
Ask the candidate to explain, unprompted, why async fn being legal inside a trait definition on modern stable Rust does NOT automatically grant that trait dyn Trait support. The gap between "I can write the syntax" and "I understand the vtable/sizedness constraint that makes it non-object-safe" is exactly what this exercise is built to surface — and it's precisely the gap that leads engineers to reach for the async-trait crate (or this hand-written equivalent) in real codebases.

// Concurrency & Async Exercise 74 · 60 min
W74 · Tokio Structured Concurrency — select! with Cancellation & Cleanup
tokio::select! cancellation safety Drop-on-cancel RAII Hard
Prompt
"Race a 'real work' async task against a cancellation signal using tokio::select!. The work task holds a resource (an Arc<AtomicUsize> active-count incremented at start) that must be decremented even if the work future is cancelled mid-flight — select! drops the losing branch's future outright, it does not resume it to run 'the rest of the function'. Prove the correct pattern is a Drop-based RAII guard by ALSO writing the broken version (increment, await, decrement as plain sequential code) and demonstrating it leaks state on cancellation."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::sync::oneshot;

// TODO: struct ActiveGuard — increments a shared AtomicUsize on construction, decrements
// it on Drop, regardless of how the enclosing future stops running.

// TODO: async fn safe_work(counter, work_ms) -> &'static str — uses the guard, so a
// select! cancellation mid-flight still cleans up correctly.

// TODO: async fn broken_work(counter, work_ms) -> &'static str — the WRONG pattern:
// increments, awaits, then decrements as plain sequential code (no guard).

// TODO: race_safe / race_broken — each races its work fn against a oneshot cancel signal
// via tokio::select!

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // TODO: test the normal path, a cancelled-mid-flight safe path, and the broken path
}

fn main() {
    let counter = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));

    // 1. Normal path: work finishes before any cancel signal arrives, count returns to zero.
    let (tx, rx) = oneshot::channel::<()>();
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(500)).await;
        let _ = tx.send(());
    });
    let outcome = race_safe(counter.clone(), rx).await;
    assert_eq!(outcome, Some("done"));
    assert_eq!(counter.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 0);

    // 2. Cancelled mid-flight, SAFE version — the Drop guard must still fire.
    let (tx, rx) = oneshot::channel::<()>();
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(20)).await;
        let _ = tx.send(());
    });
    let outcome = race_safe(counter.clone(), rx).await;
    assert_eq!(outcome, None, "cancellation should have won the race");
    assert_eq!(
        counter.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 0,
        "Drop guard must return active-count to zero even when cancelled mid-flight"
    );

    // 3. The CONTRASTING broken version: same race, same timing, but relies on sequential
    // cleanup code AFTER the .await — select! drops the losing future instead of resuming
    // it, so that cleanup line never executes, and the counter is left non-zero.
    let (tx, rx) = oneshot::channel::<()>();
    tokio::spawn(async move {

    });
    let outcome = race_broken(counter.clone(), rx).await;
    assert_eq!(outcome, None, "cancellation should have won the race");
    assert_eq!(
        counter.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 1,
        "broken pattern (cleanup after .await) leaks the increment when cancelled — this is the whole point of the exercise"
    );

    counter.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
    assert_eq!(counter.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 0);

Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::sync::oneshot;

// RAII guard: increments on construction, decrements on Drop — regardless of HOW the
// enclosing future stops running (normal completion, or `select!` dropping the losing
// branch mid-poll). This Drop-on-cancel behavior is the entire mechanism async
// cancellation safety relies on in Rust.
struct ActiveGuard {
    counter: Arc<AtomicUsize>,
}

impl ActiveGuard {
    fn new(counter: Arc<AtomicUsize>) -> Self {
        counter.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
        Self { counter }
    }
}

impl Drop for ActiveGuard {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        self.counter.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
    }
}

// The CORRECT, cancellation-safe pattern: the guard's Drop is the only thing that ever
// decrements the count, so it fires no matter where in this function `select!` cuts us off.
async fn safe_work(counter: Arc<AtomicUsize>, work_ms: u64) -> &'static str {
    let _guard = ActiveGuard::new(counter);
    tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(work_ms)).await;
    "done"
    // `_guard` drops here on normal completion, or the instant `select!` drops this
    // future early if the cancellation branch wins — same code path either way.
}

// The BROKEN, non-cancellation-safe pattern: "increment, await, decrement" written as
// plain sequential code. If `select!` drops this future while it's suspended at the
// `.await`, the decrement on the next line NEVER RUNS, because dropping a future simply
// discards it — it does not resume execution to run "the rest of the function".
async fn broken_work(counter: Arc<AtomicUsize>, work_ms: u64) -> &'static str {
    counter.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
    tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(work_ms)).await;
    // If we get cancelled at the `.await` above, execution NEVER reaches here.
    counter.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
    "done"
}

async fn race_safe(counter: Arc<AtomicUsize>, cancel: oneshot::Receiver<()>) -> Option<&'static str> {
    tokio::select! {
        result = safe_work(counter, 200) => Some(result),
        _ = cancel => None,
    }
}

async fn race_broken(counter: Arc<AtomicUsize>, cancel: oneshot::Receiver<()>) -> Option<&'static str> {
    tokio::select! {
        result = broken_work(counter, 200) => Some(result),
        _ = cancel => None,
    }
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let counter = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));

    // 1. Normal path: work finishes before any cancel signal arrives, count returns to zero.
    let (tx, rx) = oneshot::channel::<()>();
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(500)).await;
        let _ = tx.send(());
    });
    let outcome = race_safe(counter.clone(), rx).await;
    assert_eq!(outcome, Some("done"));
    assert_eq!(counter.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 0);

    // 2. Cancelled mid-flight, SAFE version — the Drop guard must still fire.
    let (tx, rx) = oneshot::channel::<()>();
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(20)).await;
        let _ = tx.send(());
    });
    let outcome = race_safe(counter.clone(), rx).await;
    assert_eq!(outcome, None, "cancellation should have won the race");
    assert_eq!(
        counter.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 0,
        "Drop guard must return active-count to zero even when cancelled mid-flight"
    );

    // 3. The CONTRASTING broken version: same race, same timing, but relies on sequential
    // cleanup code AFTER the .await — select! drops the losing future instead of resuming
    // it, so that cleanup line never executes, and the counter is left non-zero.
    let (tx, rx) = oneshot::channel::<()>();
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(20)).await;
        let _ = tx.send(());
    });
    let outcome = race_broken(counter.clone(), rx).await;
    assert_eq!(outcome, None, "cancellation should have won the race");
    assert_eq!(
        counter.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 1,
        "broken pattern (cleanup after .await) leaks the increment when cancelled — this is the whole point of the exercise"
    );

    counter.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
    assert_eq!(counter.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 0);

    println!("W74 ok: safe-cancel restored count to 0; broken-cancel leaked to 1 as expected");
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Uses a Drop impl (RAII guard) to decrement the shared counter, not sequential cleanup code placed after the .await — recognizing that select! drops the LOSING branch's future outright rather than resuming it to run "the rest of the function".
  • ★★★Deliberately writes AND tests a broken/contrasting version to prove understanding of WHY the Drop-guard pattern is required, not just applying it by rote.
  • ★★Correctly reasons that tokio::select! polls every branch and drops all but the winner — understanding this drop-based cancellation semantics rather than assuming some cooperative "check a cancel token" model exists implicitly.
  • ★Picks tokio::sync::oneshot as the natural primitive for a single-value, single-consumer cancellation signal, rather than reaching for a heavier general-purpose channel.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What if the guarded resource ALSO needs an async cleanup step, like notifying another task — can Drop still do that?" — No: Drop is synchronous only and cannot .await anything. Real systems handle this by having Drop enqueue a cleanup request onto a channel or spawn a detached cleanup task, since Drop itself can never perform async I/O directly.
  • P2"Is every tokio operation cancellation-safe just because it's inside select!, the way sleep and oneshot::recv are here?" — No. A future is cancellation-safe only if being dropped mid-poll never leaves EXTERNAL state (not just its own fields) in a bad state. Tokio's docs explicitly call out which operations ARE cancellation-safe versus which are NOT (e.g. some AsyncWriteExt methods where a partial write could be silently lost) — always check per-API, never assume.
  • P3"This example uses one Drop guard for one simple counter — what makes cancellation safety genuinely hard in a real system?" — Multi-step operations spanning multiple resources/awaits, where a cancellation landing between step 1 and step 2 leaves things in a half-done, hard-to-reason-about state (e.g. a distributed write committed on node A but not yet B). Drop-based cleanup trivially fixes single, local, synchronously-undoable resources; cross-await multi-resource invariants need far more deliberate design (idempotent retries, explicit compensating actions).
🎯 Senior angle
Show the candidate ONLY the broken version and ask them to name the bug precisely. A senior engineer should immediately identify it as select!'s drop-based cancellation model discarding the future mid-flight — not gesture vaguely at "a race condition" or "async is tricky." The ability to name the EXACT mechanism (future dropped, not resumed) versus a fuzzy intuition is exactly the signal this exercise targets.

// Concurrency & Async Exercise 75 · 60 min
W75 · Tokio mpsc Pipeline — Backpressure & Graceful Shutdown
bounded mpsc backpressure cascading graceful shutdown Medium
Prompt
"Build a multi-stage pipeline (producer → stage1 → stage2 → sink, each its own spawned task) using bounded tokio::sync::mpsc channels, so a slow downstream consumer naturally applies backpressure to upstream producers — instrument how many times the producer actually had to wait on a full channel. Then implement graceful shutdown: when the producer finishes, each stage must fully drain its inbound channel before closing its own outbound sender, cascading the shutdown downstream one stage at a time — not an abrupt task-abort."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::sync::mpsc;

const CHANNEL_CAP: usize = 4;

// TODO: async fn stage_double(inbound, outbound) — doubles each value, forwards
// downstream, and must let dropping its inbound sender cascade into closing outbound.

// TODO: async fn stage_sink(inbound, results) — slow terminal consumer

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // TODO: wire producer -> stage1 -> stage2 -> sink via bounded mpsc channels,
    // instrument backpressure, and confirm a clean cascading shutdown
}

fn main() {
    let (producer_tx, stage1_rx) = mpsc::channel::<u32>(CHANNEL_CAP);
    let (stage1_tx, stage2_rx) = mpsc::channel::<u32>(CHANNEL_CAP);
    let (stage2_tx, sink_rx) = mpsc::channel::<u32>(CHANNEL_CAP);

    let results = Arc::new(tokio::sync::Mutex::new(Vec::new()));

    let stage1_handle = tokio::spawn(stage_double(stage1_rx, stage1_tx));
    let stage2_handle = tokio::spawn(stage_double(stage2_rx, stage2_tx));
    let sink_handle = tokio::spawn(stage_sink(sink_rx, results.clone()));

    const N: u32 = 20;
    let waited_count = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let waited_count_for_producer = waited_count.clone();

    let producer_handle = tokio::spawn(async move {
        for i in 0..N {
            // Instrument backpressure directly: try_send tells us immediately whether the
            // bounded channel is full, WITHOUT itself blocking — falling back to the real
            // (awaiting) send counts as one genuine "had to wait" occurrence.
            match producer_tx.try_send(i) {
                Ok(()) => {}
                Err(mpsc::error::TrySendError::Full(v)) => {
                    waited_count_for_producer.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
                    producer_tx.send(v).await.expect("stage1 still alive");
                }
                Err(mpsc::error::TrySendError::Closed(_)) => unreachable!("receiver outlives producer"),
            }
        }
        // Dropping `producer_tx` here closes the very first channel, which starts the
        // whole cascading shutdown: stage1 drains, drops ITS sender, stage2 drains, drops
        // ITS sender, sink drains and returns.
    });

    // Every spawned task is actually joined (not aborted) — proves the cascade genuinely
    // completed rather than the process just exiting with tasks still technically alive.
    producer_handle.await.expect("producer task panicked");
    stage1_handle.await.expect("stage1 task panicked");
    stage2_handle.await.expect("stage2 task panicked");
    sink_handle.await.expect("sink task panicked");

    let final_results = results.lock().await.clone();
    let expected: Vec<u32> = (0..N).map(|i| i * 4).collect();
    assert_eq!(final_results, expected);

    assert!(
        waited_count.load(Ordering::SeqCst) > 0,
        "expected the producer to have to wait on a full channel at least once"
    );

    println!(
        "W75 ok: {} items delivered in order; producer waited on backpressure {} times",
        final_results.len(), waited_count.load(Ordering::SeqCst)
    );
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::sync::mpsc;

const CHANNEL_CAP: usize = 4;

// Stage that doubles each value, forwarding downstream until its inbound channel closes.
async fn stage_double(
    mut inbound: mpsc::Receiver<u32>,
    outbound: mpsc::Sender<u32>,
) {
    // `recv()` returns `None` once every sender for `inbound` has been dropped AND the
    // channel is drained — so this loop naturally finishes draining whatever was already
    // buffered before falling through.
    while let Some(v) = inbound.recv().await {
        outbound.send(v * 2).await.expect("sink stage still alive");
    }
    // `outbound` drops here, closing this stage's send half and signaling the NEXT stage
    // to shut down in turn once ITS buffer drains — a clean cascade, not an abrupt abort.
}

// Slow terminal sink: deliberately throttled so the bounded channel upstream fills up and
// applies real backpressure on the producer.
async fn stage_sink(mut inbound: mpsc::Receiver<u32>, results: Arc<tokio::sync::Mutex<Vec<u32>>>) {
    while let Some(v) = inbound.recv().await {
        tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(5)).await;
        results.lock().await.push(v);
    }
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let (producer_tx, stage1_rx) = mpsc::channel::<u32>(CHANNEL_CAP);
    let (stage1_tx, stage2_rx) = mpsc::channel::<u32>(CHANNEL_CAP);
    let (stage2_tx, sink_rx) = mpsc::channel::<u32>(CHANNEL_CAP);

    let results = Arc::new(tokio::sync::Mutex::new(Vec::new()));

    let stage1_handle = tokio::spawn(stage_double(stage1_rx, stage1_tx));
    let stage2_handle = tokio::spawn(stage_double(stage2_rx, stage2_tx));
    let sink_handle = tokio::spawn(stage_sink(sink_rx, results.clone()));

    const N: u32 = 20;
    let waited_count = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let waited_count_for_producer = waited_count.clone();

    let producer_handle = tokio::spawn(async move {
        for i in 0..N {
            // Instrument backpressure directly: try_send tells us immediately whether the
            // bounded channel is full, WITHOUT itself blocking — falling back to the real
            // (awaiting) send counts as one genuine "had to wait" occurrence.
            match producer_tx.try_send(i) {
                Ok(()) => {}
                Err(mpsc::error::TrySendError::Full(v)) => {
                    waited_count_for_producer.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
                    producer_tx.send(v).await.expect("stage1 still alive");
                }
                Err(mpsc::error::TrySendError::Closed(_)) => unreachable!("receiver outlives producer"),
            }
        }
        // Dropping `producer_tx` here closes the very first channel, which starts the
        // whole cascading shutdown: stage1 drains, drops ITS sender, stage2 drains, drops
        // ITS sender, sink drains and returns.
    });

    // Every spawned task is actually joined (not aborted) — proves the cascade genuinely
    // completed rather than the process just exiting with tasks still technically alive.
    producer_handle.await.expect("producer task panicked");
    stage1_handle.await.expect("stage1 task panicked");
    stage2_handle.await.expect("stage2 task panicked");
    sink_handle.await.expect("sink task panicked");

    let final_results = results.lock().await.clone();
    let expected: Vec<u32> = (0..N).map(|i| i * 4).collect();
    assert_eq!(final_results, expected);

    assert!(
        waited_count.load(Ordering::SeqCst) > 0,
        "expected the producer to have to wait on a full channel at least once"
    );

    println!(
        "W75 ok: {} items delivered in order; producer waited on backpressure {} times",
        final_results.len(), waited_count.load(Ordering::SeqCst)
    );
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Uses BOUNDED mpsc channels (not unbounded) as the deliberate mechanism producing backpressure — recognizing an unbounded channel would let the producer race arbitrarily far ahead of a slow consumer, growing memory without limit.
  • ★★★Implements shutdown purely via channel-closing (dropping senders) cascading stage-to-stage, rather than threading an explicit "stop" flag through every stage — recognizing that closing the last sender of a channel IS the shutdown signal.
  • ★★Drains fully before closing its own outbound sender — a stage that exited early on some other signal without fully draining would silently drop buffered, already-in-flight data.
  • ★Instruments backpressure concretely (e.g. via try_send + a counter) rather than assuming it happened because the test "worked" — turning an invisible runtime property into a directly-assertable fact.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What happens to already-buffered items if a stage was killed via JoinHandle::abort() instead of allowed to drain naturally?" — Buffered items can be permanently stranded (never delivered downstream), and any of the stage's own cleanup/Drop logic mid-poll gets skipped. The cascading-close-then-drain approach used here guarantees no data loss, whereas abort() is fundamentally a "stop wherever you happen to be" operation.
  • P2"Could a stage blocked on send().await while waiting for downstream backpressure ever deadlock this pipeline?" — Not here, because it's a strictly linear pipeline (no cycles) — a stage blocked sending downstream simply stops pulling more from upstream, propagating backpressure further upstream in turn. A CYCLE in the pipeline graph, by contrast, genuinely could deadlock if every stage were simultaneously blocked sending into a full channel only the next stage in the cycle could drain.
  • P3"How would you bound MEMORY, not just item count, if items were large or arrived in unpredictable bursts?" — A bounded channel capacity only bounds the COUNT of in-flight items per hop. True memory bounding for variable-sized items typically needs a byte-budget-aware channel (a semaphore permitting N bytes, not N items) or explicit chunking/streaming of large items — worth naming as a real limitation of simple bounded-mpsc backpressure.
🎯 Senior angle
The strongest signal is whether a candidate reaches for bounded channels and channel-closure-driven shutdown as the DEFAULT design, unprompted. Many candidates default to unbounded channels "to be safe" plus an explicit shutdown flag or broadcast signal — both work, but reveal they haven't internalized that Rust's channel-closing semantics already give graceful shutdown almost for free.

// Concurrency & Async Exercise 76 · 45 min
W76 · Async Mutex vs std Mutex — the Cross-Await Send Trap
Send auto-trait guard held across .await tokio::sync::Mutex Medium
Prompt
"Write two versions of an async function that increments a shared counter with an .await in between checking and acting on it, guarded by a lock. Version A uses std::sync::Mutex structured so its guard is never held across the .await (re-acquiring the lock afterward instead). Version B uses tokio::sync::Mutex and safely holds its guard across the .await. Both must work correctly when spawned across many concurrent tokio::spawn tasks. Explain precisely why holding a std::sync::MutexGuard across an await point breaks a future's Send-ness — not merely that it's 'slow.'"
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex as StdMutex};
use tokio::sync::Mutex as TokioMutex;
use tokio::time::Duration;

// TODO: async fn increment_std_mutex(counter: &StdMutex) — must NOT hold the
// std::sync::MutexGuard across an .await point (re-acquire the lock after instead)

// TODO: async fn increment_tokio_mutex(counter: &TokioMutex) — CAN safely hold
// its guard across an .await

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // TODO: spawn many concurrent tasks calling each version, confirm no lost updates,
    // and confirm real concurrency actually occurred
}

fn main() {
    const TASKS: usize = 50;

    let std_counter = Arc::new(StdMutex::new(0u64));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..TASKS {
        let c = std_counter.clone();
        handles.push(tokio::spawn(async move { increment_std_mutex(&c).await; }));
    }
    for h in handles { h.await.expect("task panicked"); }
    assert_eq!(*std_counter.lock().unwrap(), TASKS as u64);

    let tokio_counter = Arc::new(TokioMutex::new(0u64));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..TASKS {
        let c = tokio_counter.clone();
        handles.push(tokio::spawn(async move { increment_tokio_mutex(&c).await; }));
    }
    for h in handles { h.await.expect("task panicked"); }
    assert_eq!(*tokio_counter.lock().await, TASKS as u64);

    // Sanity: prove real concurrency actually happened (tasks interleaved), so the above
    // passing isn't an accident of everything secretly running sequentially.
    let overlap_flag = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..8 {
        let flag = overlap_flag.clone();
        handles.push(tokio::spawn(async move {
            flag.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
            tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(5)).await;
        }));
    }
    tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1)).await;
    let mid_flight = overlap_flag.load(Ordering::SeqCst);
    for h in handles { h.await.unwrap(); }
    assert!(mid_flight >= 2, "expected multiple tasks to have started concurrently");

    println!(
        "W76 ok: std-mutex counter={} tokio-mutex counter={} concurrent-starts-observed={}",
        std_counter.lock().unwrap(), tokio_counter.lock().await, mid_flight
    );
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex as StdMutex};
use tokio::sync::Mutex as TokioMutex;
use tokio::time::Duration;

// std::sync::MutexGuard held across a suspend point makes the ENCLOSING FUTURE non-Send:
// an async fn's state machine captures every local alive across an .await as a field of
// the generated future type, so a non-Send guard held there poisons the whole future's
// Send-ness — and tokio::spawn requires the future it's given to BE Send. This is why the
// broken form below (commented out) fails to COMPILE, not just "is risky at runtime":
//   async fn broken(counter: &StdMutex) {
//       let mut guard = counter.lock().unwrap();
//       some_async_io().await;           // guard is a live local across this .await
//       *guard += 1;
//   }
//   // error[E0277]: `MutexGuard<'_, u64>` cannot be sent between threads safely
//   //   note: future is not `Send` as this value is used across an await
async fn increment_std_mutex(counter: &StdMutex<u64>) {
    {
        let guard = counter.lock().unwrap();
        let _seen = *guard;
        // guard drops HERE at end of scope, BEFORE the await below — so no non-Send
        // value is ever alive across a suspend point.
    }
    tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_micros(200)).await;
    let mut guard = counter.lock().unwrap();  // re-acquire AFTER the await instead
    *guard += 1;
}

// tokio::sync::Mutex's guard IS Send by design — .lock() itself is an async fn that
// queues the waiter and yields to the executor instead of blocking an OS thread, so the
// guard is just an ordinary Send value. Holding it across further .await points is fully
// legal — this is exactly what made version A's naive form fail to compile.
async fn increment_tokio_mutex(counter: &TokioMutex<u64>) {
    let mut guard = counter.lock().await;
    let _seen = *guard;
    tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_micros(200)).await; // guard is STILL held here — fine
    *guard += 1;
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    const TASKS: usize = 50;

    let std_counter = Arc::new(StdMutex::new(0u64));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..TASKS {
        let c = std_counter.clone();
        handles.push(tokio::spawn(async move { increment_std_mutex(&c).await; }));
    }
    for h in handles { h.await.expect("task panicked"); }
    assert_eq!(*std_counter.lock().unwrap(), TASKS as u64);

    let tokio_counter = Arc::new(TokioMutex::new(0u64));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..TASKS {
        let c = tokio_counter.clone();
        handles.push(tokio::spawn(async move { increment_tokio_mutex(&c).await; }));
    }
    for h in handles { h.await.expect("task panicked"); }
    assert_eq!(*tokio_counter.lock().await, TASKS as u64);

    // Sanity: prove real concurrency actually happened (tasks interleaved), so the above
    // passing isn't an accident of everything secretly running sequentially.
    let overlap_flag = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..8 {
        let flag = overlap_flag.clone();
        handles.push(tokio::spawn(async move {
            flag.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
            tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(5)).await;
        }));
    }
    tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1)).await;
    let mid_flight = overlap_flag.load(Ordering::SeqCst);
    for h in handles { h.await.unwrap(); }
    assert!(mid_flight >= 2, "expected multiple tasks to have started concurrently");

    println!(
        "W76 ok: std-mutex counter={} tokio-mutex counter={} concurrent-starts-observed={}",
        std_counter.lock().unwrap(), tokio_counter.lock().await, mid_flight
    );
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Correctly identifies that the compile-time issue is the enclosing FUTURE losing its Send bound (because a non-Send guard becomes a field of the generated state machine) — not a vague "std Mutex isn't async-aware" hand-wave.
  • ★★★Structures the std Mutex version to scope-drop its guard before the await and re-acquire afterward, rather than reaching immediately for tokio::sync::Mutex everywhere by default — recognizing std Mutex is still the cheaper, correct choice when you don't need to hold it across a suspend point.
  • ★★Knows specifically WHY tokio::sync::Mutex's guard is safely Send-holdable across awaits (.lock() is itself an async fn that queues/yields rather than blocking an OS thread) rather than just knowing "use the tokio one for async code" as a rule of thumb.
  • ★Includes a concrete comment showing the actual compiler error (E0277 / "future is not Send") a naive holding-across-await version would produce, rather than only asserting the fix works.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Is tokio::sync::Mutex strictly better for async code in general, so should you just always use it?" — No: it's strictly more expensive for the common case where you DON'T hold the lock across an await (extra async machinery, task-queue-based waiting instead of a cheap OS futex/spin). The standard guidance is to default to std Mutex and reach for tokio's version only when you provably need to hold the guard across a suspend point — using it everywhere "just in case" is a common anti-pattern.
  • P2"Does std Mutex's blocking behavior actually matter inside an async runtime, beyond just 'compiling or not'?" — Yes: a thread blocked on std::sync::Mutex::lock() blocks the ENTIRE OS thread, which on a multi-threaded tokio runtime can stall every other task scheduled onto that same worker thread — not just the one waiting. tokio::sync::Mutex's .lock().await yields control back to the executor while waiting, letting other tasks run on that thread meanwhile. This is why holding std Mutex for anything beyond a very short, non-blocking critical section is risky even when it compiles.
  • P3"This exercise's std Mutex critical sections are tiny — what's the actual rule of thumb for when blocking is fine even in async code?" — A commonly-cited guideline: if the critical section does no I/O, no other .await, and completes in a small, bounded amount of CPU time (microseconds, not milliseconds), briefly blocking a worker thread is generally acceptable. Anything unpredictably long, or that itself needs to await something, should never be done while holding a std Mutex guard on an async runtime.
🎯 Senior angle
The E0277 "future is not Send" error this exercise revolves around is one every async Rust engineer eventually hits. The differentiator is whether a candidate can explain the full causal chain — non-Send local alive across an await → generated future struct contains a non-Send field → the future itself becomes non-Send → tokio::spawn's Send bound rejects it — rather than pattern-matching "oh, just use tokio::sync::Mutex" without understanding why that specific fix works.

// Distributed Systems Exercise 77 · 60 min
W77 · Memory Ordering Deep-Dive — Acquire/Release/Relaxed/SeqCst
compare_exchange spinlock Release/Acquire happens-before Relaxed vs. Acquire/Release message-passing pattern Hard
Prompt
"Build TWO concrete, runnable demonstrations of why Ordering choice matters, not just that it compiles. (1) A minimal spinlock built from an AtomicBool using compare_exchange/compare_exchange_weak with explicit Ordering::Acquire on the locking CAS and Ordering::Release on unlock — then, as a deliberately-broken comparison, a second version using Ordering::Relaxed for both, with a comment explaining specifically what can go wrong (a thread that "acquires" the relaxed lock has no guarantee it sees writes made by the previous lock-holder before that holder's Relaxed unlock, because Relaxed provides no happens-before edge — only atomicity of the flag itself, never visibility of memory operations around it). (2) The classic message-passing pattern: thread A writes a payload to a plain, non-atomic shared variable, THEN sets an AtomicBool flag with Release; thread B spins on the flag with Acquire and, upon seeing it true, reads the payload. Demonstrate why Release/Acquire on that one flag is what makes it sound for thread B to read the plain payload with no synchronization of its own, and comment on why Relaxed on the flag in this exact pattern would be undefined behavior even though it "usually works" on x86."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::cell::UnsafeCell;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, Ordering};

struct SpinLock { locked: AtomicBool, data: UnsafeCell<u64> }
unsafe impl Sync for SpinLock {}

// TODO: impl SpinLock — lock() via compare_exchange_weak with EXPLICIT Acquire,
// unlock() via store with EXPLICIT Release. Then write a second, deliberately-
// broken BrokenRelaxedSpinLock using Relaxed everywhere, with a comment on WHY.

struct Handoff { payload: UnsafeCell<u64>, ready: AtomicBool }
unsafe impl Sync for Handoff {}

// TODO: impl Handoff — send() writes payload then Release-stores ready;
// recv() Acquire-spins on ready then reads payload. Explain in a comment why
// Relaxed on `ready` here would be UB, not just "less optimal".


fn main() {
    // ── Test 1: Acquire/Release spinlock under real concurrent contention ──
    // Enough threads * enough increments that a lost-update race would show
    // up statistically almost every run if the ordering were wrong.
    const THREADS: usize = 8;
    const INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD: u64 = 200_000;

    let lock = Arc::new(SpinLock::new(0));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..THREADS {
        let lock = Arc::clone(&lock);
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            for _ in 0..INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD {
                lock.with_lock(|counter| *counter += 1);
            }
        }));
    }
    for h in handles {
        h.join().unwrap();
    }
    let final_count = lock.with_lock(|c| *c);
    assert_eq!(final_count, THREADS as u64 * INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD);  // exact count under real contention proves the ordering, not luck
    println!(
        "spinlock stress test: {} threads x {} increments -> exact count {}",
        THREADS, INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD, final_count
    );

    // Smoke-test the broken relaxed lock single-threaded only: single-threaded
    // execution has no concurrent contention, so it cannot demonstrate the bug
    // (the bug is specifically about visibility ACROSS threads) — this just
    // proves the type compiles and behaves like a lock in isolation. We do NOT
    // run it under multi-thread contention: the failure it exhibits is a real
    // data race (UB), so any observed outcome would prove nothing and risks a
    // flaky, CPU- and optimizer-dependent test.
    let broken = BrokenRelaxedSpinLock::new(0);
    broken.lock();
    unsafe {
        *broken.data.get() += 1;
    }
    broken.unlock();
    assert_eq!(unsafe { *broken.data.get() }, 1);

    // ── Test 2: Release/Acquire message passing, repeated many times ──
    // Looping the whole producer/consumer trial many times makes correctness
    // convincing rather than trivially true by luck on a single run.
    const TRIALS: u64 = 100;
    for trial in 0..TRIALS {
        let handoff = Arc::new(Handoff::new());
        let producer = {
            let handoff = Arc::clone(&handoff);
            thread::spawn(move || handoff.send(trial * 7 + 3))
        };
        let consumer = {
            let handoff = Arc::clone(&handoff);
            thread::spawn(move || handoff.recv())
        };
        producer.join().unwrap();
        let received = consumer.join().unwrap();
        assert_eq!(received, trial * 7 + 3);  // looped 100x — a race would very likely surface at least once
    }
    println!("message-passing handoff verified correct across {} trials", TRIALS);

    // Smoke-test the broken relaxed handoff single-threaded only, for the same
    // reason as above: exercising it under real contention would be
    // demonstrating undefined behavior, which a test cannot reliably assert on.
    let broken_handoff = BrokenRelaxedHandoff::new();
    broken_handoff.send(42);
    assert_eq!(broken_handoff.recv(), 42);

    let probe = AtomicU64::new(9);
    assert_eq!(probe.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 9);

    println!("W77 all checks passed");
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::cell::UnsafeCell;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, AtomicU64, Ordering};
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::thread;

// ─── Part 1: spinlock built on compare_exchange ────────────────────────────

/// A minimal spinlock: `false` = unlocked, `true` = locked.
/// Correct pairing: Acquire on the successful lock CAS, Release on unlock.
struct SpinLock {
    locked: AtomicBool,
    data: UnsafeCell<u64>,
}
unsafe impl Sync for SpinLock {}

impl SpinLock {
    fn new(init: u64) -> Self {
        Self { locked: AtomicBool::new(false), data: UnsafeCell::new(init) }
    }

    /// Acquire on the successful CAS means no read/write in the critical section
    /// below can be reordered to happen BEFORE this — and it synchronizes-with
    /// the Release store that unlocked last time, making every write the previous
    /// holder made inside its critical section visible here.
    fn lock(&self) {
        while self
            .locked
            .compare_exchange_weak(false, true, Ordering::Acquire, Ordering::Relaxed)
            .is_err()
        {
            std::hint::spin_loop();
        }
    }

    /// Release means every read/write in the critical section above is guaranteed
    /// visible to whichever thread's next Acquire-lock observes this store — that
    /// Release-then-Acquire pair on the SAME atomic forms the happens-before edge.
    fn unlock(&self) {
        self.locked.store(false, Ordering::Release);
    }

    fn with_lock<R>(&self, f: impl FnOnce(&mut u64) -> R) -> R {
        self.lock();
        let r = f(unsafe { &mut *self.data.get() });
        self.unlock();
        r
    }
}

/// Deliberately-broken comparison: same CAS-based flag, but Relaxed everywhere.
/// Relaxed only guarantees the flag itself is read/written atomically (no torn
/// reads, no lost updates to the BOOL) — it gives NO happens-before edge. A
/// thread that "acquires" this lock has no guarantee it observes writes the
/// PREVIOUS holder made inside ITS critical section before that holder's
/// Relaxed unlock, because nothing prevents the compiler or CPU from
/// reordering those writes to appear after the flag flip on either side.
/// Concretely: thread A writes `data = 5` then relaxed-stores `locked = false`;
/// thread B relaxed-CASes `locked` false->true and reads `data` — B is allowed
/// to see a stale/torn `data` even though it correctly observed `locked` become
/// available, because the flag and the payload have no ordering relationship
/// under Relaxed. This is real, observable memory-reordering UB, not a
/// theoretical nit — it's exactly why every real lock uses acquire/release
/// (or stronger) on its guard variable.
struct BrokenRelaxedSpinLock {
    locked: AtomicBool,
    data: UnsafeCell<u64>,
}
unsafe impl Sync for BrokenRelaxedSpinLock {}

impl BrokenRelaxedSpinLock {
    fn new(init: u64) -> Self {
        Self { locked: AtomicBool::new(false), data: UnsafeCell::new(init) }
    }
    fn lock(&self) {  // BOTH sides Relaxed — atomicity of the flag only, no visibility guarantee
        while self
            .locked
            .compare_exchange_weak(false, true, Ordering::Relaxed, Ordering::Relaxed)
            .is_err()
        {
            std::hint::spin_loop();
        }
    }
    fn unlock(&self) {
        self.locked.store(false, Ordering::Relaxed);
    }
}

// ─── Part 2: message passing via a Release/Acquire flag ────────────────────

/// `payload` is a PLAIN, non-atomic field. It is only sound for thread B to
/// read it without its own synchronization because of the Release-store /
/// Acquire-load pair on `ready`, which establishes a happens-before edge
/// between "A's write to payload" and "B's read of payload".
struct Handoff {
    payload: UnsafeCell<u64>,
    ready: AtomicBool,
}
unsafe impl Sync for Handoff {}

impl Handoff {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self { payload: UnsafeCell::new(0), ready: AtomicBool::new(false) }
    }

    /// Thread A: write the plain payload FIRST, then publish with a Release
    /// store. Release guarantees the payload write cannot be reordered to
    /// happen AFTER this store becomes visible to another thread.
    fn send(&self, value: u64) {
        unsafe {
            *self.payload.get() = value;
        }
        self.ready.store(true, Ordering::Release);
    }

    /// Thread B: spin with Acquire until the flag is visible true. Once the
    /// Acquire load observes A's Release store, it "synchronizes-with" it —
    /// every write A made before the Release is now guaranteed visible to
    /// every read B makes after this Acquire. That contract is what makes the
    /// plain `payload` read below safe with zero locking of its own.
    fn recv(&self) -> u64 {
        while !self.ready.load(Ordering::Acquire) {
            std::hint::spin_loop();
        }
        unsafe { *self.payload.get() }
    }
}

/// Deliberately-broken comparison: same shape, but Relaxed on the flag.
/// Relaxed gives atomicity of the flag bit alone — NO happens-before edge to
/// the plain `payload` write/read around it. The compiler is free to reorder
/// A's payload write to after its flag store, and the CPU is free to reorder
/// them too on weaker-memory-model architectures (ARM, POWER). This is
/// undefined behavior in the Rust/C++ memory model even though it "usually
/// works" on x86: x86's strong TSO model happens to forbid store-store
/// reordering for plain stores in practice, which hides the bug on that ONE
/// architecture — but UB also means the optimizer is free to exploit the
/// Relaxed ordering (e.g. hoisting/merging loads) in ways that can break this
/// even ON x86. "Usually works" is not "correct".
struct BrokenRelaxedHandoff {
    payload: UnsafeCell<u64>,
    ready: AtomicBool,
}
unsafe impl Sync for BrokenRelaxedHandoff {}

impl BrokenRelaxedHandoff {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self { payload: UnsafeCell::new(0), ready: AtomicBool::new(false) }
    }
    fn send(&self, value: u64) {
        unsafe {
            *self.payload.get() = value;
        }
        self.ready.store(true, Ordering::Relaxed);  // no happens-before edge to the payload write above
    }
    fn recv(&self) -> u64 {
        while !self.ready.load(Ordering::Relaxed) {
            std::hint::spin_loop();
        }
        unsafe { *self.payload.get() }
    }
}

fn main() {
    // ── Test 1: Acquire/Release spinlock under real concurrent contention ──
    // Enough threads * enough increments that a lost-update race would show
    // up statistically almost every run if the ordering were wrong.
    const THREADS: usize = 8;
    const INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD: u64 = 200_000;

    let lock = Arc::new(SpinLock::new(0));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..THREADS {
        let lock = Arc::clone(&lock);
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            for _ in 0..INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD {
                lock.with_lock(|counter| *counter += 1);
            }
        }));
    }
    for h in handles {
        h.join().unwrap();
    }
    let final_count = lock.with_lock(|c| *c);
    assert_eq!(final_count, THREADS as u64 * INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD);  // exact count under real contention proves the ordering, not luck
    println!(
        "spinlock stress test: {} threads x {} increments -> exact count {}",
        THREADS, INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD, final_count
    );

    // Smoke-test the broken relaxed lock single-threaded only: single-threaded
    // execution has no concurrent contention, so it cannot demonstrate the bug
    // (the bug is specifically about visibility ACROSS threads) — this just
    // proves the type compiles and behaves like a lock in isolation. We do NOT
    // run it under multi-thread contention: the failure it exhibits is a real
    // data race (UB), so any observed outcome would prove nothing and risks a
    // flaky, CPU- and optimizer-dependent test.
    let broken = BrokenRelaxedSpinLock::new(0);
    broken.lock();
    unsafe {
        *broken.data.get() += 1;
    }
    broken.unlock();
    assert_eq!(unsafe { *broken.data.get() }, 1);

    // ── Test 2: Release/Acquire message passing, repeated many times ──
    // Looping the whole producer/consumer trial many times makes correctness
    // convincing rather than trivially true by luck on a single run.
    const TRIALS: u64 = 100;
    for trial in 0..TRIALS {
        let handoff = Arc::new(Handoff::new());
        let producer = {
            let handoff = Arc::clone(&handoff);
            thread::spawn(move || handoff.send(trial * 7 + 3))
        };
        let consumer = {
            let handoff = Arc::clone(&handoff);
            thread::spawn(move || handoff.recv())
        };
        producer.join().unwrap();
        let received = consumer.join().unwrap();
        assert_eq!(received, trial * 7 + 3);  // looped 100x — a race would very likely surface at least once
    }
    println!("message-passing handoff verified correct across {} trials", TRIALS);

    // Smoke-test the broken relaxed handoff single-threaded only, for the same
    // reason as above: exercising it under real contention would be
    // demonstrating undefined behavior, which a test cannot reliably assert on.
    let broken_handoff = BrokenRelaxedHandoff::new();
    broken_handoff.send(42);
    assert_eq!(broken_handoff.recv(), 42);

    let probe = AtomicU64::new(9);
    assert_eq!(probe.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 9);

    println!("W77 all checks passed");
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Names the actual failure mode of the Relaxed spinlock precisely — not "it's less safe" but specifically that Relaxed gives atomicity of the flag bit with zero happens-before guarantee, so a new lock-holder can observe stale/torn state written under the PREVIOUS critical section even though it correctly observed the flag transition. Candidates who wave at "Relaxed is faster but riskier" without being able to articulate the exact visibility gap haven't internalized the memory model, just memorized a warning.
  • ★★★Explains WHY Release must go on the write side and Acquire on the read side, not just that they're the "correct pair" — Release prevents preceding writes from being reordered past the store; Acquire prevents following reads from being reordered before the load. Together, once the Acquire observes the Release's value, everything the writer did BEFORE its Release becomes visible to everything the reader does AFTER its Acquire — a directional contract, not a symmetric "these two go together" fact.
  • ★★★Refuses to "prove" the Relaxed version is broken by running it once and eyeballing the output — a strong candidate recognizes that a data race is undefined behavior, so any single observed run (including one that "looks correct") is not evidence of correctness, and single-threaded exercise of the broken types proves nothing about the concurrent bug; a weaker candidate tries to write a flaky "prove it fails" test and gets confused when it doesn't reliably fail.
  • ★★Loops the message-passing trial many times rather than trusting one run — correctness claims about concurrent code demonstrated on a single execution are weak evidence; repeating the producer/consumer handoff across many fresh thread pairs is the difference between "it happened to work" and "it is convincingly, repeatably correct."
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Where does SeqCst fit relative to Acquire/Release, and when would you actually reach for it over the pair you just used?" — SeqCst gives everything Acquire/Release gives PLUS a single, globally-agreed total order across ALL SeqCst operations on ALL atomics in the program, which Acquire/Release alone does not guarantee (two independent Acquire/Release pairs on different atomics can be observed in different relative orders by different threads). You reach for SeqCst when correctness depends on multiple threads agreeing on the relative order of operations on DIFFERENT atomic variables — e.g. Dekker's-algorithm-style mutual exclusion built from two separate flags — not for a single lock or a single handoff flag, where Acquire/Release is sufficient and cheaper on architectures where SeqCst requires extra fences (notably ARM).
  • P2"Why does compare_exchange take TWO orderings — one for success, one for failure — and what should the failure ordering be here?" — The success ordering governs the memory effects when the CAS actually swaps the value (here, Acquire, since that's the "I now hold the lock" transition); the failure ordering governs the (much weaker) guarantees when the CAS merely reads the current value without swapping — since a failed CAS makes no forward progress and establishes no critical-section entry, Relaxed is correct and standard for the failure case, and using something stronger there would just be paying for guarantees you don't need. This split exists precisely because success and failure are semantically different operations, not just two outcomes of "the same operation."
  • P3"This spinlock busy-waits with spin_loop() — in a real system, when is that actually the right choice over parking the thread (e.g. via a Condvar or futex)?" — Spinning is right when the expected wait is shorter than the cost of a context switch to sleep and back (typically low-single-digit microseconds or less), and specifically wrong under long or unpredictable contention, where a spinning thread burns a full CPU core doing nothing productive and can even starve the very thread holding the lock on an oversubscribed system (lock holder gets preempted while a spinner keeps the core busy). Production spinlocks in real systems (e.g. inside a kernel or a database's buffer-pool latch) almost always spin for a short bounded number of iterations THEN fall back to a real block/park, which is exactly the adaptive-locking strategy worth naming here.
🎯 Senior angle
A mid-level answer treats orderings as a checklist ("use Acquire on reads, Release on writes") applied by pattern-matching. A senior answer can explain WHY each specific ordering is required for each specific operation in terms of the happens-before relation it does or doesn't establish — and, just as importantly, can say precisely what would go wrong, in what order of operations, if a weaker ordering were substituted, rather than reciting "it's undefined behavior" as an incantation. The refusal to "test" the broken variants under real contention (because a data race can't be reliably demonstrated to fail) is itself a strong signal of genuine understanding of what UB means.

    // convincing rather than trivially true by luck on a single run.
    const TRIALS: u64 = 100;
    for trial in 0..TRIALS {
        let handoff = Arc::new(Handoff::new());
        let producer = {
            let handoff = Arc::clone(&handoff);
            thread::spawn(move || handoff.send(trial * 7 + 3))
        };
        let consumer = {
            let handoff = Arc::clone(&handoff);
            thread::spawn(move || handoff.recv())
        };
        producer.join().unwrap();
        let received = consumer.join().unwrap();
        assert_eq!(received, trial * 7 + 3);  // looped 100x — a race would very likely surface at least once
    }
    println!("message-passing handoff verified correct across {} trials", TRIALS);

    // Smoke-test the broken relaxed handoff single-threaded only, for the same
    // reason as above: exercising it under real contention would be
    // demonstrating undefined behavior, which a test cannot reliably assert on.
    let broken_handoff = BrokenRelaxedHandoff::new();
    broken_handoff.send(42);
    assert_eq!(broken_handoff.recv(), 42);

    let probe = AtomicU64::new(9);
    assert_eq!(probe.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 9);

    println!("W77 all checks passed");
}

    const THREADS: usize = 8;

    let broken = BrokenRelaxedSpinLock::new(0);

    assert_eq!(unsafe { *broken.data.get() }, 1);

    // ── Test 2: Release/Acquire message passing, repeated many times ──
    // Looping the whole producer/consumer trial many times makes correctness

        };

            let handoff = Arc::clone(&handoff);
            thread::spawn(move || handoff.recv())
        };
        producer.join().unwrap();
        let received = consumer.join().unwrap();
        assert_eq!(received, trial * 7 + 3);  // looped 100x — a race would very likely surface at least once
    }

    // reason as above: exercising it under real contention would be

W78 · G-Counter and PN-Counter CRDTs — State-Based, Grow-Only and Inc/Dec
state-based CRDT element-wise max merge commutative / idempotent composed counters Medium
Prompt
"Implement a GCounter (grow-only distributed counter CRDT): each of N simulated replicas/nodes owns its own slot in a HashMap<NodeId, u64> that only that node ever increments locally; the counter's current value is the sum of all slots. merge(&mut self, other: &Self) combines two replicas' states by taking the element-wise maximum of each node's slot — never the sum of the two states' totals, which would double-count. This pointwise-max merge is what makes it a valid CRDT: commutative, associative, and idempotent (merging the same state twice must be a no-op). Then implement a PnCounter (supports decrement too) by internally composing two GCounters — a p counter for increments, an n counter for decrements — defining the value as p.value() - n.value(), with merge just merging both inner counters independently."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::collections::HashMap;

type NodeId = u32;

struct GCounter { counts: HashMap<NodeId, u64> }

// TODO: impl GCounter — new(), increment(node, amount) [only touches own slot],
// value() [sum of all slots], merge(&other) [ELEMENT-WISE MAX per slot, not sum!]

struct PnCounter { p: GCounter, n: GCounter }

// TODO: impl PnCounter — increment/decrement route to p/n respectively,
// value() = p.value() - n.value(), merge() merges both inner counters

fn main() {
    // ── G-Counter: three replicas increment independently ──
    const NODE_A: NodeId = 1;
    const NODE_B: NodeId = 2;
    const NODE_C: NodeId = 3;

    let mut replica_a = GCounter::new();
    replica_a.increment(NODE_A, 5);
    replica_a.increment(NODE_A, 2); // 7 total on A's own slot

    let mut replica_b = GCounter::new();
    replica_b.increment(NODE_B, 3);
    replica_b.increment(NODE_B, 4); // 7 total on B's own slot

    let mut replica_c = GCounter::new();
    replica_c.increment(NODE_C, 10); // 10 total on C's own slot

    let expected_total = 7 + 7 + 10;

    // Merge ordering 1 (sequential-looking): A <- B, A <- C, then propagate.
    let mut order1_a = replica_a.clone();
    order1_a.merge(&replica_b);
    order1_a.merge(&replica_c);
    let mut order1_b = replica_b.clone();
    order1_b.merge(&order1_a);
    let mut order1_c = replica_c.clone();
    order1_c.merge(&order1_b);

    // Merge ordering 2 (DIFFERENT order: C first, then B, then propagate the
    // other direction) — commutativity means the final converged value must
    // match ordering 1 exactly, regardless of merge order.
    let mut order2_c = replica_c.clone();
    order2_c.merge(&replica_a);
    let mut order2_b = replica_b.clone();
    order2_b.merge(&order2_c);
    let mut order2_a = replica_a.clone();
    order2_a.merge(&order2_b);
    order2_c.merge(&order2_a);

    assert_eq!(order1_a.value(), expected_total);
    assert_eq!(order1_b.value(), expected_total);
    assert_eq!(order1_c.value(), expected_total);
    assert_eq!(order2_a.value(), expected_total);
    assert_eq!(order2_c.value(), expected_total);
    assert_eq!(order1_a.value(), order2_a.value());  // commutativity across two DIFFERENT merge orderings
    println!("G-Counter commutativity: both merge orderings converge to {}", expected_total);

    // Idempotence: merging a replica's state into itself must be a no-op.
    let mut self_merged = order1_a.clone();
    let before = self_merged.value();
    self_merged.merge(&order1_a.clone());
    assert_eq!(self_merged.value(), before);
    assert_eq!(self_merged.counts, order1_a.counts);
    println!("G-Counter idempotence: self-merge left value unchanged at {}", before);

    // Sanity: merging is also a no-op when repeated against an unrelated
    // already-merged state that contributes nothing new.
    let mut redundant = order1_a.clone();
    redundant.merge(&replica_b);
    assert_eq!(redundant.value(), order1_a.value());

    // ── PN-Counter: concurrent increments AND decrements across replicas ──
    let mut pn_a = PnCounter::new();
    pn_a.increment(NODE_A, 20);
    pn_a.decrement(NODE_A, 3);

    let mut pn_b = PnCounter::new();
    pn_b.increment(NODE_B, 5);
    pn_b.decrement(NODE_B, 8);

    let mut pn_c = PnCounter::new();
    pn_c.increment(NODE_C, 1);

    // Net expected: increments (20 + 5 + 1) - decrements (3 + 8) = 26 - 11 = 15.
    let expected_net: i64 = (20 + 5 + 1) - (3 + 8);

    pn_a.merge(&pn_b);
    pn_a.merge(&pn_c);
    pn_b.merge(&pn_a);
    pn_c.merge(&pn_b);

    assert_eq!(pn_a.value(), expected_net);
    assert_eq!(pn_b.value(), expected_net);
    assert_eq!(pn_c.value(), expected_net);
    println!("PN-Counter converged net value across replicas: {}", expected_net);

    println!("W78 all checks passed");
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::collections::HashMap;

type NodeId = u32;

/// Grow-only counter CRDT. Each node owns exactly one slot in `counts` and is
/// the ONLY writer to that slot (locally, via `increment`). The counter's
/// logical value is the sum across all known slots.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct GCounter {
    counts: HashMap<NodeId, u64>,
}

impl GCounter {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self { counts: HashMap::new() }
    }

    /// Local-only mutation: a node may only ever increment its OWN slot.
    fn increment(&mut self, node: NodeId, amount: u64) {
        *self.counts.entry(node).or_insert(0) += amount;
    }

    fn value(&self) -> u64 {
        self.counts.values().sum()
    }

    /// Merge takes the ELEMENT-WISE MAXIMUM per node slot, never the sum of the
    /// two totals — summing would double-count whatever both replicas already
    /// agreed on. Per-slot max is exactly what makes this commutative,
    /// associative, and idempotent (a valid join over a join-semilattice): each
    /// slot only ever grows, so "most-advanced observed state per node" is a
    /// safe, order-independent merge.
    fn merge(&mut self, other: &Self) {
        for (&node, &count) in &other.counts {
            let entry = self.counts.entry(node).or_insert(0);
            *entry = (*entry).max(count);  // max, NEVER +=, or convergence double-counts
        }
    }
}

/// Increment/decrement counter composed of two G-Counters: P tracks all
/// increments, N tracks all decrements (as increments to N's own slots).
/// Logical value is P.value() - N.value(); merging just merges both inner
/// G-Counters independently, so PN-Counter inherits G-Counter's CRDT
/// properties for free.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct PnCounter {
    p: GCounter,
    n: GCounter,
}

impl PnCounter {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self { p: GCounter::new(), n: GCounter::new() }
    }

    fn increment(&mut self, node: NodeId, amount: u64) {
        self.p.increment(node, amount);
    }

    fn decrement(&mut self, node: NodeId, amount: u64) {
        self.n.increment(node, amount);
    }

    fn value(&self) -> i64 {
        self.p.value() as i64 - self.n.value() as i64  // net value, never a shared slot for both directions
    }

    fn merge(&mut self, other: &Self) {
        self.p.merge(&other.p);
        self.n.merge(&other.n);
    }
}

fn main() {
    // ── G-Counter: three replicas increment independently ──
    const NODE_A: NodeId = 1;
    const NODE_B: NodeId = 2;
    const NODE_C: NodeId = 3;

    let mut replica_a = GCounter::new();
    replica_a.increment(NODE_A, 5);
    replica_a.increment(NODE_A, 2); // 7 total on A's own slot

    let mut replica_b = GCounter::new();
    replica_b.increment(NODE_B, 3);
    replica_b.increment(NODE_B, 4); // 7 total on B's own slot

    let mut replica_c = GCounter::new();
    replica_c.increment(NODE_C, 10); // 10 total on C's own slot

    let expected_total = 7 + 7 + 10;

    // Merge ordering 1 (sequential-looking): A <- B, A <- C, then propagate.
    let mut order1_a = replica_a.clone();
    order1_a.merge(&replica_b);
    order1_a.merge(&replica_c);
    let mut order1_b = replica_b.clone();
    order1_b.merge(&order1_a);
    let mut order1_c = replica_c.clone();
    order1_c.merge(&order1_b);

    // Merge ordering 2 (DIFFERENT order: C first, then B, then propagate the
    // other direction) — commutativity means the final converged value must
    // match ordering 1 exactly, regardless of merge order.
    let mut order2_c = replica_c.clone();
    order2_c.merge(&replica_a);
    let mut order2_b = replica_b.clone();
    order2_b.merge(&order2_c);
    let mut order2_a = replica_a.clone();
    order2_a.merge(&order2_b);
    order2_c.merge(&order2_a);

    assert_eq!(order1_a.value(), expected_total);
    assert_eq!(order1_b.value(), expected_total);
    assert_eq!(order1_c.value(), expected_total);
    assert_eq!(order2_a.value(), expected_total);
    assert_eq!(order2_c.value(), expected_total);
    assert_eq!(order1_a.value(), order2_a.value());  // commutativity across two DIFFERENT merge orderings
    println!("G-Counter commutativity: both merge orderings converge to {}", expected_total);

    // Idempotence: merging a replica's state into itself must be a no-op.
    let mut self_merged = order1_a.clone();
    let before = self_merged.value();
    self_merged.merge(&order1_a.clone());
    assert_eq!(self_merged.value(), before);
    assert_eq!(self_merged.counts, order1_a.counts);
    println!("G-Counter idempotence: self-merge left value unchanged at {}", before);

    // Sanity: merging is also a no-op when repeated against an unrelated
    // already-merged state that contributes nothing new.
    let mut redundant = order1_a.clone();
    redundant.merge(&replica_b);
    assert_eq!(redundant.value(), order1_a.value());

    // ── PN-Counter: concurrent increments AND decrements across replicas ──
    let mut pn_a = PnCounter::new();
    pn_a.increment(NODE_A, 20);
    pn_a.decrement(NODE_A, 3);

    let mut pn_b = PnCounter::new();
    pn_b.increment(NODE_B, 5);
    pn_b.decrement(NODE_B, 8);

    let mut pn_c = PnCounter::new();
    pn_c.increment(NODE_C, 1);

    // Net expected: increments (20 + 5 + 1) - decrements (3 + 8) = 26 - 11 = 15.
    let expected_net: i64 = (20 + 5 + 1) - (3 + 8);

    pn_a.merge(&pn_b);
    pn_a.merge(&pn_c);
    pn_b.merge(&pn_a);
    pn_c.merge(&pn_b);

    assert_eq!(pn_a.value(), expected_net);
    assert_eq!(pn_b.value(), expected_net);
    assert_eq!(pn_c.value(), expected_net);
    println!("PN-Counter converged net value across replicas: {}", expected_net);

    println!("W78 all checks passed");
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Merges with element-wise max, not sum — this is the single make-or-break line of the whole exercise. A candidate who writes self.counts[node] += other.counts[node] has built something that looks right on a first merge and silently double-counts on every subsequent one; catching this on their own, or immediately after being told "your merge over-counts," is the core signal.
  • ★★★Enforces (or at least states out loud) that a node only ever increments its OWN slot — the entire scheme's safety depends on no two replicas ever racing to write the same map entry; if increments could target arbitrary slots, the "one writer per slot" invariant that makes max-merge safe collapses. A candidate who spots this on their own, even if the exercise's simple API doesn't strictly enforce it in the type system, is showing real CRDT understanding rather than just copying a formula.
  • ★★Composes PN-Counter from two G-Counters instead of reinventing a signed-delta merge — recognizing that decrement can be modeled as "increment a second, separate grow-only counter" and that merging two independent G-Counters is sufficient to make the whole thing converge correctly is the standard, elegant CRDT composition technique, and reusing already-proven building blocks is a strong instinct in general, not just here.
  • ★★Can state the three CRDT convergence properties by name (commutative, associative, idempotent) and explain in their own words why THIS SPECIFIC merge function has each one — not just "CRDTs always converge" as a slogan, but the actual algebraic reason (per-slot max forms a join-semilattice, and joins over a semilattice are automatically commutative/associative/idempotent).
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What happens to this design as the number of nodes grows into the thousands, and does it ever ship over the network in practice?" — The state size grows linearly with the number of distinct nodes that have EVER incremented the counter, since every node gets a permanent slot even after it stops participating — for a long-lived system with high node churn (e.g. ephemeral serverless workers), this is a real, unbounded growth problem, sometimes addressed by periodically "retiring" long-dormant slots via an out-of-band garbage-collection protocol that all replicas must agree has safely observed those slots' final values first.
  • P2"This is a state-based CRDT (you ship the whole counter and merge). What's the alternative, and why might you pick it instead?" — Operation-based (CmRDT) CRDTs ship individual operations (e.g. "increment node A by 3") over a reliable, causally-ordered broadcast channel instead of the whole state; they can be much cheaper on the wire for large states with small deltas, but they push the "exactly-once, causally-ordered delivery" burden onto the network layer instead of onto the merge function — state-based CRDTs' big advantage is that merge is idempotent and commutative enough to tolerate duplicate delivery, out-of-order delivery, and even partial network partitions with zero extra coordination.
  • P3"Could you build a G-Set (grow-only set) or a counter that supports 'set to exact value' using the same max-merge idea? Why or why not?" — A G-Set works trivially (union is also commutative/associative/idempotent — a different join-semilattice operation on the same underlying algebraic structure), but "last-writer-wins set to an exact value" does NOT work with a pure max-merge unless you attach a total-order tiebreaker (commonly a (timestamp, node-id) pair) to each value, because plain integer values have no meaningful "max" that corresponds to "more recent" — this is exactly the LWW-Register CRDT, and probing whether the candidate spots that ordinary max-of-values isn't the same concept as max-of-a-monotonic-counter is a good gauge of whether they understand the underlying lattice requirement or just pattern-matched this one counter.
🎯 Senior angle
A mid-level answer gets the happy path working — three replicas increment, merge once, get the right sum. A senior answer proactively tests the properties that make it a CRDT rather than just "a counter that happens to combine correctly once": commutativity across different merge orders, and idempotence of a self-merge. Being able to explain WHY max-merge has these properties (it's a join over a semilattice, and joins are inherently order- and repetition-insensitive) rather than just observing that the assertions pass is what separates "implemented the recipe" from "understands why the recipe works."
