// Distributed Systems Exercise 79 · 60 min
W79 · OR-Set CRDT — Observed-Remove Set, Correct Concurrent Add/Remove
unique per-add tags add-wins semantics tombstone set causal concurrency Hard
Prompt
"Implement an OR-Set (Observed-Remove Set) — the CRDT that correctly handles the specific hard case a naive 'just track added and removed elements in two plain sets' design gets wrong: element E is added on replica 1 (tagged (E, tag_1)), then removed there; concurrently and independently, replica 2 also adds E (tagged (E, tag_2)) without ever having observed replica 1's removal. After merging both replicas, E must still be present, because replica 2's add was concurrent with — not causally after — replica 1's remove, so it must not be silently erased. Implement this via unique per-add tags ((element, replica_id, local_counter)) stored in an added set, a removed tombstone set of specific tags explicitly removed, and contains(e) defined as 'at least one tag for e exists in added-tags minus removed-tags.' remove(e) on a replica must tombstone only the tags for e that that replica has currently observed — never a tag it's never heard of yet. This 'remove only what you've seen' rule is exactly what makes the concurrent-add-vs-remove case above resolve correctly: 'add wins' over a causally-concurrent remove."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::collections::HashSet;
use std::hash::Hash;

type ReplicaId = u32;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Tag { replica: ReplicaId, counter: u64 }

struct OrSet<E: Eq + Hash + Clone> {
    replica: ReplicaId,
    next_counter: u64,
    added: HashSet<(E, Tag)>,
    removed: HashSet<(E, Tag)>,
}

// TODO: impl OrSet — new(replica), add(element) [mints a fresh unique Tag],
// remove(&element) [tombstones ONLY tags this replica has already observed],
// contains(&element) [added minus removed, per-tag], merge(&other) [union both sets]

fn main() {
    const REPLICA_1: ReplicaId = 1;
    const REPLICA_2: ReplicaId = 2;

    // ── Scenario 1: concurrent add-after-independent-remove — "add wins" ──
    // Replica 1 adds E, then removes it (it has seen and can tombstone its own
    // tag). Replica 2, WITHOUT ever observing replica 1's state, ALSO
    // independently adds E with its own fresh, unrelated tag.
    let mut replica1 = OrSet::new(REPLICA_1);
    replica1.add("E");
    replica1.remove(&"E"); // replica 1 tombstones only the tag it has seen (its own)
    assert!(!replica1.contains(&"E"));

    let mut replica2 = OrSet::new(REPLICA_2);
    replica2.add("E"); // concurrent, causally independent of replica 1's remove

    // After merging both directions, E MUST still be present: replica 2's add
    // tag was never observed by replica 1 at remove time, so it was never
    // tombstoned, and "add wins" over a causally-concurrent remove.
    let mut merged_1_then_2 = replica1.clone();
    merged_1_then_2.merge(&replica2);
    assert!(
        merged_1_then_2.contains(&"E"),
        "a naive add/remove-set design would incorrectly lose E here"
    );

    let mut merged_2_then_1 = replica2.clone();
    merged_2_then_1.merge(&replica1);
    assert!(merged_2_then_1.contains(&"E"));
    println!("scenario 1 (concurrent add survives independent remove): PASS");

    // ── Scenario 2: causally-ordered remove, THEN a fresh later re-add ──
    // Replica 2 first receives replica 1's full add+remove history for E (so it
    // now has genuinely seen that specific tag get removed), THEN independently
    // re-adds E with a brand-new tag of its own. The fresh add must be visible
    // after merging — a later, genuinely-new add is never confused with the
    // old, already-tombstoned tag.
    let mut r1_seq = OrSet::new(REPLICA_1);
    r1_seq.add("E");
    r1_seq.remove(&"E");

    let mut r2_seq = OrSet::new(REPLICA_2);
    r2_seq.merge(&r1_seq); // r2 now has causally observed r1's add+remove
    assert!(!r2_seq.contains(&"E")); // correctly absent right after merging in the removal
    r2_seq.add("E"); // fresh, independent re-add with a NEW tag
    assert!(r2_seq.contains(&"E")); // the new tag is live and untouched by the old tombstone

    let mut r1_after_merge = r1_seq.clone();
    r1_after_merge.merge(&r2_seq);
    assert!(r1_after_merge.contains(&"E")); // propagates back correctly too
    println!("scenario 2 (causal remove then fresh re-add): PASS");

    // ── Scenario 3: no cross-contamination between distinct elements ──
    // Removing one element on one replica must not affect a totally different
    // element added later with a different tag.
    let mut r1_cross = OrSet::new(REPLICA_1);
    r1_cross.add("X");
    r1_cross.remove(&"X");
    r1_cross.add("Y"); // unrelated element, unrelated tag

    assert!(!r1_cross.contains(&"X"));
    assert!(r1_cross.contains(&"Y"));

    let mut r2_cross = OrSet::new(REPLICA_2);
    r2_cross.merge(&r1_cross);
    assert!(!r2_cross.contains(&"X"));
    assert!(r2_cross.contains(&"Y")); // Y's tag was never touched by X's tombstone
    println!("scenario 3 (no cross-contamination between elements): PASS");

    println!("W79 all checks passed");
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::collections::HashSet;
use std::hash::Hash;

type ReplicaId = u32;

/// A globally-unique tag stamped on every `add`: (replica that did the add, a
/// per-replica monotonically increasing counter). Two adds of the SAME element
/// on the SAME replica get DIFFERENT tags, and no two replicas ever mint the
/// same tag, because each replica only increments its own counter.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Tag {
    replica: ReplicaId,
    counter: u64,
}

/// Observed-Remove Set. `added` holds every (element, tag) pair ever observed
/// by this replica. `removed` holds the specific tags this replica has
/// explicitly tombstoned. `contains(e)` is "at least one tag for e in added
/// minus removed" — an element with ANY live (non-tombstoned) tag is present,
/// so a concurrent add (with a brand-new tag the remover never saw) always
/// wins over a causally-earlier remove.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct OrSet<E: Eq + Hash + Clone> {
    replica: ReplicaId,
    next_counter: u64,
    added: HashSet<(E, Tag)>,
    removed: HashSet<(E, Tag)>,
}

impl<E: Eq + Hash + Clone> OrSet<E> {
    fn new(replica: ReplicaId) -> Self {
        Self { replica, next_counter: 0, added: HashSet::new(), removed: HashSet::new() }
    }

    /// Mint a fresh, globally-unique tag for this replica and record the
    /// (element, tag) pair as added.
    fn add(&mut self, element: E) {
        let tag = Tag { replica: self.replica, counter: self.next_counter };
        self.next_counter += 1;
        self.added.insert((element, tag));
    }

    /// Tombstone ONLY the tags for `element` that THIS replica has currently
    /// observed (i.e. already present in its own `added` set) — never a tag it
    /// has never heard of. This "remove only what you've seen" rule is exactly
    /// what makes a causally-concurrent add on another replica (whose tag this
    /// replica cannot possibly know about yet) survive the remove: that unseen
    /// tag simply never gets tombstoned here, and once merged in later it stays
    /// live because it was never in anyone's removed set.
    fn remove(&mut self, element: &E) {
        for (e, tag) in self.added.iter() {
            if e == element {
                self.removed.insert((e.clone(), *tag));
            }
        }
    }

    fn contains(&self, element: &E) -> bool {
        self.added
            .iter()
            .any(|(e, tag)| e == element && !self.removed.contains(&(e.clone(), *tag)))
    }

    /// Merge is a straightforward union of both `added` and `removed` sets —
    /// once a tag is known to have been removed by ANY replica, it stays
    /// tombstoned everywhere after merging (tombstones never get un-set).
    fn merge(&mut self, other: &Self) {
        for pair in &other.added {
            self.added.insert(pair.clone());
        }
        for pair in &other.removed {
            self.removed.insert(pair.clone());
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    const REPLICA_1: ReplicaId = 1;
    const REPLICA_2: ReplicaId = 2;

    // ── Scenario 1: concurrent add-after-independent-remove — "add wins" ──
    // Replica 1 adds E, then removes it (it has seen and can tombstone its own
    // tag). Replica 2, WITHOUT ever observing replica 1's state, ALSO
    // independently adds E with its own fresh, unrelated tag.
    let mut replica1 = OrSet::new(REPLICA_1);
    replica1.add("E");
    replica1.remove(&"E"); // replica 1 tombstones only the tag it has seen (its own)
    assert!(!replica1.contains(&"E"));

    let mut replica2 = OrSet::new(REPLICA_2);
    replica2.add("E"); // concurrent, causally independent of replica 1's remove

    // After merging both directions, E MUST still be present: replica 2's add
    // tag was never observed by replica 1 at remove time, so it was never
    // tombstoned, and "add wins" over a causally-concurrent remove.
    let mut merged_1_then_2 = replica1.clone();
    merged_1_then_2.merge(&replica2);
    assert!(
        merged_1_then_2.contains(&"E"),
        "a naive add/remove-set design would incorrectly lose E here"
    );

    let mut merged_2_then_1 = replica2.clone();
    merged_2_then_1.merge(&replica1);
    assert!(merged_2_then_1.contains(&"E"));
    println!("scenario 1 (concurrent add survives independent remove): PASS");

    // ── Scenario 2: causally-ordered remove, THEN a fresh later re-add ──
    // Replica 2 first receives replica 1's full add+remove history for E (so it
    // now has genuinely seen that specific tag get removed), THEN independently
    // re-adds E with a brand-new tag of its own. The fresh add must be visible
    // after merging — a later, genuinely-new add is never confused with the
    // old, already-tombstoned tag.
    let mut r1_seq = OrSet::new(REPLICA_1);
    r1_seq.add("E");
    r1_seq.remove(&"E");

    let mut r2_seq = OrSet::new(REPLICA_2);
    r2_seq.merge(&r1_seq); // r2 now has causally observed r1's add+remove
    assert!(!r2_seq.contains(&"E")); // correctly absent right after merging in the removal
    r2_seq.add("E"); // fresh, independent re-add with a NEW tag
    assert!(r2_seq.contains(&"E")); // the new tag is live and untouched by the old tombstone

    let mut r1_after_merge = r1_seq.clone();
    r1_after_merge.merge(&r2_seq);
    assert!(r1_after_merge.contains(&"E")); // propagates back correctly too
    println!("scenario 2 (causal remove then fresh re-add): PASS");

    // ── Scenario 3: no cross-contamination between distinct elements ──
    // Removing one element on one replica must not affect a totally different
    // element added later with a different tag.
    let mut r1_cross = OrSet::new(REPLICA_1);
    r1_cross.add("X");
    r1_cross.remove(&"X");
    r1_cross.add("Y"); // unrelated element, unrelated tag

    assert!(!r1_cross.contains(&"X"));
    assert!(r1_cross.contains(&"Y"));

    let mut r2_cross = OrSet::new(REPLICA_2);
    r2_cross.merge(&r1_cross);
    assert!(!r2_cross.contains(&"X"));
    assert!(r2_cross.contains(&"Y")); // Y's tag was never touched by X's tombstone
    println!("scenario 3 (no cross-contamination between elements): PASS");

    println!("W79 all checks passed");
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Understands WHY a naive "one added-set + one removed-set of bare elements" design fails before being told — in that design, once E is removed anywhere, it's gone from the removed-set-of-elements forever, so replica 2's later, causally-unrelated add of E would be silently swallowed by a remove it never even knew about. Recognizing that the fix requires per-add IDENTITY (not just per-element membership) is the entire conceptual leap this exercise is testing.
  • ★★★Implements remove as "tombstone only tags I've already observed", not "tombstone all conceivable tags for this element" — a candidate who tries to make remove somehow reach into tags it hasn't seen yet (impossible in a real distributed system, since a replica can only act on state it has) either doesn't understand the causality constraint or is unconsciously assuming global knowledge the algorithm must not require.
  • ★★Writes the exact "concurrent add survives independent remove" test unprompted, or immediately recognizes it as the critical test when asked what to verify — rather than only testing the easy, causally-ordered happy path (add, then remove, then check absent), which a broken implementation would also pass.
  • ★Notices tombstones only ever grow and can name the practical consequence (state size grows unboundedly with delete history) even without being asked to solve it — a natural segue into garbage-collecting old tombstones once all replicas are known to have observed them, the standard real-world OR-Set follow-up problem.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"Why 'add-wins' specifically — couldn't you just as validly design a 'remove-wins' OR-Set instead, where a concurrent remove beats a concurrent add?" — You absolutely could, and it's a real, named design choice (sometimes called a 2P-Set variant or 'remove-wins set'), not a law of nature; add-wins is simply the more common default because in most real applications (e.g. a shopping cart, a shared tag list, presence sets) silently losing something a user explicitly, intentionally added is judged a worse user-visible failure mode than an item lingering one merge cycle longer than a concurrent delete intended — it's a product/semantics decision encoded into the CRDT's merge rule, and a good candidate recognizes it as a choice rather than an inevitability.
  • P2"The removed/tombstone set only ever grows in this implementation — how would a real system garbage-collect it without breaking correctness?" — Only after every replica has causally observed BOTH the add and its corresponding remove (i.e. the tombstone has fully propagated everywhere and no replica can possibly still be holding an un-merged copy of that add without also having its remove) can a tombstone be safely dropped from `removed` AND its corresponding tag purged from `added` — this requires an out-of-band mechanism (often vector-clock-based causal stability tracking, or a periodically-run "everyone acknowledge" protocol) to determine that safe point; dropping a tombstone too early can resurrect an element that a later-arriving remove was still relying on being tombstoned.
  • P3"Compare this OR-Set's memory/complexity cost to the G-Counter from the previous exercise — why does correctly handling concurrent add/remove require so much more machinery than a counter that only ever grows?" — A G-Counter's per-node slot has no analogue to "remove," so a single scalar per replica is always enough state (bounded by node count) — there's no need to ever distinguish WHICH increment happened, only how many. An OR-Set must distinguish individual elements' individual insertion EVENTS from each other (because removal is selective and per-instance, not "reset everything"), which forces it to carry one tag per add forever (until garbage collection) instead of one integer per node — the fundamental reason "add and never remove" CRDTs are so much cheaper than "add and remove" CRDTs in general.
🎯 Senior angle
The entire value of this exercise lives in one specific, easy-to-miss scenario: a concurrent add that the remover never observed. A mid-level implementation that only tests "add then remove then check absent" will pass its own tests while being fundamentally broken for real concurrent use, which is precisely the trap a naive two-plain-sets design falls into in production. A senior candidate writes the adversarial concurrent scenario as their FIRST test, not an afterthought, because they understand that a CRDT's entire reason for existing is correctness under concurrent, causally-unordered operations — the easy sequential case was never the hard part.

    // Replica 1 adds E, then removes it (it has seen and can tombstone its own

    // tag was never observed by replica 1 at remove time, so it was never

    // now has genuinely seen that specific tag get removed), THEN independently

    // after merging — a later, genuinely-new add is never confused with the

    r1_seq.remove(&"E");

    r2_seq.merge(&r1_seq); // r2 now has causally observed r1's add+remove
    assert!(!r2_seq.contains(&"E")); // correctly absent right after merging in the removal
    r2_seq.add("E"); // fresh, independent re-add with a NEW tag

    r1_after_merge.merge(&r2_seq);
    assert!(r1_after_merge.contains(&"E")); // propagates back correctly too

// Distributed Systems Exercise 80 · 45 min
W80 · Vector Clocks for Causality Tracking
HashMap<NodeId, u64> element-wise max on receive Before / After / Equal / Concurrent not a total order Medium
Prompt
"Implement a VectorClock that tracks causality between events across nodes without ever imposing a false total order on events that aren't actually related. Wrap a HashMap<NodeId, u64> — one logical counter per node — and provide increment(&mut self, node: NodeId), called when a node bumps its own component on a local event, and merge(&mut self, other: &VectorClock), the standard receive-event rule: take the element-wise max of every component against the sender's clock, then increment your own component. Provide compare(&self, other: &Self) -> CausalOrder returning one of Before, After, Equal, or Concurrent, using the standard component-wise rule (self is Before other if every one of self's components is ≤ the matching component of other, with at least one strictly less — symmetric for After). Unlike a Lamport timestamp, which would force a total order onto every pair of events, two vector clocks can be legitimately incomparable — that's what Concurrent is for."
Starter code to hand to candidate
use std::collections::HashMap;

type NodeId = u32;

struct VectorClock {
    owner: NodeId,
    counts: HashMap<NodeId, u64>,
}

enum CausalOrder { Before, After, Equal, Concurrent }

// TODO: impl VectorClock — new(owner), increment(&mut self, node: NodeId),
//       merge(&mut self, other: &VectorClock) — max every component, THEN increment own,
//       compare(&self, other: &VectorClock) -> CausalOrder — must be able to return Concurrent,
//       not just force everything into a total order.

fn main() {
    // Two nodes that each do a purely local event and never exchange a message.
    let mut clock_a = VectorClock::new(0);
    clock_a.increment(0);
    let mut clock_b = VectorClock::new(1);
    clock_b.increment(1);
    assert_eq!(clock_a.compare(&clock_b), CausalOrder::Concurrent);  // a Lamport clock would falsely order these
    assert_eq!(clock_b.compare(&clock_a), CausalOrder::Concurrent);

    // A genuine causal chain: A's event -> message to B -> B merges -> B's own event.
    let a_before = clock_a.clone();
    let mut clock_b2 = VectorClock::new(1);
    clock_b2.merge(&clock_a);
    clock_b2.increment(1);
    assert_eq!(clock_b2.compare(&a_before), CausalOrder::After);  // causality preserved across the message
    assert_eq!(a_before.compare(&clock_b2), CausalOrder::Before);

    // Reflexive / equal case.
    let clock_a_copy = clock_a.clone();
    assert_eq!(clock_a.compare(&clock_a_copy), CausalOrder::Equal);

    println!("vector clock tests passed: {:?}", clock_b2);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::collections::HashMap;

type NodeId = u32;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct VectorClock {
    owner: NodeId,
    counts: HashMap<NodeId, u64>,
}

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum CausalOrder {
    Before,
    After,
    Equal,
    Concurrent,
}

impl VectorClock {
    fn new(owner: NodeId) -> Self {
        VectorClock { owner, counts: HashMap::new() }
    }

    fn get(&self, node: NodeId) -> u64 {
        *self.counts.get(&node).unwrap_or(&0)
    }

    fn increment(&mut self, node: NodeId) {
        let entry = self.counts.entry(node).or_insert(0);
        *entry += 1;
    }

    /// The "receive event" rule: fold in the sender's knowledge component-wise via
    /// MAX (never overwrite, never go backwards), THEN advance our own component —
    /// receiving a message is itself a local event.
    fn merge(&mut self, other: &VectorClock) {
        for (&node, &their_count) in other.counts.iter() {
            let mine = self.counts.entry(node).or_insert(0);
            *mine = (*mine).max(their_count);  // element-wise max — never take the sender's value if ours is already ahead
        }
        self.increment(self.owner);  // receiving IS a local event too — bump our own component after merging
    }

    /// Component-wise partial order: self is Before other iff every component of
    /// self is <= the matching component of other, with at least one strictly less.
    /// If self has SOME components strictly less AND others strictly greater than
    /// other, the two events are causally unrelated — Concurrent, not falsely ordered.
    fn compare(&self, other: &VectorClock) -> CausalOrder {
        let mut nodes: Vec<NodeId> = self.counts.keys().chain(other.counts.keys()).copied().collect();
        nodes.sort_unstable();
        nodes.dedup();

        let mut self_strictly_less = false;
        let mut self_strictly_greater = false;
        for node in nodes {
            let a = self.get(node);
            let b = other.get(node);
            if a < b {
                self_strictly_less = true;
            } else if a > b {
                self_strictly_greater = true;
            }
        }

        match (self_strictly_less, self_strictly_greater) {  // BOTH true = incomparable, i.e. Concurrent
            (false, false) => CausalOrder::Equal,
            (true, false) => CausalOrder::Before,
            (false, true) => CausalOrder::After,
            (true, true) => CausalOrder::Concurrent,
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    // Two nodes that each do a purely local event and never exchange a message.
    let mut clock_a = VectorClock::new(0);
    clock_a.increment(0);
    let mut clock_b = VectorClock::new(1);
    clock_b.increment(1);
    assert_eq!(clock_a.compare(&clock_b), CausalOrder::Concurrent);  // a Lamport clock would falsely order these
    assert_eq!(clock_b.compare(&clock_a), CausalOrder::Concurrent);

    // A genuine causal chain: A's event -> message to B -> B merges -> B's own event.
    let a_before = clock_a.clone();
    let mut clock_b2 = VectorClock::new(1);
    clock_b2.merge(&clock_a);
    clock_b2.increment(1);
    assert_eq!(clock_b2.compare(&a_before), CausalOrder::After);  // causality preserved across the message
    assert_eq!(a_before.compare(&clock_b2), CausalOrder::Before);

    // Reflexive / equal case.
    let clock_a_copy = clock_a.clone();
    assert_eq!(clock_a.compare(&clock_a_copy), CausalOrder::Equal);

    println!("vector clock tests passed: {:?}", clock_b2);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Increments after merging, not before or never — the receive-event rule is "max, then increment," in that order; a candidate who forgets the post-merge increment entirely will still pass the easy causal-chain check by accident in some orderings, but will subtly break the "two clocks with the identical vector are truly Equal" reflexive property the moment a node receives a message without generating a new local observation of its own — probe for this explicitly if it isn't obviously right.
  • ★★★Correctly produces Concurrent instead of silently picking a side — this is the entire point of the exercise. A candidate who writes compare as if it returns a total order (e.g. by comparing sums of components, or by falling back to node-id tie-breaking) has built a Lamport clock with extra bytes, not a vector clock, and has thrown away the one property that makes vector clocks worth their memory cost.
  • ★★Treats a missing component as 0, not as "undefined" or a panic — two clocks that have never heard of each other's nodes must still be comparable (a node with zero events for some other node is exactly equivalent to that node's counter reading zero); an implementation that panics or errors on a missing key in the other clock's map has a real correctness bug, not just a style nit.
  • ★Uses HashMap sparsely rather than pre-sizing for every node up front — real vector-clock implementations (e.g. in Riak/Dynamo-style stores) often only ever store entries for nodes that have actually generated an event, which is exactly what entry().or_insert(0) gives you for free; a candidate who eagerly zero-fills every known node's slot on construction isn't wrong, just less idiomatic and slightly more wasteful at scale with many rarely-active nodes.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"What's the actual practical problem with vector clocks that keeps real systems from just using them everywhere?" — Unbounded growth: the clock's size is proportional to the number of distinct nodes that have EVER written to a given piece of data, which is fine for a small, stable cluster but becomes a real storage and bandwidth cost in systems with many clients or high churn (this is precisely why Riak eventually added "clock pruning" / vector-clock truncation heuristics, and why some systems switch to dotted version vectors or just accept Lamport-clock-plus-tiebreak approximations for high-cardinality actor sets).
  • P2"If compare returns Concurrent for two writes to the same key, what does the SYSTEM do with that information — it can't just pick one?" — This is exactly the "sibling" / conflict problem Dynamo-style stores hand back to the application (or resolve with an app-supplied merge function, i.e. a CRDT) rather than silently discarding one write: Riak literally returns both sibling values to the client on a concurrent write and lets the application (or a last-writer-wins policy, accepting its weaker guarantees) decide, because there is no data-agnostic way to know which concurrent update "should" win.
  • P3"How would you adapt this so a NEW node can join the cluster after some events have already happened, without needing every existing clock updated retroactively?" — Because the underlying structure is a sparse map rather than a fixed-size array, a brand-new node simply starts with an empty (all-implicit-zero) clock and begins appearing as a key in other nodes' maps the first time it merges with them — no retroactive rewrite of history is needed, which is precisely why the exercise specifies a HashMap "or fixed-size array for N KNOWN nodes" as an explicit alternative: the array variant is faster/denser but requires membership to be fixed in advance.
🎯 Senior angle
A mid-level candidate gets the happy-path causal chain working and stops. A senior candidate treats Concurrent as the actual design goal rather than an edge case to tolerate — they'll proactively construct a scenario where two updates are genuinely unordered and show the comparator refuses to fabricate an answer, and they can articulate why that refusal is valuable (it's the signal an application-level conflict resolver needs to trigger merge logic) rather than treating it as a limitation to work around.

    assert_eq!(clock_a.compare(&clock_a_copy), CausalOrder::Equal);

// Distributed Systems Exercise 81 · 60 min
W81 · Gossip / Anti-Entropy Protocol for Eventual Consistency
push-pull state exchange std::sync::mpsc as "the network" last-writer-wins by version transitive propagation Medium
Prompt
"Simulate N nodes, each an OS thread holding a small key-value map where every key carries a version number for last-writer-wins conflict resolution, communicating over std::sync::mpsc channels standing in for a network. Each node periodically picks one peer and does a full push-pull anti-entropy exchange: send your entire local state, receive the peer's entire state back over the same round-trip, and merge (last-writer-wins per key by version) — repeat for a bounded number of rounds. Prove eventual convergence: after enough rounds, all N nodes hold an identical final state, even though updates were injected at different nodes at different times and no node ever talked to every other node directly — that's the entire point of gossip: information spreads transitively, node-to-node, with no broadcast and no coordinator."
Starter code to hand to candidate
struct VersionedValue { value: String, version: u64 }
type NodeState = HashMap<String, VersionedValue>;

struct GossipRequest { from: usize, state: NodeState, reply_tx: Sender<NodeState> }

// TODO: fn merge_state(local: &mut NodeState, incoming: &NodeState) — last-writer-wins by version
// TODO: spawn N node threads over mpsc; each round pick ONE peer, push your state + a reply
//       channel, block for the peer's state back (push-PULL), then merge it in.
// TODO: prove eventual convergence — after enough rounds, ALL N nodes' maps are identical,
//       including at a node that never directly gossiped with the node an update originated at.

fn main() {
    // 6-node ring: each node's ONLY gossip partners are its two ring neighbors
    // (a fixed, low-fanout partial view, not full membership) — this is what
    // lets us PROVE that a diametrically-opposite pair (0 and 3) never gossips
    // directly, while every round still makes a genuinely random pick between
    // its two available neighbors (satisfying "picks one random peer").
    const N: usize = 6;
    let neighbors_of = |i: usize| -> [usize; 2] { [(i + N - 1) % N, (i + 1) % N] };

    let mut txs: Vec<Sender<GossipRequest>> = Vec::with_capacity(N);
    let mut rxs: Vec<Receiver<GossipRequest>> = Vec::with_capacity(N);
    for _ in 0..N {
        let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();
        txs.push(tx);
        rxs.push(rx);
    }

    let states: Vec<Arc<Mutex<NodeState>>> = (0..N).map(|_| Arc::new(Mutex::new(NodeState::new()))).collect();
    let contacted: Vec<Arc<Mutex<Vec<usize>>>> = (0..N).map(|_| Arc::new(Mutex::new(Vec::new()))).collect();
    let running: Vec<Arc<AtomicBool>> = (0..N).map(|_| Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(true))).collect();

    // The update injected "at node 0 only" — no other node ever writes this key.
    states[0].lock().unwrap().insert(
        "x".to_string(),
        VersionedValue { value: "node0-update".to_string(), version: 1 },
    );

    // A genuine last-writer-wins conflict: node1 writes key "y" first, then
    // node3 independently writes a HIGHER version for the same key a little
    // later — the higher version must win everywhere after convergence.
    let injector_states = (states[1].clone(), states[3].clone());
    let injector = thread::spawn(move || {
        injector_states.0.lock().unwrap().insert(
            "y".to_string(),
            VersionedValue { value: "node1-first-write".to_string(), version: 1 },
        );
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(15));
        injector_states.1.lock().unwrap().insert(
            "y".to_string(),
            VersionedValue { value: "node3-later-write".to_string(), version: 2 },
        );
    });

    // Responder threads: passively answer inbound gossip requests from
    // whichever neighbor happens to pick this node this round.
    let mut responder_handles = Vec::with_capacity(N);
    for (i, rx) in rxs.into_iter().enumerate() {
        let state = states[i].clone();
        let contacted_log = contacted[i].clone();
        let running_flag = running[i].clone();
        responder_handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            loop {
                match rx.recv_timeout(Duration::from_millis(10)) {
                    Ok(req) => {
                        let mut local = state.lock().unwrap();
                        merge_state(&mut local, &req.state);
                        contacted_log.lock().unwrap().push(req.from);  // log EVERY pairwise contact, not just self-initiated ones
                        let _ = req.reply_tx.send(local.clone());
                    }
                    Err(_) => {
                        if !running_flag.load(Ordering::SeqCst) { break; }
                    }
                }
            }
        }));
    }

    // Initiator threads: each round, pick ONE random neighbor and do a full
    // push-pull state exchange with it.
    let mut initiator_handles = Vec::with_capacity(N);
    for i in 0..N {
        let peer_txs = txs.clone();
        let state = states[i].clone();
        let contacted_log = contacted[i].clone();
        let seed = (i as u64 + 1)
            .wrapping_mul(0x9E3779B97F4A7C15)
            ^ SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).unwrap().as_nanos() as u64;
        let mut rng = SimpleRng::new(seed);
        let peers = neighbors_of(i);
        initiator_handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            for _round in 0..ROUNDS {
                let peer = rng.choose(&peers);
                let (reply_tx, reply_rx) = mpsc::channel();
                let snapshot = state.lock().unwrap().clone();
                if peer_txs[peer].send(GossipRequest { from: i, state: snapshot, reply_tx }).is_err() {
                    continue;
                }
                if let Ok(peer_state) = reply_rx.recv_timeout(Duration::from_millis(200)) {
                    let mut local = state.lock().unwrap();
                    merge_state(&mut local, &peer_state);
                    contacted_log.lock().unwrap().push(peer);
                }
                thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(2));
            }
        }));
    }

    injector.join().unwrap();
    for h in initiator_handles { h.join().unwrap(); }
    // Give any in-flight responder replies a moment to land, then stop responders.
    thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(50));
    for flag in &running { flag.store(false, Ordering::SeqCst); }
    for h in responder_handles { h.join().unwrap(); }

    // --- Node 0 and node 3 are diametrically opposite on the 6-node ring, so
    // neither is ever in the other's neighbor list — assert they truly never
    // gossiped directly, in EITHER direction.
    assert!(!contacted[3].lock().unwrap().contains(&0), "node3 must never have contacted node0 directly");
    assert!(!contacted[0].lock().unwrap().contains(&3), "node0 must never have contacted node3 directly");

    // --- Yet node0's update reached node3 anyway, transitively, hop by hop
    // around the ring (0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3, or 0 -> 5 -> 4 -> 3) — proof gossip's
    // information spread without a broadcast or a central coordinator.
    let node3_state = states[3].lock().unwrap().clone();
    assert_eq!(node3_state.get("x"), Some(&VersionedValue { value: "node0-update".to_string(), version: 1 }));  // arrived with zero direct contact

    // --- Last-writer-wins actually resolved the "y" conflict to the HIGHER
    // version everywhere, not just at the two nodes that wrote it.
    for i in 0..N {
        let s = states[i].lock().unwrap();
        assert_eq!(s.get("y"), Some(&VersionedValue { value: "node3-later-write".to_string(), version: 2 }), "node {} did not converge", i);
    }

    // --- Full convergence: every node's final map is pairwise identical to
    // every other node's, even though updates originated at different nodes
    // at different times and no node ever talked to every other node.
    let reference = states[0].lock().unwrap().clone();
    for i in 1..N {
        let other = states[i].lock().unwrap();
        assert_eq!(*other, reference, "node {} diverged from node 0's final state", i);  // ALL N nodes pairwise identical
    }

    println!("gossip convergence test passed: {} nodes, {} keys converged", N, reference.len());
}

use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, Ordering};
use std::sync::mpsc::{self, Receiver, Sender};
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;
use std::time::{Duration, SystemTime, UNIX_EPOCH};

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
struct VersionedValue {
    value: String,
    version: u64,
}

type NodeState = HashMap<String, VersionedValue>;

/// A push-pull gossip request: `from` carries the sender's own state so the
/// receiver can merge it in immediately, and `reply_tx` is a one-shot channel
/// the receiver uses to push its (post-merge) state straight back — this is
/// what makes each exchange "push-pull" rather than one-directional.
struct GossipRequest {
    from: usize,
    state: NodeState,
    reply_tx: Sender<NodeState>,
}

/// Last-writer-wins merge: an incoming key only overwrites the local copy if
/// its version is strictly higher — ties and staler versions are dropped.
fn merge_state(local: &mut NodeState, incoming: &NodeState) {
    for (key, incoming_val) in incoming {
        let should_overwrite = match local.get(key) {
            Some(local_val) => incoming_val.version > local_val.version,  // STRICTLY higher wins; ties keep the local copy
            None => true,
        };
        if should_overwrite {
            local.insert(key.clone(), incoming_val.clone());
        }
    }
}

/// Minimal dependency-free xorshift64 PRNG — good enough for picking a gossip
/// peer, not for anything cryptographic.
struct SimpleRng { state: u64 }

impl SimpleRng {
    fn new(seed: u64) -> Self { SimpleRng { state: seed | 1 } }
    fn next_u64(&mut self) -> u64 {
        let mut x = self.state;
        x ^= x << 13; x ^= x >> 7; x ^= x << 17;
        self.state = x;
        x
    }
    fn choose(&mut self, options: &[usize]) -> usize {
        options[(self.next_u64() as usize) % options.len()]
    }
}

const ROUNDS: usize = 80;

fn main() {
    // 6-node ring: each node's ONLY gossip partners are its two ring neighbors
    // (a fixed, low-fanout partial view, not full membership) — this is what
    // lets us PROVE that a diametrically-opposite pair (0 and 3) never gossips
    // directly, while every round still makes a genuinely random pick between
    // its two available neighbors (satisfying "picks one random peer").
    const N: usize = 6;
    let neighbors_of = |i: usize| -> [usize; 2] { [(i + N - 1) % N, (i + 1) % N] };

    let mut txs: Vec<Sender<GossipRequest>> = Vec::with_capacity(N);
    let mut rxs: Vec<Receiver<GossipRequest>> = Vec::with_capacity(N);
    for _ in 0..N {
        let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();
        txs.push(tx);
        rxs.push(rx);
    }

    let states: Vec<Arc<Mutex<NodeState>>> = (0..N).map(|_| Arc::new(Mutex::new(NodeState::new()))).collect();
    let contacted: Vec<Arc<Mutex<Vec<usize>>>> = (0..N).map(|_| Arc::new(Mutex::new(Vec::new()))).collect();
    let running: Vec<Arc<AtomicBool>> = (0..N).map(|_| Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(true))).collect();

    // The update injected "at node 0 only" — no other node ever writes this key.
    states[0].lock().unwrap().insert(
        "x".to_string(),
        VersionedValue { value: "node0-update".to_string(), version: 1 },
    );

    // A genuine last-writer-wins conflict: node1 writes key "y" first, then
    // node3 independently writes a HIGHER version for the same key a little
    // later — the higher version must win everywhere after convergence.
    let injector_states = (states[1].clone(), states[3].clone());
    let injector = thread::spawn(move || {
        injector_states.0.lock().unwrap().insert(
            "y".to_string(),
            VersionedValue { value: "node1-first-write".to_string(), version: 1 },
        );
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(15));
        injector_states.1.lock().unwrap().insert(
            "y".to_string(),
            VersionedValue { value: "node3-later-write".to_string(), version: 2 },
        );
    });

    // Responder threads: passively answer inbound gossip requests from
    // whichever neighbor happens to pick this node this round.
    let mut responder_handles = Vec::with_capacity(N);
    for (i, rx) in rxs.into_iter().enumerate() {
        let state = states[i].clone();
        let contacted_log = contacted[i].clone();
        let running_flag = running[i].clone();
        responder_handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            loop {
                match rx.recv_timeout(Duration::from_millis(10)) {
                    Ok(req) => {
                        let mut local = state.lock().unwrap();
                        merge_state(&mut local, &req.state);
                        contacted_log.lock().unwrap().push(req.from);  // log EVERY pairwise contact, not just self-initiated ones
                        let _ = req.reply_tx.send(local.clone());

                    Err(_) => {

    }

    // Initiator threads: each round, pick ONE random neighbor and do a full
    // push-pull state exchange with it.
    let mut initiator_handles = Vec::with_capacity(N);
    for i in 0..N {
        let peer_txs = txs.clone();
        let state = states[i].clone();
        let contacted_log = contacted[i].clone();
        let seed = (i as u64 + 1)
            .wrapping_mul(0x9E3779B97F4A7C15)
            ^ SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).unwrap().as_nanos() as u64;
        let mut rng = SimpleRng::new(seed);
        let peers = neighbors_of(i);
        initiator_handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            for _round in 0..ROUNDS {
                let peer = rng.choose(&peers);
                let (reply_tx, reply_rx) = mpsc::channel();
                let snapshot = state.lock().unwrap().clone();
                if peer_txs[peer].send(GossipRequest { from: i, state: snapshot, reply_tx }).is_err() {
                    continue;

                if let Ok(peer_state) = reply_rx.recv_timeout(Duration::from_millis(200)) {
                    let mut local = state.lock().unwrap();
                    merge_state(&mut local, &peer_state);

                }

    }

    injector.join().unwrap();
    for h in initiator_handles { h.join().unwrap(); }
    // Give any in-flight responder replies a moment to land, then stop responders.
    thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(50));
    for flag in &running { flag.store(false, Ordering::SeqCst); }
    for h in responder_handles { h.join().unwrap(); }

    // --- Node 0 and node 3 are diametrically opposite on the 6-node ring, so
    // neither is ever in the other's neighbor list — assert they truly never
    // gossiped directly, in EITHER direction.
    assert!(!contacted[3].lock().unwrap().contains(&0), "node3 must never have contacted node0 directly");
    assert!(!contacted[0].lock().unwrap().contains(&3), "node0 must never have contacted node3 directly");

    // --- Yet node0's update reached node3 anyway, transitively, hop by hop
    // around the ring (0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3, or 0 -> 5 -> 4 -> 3) — proof gossip's
    // information spread without a broadcast or a central coordinator.
    let node3_state = states[3].lock().unwrap().clone();
    assert_eq!(node3_state.get("x"), Some(&VersionedValue { value: "node0-update".to_string(), version: 1 }));  // arrived with zero direct contact

    // --- Last-writer-wins actually resolved the "y" conflict to the HIGHER
    // version everywhere, not just at the two nodes that wrote it.
    for i in 0..N {
        let s = states[i].lock().unwrap();
        assert_eq!(s.get("y"), Some(&VersionedValue { value: "node3-later-write".to_string(), version: 2 }), "node {} did not converge", i);
    }

    // --- Full convergence: every node's final map is pairwise identical to
    // every other node's, even though updates originated at different nodes
    // at different times and no node ever talked to every other node.
    let reference = states[0].lock().unwrap().clone();
    for i in 1..N {
        let other = states[i].lock().unwrap();
        assert_eq!(*other, reference, "node {} diverged from node 0's final state", i);  // ALL N nodes pairwise identical
    }

    println!("gossip convergence test passed: {} nodes, {} keys converged", N, reference.len());
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Implements a genuine PUSH-PULL round-trip, not a one-way push — the whole point of anti-entropy gossip over a fire-and-forget push is that each exchange moves information in both directions per contact, roughly halving the number of pairwise exchanges needed for full convergence; a candidate who only sends state and never waits for the peer's state back has built a weaker, slower-converging broadcast-rumor protocol instead, and should be pushed to explain the difference.
  • ★★★Restricts each node to a genuinely limited peer set rather than letting every node gossip with any of the other N-1 nodes — a fully-random-over-everyone topology makes it nearly impossible to construct a provable "this pair never talked directly" test case (random chance will eventually connect any two nodes), so a candidate who reaches for a low-fanout, fixed-degree topology (a ring, a small fixed peer list) specifically to make the transitivity property testable is showing real protocol-design maturity, not just Rust skill.
  • ★★Merges by comparing versions, never by wall-clock arrival order — a subtly wrong implementation that just does "whichever state I heard about most recently wins" instead of comparing the embedded version numbers will still often look like it converges in a small, fast test, but it silently loses updates whenever a stale gossip message happens to arrive after a fresher one purely due to thread-scheduling luck.
  • ★Uses a bounded number of rounds with generous timing margins, not a fixed sleep-and-hope duration — hard-coding "sleep exactly 500ms and assume convergence happened" is exactly the kind of flaky test this exercise is meant to catch a candidate writing; bounding by round COUNT with a large enough round budget (or by actively polling for convergence with a timeout) is the more defensible pattern.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"How does the number of gossip rounds needed to reach full convergence scale with the number of nodes N, roughly?" — For a well-mixed random-peer topology, it's O(log N) rounds because the number of nodes that have heard a rumor roughly doubles each round (epidemic/exponential spread) — but our fixed-degree RING topology is the deliberately worse case, needing O(N) rounds since information can only hop one position per round in the worst direction; a candidate who can name this trade-off (low-fanout topologies are easier to reason about and test, but slower to converge, than richer random-peer topologies) is showing real depth.
  • P2"Real gossip protocols (e.g. Cassandra's, SWIM) also gossip FAILURE DETECTION, not just data — how would you extend this to detect a node that's gone silent?" — Piggyback a per-node heartbeat counter or last-seen timestamp on every gossip exchange alongside the data payload; if a node's heartbeat hasn't advanced for several rounds according to what OTHER nodes are reporting about it (not just your own direct observation, which could be a network partition rather than an actual crash), mark it suspected/dead — this is essentially what SWIM's suspicion mechanism and Cassandra's phi-accrual failure detector do, layering failure detection on top of the exact same anti-entropy channel used for data.
  • P3"This exchanges the ENTIRE state map every round — what breaks as the dataset grows to millions of keys, and what's the standard fix?" — Full-state push-pull is O(dataset size) per gossip round regardless of how few keys actually changed, which becomes prohibitively expensive bandwidth-wise at scale; the standard fix is a Merkle tree (or similar digest structure) per node so peers first exchange just a small root-hash comparison, then recursively diff down the tree to find only the actually-divergent key ranges — this is precisely the mechanism Cassandra and Dynamo use for their anti-entropy repair processes instead of naive full-state exchange.
🎯 Senior angle
Anyone can make two threads swap a HashMap and call it "gossip." What separates a senior answer is designing the test topology specifically to make the interesting property provable — recognizing that fully random peer selection makes "this pair never talked" essentially unfalsifiable in a short test run, and deliberately constraining the topology (a ring, a fixed low-fanout view) so the transitivity claim has real teeth. That instinct — shape the experiment so a claim can actually be disproven if it's false — is the same instinct that separates a good chaos-engineering test from a vibes-based one.

// Distributed Systems Exercise 82 · 90 min
W82 · Simplified Raft Leader Election
randomized election timeout term + voted_for semantics majority vote → Leader heartbeats reset timers Hard
Prompt
"Implement only the leader-election portion of Raft (no log replication) for N simulated nodes over std::sync::mpsc channels. Each node tracks a current_term and a voted_for that resets whenever the term changes, and starts as a Follower. A node that receives no heartbeat or vote request before a randomized election timeout elapses becomes a Candidate — the randomization is mandatory and must actually vary per node, since without jitter every follower can time out and start an election in perfect lockstep forever. On becoming a candidate: increment its term, vote for itself, and broadcast RequestVote(term, candidate_id). A node grants a vote only if the requester's term is >= its own current term and it hasn't already voted for someone else this term (implement the real voted_for-reset-on-new-term and one-vote-per-term rules correctly — this is the most commonly botched Raft detail). A candidate that gets votes from a strict majority (> N/2) becomes Leader and sends periodic empty AppendEntries heartbeats, which reset followers' election timers and prevent new elections while the leader is alive."
Starter code to hand to candidate
enum Role { Follower, Candidate, Leader }

enum Msg {
    RequestVote { term: u64, candidate_id: usize },
    VoteGranted { term: u64, voter_id: usize },
    AppendEntries { term: u64, leader_id: usize },
}

// TODO: fn run_node(...) per-node event loop over its own mpsc Receiver<Msg>:
//       - RANDOMIZED election timeout (must vary per node) that, on expiry, promotes
//         Follower/Candidate -> new Candidate term, votes for self, broadcasts RequestVote
//       - grant a vote only if requester's term >= current_term AND not already voted this term
//       - on strict majority of votes for the current term -> Leader, start heartbeating
//       - any AppendEntries/RequestVote with term >= current_term resets the election timer

fn main() {
    const N: usize = 5;

    let mut txs: Vec<Sender<Msg>> = Vec::with_capacity(N);
    let mut rxs: Vec<Receiver<Msg>> = Vec::with_capacity(N);
    for _ in 0..N { let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel(); txs.push(tx); rxs.push(rx); }

    let leaders_by_term: LeadersByTerm = Arc::new(Mutex::new(HashMap::new()));
    let vote_history: VoteHistory = Arc::new(Mutex::new(HashMap::new()));
    let alive_flags: Vec<Arc<AtomicBool>> = (0..N).map(|_| Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(true))).collect();
    let mut handles: Vec<Option<thread::JoinHandle<()>>> = Vec::with_capacity(N);

    for (id, rx) in rxs.into_iter().enumerate() {
        let peers = txs.clone(); let alive = alive_flags[id].clone();
        let leaders = leaders_by_term.clone(); let history = vote_history.clone();
        handles.push(Some(thread::spawn(move || { run_node(id, N, rx, peers, alive, leaders, history); })));
    }

    // --- Phase 1: a leader must emerge for some term within a generous bound.
    let (initial_term, initial_leader) = wait_for_leader_after(&leaders_by_term, 0, Duration::from_secs(3))
        .expect("no leader was elected within the time bound");

    // --- Kill (stop ticking) the elected leader, simulating a crash.
    alive_flags[initial_leader].store(false, Ordering::SeqCst);
    if let Some(h) = handles[initial_leader].take() { h.join().unwrap(); }

    // --- Phase 2: the remaining N-1 nodes must elect a NEW leader with a
    // strictly higher term once the old leader stops sending heartbeats.
    let (new_term, new_leader) = wait_for_leader_after(&leaders_by_term, initial_term, Duration::from_secs(3))
        .expect("no replacement leader was elected after the original leader was killed");
    assert!(new_term > initial_term, "replacement leader's term must be strictly higher than the original");
    assert_ne!(new_leader, initial_leader);

    for flag in &alive_flags { flag.store(false, Ordering::SeqCst); }
    for h in handles.into_iter().flatten() { h.join().unwrap(); }

    // --- Invariant 1: no term EVER had more than one leader recorded.
    let final_leaders = leaders_by_term.lock().unwrap();
    for (term, ids) in final_leaders.iter() {
        assert!(ids.len() <= 1, "term {} had {} simultaneous leaders: {:?}", term, ids.len(), ids);  // never two leaders, same term
    }
    assert!(final_leaders.len() >= 2, "expected at least two distinct terms to have produced a leader");

    // --- Invariant 2: no node ever voted for two different candidates within
    // the same term (the single most commonly botched Raft detail).
    let history = vote_history.lock().unwrap();
    for (&voter, entries) in history.iter() {
        let mut term_to_candidate: HashMap<u64, usize> = HashMap::new();
        for &(term, candidate) in entries {
            match term_to_candidate.get(&term) {
                Some(&existing) => assert_eq!(existing, candidate, "node {} voted for two different candidates in term {}", voter, term),
                None => { term_to_candidate.insert(term, candidate); }
            }
        }
    }

    println!("raft election test passed: initial leader={} (term {}), replacement leader={} (term {})", initial_leader, initial_term, new_leader, new_term);
}
Full solution key — reveal after candidate finishes 
use std::collections::{HashMap, HashSet};
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, Ordering};
use std::sync::mpsc::{self, Receiver, Sender};
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;
use std::time::{Duration, Instant, SystemTime, UNIX_EPOCH};

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum Role { Follower, Candidate, Leader }

enum Msg {
    RequestVote { term: u64, candidate_id: usize },
    VoteGranted { term: u64, voter_id: usize },
    AppendEntries { term: u64, leader_id: usize },
}

/// Dependency-free xorshift64 PRNG — used purely to jitter election timeouts.
struct SimpleRng { state: u64 }

impl SimpleRng {
    fn new(seed: u64) -> Self { SimpleRng { state: seed | 1 } }
    fn next_u64(&mut self) -> u64 {
        let mut x = self.state;
        x ^= x << 13; x ^= x >> 7; x ^= x << 17;
        self.state = x;
        x
    }
}

const HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL: Duration = Duration::from_millis(20);
const POLL_INTERVAL: Duration = Duration::from_millis(5);

/// Randomized election timeout, 150-300ms — the jitter is what stops every
/// follower from timing out and becoming a candidate in perfect lockstep,
/// which would otherwise cause elections to split forever.
fn random_timeout(rng: &mut SimpleRng) -> Duration {
    Duration::from_millis(150 + (rng.next_u64() % 150))
}

type LeadersByTerm = Arc<Mutex<HashMap<u64, HashSet<usize>>>>;
type VoteHistory = Arc<Mutex<HashMap<usize, Vec<(u64, usize)>>>>;

fn record_vote(history: &VoteHistory, voter: usize, term: u64, candidate: usize) {
    history.lock().unwrap().entry(voter).or_insert_with(Vec::new).push((term, candidate));
}

fn run_node(
    id: usize, n: usize, rx: Receiver<Msg>, peers: Vec<Sender<Msg>>,
    alive: Arc<AtomicBool>, leaders_by_term: LeadersByTerm, vote_history: VoteHistory,
) {
    let seed = (id as u64 + 1).wrapping_mul(0x9E3779B97F4A7C15)
        ^ SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).unwrap().as_nanos() as u64;
    let mut rng = SimpleRng::new(seed);

    let mut current_term: u64 = 0;
    let mut voted_for: Option<usize> = None;
    let mut role = Role::Follower;
    let mut votes_received: HashSet<usize> = HashSet::new();
    let mut election_deadline = Instant::now() + random_timeout(&mut rng);
    let mut next_heartbeat = Instant::now();
    // Tracks which leader_id this node has seen claim each term via a heartbeat —
    // lets a follower catch, in real time, the exact bug this exercise is
    // designed to prevent: two different leaders both claiming the same term.
    let mut known_leader_for_term: HashMap<u64, usize> = HashMap::new();

    let broadcast = |msg_for: &dyn Fn() -> Msg, peers: &[Sender<Msg>]| {
        for (peer_id, tx) in peers.iter().enumerate() {
            if peer_id != id { let _ = tx.send(msg_for()); }
        }
    };

    while alive.load(Ordering::SeqCst) {
        let now = Instant::now();

        if role != Role::Leader && now >= election_deadline {
            current_term += 1;
            role = Role::Candidate;
            voted_for = Some(id);
            votes_received.clear();
            votes_received.insert(id);
            record_vote(&vote_history, id, current_term, id);
            election_deadline = now + random_timeout(&mut rng);

            if votes_received.len() * 2 > n {  // STRICT majority — self-vote alone only wins for n == 1
                role = Role::Leader;
                leaders_by_term.lock().unwrap().entry(current_term).or_default().insert(id);
                next_heartbeat = Instant::now();
            } else {
                let term = current_term;
                broadcast(&|| Msg::RequestVote { term, candidate_id: id }, &peers);
            }
        }

        if role == Role::Leader && Instant::now() >= next_heartbeat {
            next_heartbeat = Instant::now() + HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL;
            let term = current_term;
            broadcast(&|| Msg::AppendEntries { term, leader_id: id }, &peers);
        }

        match rx.recv_timeout(POLL_INTERVAL) {
            Ok(Msg::RequestVote { term, candidate_id }) => {
                if term > current_term { current_term = term; voted_for = None; role = Role::Follower; }  // discovering a higher term ALWAYS resets voted_for
                let can_grant = term >= current_term && (voted_for.is_none() || voted_for == Some(candidate_id));  // one vote per term, period
                if can_grant {
                    voted_for = Some(candidate_id);
                    record_vote(&vote_history, id, current_term, candidate_id);
                    election_deadline = Instant::now() + random_timeout(&mut rng);
                    let _ = peers[candidate_id].send(Msg::VoteGranted { term: current_term, voter_id: id });
                }
            }
            Ok(Msg::VoteGranted { term, voter_id }) => {
                if role == Role::Candidate && term == current_term {
                    votes_received.insert(voter_id);
                    if votes_received.len() * 2 > n {
                        role = Role::Leader;
                        leaders_by_term.lock().unwrap().entry(current_term).or_default().insert(id);
                        next_heartbeat = Instant::now();
                        let term = current_term;
                        broadcast(&|| Msg::AppendEntries { term, leader_id: id }, &peers);
                    }
                }
            }
            Ok(Msg::AppendEntries { term, leader_id }) => {
                if term >= current_term {
                    if term > current_term { current_term = term; voted_for = None; }
                    role = Role::Follower;
                    election_deadline = Instant::now() + random_timeout(&mut rng);  // heartbeat resets the timer — this is what stops new elections while the leader lives
                    match known_leader_for_term.get(&term) {
                        Some(&existing) => assert_eq!(existing, leader_id, "node {} saw two leaders claim term {}", id, term),
                        None => { known_leader_for_term.insert(term, leader_id); }
                    }
                }
            }
            Err(_) => {
                // poll timeout (or, at shutdown, a disconnected channel) — loop and re-check state
            }
        }
    }
}

/// Polls `leaders_by_term` until it finds a leader for a term strictly greater
/// than `after_term`, or gives up after `max_wait`.
fn wait_for_leader_after(leaders_by_term: &LeadersByTerm, after_term: u64, max_wait: Duration) -> Option<(u64, usize)> {
    let deadline = Instant::now() + max_wait;
    loop {
        {
            let map = leaders_by_term.lock().unwrap();
            let best = map.iter()
                .filter(|&(&term, _)| term > after_term)
                .filter_map(|(&term, ids)| ids.iter().next().map(|&id| (term, id)))
                .max_by_key(|&(term, _)| term);
            if let Some(found) = best { return Some(found); }
        }
        if Instant::now() >= deadline { return None; }
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(10));
    }
}

fn main() {
    const N: usize = 5;

    let mut txs: Vec<Sender<Msg>> = Vec::with_capacity(N);
    let mut rxs: Vec<Receiver<Msg>> = Vec::with_capacity(N);
    for _ in 0..N { let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel(); txs.push(tx); rxs.push(rx); }

    let leaders_by_term: LeadersByTerm = Arc::new(Mutex::new(HashMap::new()));
    let vote_history: VoteHistory = Arc::new(Mutex::new(HashMap::new()));
    let alive_flags: Vec<Arc<AtomicBool>> = (0..N).map(|_| Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(true))).collect();
    let mut handles: Vec<Option<thread::JoinHandle<()>>> = Vec::with_capacity(N);

    for (id, rx) in rxs.into_iter().enumerate() {
        let peers = txs.clone(); let alive = alive_flags[id].clone();
        let leaders = leaders_by_term.clone(); let history = vote_history.clone();
        handles.push(Some(thread::spawn(move || { run_node(id, N, rx, peers, alive, leaders, history); })));
    }

    // --- Phase 1: a leader must emerge for some term within a generous bound.
    let (initial_term, initial_leader) = wait_for_leader_after(&leaders_by_term, 0, Duration::from_secs(3))
        .expect("no leader was elected within the time bound");

    // --- Kill (stop ticking) the elected leader, simulating a crash.
    alive_flags[initial_leader].store(false, Ordering::SeqCst);
    if let Some(h) = handles[initial_leader].take() { h.join().unwrap(); }

    // --- Phase 2: the remaining N-1 nodes must elect a NEW leader with a
    // strictly higher term once the old leader stops sending heartbeats.
    let (new_term, new_leader) = wait_for_leader_after(&leaders_by_term, initial_term, Duration::from_secs(3))
        .expect("no replacement leader was elected after the original leader was killed");
    assert!(new_term > initial_term, "replacement leader's term must be strictly higher than the original");
    assert_ne!(new_leader, initial_leader);

    for flag in &alive_flags { flag.store(false, Ordering::SeqCst); }
    for h in handles.into_iter().flatten() { h.join().unwrap(); }

    // --- Invariant 1: no term EVER had more than one leader recorded.
    let final_leaders = leaders_by_term.lock().unwrap();
    for (term, ids) in final_leaders.iter() {
        assert!(ids.len() <= 1, "term {} had {} simultaneous leaders: {:?}", term, ids.len(), ids);  // never two leaders, same term
    }
    assert!(final_leaders.len() >= 2, "expected at least two distinct terms to have produced a leader");

    // --- Invariant 2: no node ever voted for two different candidates within
    // the same term (the single most commonly botched Raft detail).
    let history = vote_history.lock().unwrap();
    for (&voter, entries) in history.iter() {
        let mut term_to_candidate: HashMap<u64, usize> = HashMap::new();
        for &(term, candidate) in entries {
            match term_to_candidate.get(&term) {
                Some(&existing) => assert_eq!(existing, candidate, "node {} voted for two different candidates in term {}", voter, term),
                None => { term_to_candidate.insert(term, candidate); }
            }
        }
    }

    println!("raft election test passed: initial leader={} (term {}), replacement leader={} (term {})", initial_leader, initial_term, new_leader, new_term);
}
What to look for — unprompted signals
  • ★★★Actually randomizes the election timeout PER NODE, and can explain why — a candidate who uses a fixed timeout (even a "reasonable" one like 200ms for everyone) will produce a simulation that either never elects a leader (every follower times out simultaneously, splits the vote forever) or does so only by lucky thread-scheduling jitter; ask them directly what happens with zero jitter if they don't hit the bug organically.
  • ★★★Resets voted_for exactly when the term changes, and ONLY then — a very common bug is resetting voted_for every time a RequestVote is merely received (regardless of term), which silently breaks the one-vote-per-term guarantee and can let a single term receive two granted votes from the same node; equally common is never resetting it, which permanently locks a node out of voting in any future term.
  • ★★★Computes majority as votes.len() * 2 > n, not votes.len() >= n / 2 — integer division silently rounds down, so for N=5 the wrong formula treats 2 votes (out of 5, i.e. 5/2=2) as a majority when the real threshold is 3; this is a one-character bug class that a good candidate should catch just by reasoning about a concrete odd N, without needing a test to fail first.
  • ★★Treats an AppendEntries heartbeat and a RequestVote from a HIGHER term identically w.r.t. term/role updates — both must cause current_term to advance and the receiving node to become (or remain) a Follower; a candidate who only handles the "discover higher term" logic in one message handler and not the other will pass simple tests but fail the moment a partitioned-then-reconnected node's stale messages interact with a genuinely newer cluster state.
Follow-up probes
  • P1"This only implements leader election — what's the next thing you'd need to add to make this a usable replicated log, and what NEW failure mode does it introduce?" — Log replication: the leader must append client commands to its own log and replicate them via (non-empty) AppendEntries, tracking each follower's match_index/next_index and only committing once a majority has durably stored an entry. The new failure mode is exactly what the leader-election phase alone can't protect against: a leader elected with a STALE log (possible if it wasn't part of the most recent majority commit) — which is why real Raft's RequestVote also carries lastLogIndex/lastLogTerm so voters can refuse a candidate whose log is behind theirs, a check this simplified election-only exercise deliberately omits.
  • P2"Two nodes both become candidates in the same term and neither gets a majority — what happens, concretely, in THIS implementation?" — Each candidate already voted for itself and will refuse to vote for the other (one-vote-per-term), so the term ends in a split vote with no leader; both candidates' own randomized election timers will eventually re-fire (independently, since they're jittered), each starting a NEW, higher term and retrying — the randomization is exactly what makes it overwhelmingly likely the retry timers desync enough for one to get a head start and win the next term outright.
  • P3"Why does a candidate vote for itself IMMEDIATELY rather than waiting to see if anyone else's RequestVote arrives first?" — Because votes are strictly per-term and a node can cast at most one, self-voting atomically at the moment of becoming a candidate is what guarantees the candidate's own vote is never lost to a race against an incoming competing RequestVote for the same term; if a node instead sent its RequestVote broadcast before recording its own self-vote, another node's higher-priority message could theoretically slip in and cause the candidate to end up voting for a competitor in its OWN election term — self-vote-then-broadcast is the only ordering that closes that window.
🎯 Senior angle
Getting a leader elected once is easy; the interesting signal is what a candidate does with the FAILURE path. A senior engineer will proactively simulate the leader crash themselves (not wait to be told to) and reason out loud about term monotonicity as the actual safety invariant — "the new leader's term must be strictly higher, and every node's current_term only ever moves forward" — rather than treating "a new leader got elected" as sufficient. That framing (term as a monotonic epoch counter, not just an election counter) is exactly the mental model Raft's actual safety proof rests on.

// Answer by code:
// This only implements leader election — what's the next thing you'd need to add to make this a usable replicated log, and what NEW failure mode does it introduce?
fn harden_w82_1() {
    // use: core types from the main exercise
    todo!()
}

fn main() {
    // Harden · This only implements leader election — what's the next thing you'd ne…
    harden_w82_1();
    // Parent exercise still holds after the harden change:
    const N: usize = 5;

    let mut txs: Vec<Sender<Msg>> = Vec::with_capacity(N);
    let mut rxs: Vec<Receiver<Msg>> = Vec::with_capacity(N);
    for _ in 0..N { let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel(); txs.push(tx); rxs.push(rx); }

    let leaders_by_term: LeadersByTerm = Arc::new(Mutex::new(HashMap::new()));
    let vote_history: VoteHistory = Arc::new(Mutex::new(HashMap::new()));
    let alive_flags: Vec<Arc<AtomicBool>> = (0..N).map(|_| Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(true))).collect();
    let mut handles: Vec<Option<thread::JoinHandle<()>>> = Vec::with_capacity(N);

    for (id, rx) in rxs.into_iter().enumerate() {
        let peers = txs.clone(); let alive = alive_flags[id].clone();
        let leaders = leaders_by_term.clone(); let history = vote_history.clone();
        handles.push(Some(thread::spawn(move || { run_node(id, N, rx, peers, alive, leaders, history); })));
    }

    // --- Phase 1: a leader must emerge for some term within a generous bound.
    let (initial_term, initial_leader) = wait_for_leader_after(&leaders_by_term, 0, Duration::from_secs(3))
        .expect("no leader was elected within the time bound");

    // --- Kill (stop ticking) the elected leader, simulating a crash.
    alive_flags[initial_leader].store(false, Ordering::SeqCst);
    if let Some(h) = handles[initial_leader].take() { h.join().unwrap(); }

    // --- Phase 2: the remaining N-1 nodes must elect a NEW leader with a
    // strictly higher term once the old leader stops sending heartbeats.
    let (new_term, new_leader) = wait_for_leader_after(&leaders_by_term, initial_term, Duration::from_secs(3))
        .expect("no replacement leader was elected after the original leader was killed");
    assert!(new_term > initial_term, "replacement leader's term must be strictly higher than the original");
    assert_ne!(new_leader, initial_leader);

    for flag in &alive_flags { flag.store(false, Ordering::SeqCst); }
    for h in handles.into_iter().flatten() { h.join().unwrap(); }

    // --- Invariant 1: no term EVER had more than one leader recorded.
    let final_leaders = leaders_by_term.lock().unwrap();
    for (term, ids) in final_leaders.iter() {
        assert!(ids.len() <= 1, "term {} had {} simultaneous leaders: {:?}", term, ids.len(), ids);  // never two leaders, same term
    }
    assert!(final_leaders.len() >= 2, "expected at least two distinct terms to have produced a leader");

    // --- Invariant 2: no node ever voted for two different candidates within
    // the same term (the single most commonly botched Raft detail).
    let history = vote_history.lock().unwrap();
    for (&voter, entries) in history.iter() {
        let mut term_to_candidate: HashMap<u64, usize> = HashMap::new();
        for &(term, candidate) in entries {
            match term_to_candidate.get(&term) {
                Some(&existing) => assert_eq!(existing, candidate, "node {} voted for two different candidates in term {}", voter, term),
                None => { term_to_candidate.insert(term, candidate); }
            }
        }
    }

    println!("raft election test passed: initial leader={} (term {}), replacement leader={} (term {})", initial_leader, initial_term, new_leader, new_term);
}

// Distributed Systems Exercise 83 · 75 min
W83 · Dynamo-Style Quorum Read/Write (N/W/R) with Read Repair
tunable N/W/R quorum W+R>N ⇒ read-your-writes read repair simulated replica outages Hard
Prompt
"Implement a quorum-based replicated key-value store over N simulated replicas with configurable W (write quorum) and R (read quorum) such that W + R > N guarantees read-your-writes consistency — the core Dynamo/Cassandra-style tunable-consistency trade-off. put(key, value) must write (with a version) to at least W replicas before returning success; get(key) must read from at least R replicas and return the value with the highest version among the responses actually received. Then implement read repair: whenever a get observes that some of the replicas it read from returned a stale (lower-version) value compared to the winner, it must proactively write the winning value back to those stale replicas before returning, so future reads need to repair fewer replicas over time. Simulate up to N - W (or N - R) replicas being down via a mock is_up flag, and show the operation still succeeds using a different subset — as long as enough replicas remain up to satisfy the quorum, and fails loudly otherwise."
Starter code to hand to candidate
struct VersionedValue { value: String, version: u64 }
enum StoreError { QuorumUnavailable }

struct Replica { is_up: bool, store: HashMap<String, VersionedValue> }
struct QuorumStore { replicas: Vec<Replica>, w: usize, r: usize }

// TODO: impl QuorumStore —
//   put(candidates, key, value, version): write to >= w UP replicas from `candidates`,
//     atomically (a quorum failure must leave ZERO partial writes behind), else error
//   get(candidates, key): read from >= r UP replicas, return the HIGHEST-version value seen,
//     then READ-REPAIR: write that winner back to every replica just read that was stale

fn main() {
    const N: usize = 5;
    const W: usize = 3;
    const R: usize = 3;
    assert!(W + R > N, "W+R>N is the whole point — read-your-writes is not guaranteed otherwise");

    // --- Read-your-writes via the pigeonhole overlap property: a put's W=3
    // write set and a get's R=3 read set are BOTH 3-subsets of only 5
    // replicas, so 3+3=6 > 5 forces them to share at least one replica.
    let put_set = [0usize, 1, 2];
    let read_sets: [[usize; 3]; 3] = [[2, 3, 4], [0, 3, 4], [1, 3, 4]];
    for read_set in read_sets {
        let mut store = QuorumStore::new(N, W, R);
        store.put(&put_set, "k", "just-written", 1).expect("put should succeed with 3 of 3 candidates up");
        let overlap = read_set.iter().any(|idx| put_set.contains(idx));
        assert!(overlap, "test setup bug: read set must overlap put set");
        let value = store.get(&read_set, "k").expect("get should succeed with 3 of 3 candidates up");
        assert_eq!(value, "just-written", "read-your-writes violated for read set {:?}", read_set);
    }

    // --- Read repair must actually mutate a stale replica's STORED data, not
    // just return the right value to the caller.
    let mut store = QuorumStore::new(N, W, R);
    store.put(&[0, 1, 2], "k", "v1", 1).unwrap();
    // Second write only reaches replicas 2,3,4 — replicas 0,1 are left stale.
    store.put(&[2, 3, 4], "k", "v2", 2).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(store.replicas[0].store.get("k").unwrap().version, 1, "replica 0 should still be stale before the read");

    let value = store.get(&[0, 1, 2], "k").expect("get should succeed: 3 of 3 candidates up");
    assert_eq!(value, "v2", "get must return the highest-version value seen");
    assert_eq!(store.replicas[0].store.get("k").unwrap().version, 2, "read repair should have overwritten replica 0's STORED version");  // not just the return value — the replica itself
    assert_eq!(store.replicas[1].store.get("k").unwrap().version, 2, "replica 1 was also stale and read from, so it must be repaired too");

    // --- Availability: with exactly N-W (or N-R) replicas down, operations
    // still succeed using the remaining replicas that exactly meet quorum.
    let mut store = QuorumStore::new(N, W, R);
    store.set_up(3, false);
    store.set_up(4, false);
